### Milestone 212 — DONE (an experimental state search: exploration from mid-run snapshots, with new faults and timing for the rest of a run; on the bug benchmark and on etcd 3.5.5 it did not help; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** `hydo explore --search state` keeps snapshots that runs took at rare moments and
runs the rest of a run again from them, with new faults. It is experimental and opt-in, and
without the option nothing changes. On hvx it did not help. It ran on the slow benchmark defects d7 and
d10 at about the same worker seconds as the plain exploration. It found each defect in 2 of 5
seed ranges, and the plain exploration in 3 of 5. On etcd 3.5.5 neither found the second symptom of issue 14685 in
5 ranges each. Its branches cost about two thirds of a fresh run and did not fail more often.
The Qdrant flaky test on KVM was not measured.

**Why, and what was different from the earlier attempts.** The explorer draws every schedule
from its seed and runs it from S1. The user approved (2026-11-13) closing that gap by exploring
from mid-run states near rare events. The design, written before the prototype, is
`docs/design/state-search.md`. It names why Milestones 41, 43, 44, 45, 139, and 209 found
nothing. Milestone 45, the closest, branched one schedule at its rarest assertion with 6 tick
jitter variants. The variants repeated each other, and its budget counted a variant as a run.
The state search changes three things:

- A branch draws new faults for the rest of the run, moved into the remaining steps. On KVM and
  on the Mac it also draws new timing.
- The cost is the worker's wall time. It includes the snapshots and the restores.
- Half of the schedules stay the plain exploration's.

**Built** (opt-in; without `--search state` nothing changes):

- `hydo explore --search state` and its options:
  - `--state-mix`: branches per 1,000 once the corpus has an entry, default 500. With 0 the
    search runs the plain exploration's schedules with the same bookkeeping and no snapshots.
  - `--state-corpus` (default 4 on hvx, 32 otherwise), `--state-rare` (default 2),
    `--state-snaps` (snapshots per run, default 2), and `--state-stop`.

  The search runs on one worker, which holds the snapshots (hydo-explore `src/state.rs`,
  `run.rs` `state_search`). Each run is a line of `state-search.jsonl` in the exploration's
  folder. The results formats are unchanged.
- The host controller (hydo-control `src/search.rs`). `RecLink` records every stop of a run (the
  engine's report and the commands sent). It takes `SNAP` at stops whose guest console shows a
  rare feature: an SDK assertion record, or a console-line class with numbers made `#`. For a
  target whose console shows no feature, it takes `SNAP` at stops spread over the median guest
  clock. `BranchLink` replays a parent's stops to a branch's controller, requires the parent's
  commands, and goes live at the snapshot after `RESUME`, with no resynchronisation.
  `agent::check_branch` runs that replay without a VM first and refuses a branch whose prefix
  differs. The runner gained `Link::before_step` and `Link::timing`, both inert for every
  existing link.
- A branch's schedule is one schedule string. A fault branch is an ordinary schedule. A timing
  branch has the new host token `br=<clock>` followed by timing tokens. The parser has
  `branch_points`, `without_branch_points`, and `BRANCH_KEYS` (hydo-schedule). The host
  controller takes the token out of the engine's schedule. At the first stop whose clock
  reaches it, the controller sends the new engine command `TIME <tokens>` (`SwitchLink`). A
  branch and a run from S1 do this alike.
- The KVM and Mac engines keep tick jitter and forced preemption points in a snapshot (before,
  such a `SNAP` was refused) and take `TIME`. hvx refuses `TIME`, and `hydo_engine::refusal`
  refuses `br=` for hvx before any VM.
- A branch keeps the step range in progress. The controller runs the workload in step ranges
  split at fault steps (`HYDO_FROM`, `HYDO_TO`), so a new fault inside the running range would
  change the run from that range's start. A branch keeps every fault of its parent that starts at
  or before the end of the range in progress, and moves the fresh seed's faults after it.
- After the measurements: a branch never has both an `N=` and an `O=` window. The strategies
  never draw both, and 17 measured branches with both ended in `ERROR tc setup failed` where the
  windows met. The branch keeps its parent's window and drops the fresh seed's
  (`state::tests::a_branch_never_has_both_network_windows`).

**Checks.** Branches replay bit for bit from a fresh boot. On hvx, 6 of 6 branches of the d7
image gave their fingerprints again under `hydo run`. On the Mac, 9 of 9 fault branches of the Redis
example did, and 9 of 9 timing branches. The Mac fast `hydo-bench rebaseline --check` gave all
76 schedules their recorded values. On hvx, the recorded schedules of etcd-3.5.5, redis,
redis-netem, redis-freeze and redis-hist gave every recorded value, and the pinned reproducers
gave `a76d7fe857fdb37c` and `efbde7b57264be0f`. The tests are these:

- hydo-control's `search::a_branch_equals_its_schedule_run_from_s1`;
- the unit tests of `state.rs`: the branch rule, branch points, the range in progress, and the
  search's determinism;
- hydo-schedule's `branch_points`.

 The explorer's identity goldens did not change.

**Measurements** (hvx, the bare-metal machine; the tables are in `docs/design/state-search.md`,
section "Measurements"). Each target ran 5 seed ranges. The plain exploration ran with
`--state-mix 0`. The budgets were 60 plain runs against 80 state-search runs on the benchmark,
and 80 against 100 on etcd, which cost about the same worker seconds. A benchmark detection is a
failure with the defect's signature whose schedule passes on the control image from a fresh
boot (hydo-bench's rule). The control runs are why the raw counts mislead: in the d7 search of
seeds 4001–4080, all 14 runs with d7's signature failed on the control image too.

| target | ranges with a detection, plain | state search | median worker seconds, plain | state search |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| d7 | 3 of 5 | 2 of 5 | 418 s | 503 s (no detection) |
| d10 | 3 of 5 | 2 of 5 | 474 s | 570 s (no detection) |
| d4 | 5 of 5 | 4 of 5 | 98 s | 115 s |
| d6 | 5 of 5 | 5 of 5 | 28 s | 28 s |
| etcd 14685, `client.revisions_monotonic` | 0 of 5 | 0 of 5 | none in 816–879 s | none in 810–866 s |

The state search was earlier in 3 of 20 benchmark ranges, each time by a branch (d10 once, d6
twice), and later or without a detection in 6. At equal worker seconds the plain explorations
showed 21 distinct failure classes over the 20 benchmark ranges and the state searches 16. The
state search found no class that the plain exploration missed in the same range. On etcd the
classes were the same in every range. A branch's median wall time was 4.0 to 5.4 s, against 6.0
to 9.9 s for a fresh run. Branches failed in 0.5 to 7.7 % of the runs, fresh runs in 1.5 to
30.6 %.

**Left** (open item 85):

- the Qdrant flaky test on KVM;
- the KVM engine's change on a real KVM host;
- the shrinker and `br=`;
- timing branches on hvx;
- one worker per search.

### Milestone 217 (tentative number) — DONE (TigerBeetle's issue 3960, two holds that expire on the same nanosecond: not found blind; replayed on hvx with the guest's clock; the replica stops on 0.16.29, 0.16.45 and 0.17.9 and stops again at every restart; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** TigerBeetle's issue 3960 shows a replica that stops on `assert(expires_at <=
timestamp_event)` in its expiry pulse, with a unit test of the state machine. The example
`hydo/onboard/examples/tigerbeetle` got holds (pending transfers with timeouts), settlements and
a business check of holds, and a second project, `tie/`, that makes the tie on purpose. Every
run used hydo 0.3.1's Linux release and hvx on the bare-metal machine. One or two VMs of this
session ran at a time. No hydo code changed. The example's RESULTS.md has the details (the section on issue
3960).

**The condition.** Since 0.16.29 (commit `499fcd4b1`) a pulse at the timestamp T gives the k-th
of its n expired holds the timestamp T - n + k. Two holds with one expiry e and a pulse at T = e
give the first of them e - 1, before its expiry. Up to 0.16.28 every expired hold gets T.

**Blind.** The single replica with the drivers `parallel_driver_hold` and
`parallel_driver_settle` ran 150 schedules: the process strategy twice with `--more-faults`,
once with `--timing`, once with `--new-faults`, and the random strategy with both (2,110 s). The
only failures were 7 disk-fault runs of the random strategy, TigerBeetle's documented behaviour.
Over 95 distinct workloads (2,983 holds in 651 batches) no two holds shared an expiry. The
nearest pair of batches was 543,848 ns from a whole number of seconds apart, where a tie needs at
most 7 ns. hvx puts more pairs within 10 ms of whole seconds than uniform times would (108
against 37.6), but none within 100 µs.

**Two false findings of the new check, fixed.** The recovery boot's clock started at
`guest.clock_start` again, so after a power cut no hold expired (19 of 30 runs). Every manifest
of the example sets `guest.clock_after_cut: 60` now. After a backward clock step the holds
expired late by the guest's clock (12 of 30), since TigerBeetle's timestamps never run
backwards. `final_holds` now demands only that a hold more than 1 s past its expiry holds no
amount.

**Directed.** `tie/workload/singleton_driver_tie` sets the guest's clock to whole seconds with
`date -s` for one request each and an hour back in between. With the clock behind, the replica
timestamps by its counter alone (+ 1 per client session, + 1 + n per batch of n). A request
through a running REPL session (under `script`, which gives the REPL a terminal) reaches the
replica k × 999,848 + 1 ns after the clock was set. Anchors with equal k let the counter put Y
exactly d seconds after X, and put the pulse on the tied expiry + V (the knob `V`). Twice each,
one fingerprint each:

| release | schedule | verdict | fp |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.17.9 | `disk=none dseed=1 \| run V=0` | `ERROR restart after the faults (tigerbeetle_0)`: `panic: reached unreachable code`, and again after hydo's restart (SIGABRT) | `f291537d8a266c67` |
| 0.17.9 | `... V=1` | OK; the pulse expired the three holds | `9b5d243994b8a8be` |
| 0.16.45 | `... V=0` | `ERROR restart after the faults`, the same panic twice | `171200ffc4859485` |
| 0.16.29 | `... V=0` | `ERROR restart after the faults`, the same panic twice | `84620a7023e63331` |
| 0.16.28 | `... V=0` | OK; the pulse at the tie expired the three holds | `bd504f1894c2b0fd` |

The release binaries are stripped, so the log names no assert; the panic comes exactly at T = e
and on the releases since the change. A restarted replica executes the pulse from its
write-ahead log again and stops: holds and transfers of ordinary clients stop a replica for
good.

**Not done** (open item 86): the three-replica cluster, the Mac engine (`ERROR boot: SPIN`, open
item 13), and a build with symbols. An upstream comment is drafted, not posted.

**Tests.** `cargo test -p hydo-explore --test it identity::` passes after re-recording the quick
golden with `HYDO_BLESS=1`: only its `input` lines of the example changed. Four full-tier
goldens already name other changed inputs on main: the corpus and answer goldens of
hydo-control, hydo-explore, hydo-build and hydo-manifest. Those inputs include
`.github/workflows/release.yml`, `action/action.yml`, and the etcd and Formance examples. The
goldens now also name this example's manifests, and they were not re-recorded.
`public_content::` and `docs::` pass.

### Milestone 218 (tentative number) - DONE (Lago onboarded on the Mac engine as an experiment in business bugs; a subscription cancelled while Redis is down is never invoiced, known upstream as lago-api issue 6901; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** Lago v1.57.0, open-source usage-based billing (a Rails API, a Sidekiq worker and a
clockwork clock on PostgreSQL 15 and Redis 7), runs unmodified from its official images in
`hydo/onboard/examples/lago` (RESULTS.md). The import started from Lago's own
`docker-compose.yml`, cut down to six of its eight services: the web front end and the PDF
renderer are left out. The experiment gave it two kinds of rules. Seven billing rules read Lago's
own tables: every acknowledged event stored once, every acknowledged event of a charge paid in
advance charged once, invoice totals equal to their fees, one invoice per subscription and
period, every period invoiced after its billing tick, and every invoice in a final state. One
generic rule compares the client's acknowledged operations with Lago's totals per subscription,
and knows nothing about billing. Every run used the Mac engine with the published 0.3.1 release
files. The bare-metal machine ran another agent's campaign. Nothing recorded moved, and no hydo
code changed.

**What was found.**

- A Lago bug, known upstream as lago-api issue 6901 (open). A subscription that is cancelled
  while Redis is down is terminated in PostgreSQL, but `BillSubscriptionJob.perform_after_commit`
  fails at its uniqueness lock and the API answers 500. The retry gets 404, and the period is
  never invoiced. The swarm exploration found it without being told (seed 36). The hand
  schedule `disk=none | run K=redis@1+4` gives `30be47e1ed697d48` twice, and five requests
  reproduce it with Docker and without hydo. A comment for the issue is drafted, not posted.
- A Sidekiq bug, not Lago's: a Redis error during the first `cleanup` of Sidekiq's scheduler
  thread (in `initial_wait`, outside the loop's `rescue`) ends the thread. Lock retries of
  `Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceChargeJob` then wait in the `schedule` set for good, and
  acknowledged transfers are never charged. Not checked outside hydo.
- Documented or known behaviour: a power cut loses the jobs that make fees paid in advance
  (Redis without an append-only file in Lago's own file, and Sidekiq's open-source fetch; the
  build parameter `redis_aof=yes` separates the two). A billing day that the clock skips is never
  invoiced (Lago issue 354). After a backward clock step of 30 s or more, a termination can fall
  before usage that Lago already acknowledged, which is then never billed. These are clock and
  deployment effects.
- The consistency rules (totals, one invoice per period, one fee per event, final states, events
  stored) never failed.

**Which kind of rule found what.** The generic rule failed in every run that broke a business
result: 11 of 20 in exploration A, 3 of 20 in B, 3 of 16 hand schedules. The billing rules failed
in 8, 3 and 3 of them, and named the mechanism each time. The three that only the generic rule
caught were usage dropped by a termination after a clock step. Two billing rules (transfers
charged, periods invoiced) did all of the billing rules' work.

**Runs.** 56 schedules and about 30 directed runs on the Mac engine:

| exploration | strategy | schedules | failures |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `process --new-faults`, seeds 1-20, before the check fixes | 20 | 12, all clock or power-cut effects |
| B | `swarm --new-faults`, seeds 21-40, the final image | 20 | 8: the Lago bug, a skipped billing day, a clock artifact, 4 disk I/O errors, a lying disk |
| C | hand schedules at the billing tick (`T=0:900`) with one fault each | 16 | 3, Redis killed or cut off (the Sidekiq scheduler) |

The final image, `af496f66…`, passes `disk=none | run` twice with one fingerprint (RESULTS.md).
The three saved regressions expect a violation.

**What hydo lacked.** Open items 87 to 93: `eventually_` commands that run after the
`eventually_` checks, the seed's records not carried into the run, a check's output beyond its
last line, one shrink per signature, the importer's idle job service as a fault target, clock steps
that cannot aim at a time of day, and the identity test reading git-ignored outputs.

### Milestone 219 (tentative number) — DONE, STAGES 2 TO 4 (several vCPUs on the KVM engine: the engine runs 2 to 8 vCPUs in turns of counted exits, Linux boots on them with the pinned SMP guest kernel; a determinism bug of the guest kernel found and fixed, after which every schedule gave one fingerprint on two AMD models; nats-server's flaky test passes at 7 of 28 turn settings; one vCPU unchanged; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** Stages 2 and 3 of `docs/design/kvm-vcpus.md`. With `--vcpus N` the KVM engine runs
N vCPUs of one VM one at a time from its thread, in turns of counted exits, with an x2APIC per
vCPU in the engine, and boots Linux with `bzImage-kvm-smp`. The release's Redis example runs on 2
and 4 vCPUs. Each schedule gave one fingerprint twice, and the same on AMD EPYC 7763 and 9V45.
Without the option the engine runs the code of before: `hv/kvm/kvm-check.sh` gave Milestone 210's
AMD values, and the scripted one-vCPU pins pass. No recorded value moved.

The first SMP kernel had a determinism bug: vCPU 1 ran user code with CR4.TSD clear, so a
program's RDTSC there read the TSC of the host's CPU. The section "The determinism bug" below has
the cause, how it was found, and the fix. Every several-vCPU value in the tables before that
section was made with the kernel that had the bug and is superseded by the values in it.

**The engine** (`hydo/crates/hydo-kvm`):

- `smp.rs`: whose turn it is, the turn length (`q=` exits, or seeded lengths with `qs=` by hvx's
  rule), each vCPU's run state (ready, halted, stopped, waiting for STARTUP), its x2APIC and its
  MSR model.
- `vmm.rs`: the vCPUs, vCPU 0 first. A turn ends after `q` exits, at a HLT, at an OUT to the relax
  port `0x5f0`, or at a spin the observer proves while another vCPU can run. When no vCPU can run,
  the clock jumps to the next event of any vCPU or device. The x2APIC's MSR exits go to the APIC
  model: IPIs, EOI, the APIC timer in the exit clock, INIT, and STARTUP, which starts the target
  in real mode. The 8259 PIC reaches vCPU 0 through an ExtINT LINT0. Snapshots keep every vCPU
  with its `kvm_run` flags; the fingerprint adds the other vCPUs and the several-vCPU state after
  every part of a one-vCPU fingerprint.
- `cpuid::table_smp` (APIC, x2APIC, the topology leaf, ARAT), an MP table without an I/O APIC,
  `x2apic_phys noapic` on the command line, `Hypervisor::fresh_n` (one VM file shared by its
  vCPUs), and a program per vCPU in the scripted vCPU.
- `hydo-kvm --vcpus N`; the RESULT line has `qn=`. Tick jitter and the rewind mode are refused with
  several vCPUs for now.

**The product.** `hydo run --backend kvm --vcpus N` and `hydo explore --backend kvm --vcpus N`
pass the count to the engine and look up the SMP kernel by sha256 (`hydo_kvm::kernel::SMP_TWINS`,
`hydo_engine::kvm::boot_files_n`); `hydo_engine::refusal_on` lets `q=` and `qs=` through on such a
machine. The explorer's turn tokens (`--turns`, `--sweep turns`) stay hvx's for now.

**The kernel.** `hv/kvm/linux/kernel-smp.nix` over the unchanged `kernel.nix`. The first pin was
`bzImage-kvm-smp` `a43b7bc3…`, config `d630f99e…`. It came out with the same bytes four times
from sandboxed builds on two runners (`nix-build`, then `nix-build --check`), and from the
bare-metal machine's trial build of Milestone 213. It had the determinism bug below; the pin now
is `b40b2711…`.

**The runs** (a one-off workflow on a temporary branch `tmp-kvm-vcpus2`, deleted afterwards:
https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43440090997; four jobs, every one green):

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `kvm-check.sh`, one vCPU, this branch's `hydo` (EPYC 9V45 and 9V74) | 15 of 15 on both; `2846084b7f0ab1e2` OK and `bca22e72dbf0da18` VIOLATION k:1, Milestone 210's AMD values |
| a timing branch with `br=` (Milestone 212), one vCPU | `2039c438b0971596` twice from a fresh boot and once from S1, the value of its control without `br=` |
| 2 vCPUs, `disk=none dseed=1 \| run` | OK, `cb3f16360593598e` twice on each host, `qn=231`; vCPU 1 made 6,396 of 26,560 exits |
| 2 vCPUs, `q=64` / `q=7 qs=1f` | OK, `2e44e4e7d6c7173a` (`qn=399`) / `65afef462b5bb2cb` (`qn=2476`), each twice on each host |
| 2 vCPUs, `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | VIOLATION key k:1 lost, `25b2b20d93cdf8fc`, twice on each host |
| 4 vCPUs, `disk=none dseed=1 \| run` | OK, `5ad6cb7c9b3bd84a` (`qn=503`), twice on each host |
| 2 vCPUs, from the worker's S1 against a fresh boot | not run: `hydo explore` refused `--vcpus` for KVM, fixed in this milestone |

**The S1 check and stage 4** (a third workflow run on a temporary branch `tmp-kvm-vcpus3`,
deleted afterwards: https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43446326976; AMD EPYC 7763 and 9V74,
both green):

- `hv/kvm/smp/smp-check.sh` 13 of 13 on both hosts. The run from the worker's S1 on 2 vCPUs gave
  the fresh boot's `cb3f16360593598e`. An exploration of 8 seeds on 2 vCPUs made 27 runs, and
  `hydo repro` of it gave 6 of 6 with the recorded fingerprint.
- `hv/kvm/smp/nats-check.sh`, nats-server's flaky test (`hydo/onboard/examples/nats-flaky-8363`).
  1 vCPU fails (`d6cb9210afe66ff9`); the fixed test passes on 2 vCPUs (`b0db8d6cd5ef6e7c`). Of 28
  turn settings on 2 vCPUs, 10 pass (`q=2` to `q=8`, `16`, `24`, `32`, and two of six seeded
  ones) and 18 fail, the same verdict per setting on both hosts. Turn boundaries at exits reach the
  passing order, so the design's largest risk did not hold for this test.
- 24 of the 28 settings gave one fingerprint on both hosts; `q=12`, `1024`, `2048` and `4096` gave
  one per host, with equal verdicts. Each ran once per host, so the cause is not known yet: a
  per-model difference inside the guest (Zen 3 against Zen 4), or a host-timed difference in the
  engine. `HYDO_KVM_DIAG` now lists each vCPU's state, its APIC, and the scheduler, and a repeat
  run on a branch `tmp-kvm-vcpus4` keeps every run's folder. The cause was the determinism bug
  below, and with the fixed kernel 7 of the 28 settings pass.

Also in this milestone: with several vCPUs a proven exit-free cycle with interrupts off ends the
vCPU's turn at the cycle's smallest state when another vCPU can run (before, it ended the run as a
deadlock); a cycle with a state that has interrupts on is resolved as before. The `--vcpus` help
text names KVM, and `hydo guide flaky-tests` and the manifest reference describe it.

**The determinism bug.** A repeat run on a temporary branch `tmp-kvm-vcpus4`
(https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43464674850; Intel Xeon 6975P-C, AMD EPYC 9V74 and
7763) ran `q=2`, `q=12`, `q=1024` and `q=2048` three times each. `q=2` gave one fingerprint on
each host. The other three gave three fingerprints in three runs on every host, with equal
verdicts. So the differences between hosts in the stage 4 run were a determinism bug, not a
difference between CPU models. In the engine's diagnostics every vCPU's registers, both APICs,
the scheduler, the clock and every exit count were equal, and only one 1 MiB block of RAM
differed.

How it was found:

1. RAM dumps (`hv/kvm/smp/nats-diff.sh`, run
   https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43468063420; AMD EPYC 7763 and 9V45, Intel Xeon
   Platinum 8573C) compared two runs of `q=12` word by word. One 8-byte word differed, at guest
   physical address `0x3fed52a0`, with values of about 2 to 3.4 × 10^10: the size of the guest's
   TSC after some seconds. The guest's exits were the same in both runs, so the guest stores the
   value without branching on it.
2. A temporary watch in the engine logged every change of that word with the exit, the vCPU and
   RIP (run https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43482338111, on a branch
   `tmp-kvm-vcpus7`; AMD EPYC 9V45 and 7763, Intel Xeon 6975P-C). The first change that differs
   comes at the same exit on every host, on vCPU 1: exit 17880 for `q=12`, and exit 17600 for
   `q=1024` at another word, `0x1e6f188`. The next word there holds about 56 ms in nanoseconds,
   a pair of a TSC reading and a clock reading, as Go's runtime keeps in `ticks.startTicks` and
   `startTime`.
3. The same run checked the engine. Many looks of the spin observer (`HYDO_KVM_SPIN_MS=1`),
   almost none (60 s), and the engine pinned to one host CPU each still gave three fingerprints in
   three runs. So neither the observer nor the host's scheduling is the cause.

The cause. The guest patch makes user-space RDTSC fault, so that the kernel returns the exit
clock instead. `hydo_tsd_init()`, an early initcall, sets CR4.TSD for it. KVM does not trap
RDTSC, so without TSD a program reads the TSC of the host's CPU, which KVM offsets but does not
stop. The initcall
sets TSD only on the boot CPU, and Linux 6.6.35 drops it twice on every other CPU:

- `secondary_startup_64` in `arch/x86/kernel/head_64.S` loads CR4 with MCE, PAE and PGE only;
- `cpu_init()` in `arch/x86/kernel/cpu/common.c` clears VME, PVI, TSD, and DE.

On the boot CPU, `cpu_init()` runs before the initcall, so the boot CPU keeps TSD. One vCPU never
had the bug.

The fix took three tries:

| try | change | run | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | TSD in `mmu_cr4_features` and the real-mode trampoline's CR4 | 43472281045 | no effect: `head_64.S` drops it; `q=12`, `1024`, `2048` and `4096` still gave three fingerprints on every host |
| 2 | TSD in `cr4_init()` | 43487988684 | no effect: `cpu_init()` clears it again. The new engine guard stopped every run with several vCPUs |
| 3 | TSD again in `cpu_init()`, right after its clear | 43496814855 | one fingerprint per schedule |

The fix (`hv/kvm/linux/hydo-kvm-smp.patch`) is try 3. `cpu_init()` sets TSD again right after its
clear when `hydo_tsd_forced()` is true, before the CPU can run user code. The patch of try 1 is
gone. In run 43487988684 the "ONE" lines of `nats-check.sh` were three runs without a result each,
all with the fingerprint `none`; the script now prints NO-RESULT for such a setting.

The guard. With several vCPUs, every fingerprint now checks that each started vCPU has CR4.TSD set
when vCPU 0 has it, and the run ends with a message otherwise. Try 1 also had a guard, which
looked at a vCPU that was in user code at the end of its turn. User code seldom makes an exit, so
that guard never fired. The new guard is what stopped the runs of try 2.

The kernel. `bzImage-kvm-smp` is now `b40b2711…`, config `d630f99e…` (unchanged), store path
`r23ms6f5…-hydo-kvm-guest-kernel-smp-6.6.35`. The bare-metal machine's trial build gave it first,
without warnings. In run 43496814855 each of three runners built it twice in a sandbox, with the
same bytes six times. The RDTSC audit lists the UP kernel's 10 sites.

**The runs with the fixed kernel** (run https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43496814855, on
a temporary branch `tmp-kvm-vcpus9`, deleted afterwards; AMD EPYC 9V45 and two EPYC 7763; every job
green). Every value below was the same on all three hosts, so the two AMD models agree:

- `hv/kvm/kvm-check.sh`, one vCPU: 15 of 15 checks.
- `hv/kvm/smp/smp-check.sh`: 13 of 13 checks. An exploration of 8 seeds on 2 vCPUs made 21 runs,
  and `hydo repro` of it reproduced 5 of 5 with the recorded fingerprint.
- `hv/kvm/smp/nats-check.sh`: 31 settings, each run three times; every setting gave one
  fingerprint. The 28 turn settings and their verdicts are in the example's `RESULTS.md`.

The Redis example's new several-vCPU values (each schedule twice on each host):

| vCPUs | schedule | verdict | fp | turns (`qn=`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | `disk=none dseed=1 \| run` | OK, acked=20 | `851da6841d14cbad` | 229 |
| 2 | `disk=none dseed=1 q=64 \| run` | OK | `cc2a072b654ecfe2` | 432 |
| 2 | `disk=none dseed=1 q=7 qs=1f \| run` | OK | `dcb22e9bc56af461` | 2,407 |
| 2 | `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | VIOLATION, key k:1 lost | `c3c57641abcec195` | 159 |
| 4 | `disk=none dseed=1 \| run` | OK | `b5fab129b81cb213` | 504 |

A run from the worker's S1 on 2 vCPUs gave the fresh boot's `851da6841d14cbad`. In the default
two-vCPU run, vCPU 1 made 6,338 of the workload's 26,368 counted exits. One vCPU kept its values:
the timing branch with `br=` gave `2039c438b0971596`, and nats-server's buggy test
`d6cb9210afe66ff9` (VIOLATION).

**Left.** The fix ran only on AMD. The earlier runs on Intel (Xeon 6975P-C and Platinum 8573C) had
the bug. A run with the fixed kernel on an Intel host is still to do. Also left:

- `hydo repro` of one run's folder and `hydo explain` with `--vcpus` on KVM;
- the explorer's turn tokens and turn-length search for KVM;
- `bzImage-kvm-smp` in the Linux release.

### Milestone 220 (tentative number) - DONE (`hydo report --html`: a failure as one self-contained web page, for a run, an exploration or a CI run, with the failing run's timeline and its first difference from a passing neighbour; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** `hydo report --html [DIR] [-o FILE] [--against RUN_DIR] [--diff DIFF]` writes one
HTML file, by default `DIR/report.html`. DIR is a run directory, an exploration directory or a
`hydo ci run` output directory. The goal is a failure that is easy to understand and to share.
The page holds its style sheet and one small script, the copy buttons, and loads nothing: no
script, font, style sheet or image from anywhere else. So it opens from disk, as a CI artifact
or as an attachment to an issue. It follows the reader's light or dark setting and has one
column on a phone. It is made from the directory's files only, and no VM runs.

**What the page shows.**

- A summary: the verdict, the system (from the image's name), the engine with its vCPUs, RAM
  and CPU level, the host's CPU, the hydo version with its fingerprint epoch, the schedule, and
  the fingerprint.
- Each failure. For a run, its failed checks and its diagnosis, then `hydo repro DIR` and the
  `hydo run` command line of its schedule, each with a copy button. For an exploration, each
  class and signature with its seeds, whether every re-run reproduced, and the minimal schedule
  with its verdict, its two confirmation fingerprints and the replay command. A failure that
  was not shrunk, such as an ERROR, shows its first run's schedule and command. A sentence says
  in plain words what each class means.
- The failing run's timeline: the events of `hydo inspect events`, now also readable for an
  exploration's run (`consoles/<tag>.*`). It shows the faults, the service starts and signals,
  the processes that ended, the readiness checks, the assertions, the reports, the kernel's
  lines, the forced thread switches and the verdict, with the stop and the engine's clock of
  each. The commands, snapshots and the guest's own output are behind a check box, which needs
  no script. A run without control transcripts gets the events that `hydo diff` reads from its
  consoles.
- The first difference from a passing run, as `hydo diff` finds it: the shared events before it,
  the events only one run has, and what differs inside them. It also shows the first
  difference in what the checks judge, and the first forced thread switch that differs. For a
  run the passing run is `--against`, or `--diff` (a diff.json, a `hydo diff` directory, or a
  `hydo explain` directory, whose closest neighbour with another verdict is taken), or the
  `hydo explain` directory given as DIR. For an exploration it is new: the minimal schedule's
  confirmation run against each passing shrink candidate of its signature. The page picks the
  one whose first difference comes latest, as `hydo explain` does.
- The property table: held, failed, never reached, never evaluated, with the runs of each.
- For a CI run: each finding's state against the base (new, pre-existing, still present,
  changed, fixed, unverified) with a sentence each, how hydo knows it (the proof), the replays
  on both commits, the stored first difference, and the timeline of this commit's replay.
- A section "Versions" when the results carry them. It reads a `versions` member of the
  document, or `versions.json` beside it. Its format is not defined yet (open item 94).

**Bounds.** A timeline keeps at most 400 events, its main events first, and each text at most
300 characters. A piece of evidence keeps at most 4,000 bytes. Only the first 4 failures of an
exploration or a CI run get a timeline and a diff. The page says what it left out and names the
command that shows all of it.

**Code.** `hydo/crates/hydo-cli/src/htmlreport.rs` and `htmlreport/page.rs`. `hydo inspect`'s
reader of a recorded run (`inspect::drive::Recorded`) gained `RunFiles`, the file names of a
`hydo run` directory or of an exploration's run. `diff::load_run` reads a run from its document
and those files, and `preempt::read_file` reads one records file. The results format is
unchanged. `hydo report`'s help texts name `--html` (the CLI golden is re-recorded for the help
texts only), and `hydo guide inspect` has a section "Share a failure as one page".

**Proof on this Mac, with the Mac engine and one VM at a time.** The Redis example of the 0.3.1
release was built by that release (image `fba2c11e…`) and run by this tree's `hydo`:

| run | schedule | verdict | fp |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | VIOLATION, key k:0 lost | `a2b8d71c0c467d15` |
| B | `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=always` | OK, acked=12 all present | `7147e75676d15194` |

`hydo report --html A --against B` gave a 30 KiB page. Its timeline shows the power cut before
step 12 and the recovery boot's check that finds `k:0` lost. Its diff shows where the two runs
part: the knob's value in the first command, and in what the checks judge, the recovery's
acknowledged list. `hydo explain A` ran five neighbours, and `--diff` on its directory shows the
closest one (`without C=12`). A swarm exploration, seeds 1 to 30, gave 13 failures of 4 kinds,
all reproduced: two shrunk violations, `lying-disk` and `unsafe-knob` (`disk=cut
dseed=1f16055b6d41c6d9 | run C=9 R=no`), and two kinds of ERROR under disk I/O errors. Its page
has 76 KiB. Each minimal schedule is compared with its passing shrink candidate. For
`unsafe-knob` that is the schedule without `R=no`. The pages were looked at in headless Chrome
at 1280 and 520 pixels, in light and in dark. Their script passes `node --check`. The recorded
hvx runs of `tests/fixtures/inspect/` (a power cut, and an out-of-memory provisioning with its
diagnosis) also render.

**Tests.** Golden pages in `hydo/crates/hydo-cli/tests/golden/report/` (`HYDO_BLESS=1 cargo test
-p hydo --bin hydo htmlreport` rewrites them). One is the Mac power-cut run against its passing
neighbour, from fixtures with the scratch paths replaced by `/work`. One is an exploration on the
explorer's scripted engine, seeds 1 to 12, with the consoles the page reads. One is the recorded
CI run `mac-shop-ci-run`. Each page is checked for a size bound and for no address, `src=`,
`<link>`, `@import` or `url(` at all. A test checks that a timeline of 5,050 events keeps 400,
with every fault. Another checks that text from a run is escaped, and another the section
"Versions".

**What is left.** Open item 94: the format of the version range, a real `hydo ci run` with
replay directories, a fresh hvx run, and a run with forced preemption points.

### Milestone 221 (tentative number) - DONE (`hydo versions`: in which versions of the system a finding is present, by replay and bisection; Formance Ledger's account race is introduced in v2.4.0 and still present in v2.4.18; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** Until now the versions of each finding were found by hand. Examples are the
TigerBeetle example's table for issue 3960 (M217), etcd 3.5.5 against 3.5.6 (M78, M206), and
Formance v2.3.24 against v2.4.18 (M215). `hydo versions` does it in one command. It takes a
finding and a list of the system's versions, oldest first. It builds each version's image, replays the finding's minimal
schedule on it, and says where the finding was introduced and whether the newest version still
has it. The code is `hydo/crates/hydo-cli/src/versions.rs`. The guide's section is `hydo guide
workflow`, "Which versions have a finding".

**The command.**

- The finding is a run directory, an exploration directory (each of its findings, or `--finding
  N`), or a schedule. A schedule's finding is named by `--image` (one replay there) or by the
  first failing end of the versions. `--key` picks one finding key, for example a new error kind in
  a run that passed its checks.
- The versions are one of three forms. `--param KEY=V1,V2,...` builds each with `hydo build
  --set KEY=<version>`. `--git REV,REV,...` or `--git A..B` checks out each revision as a
  detached worktree. `A..B` is A and every first-parent commit after it up to B, labelled by its
  tag when it has one. `--images NAME=IMG,...` takes ready images. `--build CMD` runs before
  each build with `HYDO_VERSION` set. `--set` adds a parameter to every build.
- Each version gets one outcome. `reproduced`: the replay gave the finding's key (the CI's
  finding key, M197). `passes`: the checks held. `fails-otherwise`: another finding failed the
  run. `cannot-run`: the version did not build, or the schedule was refused or gave no result.
- The search replays the newest version and the oldest, each stepping inward past undecided
  versions. Then it bisects every range between two decided versions whose outcomes differ. It
  assumes one change point and writes `contradiction` when the decided versions change more than
  once. `--found-on V` replays the finding's own version first. `--all` replays every version.
  A version whose image has the bytes of the finding's recorded run is answered by that record.
- Builds and replays run as child `hydo build` and `hydo run` processes. A failed build is that
  version's outcome and never ends the search. Images are kept in an image cache by a key over
  their inputs: `vk1-<hex>` over the CI's input-key lines, the build command, and for `--git` the
  commit. The build's intermediates are deleted.

**The results addition.** `versions.json` (`hydo_results::VersionsDoc`, type `versions`) has one
`Versions` per finding. Each has the schedule, the key and title, `source`, every version with
its `outcome`, `fingerprint`, `verdict`, `image_sha256` and replay number, and the answer:
`first_bad`, `last_good`, `last_bad`, `fixed_in`, `still_present_in_newest`, `contradiction`,
`replays` and a `summary` sentence. `hydo versions <dir>` writes it to `<dir>/versions/`.
`hydo report <dir>` adds the summary to the report, and `hydo report --html` (M220) shows a
section "Versions" read by these types. That page had guessed the field names before (open item
94). The schema gains the four types, and `hydo-schema-compat` and the results tests pass. The
proof's document is `hydo/schema/examples/results/v1/mac-formance-versions/versions.json`.

**Tests.** `tests/versions.rs` runs the command on the scripted engine. Its program builds a
stand-in image per version (`<program> build <manifest> <out> KEY=VALUE...`) and answers a
replay from the version in the image (`HYDO_SCRIPTED_IMAGE`). The four tests:

| test | versions | the answer |
|---|---|---|
| bisection | 1 to 8 from a parameter, the bug from 6, version 5 does not build | replays 8, 1, 4, 6; introduced in 6, 4 passes, 5 not decided; a second search builds only 5 |
| contradiction | `--all` over 1 to 4, the bug in 2 and 4; and `--found-on 2` over 1 to 5, the bug in 2 only | `contradiction` names the sequence; first bad 2, fixed in 3 |
| run directory | a recorded `result.json` | its key; `hydo report` prints the `versions:` line |
| git | tags r1 to r6 of a scratch repository, the bug from r4 | introduced in r4, r3 passes; every worktree removed |

Unit tests in `versions.rs` cover the search order, the answer, and the sentences.

**The proof on the Mac engine.** Formance Ledger's finding 1 (M215): two first uses of one
account in two assets race, and PostgreSQL logs `duplicate key value violates unique constraint
'accounts_ledger'` (error kind `027af89500d5`). A copy of the example in the session's scratch
folder took the ledger's release as a parameter (`../bin/ledger-{{ledger}}-{{arch}}`). Its
known-errors list no longer accepted the finding's two kinds. A `--build` script compiled each
tag for linux/arm64 with Go 1.27.3. With this tree's `hydo` in the 0.3.1 Mac release:

```sh
hydo build hydo/hydo.yaml --set arch=arm64 --set ledger=v2.4.18
hydo run "disk=none | run" --out run-2.4.18     # OK; 2 new error kinds, fp f479b8a7e9865610
hydo versions run-2.4.18 --key f1:error-log:21b4dcd9d9 --manifest hydo/hydo.yaml \
  --set arch=arm64 --param ledger=v2.3.24,v2.4.0,v2.4.9,v2.4.18 --build 'sh ../build-version.sh'
```

```text
  version  outcome          fingerprint       replay  verdict
  v2.3.24  passes           e08898ae773d1f14  1       HYDO-ORACLE: OK invariants=14 held (...)
  v2.4.0   reproduced       a1a0a244d9473280  2       HYDO-ORACLE: OK invariants=14 held (...)
  v2.4.9   not-replayed     -                 -
  v2.4.18  reproduced       f479b8a7e9865610  record  HYDO-ORACLE: OK invariants=14 held (...)

introduced in v2.4.0 (v2.3.24 passes); still present in v2.4.18, the newest version tried (2 replays for 4 versions)
```

The command built the v2.4.18 image with the bytes of the hand build (`62a8dd2a…`). So the

**On hvx.** The bare-metal machine ran the etcd example with this tree's `hydo` in a prefix made

`--build` that fetches each release archive by its sha256 in `build.sh`:

The recorded 3.5.5 image (`b4dc0195…`) came from the re-baseline's staging. That build kept the

### Milestone 222 (tentative number) - DONE (five fixes from the onboardings of Milestones 215, 217 and 218: sends wait for room in the receive queue, a run holds 65,536 sends, request ids in the error template, no login name in `known-errors.yaml`, a verdict for a service that stops in a run without faults, and the identity test without git-ignored files; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-13)

**In short.** This milestone closes open items 82, 83, 84 and 93, and the verdict part of open
item 86. Each fix has a test. Only runs that fail today change. The pinned reproducers, the
KVM engine's pinned fingerprints, and the recorded hvx values of the images with error logs
stayed as recorded.

**Open item 82: the recovery boot lost its carried records.** After a power cut the host sends
`$HYDO_ACKED`, the failed ids and `$HYDO_OUTCOMES` as messages of up to 3,000 bytes at one stop,
without waiting for replies. The Mac and KVM engines typed every message that was due into the
4,096-byte receive queue and dropped the bytes that did not fit. Now a due message waits in the
engine until it fits, and every later message waits behind it (`ctl_next`, `ctl_fits` and
`ctl_due` in `hydo-hvm` and `hydo-kvm` `serve.rs`). The engine types it at the first exit with
room and reports it with a `SENT` line. A `SEND` that cannot be typed at once is answered
`queued` (`SendAnswer::Queued`), as a send for a later exit always was. No message is longer than
the queue, so each one fits once the guest has read what came before it. A run in which every
message fits is the same exit for exit, so its fingerprint stays. The host's transcript records
the same sends either way. hvx sends through the host-call port and was not affected.

- Test: `hydo-kvm`'s `sends_wait_for_room_in_the_receive_queue`, on the scripted vCPU. A guest
  reads 9,000 bytes, and the host sends three messages of 3,000 bytes at one stop. The first is
  typed at once, the other two are queued and typed later, and the guest reads every byte. With
  the old `serve.rs` the test fails: all three were "typed", and the guest never read its 9,000
  bytes.
- The Mac, a copy of the Formance Ledger example with 40 rounds and the full account names in
  the client's tokens (the example itself keeps 30 rounds and short names). Its recovery boot
  carries about 5.8 KB of records. `disk=cut dseed=1 | run C=38` with the 0.3.1 release's
  engine: `hvmx: one: send 599: 2390 of 3122 bytes do not fit in the receive queue`, then
  `ERROR recovery: exit budget exhausted` after 121 s. With this tree's `hydo-hvm`
  (`HYDO_HVM_ENGINE`): `OK invariants=14 held` in 21 s, fp `3abdf57571c42ae2`, and `hydo repro`
  gave the same fingerprint. The first boot's workload fingerprint was the same in both runs
  (`c196b716a175de18`). `disk=none dseed=1 | run` of that image gave `68c7e500bd9d0eec` with
  both engines.

**Open item 83: at most 1,024 messages per run.** The limit was the size of the C engines'
array, ported to every Rust engine. A slow workload sends more: queue polls, `always_` checks
and clock reads. The limit is now `hydo_engine_proto::MAX_SENDS`, 65,536, on hvx, KVM and the
Mac. It still guards against a host controller that sends without end, and the refusal says
so: `send more than 65536 sends in one run (the limit against a host controller that sends
without end)`. So that a long run stays cheap, the engines now drop the bytes of an
acknowledged message, find an acknowledged id by binary search, and start the scans at each
exit or return after the messages that are typed or acknowledged for good (`Book::lo`). A
snapshot's copy of the book starts its scans at 0 again, because its typed messages become
retypes.

- Test: `hydo-kvm`'s `a_run_holds_more_than_1024_sends`: 3,000 messages of one byte in one run,
  each acknowledged, and the guest reads all of them.

**Open item 84: error kinds and request ids.** The default template (`nums` in
`hydo-control` `schedule/errlog.rs`) made `<id>` only of a mixed token of 16 characters or
more. Two rules are new:

- A token of 8 to 15 letters and digits is `<id>` when it changes between digits, capitals and
  small letters at every second character or more often, and repeats few characters. So
  `qjGcd4lJvd` and `k3j9x2ab01` are ids, and `thread12`, `Http2Server`, `MY012592` and Redis's
  banner `oO0OoO0OoO0Oo` keep their letters.
- The value after a trace, span, request or correlation key (`trace-id=`, `request_id:`,
  `'reqId':`) is `<id>` when it has six characters or more with a digit and a letter, or with
  capitals and small letters. So `trace-id=FXkZAHyuua`, which has no digit, is an id too.
  `clientId=producer-1` and `pid=4242` are as before.

The first version of the first rule also took Redis's banner, which every recorded Redis run
with error logs reports. The controller's recorded transcripts (`m123::`) showed that, and the
rule now asks for few repeated characters. The new test `reviewed_kinds_keep_their_templates`
gives every reviewed entry of the examples' known lists (formance-ledger, medusa,
nats-jetstream, redis-errors, the stack, and the schema's example folder; 40 entries or more)
its example line and compares the template with the listed one. All stay. The test
`request_ids_are_one_kind` has the cases above.

`hydo errors accept` wrote the login name (`$USER`) as `by:` into the known list, which is
usually a tracked file. Now it writes `by:` only with `--by`. Test: `hydo-errors`'
`accept_writes_no_name_unless_given`.

**Open item 86, the verdict.** A service that stopped in a run without faults, and did not start
again, ended the run at once with `ERROR restart after the faults (<service>)`, and no check
ran. Such a run had no faults. A run without faults has no disk fault (`ioerr`, `lying`), no
`cf=`, and only knobs and `Q=` in its guest part; timing tokens are allowed
(`RunCfg::no_faults`). In such a run the controller still tries the restart. If the service
does not come back, there is no workload retry, the final checks run, their verdict goes to the
log (`the checks with <service> stopped: ...`), and the verdict is `HYDO-ORACLE: VIOLATION service
stopped in a run without faults (<service>)`. A run with any fault keeps the old verdicts.
`hydo inspect` names the service of the new verdict. The recorded verdicts `ERROR restart after
the faults` (`hvx/redis-errors` and others) all come from runs with `disk=ioerr`, so none
changes. Test: `restart_may_fail::a_service_that_stops_in_a_run_without_faults_is_named_and_the_checks_run`,
which also checks that `K=db@1+1` and `disk=ioerr:5` keep the old verdict.

**Open item 93: the identity test read git-ignored files.** The explorer's goldens pin every file
of an example's `hydo/` folder. The list now leaves out the files that the repository's ignore
rules leave out (`git check-ignore`; tracked files are always in), and so does the list of
example manifests. Without git, nothing is left out. Test: `identity::local_outputs_are_no_inputs`
writes a file into the Formance example's `hydo/hydo-out/` and checks that it is not an input.
The identity goldens pass unchanged on a clean tree.

**Checks.**

- hvx (the bare-metal machine, this tree in its own folder, the loaded main module
  `91D86B693F4D4035C368F9B`): `deploy-metal.sh` printed `ALL PASS (35 checks)`, and the pinned
  reproducers gave `a76d7fe857fdb37c` (VIOLATION) and `efbde7b57264be0f` (OK).
  `hydo-bench rebaseline --check` over the 0.3.1 Linux release, for the three images with

  `disk=ioerr:5 dseed=1 | run` with `ERROR restart after the faults (redis)`. A ctl value
  covers the error records, so these runs show that the templates of real Redis, MySQL and
  Kafka lines stayed.
- KVM: the scripted engine tests, among them `one_vcpu_fingerprints_are_pinned`. No real KVM
  host ran this tree.
- The Mac: the Formance runs above. No other recorded Mac value was run again. No Mac image

- `cargo test --release` of hydo-control, hydo-errors, hydo-explore, hydo-engine-proto,

**Left.** The engines' change ran on the Mac and in the KVM engine's scripted tests, not on a
real KVM host. The tracked Formance example keeps 30 rounds and short names. The error rules

### Milestone 223 (tentative number) — DONE (hydo in a team's CI, stage 2: accepted findings, time budgets, shards and their merge, and a history store; 2026-11-13)

**Why.** Open item 67 left stage 2 of `docs/design/ci.md` unbuilt. The trial of 2026-11-13 showed
the most pressing gap: a known failure, such as the Redis `appendfsync everysec` window, fails
every pull request that brings it back, and a team then turns the check off.

**Built** (`hydo/crates/hydo-cli/src/ci/`, `hydo ci --help`, `hydo guide ci` sections 9 to 12):

1. **Accepted findings.** `hydo/known-findings.yaml` is a new versioned file
   (`hydo_manifest::known_findings`). Its schema `hydo/schema/known-findings-v1.json` has a
   released copy and is checked with `hydo-schema-compat`; an example is in
   `hydo/schema/examples/known-findings/v1/`. Each entry has `key`, `title`, `schedule`,
   `reason`, `who` and `date`. Like `ci.yaml` it is not staged into the image, and the image
   input key leaves it out. `hydo ci accept <key> --reason ...` (src/ci/accept.rs) takes the
   title and the minimal schedule from a recorded `ci-run.json`, and a unique prefix of a key of
   that run is enough. It appends the entry and keeps the file's other text. `who` is written only
   from `--who` and is empty otherwise. `hydo ci run` gives an accepted finding the state
   `accepted` and keeps the state it would have had in `CiFinding.accepted.state`. `fail_on`
   never fails on it, and `junit.xml` shows it as a skipped test. An entry the exploration did
   not find is replayed with its schedule. When the schedule passes, the entry is listed in
   `CiRun.stale_accepted` and in the report's section `Accepted findings this run did not find`.
2. **Time budgets.** `budget:` per mode in `hydo/ci.yaml` (`10m`, `90s`, `1h30m`) or `--budget`.
   The explorer has a new option, `--time-limit SECONDS`, for a plain seed range only. When the
   limit has passed it cancels the first runs still queued. It keeps the seeds already finalized
   in seed order and drops the results of runs that were in flight, so the explored seeds are
   always the first ones of the range (`Summary.time_limit`: `planned`, `explored`,
   `explored_seeds`, `cut`). Re-runs and shrinks of those seeds finish as usual. `hydo ci run`
   now builds the base's image before any exploration. It keeps 15 % of the budget for replays
   and regressions, gives this commit's exploration half of the rest when the base is explored
   too, and explores the base over exactly the seeds this commit explored. A partial run never
   calls a finding `fixed`: a passing replay there is `unverified` with the proof
   `head-replay-ok-partial`. The scripted-engine scenario `time_limit_cuts_at_a_seed_boundary`
   checks the cut, and that `--seeds 1-<explored>` gives the same first runs.
3. **Shards.** `--shard I/N` explores the I-th of N contiguous parts of the seed range
   (src/ci/seeds.rs; the first parts are one seed longer when the range does not divide). Each
   shard compares its part with the base and replays its own findings; only the first replays the
   saved regressions. `hydo ci merge` (src/ci/merge.rs) checks that the shards are one run and
   combines them by finding key in shard order, without a VM. A shard that proved a key new by a
   base replay makes it `new`, a key some shard's base found makes it `present`, and `fixed` needs
   every shard. A missing shard makes the merged run partial and failing. Each shard shrinks its
   own failures, so a signature found by two shards is shrunk twice; the merge keeps the lowest
   shard's minimal schedule, which is the one a single run shrinks. The action has a new input,
   `merge`, which runs `hydo ci merge` on the shards' downloaded outputs and skips the `/dev/kvm`
   step. `hydo guide ci` section 11 has the matrix workflow; actionlint 1.7.12 and shellcheck
   report nothing for it and for the action's scripts. It never ran on GitHub.
4. **History.** A directory store (src/ci/history.rs), the first form of section 4.5. `hydo ci
   record <ci-run.json> --store DIR` writes `v1/<project>/runs/<id>.json`, appends a
   `finding-event` to `v1/<project>/findings.jsonl` for each change of state, and rewrites
   `v1/<project>/state.json` (a `ci-ledger`, per branch). Both are results-format additions with
   an example in `hydo/schema/examples/results/v1/mac-redis-ci-history/`. A finding seen failing
   is `new` on the branch, or `reappeared` after `fixed`. A finding proven fixed by replay
   becomes `fixed`, and one the run did not find keeps its state. A pull request's run needs
   `--branch`, and a shard's run must be merged first. `hydo ci run --history DIR` reads the
   ledger of the target branch. It replays the open findings that neither exploration found, as
   it replays the base's findings. Such a finding is called fixed only when the base still fails
   it the same way, and a new finding that the ledger has fixed becomes `reappeared`. `--base
   main` now also names the base branch when no flag or CI variable does.

Results-format additions: `Summary.time_limit`, `CiBudget.time_limit_s`, `completed_seeds`,
`planned`, `completed`, `partial`, `shard` and `range`, `CiFinding.source`, `accepted` and
`fixed_at`, `CiRun.stale_accepted`, `shards` and `history`, the states `accepted` and
`reappeared`, and the documents `finding-event` and `ci-ledger`. `hydo/ci.yaml` format 1 adds
`budget`. The schema checks pass against the released schemas.

**Proof, on this Mac** (the Mac engine, one VM at a time, `workers: 1`, under a load average of
about 50 from other sessions). A throwaway git repository holds the 0.3.1 release's Redis
example, with `pr: {seeds: 1-20, strategy: swarm}`. The base commit has `appendfsync always`,
and the change sets `appendfsync everysec`, as in the trial. The first five rows were made twice,
once in a directory that another session deleted, with the same findings each time:

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| The change against the base | exit 1, `hydo: 1 new finding, 1 changed (failed)`: `VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost` (`f1:invariant:5ef675c8c9`), minimal schedule `disk=cut dseed=70c9101f818fe74 \| run C=14`, the base passes it; 49 runs, 4 replays, both images built |
| `hydo ci accept f1:inv --reason ...`, committed | the entry with that key and schedule, `who: ""` |
| The change with the entry | exit 0, `hydo: no new findings, 1 changed, 1 accepted (passed)`, both images from the image cache (the same input keys) |
| `--budget 90s` | exit 0, `hydo: no new findings, 1 accepted, partial: 8 of 20 seeds (passed)`; the explorer stopped before seed 9, the base explored seeds 1-8, the run took 78 s |
| `--shard 1/2`, `--shard 2/2`, `hydo ci merge` | exit 0, the same three keys with the same states and minimal schedules as the single run, and the same fault counts (`C` 12, `K` 10, `N` 13, `disk` 17); 63 runs against 49, because both shards shrank the violation |
| A nightly run of the base commit, seeds 21-60, recorded with `hydo ci record` | 3 `new` events on `main` in `findings.jsonl` |
| The change with `--history` | the three keys found by the explorations again, so no history finding was replayed |
| The change with `--history --seeds 1-8` | `hydo: no new findings, 2 fixed, 1 accepted (passed)`: neither exploration found the two run errors of the nightly run; their schedules pass on the change and fail on the base (proof `head-replay-ok-base-fails`). The same keys are present on other schedules of seeds 1-20, which is the limit that section 6.1 describes: a finding can be gone from its schedules and still exist |

Tests: `cargo test` of hydo-manifest, hydo-results, hydo-explore (every scripted-engine scenario,
whose goldens did not move) and hydo's `ci::` unit tests, `cargo test -p hydo --test it docs::`,
`cargo test -p hydo-agents --test it public_content::`, clippy and fmt. Nothing recorded moved.

**Not built** (open item 67): the history page (`hydo ci page`), the `workflow_run` recorder of
pull requests, a history branch kept by the action, budgets turned into seed counts from history,
proposed regression files, and one shrink per signature across shards.

### Milestone 224 (tentative number) - DONE (Blnk onboarded on the Mac engine and on hvx as the third experiment in business bugs; two new Blnk bugs, an overdraft limit that coalesced draws ignore and an atomic bulk that keeps its first transfer, each found by a domain rule; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-14)

**In short.** Blnk, an open source ledger in Go, runs unmodified from `main` at `67d88333`
(2026-11-11) in `hydo/onboard/examples/blnk` (RESULTS.md). Its API process saves each
transaction as `QUEUED` in PostgreSQL 16, and a worker applies it through a Redis 7.2.4 queue.
The latest release, v0.15.8, has four bugs fixed since on `main` (upstream issues 413, 418, 421
and 422), so the experiment tested `main`. Seven domain rules read Blnk's tables:

- balanced transactions;
- balances and held amounts equal to their transactions;
- one final state per queued transaction;
- holds that never commit more than they held;
- one transaction per reference;
- overdraft rules;
- atomic bulks.

One generic rule compares every balance with the client's acknowledged operations. Error logs
as findings ran beside them. The runs used the Mac engine with this tree's hydo, and hvx on the
bare-metal machine with the published 0.3.1. No hydo code changed, and nothing recorded moved.

**What was found.**

- A Blnk bug, found by the overdraft rule alone. Blnk does not save `overdraft_limit`. The
  worker loads coalesced draws, and recovered ones, from PostgreSQL without it, and an
  `allow_overdraft` without a limit skips every balance check. On hvx it shows without a fault,
  with concurrent draws only (`overdraft-limit-concurrent-draws`). Natively 20 of 20 bursts of 5
  draws went past a limit of 50.00, and 0 of 20 with a two-line patch.
- A Blnk bug, found by the bulk rule, the generic rule, and the error logs. A synchronous atomic
  bulk in queue mode refunds only applied items when a later item fails before it is queued: a
  Redis timeout, a request cancelled because the client gave up, or a reused reference. The
  earlier items stay `QUEUED`, nothing marks the batch failed, and the worker applies them; the
  answer says nothing was applied. It failed 17 of 85 explored schedules, and natively 20 of 20
  bulks with a reused reference. The tested patch marks the batch failed, rolls back under the
  batch lock, and records the waiting items as `REJECTED` in PostgreSQL. With it, the 6 failing
  schedules of one exploration hold the rule, and the native bulks have no effect.
- A deployment setting, found by the generic rule alone. With Redis's defaults (no append-only
  file, as in Blnk's Compose file), a Redis kill or a power cut loses acknowledged commits and
  voids of holds, which live only in Redis. `--set redis_aof=yes` passes the same schedule.
  Upstream issue 336 drew the same line for the expiry of holds.
- A clock effect: after an hour's backward clock step, transfers behind a lock that a killed
  worker left were rejected after their 5 retries.

Reports for both bugs are drafted, not posted.

**Runs.** 85 explored schedules and about 40 directed runs:

| exploration | engine | strategy | schedules | failures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| e2 | Mac | `process --new-faults`, seeds 1-20 | 20 | 9: the bulk bug 6, the lost commits 2, a mistake of the wait 1 |
| h1 | hvx | `swarm --new-faults`, seeds 101-125 | 25 | 15: the overdraft bug 1, the bulk bug 2, the lost commits 3, disk faults 9 |
| h2 | hvx | `process --new-faults --timing --preempt`, seeds 201-220 | 20 | 8: the overdraft bug 1 (shrunk to no fault), the bulk bug 2, the lost commits 2, the wait 2, the clock 1 |
| e4 | Mac | `process --new-faults`, seeds 41-60 | 20 | 10: the bulk bug 7, the lost commits 1, the wait 1, the clock 1 |

The final images pass `disk=none | run` twice with one fingerprint on each engine
(`c8645a2ab6f1b90f` on the Mac, `35f37b7eb11da9ed` on hvx), and the three regressions fail as
expected on both.

**Which kind of rule found what.** Each kind found what the other did not. The overdraft rule
found the first bug, which the generic rule cannot judge, since the limit is Blnk's own decision.
The generic rule found the lost commits, where every domain rule held. Across the three

(Blnk's API, Redis, and worker), never where one database transaction does (Formance).

### Milestone 226 (tentative number) - DONE (a pause of threads of the workload: `P=workload/<thread>[#<k>]@<at>~<off>:<dur>` freezes named threads with the guest kernel's cgroup v2 freezer while the other threads run on, and `hydo explore --pause-thread` draws it; Qdrant's flaky test fails on every run of one such pause on hvx, its neighbours pass, and the fix passes; the Mac and KVM engines refuse it, their guest kernels have no cgroups; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-14)

**In short.** Open item 80 asked for a pause of one thread. Milestone 216's pause of the workload
stops the whole test process, so it did not reach Qdrant's race, which needs the test's thread
held off while the update worker of the same process runs. The timed pause can now name threads:
`P=workload/tests::wal_reco@0~4433:500` stops the thread named `tests::wal_reco` 4,433 ms of
guest time after step 0 starts, for 500 ms. On hvx it fails Qdrant's
`test_wal_replay_loads_pending_to_queue` on every run with the report's line
`length: 0, op_num: Some(500)`; 1 ms earlier or later it passes; the fixed test passes. No agent
change and no image rebuild.

**How a schedule names a thread.** By its name as Linux keeps it (`/proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/comm`,
at most 15 bytes), with an optional `#<k>` for the k-th thread of that name in the order of the
thread ids. The name is chosen at the moment the pause starts, among the threads of every process
of the workload. Why a name and not a thread id or a creation number:

- A thread id depends on everything the guest started before, the image's services and the
  controller's commands too. It is the same for one schedule on one image, but it moves with any
  change before the test, and nobody can write it down in advance.
- The n-th thread created counts every helper thread of the runtime, whose number depends on the
  guest's CPUs (tokio starts one worker per CPU).
- A name is what the program gives its thread (Rust's test harness names a test's thread after
  the test, tokio names its threads), so it is the same on every engine and every vCPU count.
  `#<k>` counts only threads of that one name, in the order of their thread ids, which is the
  order of their creation. A name that matches several threads, or `*` and `?`, stops all of
  them.

The schedule language checks the form (`hydo-schedule` `ThreadSel`): letters, digits and
`_ . : + -`, `*` and `?`, at most 15 bytes (a longer name is refused with its first 15 bytes), and
`#<k>` from 1.

**How one thread is stopped.** A signal cannot do it: SIGSTOP, also sent with tgkill to one
thread, stops the whole thread group. The candidates were these:

- ptrace (`PTRACE_SEIZE` and `PTRACE_INTERRUPT` stop exactly one thread). It needs a program in
  the guest that calls ptrace. busybox has none, so the agent would have to change, and the
  agent's bytes are in every image: every image built after the change would get new bytes and
  new fingerprints.
- `SCHED_IDLE` and a busy competitor. A thread at `SCHED_IDLE` still runs a little, and on the
  Mac and KVM a busy loop makes no VM exits, so it uses no guest time (the reason Milestone 216
  left the CPU-limit model).
- The cgroup v2 freezer in threaded mode. In a cgroup whose `cgroup.type` is `threaded`, the
  threads of one process may sit in different cgroups, and `cgroup.freeze` stops exactly the
  threads of its cgroup, at their next return to user space or their next interruptible sleep.
  It needs nothing but busybox's shell, so no image changes. It was taken.

The controller's pause timer (`hydo-control` `schedule/threads.rs`) runs four guest commands:
`busybox sleep <off>`; a shell script that finds the workload's first process (the process whose
parent is the agent, that leads its own session, and whose environment has `HYDO_FROM`), lists
the threads of its session, picks the named ones, moves each into the threaded cgroup
`hydo-pause` under its own cgroup and writes `1` to `cgroup.freeze`; `busybox sleep <dur>`; and a
script that writes `0` and moves the threads back. The standard output of the workload's first
process does not identify it: busybox ash redirects a command's output in the shell itself. The
control transcript logs the threads stopped (`PAUSED workload/tests::wal_reco (timer, threads 85
tests::wal_reco)`), or, when no thread matches, the names the workload has (`PAUSED nothing: no
thread of the workload matches workload/nosuch (timer; its threads: busybox, collection.test,
tests::wal_reco, tokio-rt-worker (4))`). A kernel without cgroup v2 ends the run with an error
that says so. Every decision is the guest's own, so a schedule replays bit for bit.

The guest kernels of the Mac engine (`Image-explore`, `Image-explore-netns`) and of the KVM
engine (`bzImage-kvm`) are built from `allnoconfig` and a list without `CONFIG_CGROUPS`. Those
engines refuse a pause of threads before any VM (`hydo_engine::refusal`), and `hydo explore
--pause-thread` refuses those backends. Only hvx boots the x86_64 kernel with cgroups. A kernel
with cgroups for those engines moves their fingerprints, an epoch change.

**What changed.**

- `hydo-schedule`: `Pause::Timer` has `thread: Option<ThreadSel>`. The language test
  `thread_pauses` holds the examples and the refusals.
- `hydo-control`: the module `schedule/threads.rs` and the part `ThreadPauseTimer`. A pause
  without a thread takes Milestone 216's path exactly. The scripted agent answers the two
  scripts, and `workload_pause::a_timed_pause_of_threads_freezes_them` checks the commands, the
  log lines and the replay.
- `hydo-engine`: the refusal on the Mac and KVM engines (`thread_pause_tests`).
- `hydo-explore`: `--pause-thread <name>[,<name>...]` draws `P=workload/<name>@...` with
  `--pause-workload`'s draws, the target drawn last, so `--pause-workload` alone keeps its
  schedules. `--pause-min <ms>` sets the earliest start (default 0, which keeps Milestone 216's
  draws) and `--pause-lengths <ms>,...` the lengths (default 10 to 500 ms). The shrinker treats a
  thread pause as a pause of the workload: half the length, and the start 0. The test is
  `workload_pauses::thread_pauses_draw_the_named_threads`.
- `hydo guide faults` has the section "Pause threads of the workload", `hydo guide flaky-tests`
  the section "A test that fails when one thread stops", MANIFEST.md the token, and
  `hydo guide capabilities` the row.

**The proof on hvx.** The bare-metal machine, this tree's `hydo` and `hydo-hvx` over the 0.3.1
Linux release, the main module loaded since 2026-11-08, one vCPU. The images were rebuilt to the
recorded bytes (`9aa2213aea1a5295…`, fixed `4fbac285d9940f02…`). A run whose test output carried
the guest's uptime put the shard's reload at 4.39 s after the workload's start. Pauses of the
test's thread from 0 to 4,250 ms passed, and so did pauses of every `tokio-rt-worker`. Of the

test's thread is then waiting for the blocking task that counts deferred points, and the worker
applies all 35 queued operations before it reads the length.

| image | schedule | verdict | fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| buggy | `disk=none \| run P=workload/tests::wal_reco@0~4433:500` | VIOLATION, `length: 0, op_num: Some(500)` | `4ae6099ea6e753a6` (3 runs) |
| buggy | `disk=none \| run P=workload/tests::wal_reco@0~4432:500` | OK, `length: 35` | `ab031f4dc2b53472` (3 runs) |
| buggy | `disk=none \| run P=workload/tests::wal_reco@0~4434:500` | OK, `length: 35` | `3f2ae9a4cced6ab7` (2 runs) |
| buggy | `disk=none \| run P=workload/tests::wal_reco@0~4433:200` | OK, `length: 3` | `f929e23e369aa175` (2 runs) |
| buggy | `disk=none \| run P=workload@0~4433:500` | OK, `length: 35` | `fe44e7e86b9ea884` (2 runs) |
| buggy | `disk=none \| run` | OK, `length: 35` | `240f9805a28e2544` (2 runs, the recorded value) |

At that start the length the test read fell with the pause's length: 34, 31, 24, 19, 5 and 0 for

`hydo explore --pause-thread tests::wal_reco --pause-min 4400 --pause-max 4500 --pause-lengths

**The Mac.** The Mac engine refuses the pause (`hydo run` printed `not run (no VM was started):

### Milestone 227 (tentative number) - DONE (the explorer draws KVM turn lengths and searches them; Milestone 219's kernel fix holds on Intel; on Intel a run from a worker's S1 snapshot gave another fingerprint than a fresh boot, with several vCPUs only, and a fix waits for its run; 2026-11-14)

**In short.** `hydo explore --backend kvm --vcpus N` now draws the turn tokens `q=` and `qs=`
with `--turns`, and `--sweep turns` searches KVM turn lengths. On nats-server's flaky test both
find passing and failing schedules, and every failure reproduced. A run on six GitHub hosts,
one of them Intel, showed that Milestone 219's kernel fix holds there too. The same run found a
new difference on the Intel host only: with 2 vCPUs, a run from an explorer worker's S1 ended
with another fingerprint than the fresh boot, with the same verdict. One-vCPU values did not
move.

**The explorer** (`hydo/crates/hydo-explore`):

- `--turns` on KVM with several vCPUs draws from the stream hvx uses, so the same seeds get a
  turn token and the same `qs=`. Only the lengths differ, because a KVM turn is a number of
  counted VM exits (default 256). A third of the drawn lengths are 1 to 32 exits, a third 33 to
  255, and the rest 128 to 512.
- Before, the explorer dropped `q=` and `qs=` from every schedule for the Mac and KVM engines,
  also from a schedule written by hand. On KVM with several vCPUs it keeps them now.
- The shrinker's step to a longer turn stops at KVM's default of 256 exits.
- `--sweep turns` has KVM defaults: lengths from 1 to 4,096 exits (`--turn-range`), narrowed to
  one exit (`--turn-resolution`). `report.md` says exits there.
- `--bursts` and `--turn-margin` stay refused on KVM, because only hvx's module applies them.
- Without these options nothing changed: every fake-engine scenario, the quick identity golden
  and the corpus golden are as before. Two new fake-engine scenarios, `kvm_turns_explore` and
  `kvm_turns_sweep`, run them on a scripted copy of the nats verdict table.
- `hv/kvm/smp/turns-check.sh` runs both on the real nats example on a host with `/dev/kvm`.

**The run** (https://github.com/kakoc/hydo/actions/runs/43527210060, a one-off workflow on a
temporary branch `tmp-kvm-turns`, deleted afterwards; two jobs for the explorer and six for the
hosts). Each job built `bzImage-kvm-smp` with a sandboxed Nix and got the pin `b40b2711…`; the
host jobs built it twice.

The explorer, `turns-check.sh` on AMD EPYC 9V74 and 7763, 7 of 7 checks on both, with the same
fingerprints on both:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `hydo explore --backend kvm --vcpus 2 --turns --seeds 1-40` | 21 schedules with a drawn turn length, each 1 to 512 exits; 8 passed, 32 failed; the explorer reproduced 32 of 32 |
| `hydo repro` of that exploration | 33 of 33 with the recorded fingerprint |
| `hydo explore --backend kvm --vcpus 2 --sweep turns` | 20 runs; boundaries at `q=15` (fails) / `q=16` (passes) and `q=39` (passes) / `q=40` (fails), each length one fingerprint twice |
| `hydo repro` of the sweep | 2 of 2 |

The passing schedules of the exploration had `q=16`, `q=26`, and seeded turns with `q=7`, `15`,
`17`, `26`, `36` and `135`. The sweep's lengths that `nats-check.sh` also ran from fresh boots
(`q=1`, `2`, `16`, `32` and `4096`) gave the fresh boots' fingerprints.

The hosts, `smp-check.sh` and `nats-check.sh` with `REPEAT=3`:

| host | `nats-check.sh` | `smp-check.sh` |
|---|---|---|
| AMD EPYC 9V74 (three hosts), 9V45, 7763 | 31 of 31 settings ONE, the same fingerprints on all five | 13 of 13 |
| Intel Xeon 6975P-C | 31 of 31 settings ONE, with fingerprints of its own | 11 of 13 |

Every setting had a real fingerprint, and every host gave the verdicts of the example's
`RESULTS.md`: 7 of the 28 turn settings pass. So the kernel fix of Milestone 219 holds on Intel.
On Intel the Redis example on 2 vCPUs gave `336869d674c85757` (default turns, `qn=229`),
`545e65bb7890dd84` (`q=64`), `ff73e513f05d98ad` (`q=7 qs=1f`), `33bbb08f63126ef6` (the power
cut) and, on 4 vCPUs, `c97101859c049431`, each twice. The one-vCPU checks gave
`cc72581995fd656f` from a fresh boot and from S1.

**The Intel S1 difference.** Two checks of `smp-check.sh` failed on the Intel host only:

- `2 vCPUs from S1 equals the fresh boot`: the run from the explorer worker's S1 gave
  `d25d8c657ebe3746`, the fresh boot `336869d674c85757`. The verdict, the turn count
  (`qn=229`) and the control transcript (`ctl=1c0625b4e495b9e2`) were the same.
- `repro of the exploration`: 4 of 5. The minimal schedule `disk=lying:1 dseed=eac0b527c5ac67d9
  | run C=20` gave `f6ee32068f7a6a4c` from a fresh boot and `dff2589a3d990f49` in the explorer.

A fresh boot runs on in the VM that took S1. A run from S1 starts in a fresh VM with the saved
vCPU states loaded. With one vCPU the two agree on Intel, and with two vCPUs they agree on AMD.
So the difference is KVM state that a load into a fresh VM does not give back on Intel. The
equal transcripts and turn counts say that the guest did not run differently, so the difference
is in a part of the state that the fingerprint hashes and the guest does not read.

**The fix** (`hydo/crates/hydo-kvm/src/vmm.rs`). With several vCPUs, the machine that takes a
snapshot now goes on in a fresh VM with the snapshot's vCPU states loaded, as every run restored
from it does. A fresh boot and a run from S1 then start from the same KVM state by construction.
With one vCPU the machine goes on in its VM, as before, so no one-vCPU value can move. After each
load with several vCPUs the engine reads every vCPU back and prints the parts that differ from
the state loaded (`hydo-kvm: vCPU <i> read back after a load differs at exit <n>: ...`, at most
16 lines per process), so the next run names the part. A scripted test,
`two_vcpus_a_run_from_s1_equals_a_fresh_boot_when_a_load_changes_the_state`, gives the scripted
vCPU a load that changes DR6. Without the fix it fails, with the fix it passes. The six scripted
one-vCPU pins pass. On AMD the S1 checks passed before the fix, so a load there gives the state
back; the next run checks that the AMD several-vCPU values did not move. The fix has not run on
an Intel host yet.

**Left.**

- A runner run of the fix on several hosts, Intel among them: `smp-check.sh`, `turns-check.sh`
  and `kvm-check.sh` (a branch `tmp-kvm-s1` is ready).
- `hydo repro` of one run's folder and `hydo explain` with `--vcpus` on KVM; `bzImage-kvm-smp`
  in the Linux release.

**The proof run of the S1 fix.** Run 43535344097 on eight hosts (five Intel: Xeon 6975P-C and Xeon Platinum 8573C; three AMD: EPYC 9V74 and 7763): smp-check 13 of 13, turns-check 7 of 7 and kvm-check 15 of 15 on every host. The engine's read-back lines appear on Intel only and name one kind of field: the hidden attributes of unusable null segments (DS, FS), which Intel's VMX normalises when a state is loaded and the guest never reads. Since the snapshotting machine goes on in a VM loaded from the snapshot, a run from S1 and a fresh boot start from the same state on both vendors.

### The 0.3.2 release — published (2026-11-14)

The lead's task of 2026-11-14: release 0.3.2 with what `main` has since 0.3.1 (Milestones
210–227), cut from `main` at `b9bd4bc1`. The user decided the version: 0.3.2, not 0.4.0, because
plans pin `hydo_version: "0.3"`. Branch `worktree-agent-a2aca51c06d6b3b72`; the lead did every public step.

**The version** (`ffde09ef`). As at 0.3.1: `hydo/VERSION`, the workspace version and every
`hydo-*` entry of `[workspace.dependencies]` (not `hydo-agent-proto`), both release scripts'
default, the four SDKs and the unpublished Rust test SDK, the examples' lock files of
`hydo-assert`, README.md, docs/INSTALL.md, docs/LIMITS.md, hydo/PRODUCT.md, both quickstarts, the
CI action's and the GitLab template's examples, the guide's `ci` and `capabilities` topics,
MANIFEST.md and docs/PUBLISHING.md's commands. The guest programs that carry the version were
re-pinned, built on this Mac: `hydo-world` x86_64 `f896bea4…`, arm64 `2b1b7bd0…`;
`hydo-world-tls` `a9f4c277…`, `0ae4f3b7…`; `hydo-grpc` `21db8ce0…`, arm64 `83004951…`. The Linux
release builds the x86_64 ones on the bare-metal machine, and they matched the pins.
