### Milestone 284 (tentative number) - DONE (web apps on the Mac engine: `browser:` and `browser.explore` run on an Apple Silicon Mac; the root file system of such an image is a read-only ext4 file system on its disk, `guest.root: disk`, an opt-in format-1 key that is the default with `browser:`, which `hydo build` makes in a helper VM of the Mac engine; the guest kernel did not change, and no run ended in `SPIN`; web-shop's flaky test fails on every run of its schedule, the walk found both planted bugs blind in 20 seeds, and a Memos walk and its recording replay gave hvx's verdicts; each schedule gave one fingerprint over two runs; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**Why.** Most web developers work on a Mac, and `browser:` (Milestones 253 and 254) and the walk
through the pages (Milestones 258 to 273) ran only on hvx and KVM. Open item 51 named the cause:
the Mac engine boots an arm64 image whose whole root is the initramfs, which the guest kernel
unpacks into guest RAM, and the Playwright image is 2.4 GB of files.

**The choice: a key, not an epoch.** The root on the disk could have come with the fingerprint
epoch 4, for every arm64 image. That would move every recorded Mac value and give the lead a
re-recording pass for no gain, because a root of a few MB fits in RAM well. A key keeps every
image built before as it was. `guest.root: memory | disk` (a format-1 addition: the schema's
`RootPlace`, `hydo_manifest::validate::ROOT_PLACES`) decides; without it the root is on the disk
for an image with `browser:` and in memory for every other image. No Mac image with `browser:`
existed before, so no recorded value moves, and open item 105 gets no line. The x86_64 engines
ignore the key: their root was always on the disk.

**The build** (`hydo/crates/hydo-build/src/arm64.rs` `disk_root`, `image.rs` `mac_mkfs_root`,
`cpio.rs` `write_cpio_file`).

- The root tree is staged as before. hydo-build writes it as one newc cpio archive, not
  compressed and written as it is made, with the same entries and owners as the initramfs would
  have. The archive of web-shop is 2,546,840,484 bytes.
- The new initramfs holds busybox, an `/init` script, and copies of `/etc/hydo`,
  `/bin/busybox` and a SQL helper's configuration, the files that the host reads from an image
  (`hydo_engine::image::embedded_file`). `/init` mounts `/dev/vda1` read-only with `noatime`,
  moves `/dev` into it, and runs `switch_root /root /init`, so the agent is PID 1 on the root as
  before. web-shop's initramfs is 830,910 bytes.
- The root file system is made in a helper VM of the Mac engine (`hydo-hvm hvm run`), as the
  data disk already was. The helper's disk has two partitions: the new file system and the
  archive. The helper runs the release's mke2fs with the root options of a Linux build (no
  journal), mounts it, unpacks the archive with busybox `cpio -i -d -m -u` as root, and unmounts
  it. The new engine option `HVM_DISK_OUT_BYTES` writes back only the first partition. The
  tree, the archive and the helper's disk are removed as soon as each is no longer needed; the
  build of Memos needed 7 GB of free disk at its peak.
- The root's size is `root.size_mib`, else 1.3 times the archive in steps of 64 MiB: 3,200 MiB
  for web-shop. The disk is then the root in p1 and the data file system in p2, as on x86_64.
- A build of web-shop's walk image took 156 s on this Mac, about 60 s of it in the helper VM.
  On Linux, which has no Mac engine, hydo-build refuses `guest.root: disk` for an arm64 image.

**The guest.** Nothing in the guest kernel, the agent or the engine's run code changed. The image
boots `Image-explore-netns-cg`, the kernel of every arm64 image with `network: bridge`.
Playwright's runner, Chromium's headless shell and the config's web server ran at once; Playwright
starts Chromium without its sandbox, so no namespace or seccomp option was needed. A disk fault
can now hit a read of the root, as on the x86_64 engines.

**Loops without VM exits.** No run of this milestone ended in `SPIN`, also in the exploration's
104 runs. Chromium's and Node.js's waits are system calls, which make exits.

**The pin.** The arm64 Playwright image that the catalog pinned in Milestone 253 is
`sha256:56be08aca06bf736a928da2e3235a3b63ef71ee97313beb18c6019fea791aba4` (config
`sha256:9136e3eed8fc…`, 7 layers, 35,741 entries; the docker-save archive is 988,750,336 bytes).
hydo-build leaves out the same two systemd names with a backslash as on amd64. playwright-core
1.65.1 and `walk.mjs` are JavaScript, so the walk needed no change.

**The runs.** This milestone's programs over the 0.3.4 Mac release on an M2 Pro, one VM at a
time. The runs of the table and the exploration used images of the fingerprint epoch 3, built on
`main` at `7944ad08` with `--set variant=buggy` for web-shop:

| image | schedule | verdict | fingerprint | runs | wall time per run |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| web-shop `hydo.yaml` (`a70204c1…`) | `disk=none \| run` | OK, 3 tests passed, 6 invariants held | `e49b289c2d4f34b7` | 2 | 56 s, 50 s |
| web-shop `hydo.yaml` | `disk=none \| run H=api.add_item@1-2:delay=1000` | VIOLATION `browser.tests_pass`: Expected "2", Received "0" | `15e26130aad215fd` | 2 | 49 s, 48 s |
| web-shop `hydo-walk.yaml` (`9d2d78ca…`) | `disk=none \| run I=2` | OK, 5 invariants held | `b76ad58b5c0ae26b` | 2 | 56 s, 44 s |
| Memos (`887b86b8…`) | `disk=none \| run I=1` | OK: all 5 saved memos are in the database | `70dc50842f43b01b` | 2 | 69 s, 70 s |
| Memos | `disk=none \| run I=1,rec` | OK, with the video of step 5 (276,792 bytes) and its trace | `3efb64050c17ce3d` | 2 | 144 s, 136 s |
| Redis with `guest.root: disk` (`cef7cb4e…`) | `disk=none \| run` | OK, 20 writes acknowledged | `83d00ced9410093e` | 1 | 2 s |
| the same | `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | VIOLATION, `key k:1 lost` | `d10e597424bf4a9c` | 2 | 2 s |
| Redis, the release's example (root in memory, `9ddfc929…`) | `disk=none \| run` | OK | `a62eee5332a5b9d2` | 1 | 3 s |
| the same | `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | VIOLATION, `key k:0 lost` | `474b2874e7ef0fa2` | 2 | 3 s |

On hvx the same schedules took 48 s to 10 minutes on the shared bare-metal machine, and the walk
`I=2` took 65 s (the web-shop example's RESULTS.md). The verdicts are hvx's. The fingerprints are
the Mac engine's own.

**At the fingerprint epoch 4.** After the rebase onto `main` at `64950f8f` (Milestones 269 and
283, the epoch 4), the web-shop images were built again and gave their verdicts with one

## Milestone 288 (tentative number): a second evaluation of `hydo fuzz` by a new user

A fresh evaluator, a coding agent that played a Rust developer new to hydo, tried `hydo fuzz` on
six popular crates before the 0.4.0 release. The evaluator learned the tool only from `hydo guide
fuzz`, `hydo fuzz --help` and `hydo guide manifest`, and did not read the first evaluation (M280)
or the design notes. The binary came from `main` at `0038380d`. The page is
`docs/design/function-fuzzing-evaluation-2.md`.

The crates were strsim 0.11.1, hex 0.4.3, httparse 1.10.1, bytes 1.12.1, num-traits 0.2.19 and
chrono 0.4.45. The evaluator wrote 26 contracts on library functions, of which hydo fuzzed 24, and
37 property functions in the crates' test modules. Each crate's first useful run came 2 to 4
minutes after its copy, and each build and run took 1 to 15 seconds.

The candidates, none posted and none checked against the issue trackers:

- strsim's `sorensen_dice` divides by byte lengths: `sorensen_dice("ab", "aba")` is `0.666...`,
  and `sorensen_dice("éü", "éüé")` is `0.25`.
- httparse's `parse_chunk_size` accepts a chunk size line without a hex digit as size 0:
  `b"\r\n"` gives `Ok(Complete((2, 0)))`. RFC 9112 requires at least one digit.
- num-traits' `abs_sub(1i64, -9223372036854775807)` panics in a debug build and returns
  `-9223372036854775808` in a release build. Its documentation calls the result the positive
  difference.

Two smaller gaps: num-traits' `abs(i32::MIN)` panics in a debug build although its documentation
says that it returns `MIN`, and hex's `decode("é")` names the character `'Ã'`, which is not in the
input.

The worst problems, in order:

1. A clause on an `f64` result was decided on 0 of 1,000 calls, and the function still counted as
   `held` with exit status 0.
2. The harness fails on `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and the package copy loses the `[lints]` table
   of `Cargo.toml`. In httparse the second failure came with a message that blamed the crate.
3. Methods of types that hold pointers, trait methods and enumeration results are refused or not
   read, so in bytes and httparse every test was a hand-written property function.
4. `like` is for strings only, so a parser over bytes needs a wrapper that takes `&str`.
5. A run shows only counts, never the inputs it generated.

Open item 139 points to the page. Nothing recorded moved.

## Milestone 289 (tentative number): the blockers of `hydo fuzz` from the second evaluation

Milestone 288's evaluation found that `hydo fuzz` passed a clause it could not read, and that its
harness failed on ordinary crates. This milestone fixes both before the 0.4.0 release, in the
crate `hydo-contracts` (the module `fuzz`). The page `docs/design/function-fuzzing-evaluation-2.md`
has a section "After the fixes of M289" with the runs before and after.

**Verdicts that never pass an unread clause.**

- `f32` and `f64` values are a type of their own (`FTy::Float`). The harness writes a result's
  bits, and a clause compares it. A comparison of an integer with such a value is exact, so
  `9007199254740992.0 < 9007199254740993` holds. Arithmetic is `f64` arithmetic, and a NaN is
  unequal to everything. Floating-point parameters are generated too: edges, small fractions,
  values of an `in` range, and any bits.
- A clause that hydo decided on fewer than `--min-reach` calls is `not judged`, with the first
  reason, a `to fix:` line, and exit status 3. Before, such a clause was `held` whenever it had
  one part.
- A clause `a || ... || z` whose `z` decided too few calls, in a run where calls panicked, is
  `not reached`. The calls that panicked may be the ones that reach `z`, so the verdict is the
  panic, and no `to fix:` line asks for other inputs.

**A harness that builds on common crates.**

- The test module's `allow` list leaves out every lint that a source of the crate forbids, and
  names `unsafe_code` only for an `unsafe` function.
- The copy's `Cargo.toml` keeps the package's `[lints]` tables, or the workspace's with
  `workspace = true`. `cargo metadata` does not give them.
- Each contracted function that the run does not build a harness for gets a one-line module that
  names it (`harness::keep`). A property function that only hydo calls then stays in use when
  `--fn` names another function, so a crate that denies warnings in its tests still builds.
- When the copy does not build without any harness, hydo builds the crate with its own
  `Cargo.toml` and the same sources: in a plain copy for a package of its own, or in place with
  `--locked` for a workspace member. If that builds, the message says that hydo's copy is the
  cause, with the first error and a hint.

**Skipped functions.** A contracted function that was refused, or whose harness did not build,
makes the exit status 3 when nothing broke. The summary says so. `--allow-skipped` keeps the
status of the functions that ran.

**Bytes and the inputs.** `input buf like b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n"` gives examples for `&[u8]` and
`Vec<u8>`, and text examples give their bytes. A list of bytes shows as a byte string, and
`--input` reads one. `--show-inputs N` prints N of each function's inputs, spread over the run,
and keeps them in `fuzz.json` as `samples`.

**Evidence.** Seed 1 and 1,000 inputs on copies of the evaluation's crates, with strsim's
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` and httparse's `#![cfg_attr(test, deny(warnings))]` put back:

| Run | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| strsim `jaro`, `ensures result <= 1` | harness error E0453, exit 2 (0 of 1,000 decided with `deny`) | held on 1,000 calls, exit 0 |
| strsim `jaro`, `ensures result < 1` | (not run) | broken on 15 calls, shrunk to `a = "", b = ""` with `result = 1.0` |
| strsim, 13 functions | none built, exit 2 | 12 held, 1 broken, exit 1 |
| httparse, 5 functions | `the crate does not build in the test profile without hydo's harness`, exit 2 | 4 held, 1 broken (`text = "\r\n"`), exit 1 |
| httparse, a property over `&[u8]` with `like b"..."` | (not possible) | broken on 25 calls at `buf = b"\r\n"` |
| num-traits `abs` | clause `vacuous`, advice to change the inputs | clause `not reached`, no advice; broken by the panic |
| bytes, 6 functions and 2 refused | exit 0 | exit 3, with a line that names the 2 |

The new fixture `hydo/crates/hydo-contracts/tests/fuzz-m289` has each case: it forbids
`unsafe_code`, denies warnings with a `cfg` from its `[lints]` table, and holds `f64` results and
a parameter, an enumeration result, `abs32`, a byte parser and a trait method. The test
`fuzz::a_crate_that_forbids_unsafe_code_fuzzes_with_floats_bytes_and_honest_verdicts` checks the
verdicts and the exit statuses. Four unit tests check the floating-point wire form and
comparisons, the allow list, the kept lints, and the byte examples. Nothing recorded moved.

**Left** (open item 139): trait methods, methods of types that hold pointers, and enumeration
results are still refused or not read. A workspace member without a lock file cannot be built
apart.

### Milestone 291 (tentative number) - DONE (value properties: a `// hydo: keep` line says what must hold for a recorded value along each key's history, and a run that breaks it fails with a finding of the kind `values` whose verdict names the line, not the key; the history up to the break, with the first changing call, is in the finding, `hydo report`, `hydo report --html` and `hydo inspect values --broken`; on Blnk the run without faults, where every business rule held, now fails; the fixed build holds; one fingerprint with and without the plan; the explorer finds and shrinks the finding; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**In short.** Milestone 285 recorded values and showed their changes, but no rule judged a change,
so a person read the history only after another check had failed. A `keep` line makes the history
a property that a run can break:

```go
// hydo: keep overdraft_limit from blnk.setTransactionMetadata to model.canProcessTransaction
```

The grammar is `keep <name> [once set] [from <function>] [to <function>] [across boots]`. A
stop of `to` (every stop without it) that recorded the value is judged against a reference stop
of the same key. Without `once set` the values must be equal, and the reference is the last
earlier stop of `from` (the key's first stop without `from`). With `once set` a value once present
must not be absent or nil later. The reference is in the same boot unless the line says `across
boots`. `docs/design/value-history.md`, "Value properties", has the decisions, and section 4 of
`hydo guide values` the how-to.

**Why a comment line.** The other way was a `values:` block in `hydo.yaml`. A property names the
`as` names of `record` lines and the functions that have them, so it lives in the same sources,
and the plan's compiler checks both names: a property whose value no `record` line records, or
whose function records no such value or is ambiguous, is listed by `hydo build` as not checked.
The line can stand next to any recording function, and `from` and `to` make it read the same
anywhere.

**The parts.**

- The language (`hydo-contracts`, `lang.rs`): `SrcKeep` and `SrcContract.keeps`. A function with
  only `keep` lines gets no breakpoint.
- The plan (`plan.rs`): `Program.keeps` (`Keep`: the line, its file and line, the name, `once_set`,
  `from` and `to` as full names in the debug information, `across_boots`), skipped when empty, so
  every plan of before reads and writes as it did. `compile.rs` resolves a short name such as
  `blnk.setTransactionMetadata` by its end after `/`, `.` or `::`. The engines do not read it.
- The judge (`values.rs`): `judge_keeps` over the histories gives, per property, the keys and
  stops judged and each key's first break: the judged stop, its reference, and the first stop
  after the reference whose value broke the property (the first changing call). `break_lines`
  writes the key's history up to the break with the three stops marked.
- The run (`hydo-explore`, `contracts.rs`): `fold` judges the properties with the contracts, from
  the same records, in `hydo run` and in every explorer run. A broken property is a finding of the
  kind `values` (`hydo_results::kind::VALUES`), with `details.output` the history up to the break,
  and it turns an `OK` verdict into `VIOLATION [values <the line>] the value changed` (or `the
  value was absent after it was set`). The verdict has no key and no value, so the shrinker keeps
  one signature across keys and values; the test `value_properties::` checks that two runs that
  break at other keys give one signature. `hydo run` prints a line per property, held or broken,
  with the history of the first broken key.
- The advice (`advice.rs`): `is_values`; the title "<system> broke a value property you
  declared", and a why and a what-to-do that point at the history. The class stays the class of
  the schedule's faults, as for every check.
- The view: `hydo inspect values --broken` (only keys that broke a line); the text view prints
  each property's count and a `BROKEN:` line per broken key. The results type `values` gains
  `ValueHistory.properties` (`ValueProperty`) and `ValueKey.breaks` (`ValueBreak`), additions
  that hydo-schema-compat accepts. `hydo report` and its web page show the broken property in
  "What hydo saw" with the history, and the web page's section "How the recorded values changed"
  starts with each property, held or broken, and the first broken key's table up to the break.
- `hydo build` prints `1 value property` beside the recorded values.

**The proof on Blnk.** `values.patch` has the line in place of a blank comment line next to
`canProcessTransaction`, so the line numbers and the program's bytes stay (`blnk-values-arm64`
`e6f51ac3…`, `blnk-fixed-values-arm64` `e21aa543…`, as Milestone 285 built them). All runs used the
Mac engine with this tree's hydo and engine over the 0.3.4 Mac release's guest files, at the
fingerprint epoch 4, on `explore-ob-blnk-values-arm64.cpio.gz` (`62d83259…`, the image of
Milestone 285's last row) and its build with the fixes (`7580be81…`):

| image, schedule | with the plan | without it | the rules | the value property |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| buggy, `overdraft-limit-concurrent-draws` | `ddb6f1730f6854ea` twice | `ddb6f1730f6854ea` twice | `VIOLATION [no_overdraft]` | broken for 2 of 22 keys (`c27`, `c29`), 24 stops judged |
| buggy, `disk=none \| run` | `f52b32d3577045db` twice | `f52b32d3577045db` twice | OK; the verdict is `VIOLATION [values ...]` | broken for 3 of 66 keys (`c33`, `c54`, `c57`), 77 stops judged |
| fixed, `overdraft-limit-concurrent-draws` | `0d634838208d69f3` | `0d634838208d69f3` | OK | held, 25 stops of 22 keys |
| fixed, `disk=none \| run` | `498a8cf0e45aa1d7` | not run | OK | held, 81 stops of 66 keys |

The two runs with the plan of each buggy schedule wrote the same records (`eaf3d5fb…`, as in
Milestone 285, and `d59ee3d0…`). Each break names the first changing call: the worker's coalesced
copy (`createQueueCopy` called from `buildQueuedCoalescingBatchForScope`) has the limit 0.0, and
the decision then sees 0.0 for the queue copy. The engine's time with the plan was 5.9 s and 5.6 s
on the regression and 5.7 s and 5.8 s without it; 6.4 s and 7.3 s on the clean run, 6.5 s and 7.1
s without it.

**The exploration.** `hydo explore --strategy random --workers 2` of the buggy build on the Mac
engine (2 x 1,536 MiB of guest RAM): seeds 1 to 10 with shrinking (1,858 s), and seeds 11 to 30
with `--no-shrink --no-diagnose` (240 s). The property broke in 9 of the 30 schedules (seeds 4,
13, 15, 16, 18, 21, 25, 26, 30); the overdraft rule `no_overdraft` broke in 1 (seed 21, where the
property broke too). So the property found finding 1 first at seed 4, and the rule at seed 21.
Seed 4's failure, class `durable-defaults`, shrank in 89 runs to a schedule without a fault and
with only the draw and repay commands (`disk=none dseed=6e73e372e2338aca | run
W=:p1,r200,cparallel_driver_repay+parallel_driver_draw,...`), whose two confirmations gave
`87887f2853ae545c` twice; `report.md` shows its key's history up to the break. The schedules with
a power cut compared stops within each boot; seeds 18 and 26 broke the property in the first
boot.

**Tests and checks.** New: `hydo-contracts`'s `keeps::` (the lines and their errors, a property
from one function to another with its first changing call, `across boots`, a plain `keep`, `once
set`, the names the compiler refuses) and `hydo-explore`'s `value_properties::` (the finding, the
verdict and its signature, the advice, a held property). Two results examples recorded from the
clean run: `mac-blnk-run-values-violation/result.json` (a run with a `values` finding) and
`mac-blnk-values-broken/values.json`; `examples::` now asks for a `values` finding. `ci/test-tiers.txt`
lists the two new test files as fast. On this Mac, after the rebase onto `origin/main`: `cargo fmt --all --check`, workspace clippy with `-D
warnings`, `cargo test -p hydo-contracts`, `-p hydo-results` and `-p hydo-config`, `hydo`'s
`equivalence::cli_matches_golden`, `agents_equivalence` and `docs::`, `hydo-agents`'s
`public_content::`, `hydo-schedule`'s `language::`, `hydo-release`'s `test_tiers`,
`hydo-explore`'s `--test it` and `--test fake_engine`, `hydo-schema-compat`, `sh
ci/consolidate-tests.sh --check` and `sh ci/vale.sh`. Nothing recorded moved: a plan without
`keep` lines is the plan it was, the engines did not change, and the Blnk programs kept their
bytes.

**Left** (open item 146): a property over two names (the limit against its metadata entry), a
comparison with a constant and an order of calls are not built; the property table and `hydo
rules check` do not know the lines; `across boots` ran on synthetic records only; and an
exploration's plain problem text does not quote the history (its `report.md` and a run's report
do).

### Milestone 290 (tentative number) - DONE (a cheaper fingerprint on the Mac and KVM engines, part of the fingerprint epoch 4: the disk's part of a fingerprint is a tree of block hashes, so a fingerprint hashes again only the blocks the run wrote; the base's block hashes are made once per process on a thread of their own while the guest runs; an image of the epochs 1 to 3 keeps the byte-wise hash and its values; web-shop's `disk=none | run` takes 7.6 to 8.2 s in the engine instead of 42 to 55 s; every epoch-4 Mac and KVM fingerprint moves and waits for the pass before 0.4.0; 2026-11-17)

**Why.** Open item 145: the Mac engine hashed every byte of the guest's disk with byte-wise
FNV-1a for each fingerprint, and a run takes two (the workload's `wfp` and the run's `fp`). The
KVM engine uses the same devices (`hydo_hvm::virtio`), so it paid the same. Milestone 284
estimated 10 s of web-shop's 45 s run for its 3.4 GB disk. In a real run it was more, because the
disk's pages are not in the page cache at the run's end: an engine built for the measurement
printed 12.0 s and 13.3 s for the devices' part of the two fingerprints of one web-shop run, of
33.4 s in the engine.

**The scheme** (`hydo/crates/hydo-hvm/src/disk.rs`, `Disk::tree_hash`).

- A leaf is a 4 KiB block of the copy-on-write disk, the block that the engine already keeps per
  write. Its hash is the word-wise mix of the RAM hash (`mix64`) over the block's bytes.
- A node is a 2 MiB chunk of the disk table (512 blocks). Its hash folds its blocks' hashes in
  order with `h ^= w; h *= P; h ^= h >> 29`.
- The root continues the devices' hash with the text `hydo-disk-tree-v1`, the disk's length, and
  the chunks' hashes in order.
- The base's block and chunk hashes (8 bytes per 4 KiB, 6.5 MB for web-shop's disk) are made once
  per disk base and shared by every copy of the disk: snapshots, the durable disk of a power cut,
  reboots. The engine starts them on a thread of its own, on half of the cores, when it opens the
  disk (`Disk::hash_base_soon`). A fingerprint that comes first waits for them.
- At a fingerprint, a chunk that the run did not write gives the base's chunk hash. In a chunk it
  wrote, each written block is hashed again from its bytes, and the other blocks give the base's
  hashes.

The root is a function of the disk's bytes alone. A block written back to its old bytes gives
the base's hash again (a unit test). Each step is a bijection of the state when the other inputs
are fixed, so a change of any one byte always changes the root. Added disks (`guest.disks`) use
the same tree; their base is all zeros, so its hashes come from one block's hash. The state of
the devices, the write cache, and RAM are hashed as before.

**Why no cache file.** The base's hashes could be written beside the image by `hydo build`, or
kept in a cache by the image's digest. A cache must be checked against the disk's bytes, and that
check reads the whole disk, which costs what making the hashes costs. So the engine makes them in
memory and keeps no file, and no stale cache can exist. A worker of `hydo explore` makes them
once for all its runs.

**The block size, measured.** On this M2 Pro (12 cores), over web-shop's disk
(3,423,600,640 bytes) in the page cache:

| what | time |
|---|---|
| the byte-wise FNV-1a of every byte (epoch 3) | 4.30 s |
| the word-wise mix of every byte on one core | 0.80 s |
| the base's leaf hashes on 12 threads, leaves of 4, 16, 64 and 256 KiB | 120, 122, 104 and 110 ms |
| the root with nothing written | 17 µs |
| the root with 256, 2,560, 25,600 and 102,400 written blocks | 0.55, 3.8, 39 and 132 ms |

The leaf size does not change the base's time. A leaf of the table's block size hashes only the
written bytes again and needs no read of the base, so the leaf is 4 KiB.

**The epoch.** `hydo_image::EpochDefaults` gains `disk_tree`, on from epoch 4. The epoch stays 4:
the change joins Milestones 269 and 283 before 0.4.0. The engines read it from the image's epoch:

- The Mac engine's `Start` and the KVM engine's `Start` take `image_epoch` (in process, the
  image's epoch). The program `hydo-hvm` takes `--image-epoch N`, as `hydo-kvm` did.
- `BootSpec::engine_args` names `--image-epoch N` for both programs for every image before this
  hydo's epoch. Before, it named it to `hydo-kvm` for epoch 1 only. So the program `hydo-kvm` now
  also runs an epoch-2 image with DR6's host bits (Milestone 252), as the in-process engine did.
- The boot probes of `hydo-hvm hvm` (the helper VM of `hydo build`) keep the byte-wise hash.

hvx is not changed: its disk is in the kernel module, and the module computes its fingerprint.

**The runs on this Mac.** The base commit's programs (`74430ea2`, "before") and this milestone's
("after"), each over the 0.3.4 Mac release, one VM at a time, on web-shop's epoch-4 image built
with `--set variant=buggy` (disk `bc0ad90a…`, the disk of Milestone 284):

| programs | schedule | fingerprint | engine time | wall time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | `disk=none \| run` | `7da8112398ae9137` | 42.4, 54.7, 47.4 s | 52.4, 63.6, 54.3 s |
| after | `disk=none \| run` | `a6eef3eadef684d5` | 7.6, 8.0 s | 15.6, 15.5 s |
| before | `disk=none \| run H=api.add_item@1-2:delay=1000` | `24c270f6f56a9d85` | 29.1 s | 36.1 s |
| after | the same | `d72c2ed52f8a8630` | 7.7, 14.7 s | 14.7, 23.5 s |

The verdicts are the same: OK with 6 invariants held, and the delay's VIOLATION
`browser.tests_pass`. The before values are Milestone 284's epoch-4 values. The second delay run
ran beside a build of the workspace. The engine built for
the measurement printed each fingerprint's parts:

- with the byte-wise hash (forced in that engine): the devices 12.0 s and 13.3 s, RAM 1.0 s and
  1.0 s, and the before fingerprint `7da8112398ae9137`;
- with the tree hash made at the first fingerprint: the devices 3.56 s and 31 µs;
- with the tree hash made while the guest runs (this milestone): the devices 77 µs and 23 µs,
  and 218 µs and 23 µs, with one written block of the disk.

The run's own fingerprints now cost about 1 s each, all of it the hash of web-shop's 4 GiB of
guest RAM.

**Old images keep their values.** The release's Redis example built by the 0.3.4 Mac release
(fingerprint epoch 3, `706c8b95…` and its disk `9ddfc929…`, the quickstart's bytes) gave the

## Milestone 292 (tentative number): function fuzzing inside the VM, under faults

`hydo fuzz` tested a function natively, where no power cut, disk error or clock step can meet a
call. This milestone makes the calls inside hydo's VM under such faults, for Rust, and judges
whether a Rust developer would keep it. The design and the evaluation are the section "Inside
the virtual machine" of `docs/design/function-fuzzing.md`. The user's reference is the section
"Fuzz under faults, inside the VM" of `hydo guide fuzz`.

**What a user writes and runs.** The same `// hydo:` contract, and for a function that writes
files one more line, `// hydo: durable <check>`. The check is a property function of the crate:
it takes the function's parameters and then the call's result as an `Option`, and returns
`bool` or `Option<bool>`. Then:

```sh
hydo fuzz --vm path/to/crate
```

**How it works** (the module `fuzz::vm` of `hydo-contracts`; `hydo-cli` routes `--vm` to it):

- The copy's test program is built for `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` (or
  `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` on the Mac), statically linked, by the native build with
  `CARGO_BUILD_TARGET` and the target's `RUSTFLAGS`.
- hydo writes a project. `cases/<step>/calls` holds `--batch` inputs per workload step. `run.sh`
  is the workload: one process per call, each in its own folder `/data/fuzz/<step>.<call>`.
  `dirs.sh` is the provisioning that makes the folders and syncs, and `check.sh` is the one
  invariant. `hydo build` makes the image, and `hydo run` runs it under each schedule.
- The schedules: the first without a fault, then a power cut (`disk=cut` with `C=` or `cf=`),
  disk errors, a clock step, and a pause of the calls, in turn, from the seed.
- A call's answer is an id `<step>.<call>=<answer>` in `$HYDO_ACKED`, which the run reports at
  its end and at a power cut and carries into the recovery boot. The check runs there for each
  call that started, with `Some(result)` or `None`.
- A failure shrinks alone in an image of one step under the schedule moved to that step
  (`one_step_schedule`), `--batch` candidates per run. The report names the image and the
  schedule that replay it, and runs the replay once more to compare its fingerprint.

The contract language gains the line `durable <function>` (`lang::SrcContract::durable`). The
native `hydo fuzz` leaves the checks out of its functions and names them in `--list`
(`fuzz::split_checks`).

**The target.** `hydo/onboard/examples/fuzz-vm` holds three functions of one crate:

- `commit_all`: redb 4.6.0 transactions with its default durability;
- `save`: a save by rename with tempfile 3.27.0 and no sync;
- `save_synced`: the same save with the two syncs.

 redb is a
popular embedded key-value store whose commits promise durability. The save by rename is a
common way to write a file, and its durability depends on syncs that the code must make.

**Evidence.** On the bare-metal machine's hvx, every VM through `~/bin/hvx-run`, 200 inputs per
function (600 calls in 24 steps) and 24 schedules per seed:

| Function | Seed 1 | Seed 2 |
|---|---|---|
| `commit_all` | held: 4,465 checks, 1,465 of them after a power cut | held: 4,569 checks, 1,169 of them after a power cut |
| `save` | broken on 750 calls in 4 runs, first under `disk=cut \| run C=14`; shrunk to `text = ""` | broken on 750 calls in 4 runs, first under `disk=cut \| run C=14`; shrunk to `text = ""` |
| `save_synced` | held: 3,675 checks, 675 of them after a power cut | held: 3,905 checks, 505 of them after a power cut |

Five `cf=` cuts came in the middle of a call: four in a commit of `commit_all` (`cf=692` and
`cf=236` of seed 1, `cf=1505` and `cf=913` of seed 2), and one in `save_synced` (`cf=3748`). Each
check of the call that did not return found the database's transactions whole and in order, and
the file whole or absent. Each seed took 452 seconds. This time includes the shrink and the replay. The replay of
`save`'s smallest input gave its fingerprint again in both seeds (`dd2260cccca16aa8` and
`11464c875d1a0163`).

Natively, `hydo fuzz` held every clause of the three functions on 200 inputs.

**What the first runs taught.** Four things got in the way of real findings:

- The hvx module keeps the first 64 KiB of a VM's console. Answers on the console were lost in
  a run with disk errors, whose answers held error messages. The answers moved to
  `$HYDO_ACKED`.
- A recovery boot with about 90 KiB of carried ids logged `HVX_HC_PUT: No space left on
  device` in a loop and did not start (open item 120). An answer longer than 64 bytes goes to
  the console instead, at most 32 KiB per boot, and its check gets `None`.
- Two checks of the example were wrong. One dropped redb's database before its read. The other
  counted an `EIO` after ext4 aborted its journal as a lost commit. Both failed under the
  schedule without a fault or alone. The report now says so.
- hydo's `check.sh` compared the call ids with awk as numbers, which made some of them equal.
  Nine checks got another call's result. The script compares them as text now.

**The verdict.** A Rust developer would keep `hydo fuzz --vm` for functions that write files and
promise durability or atomicity. The first report came about one minute after the command.
It found the missing sync that native fuzzing cannot find. The finding came with a small input
and a replay. It is not yet worth it for time or concurrency. Faults meet a call only at a power
cut or a disk flush, and each call is one process on one vCPU.

**Tests.** `fuzz::vm`'s unit tests check the schedules' draw and `one_step_schedule`, and
`lang::a_durable_line_names_the_check_of_the_recovery_boot` checks the new line. Nothing
recorded moved: no engine, controller, or guest program changed.

**Left.** Open item 139 lists these parts:

- The Mac engine and KVM did not run it.
- A kill has no target, and clock steps and pauses meet a call only between steps.
- `cf=` failures are not shrunk, and the channels of the answers on hvx are small.
- A hung `hydo run` stops the fuzzing.
- Native `hydo fuzz` of a function that writes files runs every call in the current folder.

## Milestone 300 (tentative number): the use cases page

**Why.** The user asked for one place that lists every use case hydo serves or could serve, so
that the capabilities and the ideas can be gone over later and none is forgotten. The user also
shared a chart that sorts the testing techniques into four stages: before production, at deploy,
at release, and after release.

**The page.** `docs/USE-CASES.md`, a reference. It has five parts:

- An opening that defines the three status words: `built` (in `main`, with a proof run),
  `partly built` (built, with gaps that an open item or a milestone names), and `idea` (not
  built). A row that needs production traffic or real users says "not hydo's job", with the
  reason.
- The map against the chart. Each of the chart's 42 techniques has one row with what hydo has
  (the command or key), its status, and its evidence (an example or a milestone). Fourteen rows
  are not hydo's job, for example formal verification, lint, canary releases, and A/B tests.
- The use cases by who asks, in seven sections: a backend team with a database or a queue, a
  team with a web app, a library author in Rust, an embedded or device team, a team that adopts
  hydo in CI, a maintainer who receives a bug report, and someone who evaluates an upgrade or a
  dependency bump. Each section is a table of the team's questions, hydo's answer today with its
  command, and the status, followed by the ideas that would answer more.
- The ideas: 33 entries, each with what it is, why it matters, what it would need, and where it
  came from. They come from the user's brief (differential testing between versions and
  configuration as an explored dimension, both being built as Milestones 298 and 299; soak tests
  with exact resource counts; a check that an error path is reached under faults), the open items
  (13, 49, 56, 67, 68, 77, 109, 110, 113, 114, 116, 117, 119, 122, 125, 128, 131, 136, 139, 140,
  141, 142, 144, and 146), and the design pages (`ci.md`, `contracts.md`, `cost-tracking.md`,
  `explain.md`, `inspect.md`, `jepsen-gaps.md`, `messaging.md`, `value-history.md`, and
  `agent-environments.md`).
- How to keep it current.

Where a source did not say that a capability had a proof run on an engine, the row says
`partly built` and names the gap. Code coverage is one example: Intel Processor Trace exists on
hvx only, through `HVX_EXPLORE_PT_ELF`, and no guide topic describes it for users.

**The rule.** `AGENTS.md` "How to record new work" gains step 4: every milestone updates the rows
of `docs/USE-CASES.md` for each capability that it builds or changes.

**The wiring.** `ci/vale.sh` checks the page (64 documents now; the count in `AGENTS.md` said 60
and is corrected). `README.md` "Learn more" and the `docs/` row of `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` link it,
and `AGENTS.md` "Where to look" points to it.

--test it public_content::`, and `cargo test -p hydo-release --test it test_tiers`. Nothing

### Milestone 294 (tentative number) - DONE (a cheaper RAM part of the fingerprint on the Mac and KVM engines, part of the fingerprint epoch 4: guest RAM is hashed by a tree of 4 KiB page hashes on half of the cores, with a leaf mix of eight independent lanes; the KVM engine takes the hashes of the pages the guest did not write since its RAM base from the base; on the Mac write tracking by stage-2 faults was measured and not taken; a fingerprint of web-shop's 4 GiB of RAM takes about 43 ms instead of about 1 s, and its `disk=none | run` takes 5.7 to 5.9 s in the engine instead of 7.6 to 8.2 s; an image of the epochs 1 to 3 keeps its values; every epoch-4 Mac and KVM fingerprint moves again and waits for tonight's pass; 2026-11-17)

**Why.** After Milestone 290 the disk's part of a fingerprint costs microseconds, and the RAM's
part costs the most. The Mac engine hashed every byte of guest RAM with one chain of the
word-wise mix (`hydo_hvm::fnv::mix64`), and a run takes two fingerprints (the workload's `wfp`
and the run's `fp`). An engine built for the measurement printed 240 to 366 ms per fingerprint for
the Redis example's 1 GiB of RAM. On web-shop's 4 GiB it is about 1 s (Milestone 290). The KVM
engine hashed RAM page by page in the same chain. It skipped the reads of the zero pages of its
RAM base, but not their mix.

**The scheme** (`hydo/crates/hydo-hvm/src/ramtree.rs`, `hydo_hvm::ramtree`).

- A leaf is a 4 KiB page. Its hash is the word-wise mix in eight lanes: word `i` of the page goes
  into lane `i % 8`, each lane starts from the FNV offset XOR its number, and the eight lane values
  are mixed in order at the end. The lanes are independent chains, which one core runs at once.
- A node is a 2 MiB chunk (512 pages). Its hash folds its pages' hashes in order with `h ^= w;
  h *= P; h ^= h >> 29`.
- The root continues the fingerprint with the text `hydo-ram-tree-v1`, the RAM's length, and the
  chunks' hashes in order. It takes the place of `mix64` over RAM, after the devices' hash.
- The pages are hashed on half of the host's cores, 64 MiB of RAM per piece of work. The shape
  depends only on the RAM's length, so the root does not depend on the number of threads.

The root is a function of the RAM's bytes alone. Each step is a bijection of the state when the
other inputs are fixed, so a change of any one byte always changes the root. A page swapped with
another changes it too, because the nodes fold the pages in order.

**The KVM engine** (`hydo_kvm::mem`, `Mem::tree_hash`). The engine already knows which pages the
guest wrote since its RAM base (the base of a snapshot, Milestone 161): the page map lists them
(`Mem::private_pages`). Its tree hash takes three kinds of page:

- a page that RAM holds itself: hashed from its bytes, on several threads;
- another page that is nonzero in the base: the base's hash of the page, made once per base on
  several threads (`RamBase::leaves`);
- a zero page: the hash of a zero page, without a read.

The value is the tree hash of RAM's bytes, whatever the base: a page written back to the base's
bytes gives the base's value again (a unit test). Where the page map cannot be read, as on this
Mac in the tests, every page is compared with the base, which gives the same pages.

**Why the Mac engine tracks no writes.** Hypervisor.framework has no dirty-page log. A write can
be found only by a stage-2 write protection, a fault at the first write to each 16 KiB granule,
and an `hv_vm_protect` call that lifts it. An engine built for the measurement did that from the
first entry of the guest, and it re-protected what the spin observer unprotected. The faults are
not the guest's exits: no time passes, and the fingerprint stayed the same.
| run | granules written | faults | time in the fault handler | engine time with tracking, without |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| web-shop `disk=none \| run` | 38,186 of 262,144 | 38,186 and 37,971 | 151 and 180 ms | 13.0 and 14.3 s; 5.5 to 5.9 s |
| Redis `disk=none \| run` | 8,253 of 65,536 | 8,082 to 8,253 | 5.9 to 6.8 ms | 0.1 s; 0.1 s |

The most that tracking can save is the hash of the unwritten pages: about 86 ms per web-shop run
(two fingerprints of 43 ms) and about 22 ms per Redis run. In web-shop the fault handler alone
took 151 to 180 ms, and the whole run took 7 to 8 s longer. Most of that is the spin observer's
46 to 55 looks per run, after each of which the probe had to protect all of RAM again. In Redis
both the cost and the saving stay below the 0.1 s that the engine time shows. So the Mac engine
hashes every page at each fingerprint, on several threads, and keeps no write tracking.

**The hash, measured.** On this M2 Pro (12 cores) with other work on the machine, over 4 GiB of
memory, half of it nonzero:

| what | time |
|---|---|
| one chain of `mix64` over every byte (epoch 3) | 1.05 to 1.15 s |
| the tree with the one-lane leaf of `mix64`, on 1 thread | 0.95 s |
| the tree with the eight-lane leaf, on 1 thread | 0.19 s |
| the tree with the eight-lane leaf, on 6 and on 12 threads | 41 ms and 40 ms |

Six threads already read memory as fast as twelve, so the engine takes half of the cores and
leaves the other half to the explorer's other workers.

**The epoch.** `hydo_image::EpochDefaults` gains `ram_tree`, on from epoch 4. The epoch stays 4:
the change joins Milestones 269, 283, and 290 before 0.4.0. The Mac engine's `Start` and the KVM
engine's `Start` read it from the image's epoch, as `disk_tree`. The programs take the image's
epoch from `--image-epoch N` (Milestone 290). The boot probes of `hydo-hvm hvm` keep the old hash.
hvx is not changed: its fingerprint is the kernel module's.

**The runs on this Mac.** The base commit's programs (`c1d78449`, "before") and this milestone's
("after"), each over the 0.3.4 Mac release, one VM at a time. The after programs were this
milestone's with the write-tracking probe built in and turned off: they printed the time of each
RAM hash and hashed as this commit does. A last run of this commit's own programs did not get the
Mac VM lock in 30 minutes.

web-shop's epoch-4 image built with `--set variant=buggy` (disk `bc0ad90a…`, the disk of
Milestones 284 and 290), `disk=none | run`:

| programs | fingerprint | engine time | wall time | RAM hash per fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | `a6eef3eadef684d5` | 8.2, 7.6 s | 15.8, 13.9 s | about 1 s (Milestone 290) |
| after | `f67a52270a7c1d7b` | 5.7, 5.9 s | 13.0, 11.4 s | 41 to 45 ms |

The verdict is the same: OK with 6 invariants held. The before value is the after value of
Milestone 290.

**Old images keep their values.** The release's Redis example built by the 0.3.4 Mac release
(fingerprint epoch 3, `706c8b95…` and its disk `9ddfc929…`, the quickstart's bytes) gave the
fingerprints that `QUICKSTART-mac.md` and `hydo/onboard/recorded.json` record, with the before
programs once and with this milestone's twice. The after programs hashed RAM with `mix64`, 240 to
366 ms per fingerprint:

| schedule | fingerprint | engine time, before and after |
|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | `a62eee5332a5b9d2` | 0.9 s; 0.8 and 0.7 s |
| `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | `474b2874e7ef0fa2` | 1.0 s; 1.0 and 0.9 s |
| `disk=cut \| run C=12` | `2e5f02d8ff33394f` | 1.0 s; 1.2 and 1.1 s |

**New images.** The same example built with this milestone's programs (epoch 4, `31e90668…`, the

| schedule | before | after | engine time, before and after |

The before values are Milestone 290's after values.

**Tests.**

### Milestone 298 (tentative number) - DONE (differential testing between versions: `hydo compare-versions` runs the same schedules on two versions of a system and reports where the client's outcomes, the stored state, or the verdicts differ; the format-1 addition `services[].compare` prints a service's state after the verdict; normalization rules blank what may differ; `--seeds` draws schedules as `hydo explore` does and shrinks each difference; `compare.json` is a results addition; on the Mac engine Redis `always` against `everysec` differs on 4 of 10 drawn schedules, two builds of one source and `hz 1` against `hz 10` agree, and Formance Ledger v2.4.0 shows the account race that v2.3.24 does not; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**In short.** A team asks before every upgrade, dependency bump, or refactor whether the new
version behaves as the old one did. hydo repeats a run exactly, so two runs of one schedule on
two versions differ only where the versions differ. `hydo compare-versions` runs each schedule
on version A and on version B and compares what the two runs did, at three levels. It names the
first difference: the workload steps, the record, what A had and what B had, and the commands
that run it again on each side. The design is `docs/design/differential.md`. The code is
`hydo/crates/hydo-cli/src/compare.rs`, and the guide's section is `hydo guide workflow`, "Does a
new version behave the same".

**The command.**

- The two versions come as `hydo versions` makes them (Milestone 221): `--param KEY=A,B`, `--git
  A,B` with `--build`, or `--images A=IMG,B=IMG`. The code of `hydo versions` that builds the
  images and replays a schedule is shared, with its image cache.
- The schedules are given, or they are the saved regressions beside version A's image
  (`--regressions`), or they are drawn from seeds (`--seeds A-B` and the explorer's drawing
  options). The draw is the explorer's own: `hydo_explore::Drawer` reads the image's fault space
  as `hydo explore` does and gives each seed's schedule and the shrinker's candidates.
- A drawn schedule whose runs differ is shrunk with those candidates. A candidate is kept when its
  runs still differ in the same level and stream. The shrink takes at most `--shrink-budget`
  candidates (default 20), each run on both versions.
- `--again DIR` compares the runs of an earlier comparison once more, with the rules and levels
  given now, and runs no VM.
- The exit status is 0 when the versions agree on every schedule, 1 when a schedule differs, and
  2 when a side could not run.

**What is compared.** Each level is optional (`--levels`):

- `verdicts`: the verdict's kind and check, and each finding of `result.json` (kind, id and
  status).
- `observations`: the lines of `$HYDO_OUTCOMES`, read from the controller's `read` commands in the
  control transcript and the agent's replies in the agent log; the acknowledged and failed lists;
  and each `HYDO-HIST` record without its guest time, per history and process. The lists compare
  as sets of lines, so that concurrent operations that finish in another order agree.
- `state`: each line of a service's `compare:` output, and what each check printed (the
  `HYDO-ASSERT` record's output and the `HYDO-CHECK-OUT` lines).

The other streams keep their order and are aligned with `hydo diff`'s Myers alignment, so a key
that only one version stored shows as that key. Normalization rules make the rest exact:
`--ignore REGEX[=>TEXT]`, `--ignore-json PATH` (dotted, `*` for any key or index), and
`hydo/compare.yaml` (`ignore:` and `levels:`).

**The format-1 addition.** `services[].compare` names a command that prints the state a service
stored. The host controller runs it after the verdict, in the boot that gives the verdict
(`hydo-control`'s `schedule/dump.rs`). It sends each line as a console note, `HYDO-STATE
<service>: <line>`, and then `HYDO-STATE-END <service> rc=<n> lines=<n> cut=<0|1>`, at most 64
KiB per service. Without the key a run sends the same commands as before. MANIFEST.md has the
section "State for comparisons", and `project-v1.json` gains the key.

**The results addition.** `compare.json` (`hydo_results::CompareDoc`, type `compare`) has the two
versions, the levels, the rules, the search, and one `CompareSchedule` per schedule. Each has its
verdicts and fingerprints, its run directories, its replay commands, every stream's first
difference (`CompareDifference`), the index of the first difference in the run's order, and a
summary sentence. `hydo report DIR` prints it, and `hydo report --html DIR` writes a page with a
card per schedule and a folded table of every difference. The example is
`hydo/schema/examples/results/v1/mac-redis-compare/compare.json`, the Redis proof below with the
image cache's path written as `~/.hydo/versions`.

**The proof on the Mac engine.** This tree's `hydo`, `hydo-build` and `hydo-hvm` ran in a copy of
the 0.3.4 Mac release, under the shared VM lock, one comparison at a time. The Redis example of
the release got two parameters, `fsync` (`appendfsync`) and `hz`, and a `compare:` command that
prints every key and its value by key number.

```sh
hydo compare-versions "disk=none | run" "disk=cut | run C=12" --param fsync=always,everysec
```

| schedule | A `always` | B `everysec` | answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | OK, `29c457aa86c394e4` | OK, `014f83b5871aa48c` | no difference (126 records) |
| `disk=cut \| run C=12` | OK, `aaf8cd01a3d41f1b` | VIOLATION, `32f0a58c50495bc1` | the check printed `acked=12 all present` and `key k:0 lost`; only A stored the 12 keys |

`--seeds 1-10` on the same pair drew 10 schedules, and 4 differ. Each was shrunk:

| seed | minimal schedule | candidates | the first difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | `disk=none \| run K=redis@9+1 N=redis@17-18:loss,28%` | 17 | `17 unknown` in A, `17 ack` in B |
| 7 | `disk=lying:1 \| run C=1` | 9 | the recovery's check held in A and lost `k:0` in B |
| 8 | `disk=ioerr:1 \| run` | 5 | A ends `ERROR restart after the faults (redis)`; B acknowledged all 20 writes |
| 9 | `disk=ioerr:1 \| run` | 6 | the same |

Seeds 8 and 9 show a difference that no check of the example names. With `appendfsync always`
one failed disk write stops Redis, and hydo cannot start it again. With `everysec` Redis
acknowledges every write of the same schedule.

The pairs that must agree:

- Two builds of one manifest (`fsync=always`), each with its own `hydo build`, gave the same
  bytes (`d43e73fb…`). `--images first=...,second=...` on `disk=none | run`, `disk=cut | run C=12`
  and `disk=none | run K=redis@5+2`: no difference, and the same fingerprints (`29c457aa86c394e4`,
  `aaf8cd01a3d41f1b`, `2db294d06b54d34d`).
- `hz 1` against `hz 10` (`4de657b8…`) on those three schedules and `disk=ioerr:1
  dseed=9e5651b0ef953636 | run`: no difference, with other fingerprints (`8de6b9a75787ff0b`,
  `31193b877a028225`, `99f2039fca5c95ed`, `593555eb37e03266`). On seeds 1 to 10, 9 agree. Seed 2
  shrank to `disk=none dseed=975835de1c9756ce | run K=redis@9+2 N=redis@17-20:loss,14%`. Under
  packet loss the background rate moves which request runs past the client's 2 s deadline.

**A refactor: Formance Ledger v2.3.24 against v2.4.0.** A copy of the example took the ledger's
release as a parameter (`../bin/ledger-{{ledger}}-{{arch}}`). Each tag was built from GitHub's
source archive for linux/arm64 with Go 1.27.3, and the client once.

```sh
hydo compare-versions "disk=none | run" --param ledger=v2.3.24,v2.4.0 --set arch=arm64 \
  --manifest hydo/hydo.yaml
```

Both runs end `OK invariants=14 held` (`59b6f16b1e0b7479` and `469d4ba0936a06b1`), so no check
sees a change. The comparison shows three:

- Only v2.4.0 has the error kinds `027af89500d5` (PostgreSQL's `duplicate key value violates
  unique constraint 'accounts_ledger'`) and the ledger's `upserting accounts` error. It is the race
  of Milestone 215: pull request 1064 replaced `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` by a CTE in
  `UpsertAccounts`. Two first uses of one account in two assets (`o3a` and `o3b`, account `s3`
  in `U` and `E`) raced in step 0. The client's retry with its idempotency key was acknowledged,
  so the outcomes hide it.
- The acknowledgments of `c1` and `p2` came in the other order. The client's revert `r15` picks
  its transaction by that order, so it reverted `p2` in v2.3.24 (refused) and `c1` in v2.4.0
  (acknowledged).
- So every check that counts transactions printed 52 in A and 53 in B.

The first is a real change of behaviour that the checks do not see. The second is a weakness of
the workload: an operation that chooses from the order of earlier answers chooses otherwise on
another version.

**Tests.** `tests/compare.rs` runs the command on the scripted engine: a version against itself,
a change with and without a rule and with one level, and a search that shrinks each difference.
Unit tests in `compare.rs` read the recorded Redis runs of `tests/fixtures/report/redis` and
check the history records, the state dumps, the JSON rules and the lists. `schedule::dump`'s
test checks the notes. `hydo-results`' examples test reads the new example. The CLI golden is
re-recorded for the main help's new lines and the changed `hydo guide manifest`.

**What is left.** Open item 149.


## Milestone 296 (tentative number): faults inside a call, and `hydo fuzz --vm` on the Mac engine

Milestone 292's evaluation named two gaps of `hydo fuzz --vm`. Its clock steps and pauses came
between workload steps, and a call ends inside its step, so they never met a call. Code that
depends on time or on threads could not be tested. And it ran on hvx only. This milestone puts a
fault inside one call with hydo's reactions, and runs the whole tool on the Mac engine. The
design is the section "Faults inside a call" of `docs/design/function-fuzzing.md`, and the
user's reference is the section of the same name in `hydo guide fuzz`.

**What a user writes.** Nothing new. A function of time or threads gets the same contract, and
the command names it and the kinds of fault:

```sh
hydo fuzz --vm path/to/crate --fn count_twice --faults pause
```

**How a fault comes inside a call.**

- The schedule names one call with a knob, `E=<step>.<call>`. The project's manifest declares
  the knob `E`, whose `set` command writes the value to `/tmp/fz.event` in the guest.
- `run.sh` starts that call as `/tmp/fuzz-call`, a link to the harness, with
  `HYDO_FUZZ_EVENT=1`. Right before the call the harness names its thread `hydo-call`
  (`/proc/thread-self/comm`) and writes the record `HYDO-ASSERT {"t":"reachable",
  "id":"fuzz.call",...}` to the console. The threads that the function starts inherit the name.
- The reaction `A=fuzz.call+<ms>:<action>` (Milestone 139) acts `ms` milliseconds of guest
  time after the controller sees the record. The draw takes the delay from 0, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50,
  and 100 ms.
- The reactions gained four actions (`hydo_schedule::ReactAction`, the controller's
  `features/react.rs`):
  - `clock+<s>` and `clock-<s>`: the clock step of `T=` at that moment;
  - `stop-workload-<ms>`: SIGSTOP and SIGCONT of the workload's tree;
  - `stop-workload/<thread>[#<k>]-<ms>`: the cgroup freezer of Milestone 226, for the threads
    of that name;
  - `kill-workload/<name>[#<k>]`: SIGKILL of the workload's processes of that name, while the
    workload goes on.
- The draw puts the fault inside a call in two of three clock and pause schedules, in one of
  three power cuts, and in every kill (the new kind `kill`). The thread pause names the first
  thread that the function starts (`hydo-call#2`). The kill names `fuzz-call`, so a kill after
  the call's end meets no other call. hydo does not judge a killed call's `ensures`, and its
  durability check runs with `None`.
- The shrink keeps the fault. `one_step_schedule` turns `E=` into `E=0.0`, and each smaller
  input gets a run of its own with `E=0.<k>` naming it. A failure whose input passes alone
  under its first schedule is shrunk under the next two schedules under which it failed.

Only the named call writes the record, so a run's console gets one. On hvx a VM's console keeps
64 KiB, and a record per call would fill it.

**Two fixes to the controller's scripts, for the reactions only.** busybox's `timeout` leaves a
watcher that leads a session of its own and carries `HYDO_FROM`. The freeze of Milestone 226
takes the first such leader in the order of `/proc`'s names. In one shrink run on hvx it took a
watcher, saw only the thread `timeout`, and stopped nothing. The reaction's freeze and kill take
the leader whose session has the most processes. On the Mac a thread that ended between the
freeze's listing and its move ended a run in `ERROR P=workload/hydo-call#2: unexpected output
"sh: write error: No such process"`. The reaction's freeze leaves such a thread out. The timer's
freeze keeps its script, so that every recorded pause of threads sends the commands it sent
before (open item 80).

**When the fault comes.** The controller sees the record at its next stop, so the fault comes
later than its delay. A probe on hvx stepped the clock inside a call that read the clock every
millisecond:

| Delay drawn | A call that sleeps 1 ms at a time | A call in a busy loop |
|---|---|---|
| 0 ms | 1 ms after the start | not seen in 500 ms; 5 ms in the run of the input alone |
| 20 ms | 32 ms | 29 ms |
| 100 ms | 113 ms | 109 ms |

**The planted bugs and their twins.** The fuzz-vm example gained four functions and two of
crates.io. Natively, all six held on 100 inputs each.

- `wait_reply_is_honest` waits for a worker's answer with a deadline on `SystemTime`, and its
  twin `wait_reply_monotonic_is_honest` on `Instant`. The promise: an answer is the worker's,
  and "timed out" comes only after the timeout passed on the monotonic clock.
- `count_twice` counts on a worker and on the caller under one lock, and waits for the worker's
  "done" with a timeout of 500 ms. The worker needs 10 ms per count. Its twin
  `count_twice_joined` joins the worker. The promise: the total is `2 * n`.
- `crossbeam_recv_is_honest`: crossbeam-channel 0.5.17's `recv_timeout`, with the same promise
  as the waits.
- `snowflake_ids_increase`: `n` ids of rs-snowflake 0.6.0's `real_time_generate`, made 2 ms
  apart by one generator, are in increasing order. The generator reads `SystemTime`.

**Evidence: faults inside a call.** 40 inputs per function, 20 calls per workload step, seed 1.
The seed gives the same schedules on both engines.

| Functions, `--faults`, schedules | hvx | the Mac engine |
|---|---|---|
| the waits, `clock`, 16 | `SystemTime`: broken on 2 calls in 2 runs, first under `E=0.7 A=fuzz.call+5:clock+86400`; shrunk to `work_ms = 20, slack_ms = 200`. `Instant`: held on 640 calls | the same: broken on 2 calls in 2 runs, shrunk to `work_ms = 20, slack_ms = 200`. `Instant`: held on 640 calls |
| the counts, `pause`, 16 | `count_twice`: broken on 6 calls in 6 runs; shrunk under `E=1.19 A=fuzz.call+2:stop-workload-3000` to `n = 3`. `count_twice_joined`: held on 640 calls | `count_twice`: broken on 5 calls in 5 runs; shrunk under the same schedule to `n = 1`. `count_twice_joined`: held on 640 calls |
| the crates, `clock,pause`, 24 | rs-snowflake: broken on 1 call, under `E=3.15 A=fuzz.call+20:clock-30`; shrunk to `n = 12`. crossbeam-channel: held on 960 calls | rs-snowflake: broken on 2 calls in 2 runs, first under the same schedule; shrunk to `n = 12`. crossbeam-channel: held on 960 calls |

Every shrunk finding's replay gave its fingerprint again. On hvx these were `2a2350666cadc6b6`,
`6f8a8ed8a7657033`, and `c80eeeb9ad130c04`. On the Mac engine they were `8294279ee2bb5a27`,
`a377ee6167670f11`, and `654b05c7c46bccf4`. The Mac's values come from before Milestone 294's tree hash of
the guest's RAM, which moves every Mac fingerprint. The first failure of `count_twice` came under a
timed pause of the whole run, `P=workload@0~291:500`. Its input passed alone under that
schedule, so the shrink took the next schedule. The runs took 128, 196 and 193 s on hvx.

rs-snowflake's ids went back with the clock: the crate's comment names "clock is moving
backwards situation", and the code keeps no last value to compare with. It is a candidate. It is
not reported upstream and not posted.

**Evidence: the Mac engine.** `hydo fuzz --vm` needed no change of its build for the Mac. The
harness is built for `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` with `rust-lld`, and `hydo build` writes an
`-arm64.cpio.gz` image. The draw now gives `cf=` only to hvx. M292's example, 200 inputs per
function (600 calls in 24 steps), 24 schedules per seed, `--data-mib 64`:

| Function | Seed 1 | Seed 2 |
|---|---|---|
| `commit_all` | held: 4,576 checks, 1,376 of them after a power cut | held: 4,800 checks, 1,400 of them after a power cut |
| `save` | broken on 373 calls in 3 runs, first under `disk=cut \| run C=14`; shrunk to `text = ""` | broken on 925 calls in 5 runs, first under `disk=cut \| run C=14`; shrunk to `text = ""` |
| `save_synced` | held: 3,300 checks, 100 of them after a power cut | held: 3,759 checks, 359 of them after a power cut |

The replays of `save`'s smallest input gave their fingerprints again (`a373bb16002967d6` and
`ba19400d6860bca7`). A seed took 251 and 239 s, against 452 s on hvx in Milestone 292. On the
Mac a cut inside a call comes from a reaction, not from `cf=`. Seed 1 killed four calls inside
the call: two commits, a save, and a synced save.

**Two frictions of the 0.4.0 user trial (Milestone 297).** `hydo fuzz --vm --help` printed the
native help; it prints the VM's options now. A run's line printed the verdict with an empty part,
`HYDO-ORACLE: OK invariants=1 held (fuzz.checks: )`; the empty part is left out.

**The two small items of open item 139.**

- `--run-timeout S` stops a `hydo run` that takes longer than `S` seconds on the host. hydo
  kills its process group, notes the run as `TIMEOUT on this machine`, and goes on. The default
  is 600 seconds plus 2 per call of the image.
- Native `hydo fuzz` runs each call in an empty folder of its own (`HYDO_FUZZ_DIRS/<k>`) and
  removes the folders after the batch. A save of the example no longer leaves `saved.txt` in
  the current folder.

**Tests.** `fuzz::vm`'s unit tests check the draw of faults inside a call, `in_call`,
`with_call`, and `E=` in `one_step_schedule`. `language::reactions_inside_the_workload` checks
the new actions, and `react::a_reaction_acts_where_its_event_is_seen_and_replays` runs four of
them on the scripted engine. `threads::the_reaction_finds_the_largest_session` checks that the
reaction's freeze differs from the timer's only in the two places. Nothing recorded moved: a
schedule without the new actions sends the commands it sent before.

**Left.** Open item 139 lists these parts:

- The fault comes 1 to 13 ms after its delay, so a window of one millisecond is reached by chance.
- One call per run gets a fault inside it. A function of time or threads needs `--fn` and
  `--faults`.
- KVM and several vCPUs were not tried.
- The rs-snowflake candidate is not posted.
- The timer's freeze of `P=workload/<thread>` keeps both script problems (open item 80).

## Milestone 299 (tentative number): configuration as a dimension that hydo explores

Several of hydo's findings came from one setting of the system under test. Examples are Redis's
`appendfsync everysec`, Redpanda's write caching, Vikunja's SQLite `synchronous=NORMAL`, libSQL's
durability default, and NATS's `sync_interval`. Each was found by hand, one setting at a time.
This milestone makes hydo answer which settings lose acknowledged data, or break another check,
under which fault, with a minimal schedule per setting.

**What a user declares.** The setting is a build parameter (`params:`), and `configs:` (a
format-1 addition) lists the values to explore:

```yaml
params:
  appendfsync: always
configs:
  appendfsync:
    values: [always, everysec, "no"]
    service: redis
    doc: "https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/"
    tradeoff:
      everysec: "fsync every second: ... you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster"
      "no": "never fsync: ... the faster and less safe method"
```

- Each key is a parameter of `params:`. Its default comes first, listed in `values:` or not.
- `service:` names the service whose configuration it is, or a list of services (the nodes of
  a cluster that share one file).
- `tradeoff:` holds, per value, what the project's documentation says the value weakens. The
  default may have a note too, as NATS's default `sync_interval` has.
- The validator checks the shape and the service names. `apply_params` checks that each key is
  a declared parameter and that each `tradeoff:` key is one of the values. `hydo build` ignores
  `configs:`: an image is made from `params:` and `--set` alone.

**What a user runs.**

```sh
hydo explore --configs hydo/hydo.yaml --seeds 1-20 [--configs-mode all|one|pairs] [--set K=V]
hydo report hydo-out/configs
hydo report --html hydo-out/configs
```

**How it works** (`hydo-cli/src/configs.rs`, `hydo_manifest::configs`):

- The combinations: every combination up to 12 (`all`), else a set that covers every pair of
  values of two settings (`pairs`, a greedy and deterministic construction). `one` explores the
  defaults, then one setting changed at a time. The defaults are always the first combination.
- Each combination's image is made by `hydo versions`' image maker (`Maker::param_image`, now
  shared): `hydo build --set <param>=<value>` through the image cache by input key, so a second
  run builds nothing.
- Each image is explored by a child `hydo explore --image <img> --out <dir>/<NN>-<label>` with
  the same options, so each combination has a whole exploration folder and report.
- Per combination, the classes of failure come from the exploration's minimal schedules (the
  findings of `hydo versions`, with their finding keys). Each has its replay command, `hydo run
  --image <img> "<schedule>"`.
- Across the combinations each failure (one finding key) gets the combinations that found it,
  the values it needs (a setting's values it appeared with, when not all of them), and a label.
  It is the setting's documented trade-off, not a bug, when every combination that found it has
  a value with a `tradeoff:` note, and a combination without such a value was explored.
- The answer is `configs.json`, the results addition `ConfigsDoc` (type `configs`, with
  `ConfigSettingInfo`, `ConfigCombination`, `ConfigClass`, `ConfigFinding`, `ConfigValue`,
  `ConfigTradeoff`). `hydo report <dir>` prints its table, and `hydo report --html <dir>` writes
  a page with the settings, the combinations and each failure with its replay.

**Proof on the Mac** (an M2 Pro, the Mac engine, this tree's `hydo`, `hydo-build` and
`hydo-hvm` over the 0.3.4 Mac release's guest files, fingerprint epoch 4, one VM lock for each
`hydo explore --configs`, `--workers 2 --no-diagnose`).

Redis 7.2.4, the release's Redis example with `hydo/onboard/examples-mac/redis/hydo-configs.yaml`:
`appendfsync` as the parameter, no `knobs:` entry, and the fault kinds of an honest disk (`kill`, `pause`,
`network`, `oneway`, `cut`, `clock`). `hydo explore --configs hydo-configs.yaml --seeds 1-20`
took 64 s with the three builds:

| `appendfsync` | image | schedules failed | class, minimal schedule | fingerprint, twice | label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `always` (default) | `eaa6d210…` | 0 of 20 | none | | |
| `everysec` | `e150673e…` | 5 of 20 | lost acknowledged writes (`key k:0 lost`), `disk=cut dseed=63cbe1e459320dd7 \| run C=1` | `a9ad2a01638d3197` | the documented trade-off |
| `no` | `b7205c3c…` | 5 of 20 | the same, `disk=cut dseed=63cbe1e459320dd7 \| run C=1` | `4e16ac06d8a05cf3` | the documented trade-off |

The 5 failing schedules are the 5 of the 20 with a power cut (seeds 7, 11, 12, 18 and 20), on
both relaxed values. With `always` the same 5 schedules passed, so the finding needs
`everysec` or `no`, and the table names those values.

NATS 2.12.1, three nodes, `hydo/onboard/examples/nats-jetstream/hydo/hydo-configs.yaml`: the
configuration file `conf` as the parameter (the default `sync_interval` of two minutes, 10 s,
`always`), 12 workload steps, and the fault kinds `kill` and `cut`. `hydo explore --configs
hydo/hydo-configs.yaml --set nats=2.12.1 --seeds 1-20` took 113 s with the images from the

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| `nats-server-sync-10s.conf` | `ee2f8d20…` | 5 of 20 | the same schedule | `4638f825f8c84f26` | the documented trade-off |

Here the default is the relaxed value, with a `tradeoff:` note that quotes NATS's own advice
(`sync_interval: always` for strict durability, issue 7564). This is Jepsen's NATS finding 3.4,
which Milestone 141 found by hand. A first run with seeds 1-6 found nothing on any value: the

nothing. The guide says to start with 20 seeds.

Each of the four replay commands that the two tables print (`hydo run --image <cached image>
"<schedule>"`) ran once more as printed and gave the fingerprint above with the same verdict.
The six images came from the image cache by their input keys; a second `hydo explore --configs`
of the NATS manifest built nothing. The Redis images are 140 MB each and the NATS ones 1.1 GB.
