## Milestone 301 (tentative number): the frictions of the 0.4.0 trial

Milestone 297's trial of 0.4.0 found that what hydo tells a new user is sometimes false. This
milestone fixes its frictions, worst first, each with a test that would have caught it.

**1. A walk's recording showed a passing run under a failing problem.** The trial's walk
exploration of web-shop shrank seed 2 to a walk with no fault, `I=813a9e4ce991433d,n3` with every
action but those of step 2 left out. Its verdict was `The page / showed the busy element .spinner
("Loading products…") for 10.2 s, until the test ended`, and its recording replay ended `OK`.

- The cause is the watcher, not the recording. Step 2 loads `/`, goes back, reloads, and waits
  5 s. The back leaves `/` for `about:blank` while the products are loading. The new document has
  no spinner, so the page script sent no "spinner gone" event, and `check.mjs` kept the spinner of
  the old page open until the test ended, 10.2 s later, just over the 10 s limit. The recorded
  run repeated the same three actions, as Milestone 270 makes it. Recording costs guest time, so
  that run's span was under 10 s, and it passed.
- The fix: the page script sends a `doc` event when a new document starts (`hook.cjs`, only for
  the page's main frame), and `check.mjs` ends every open busy element at a `doc` event or at a
  navigation to `about:`. A spinner that stays on its own page is still a finding.
- On the Mac engine, the trial's minimal schedule gives `OK` twice with one fingerprint,
  `fe1bc2e5e2990ead`. The walk takes the same actions: `back`, `reload`, `wait 5000`. Seed 2's own
  schedule, `H=api.place_order@2-3:delay=10000,p=25 I=813a9e4ce991433d`, gives `OK` too.
  Problem 2, `H=api.get_order@3-4:reset` with its walk, still breaks
  `browser.no_page_errors` (`93b4514a28c3cf83`): the planted bug of the order page.
- A recording can still pass, because its timing is its own. `hydo explore`'s line says so in
  words. `hydo report` and `hydo report --html` of the exploration show each problem's recording,
  `replays/rec-<k>/`, and link its video, its trace and its `repro.spec.ts`. When the recorded run
  did not fail, the page says plainly that the recording does not show the failure, and why.
- Tests: `hydo-manifest`'s `a_spinner_ends_with_its_document` runs `check.mjs` with `node` over
  the trial's events (it fails without the fix), and `hydo`'s
  `a_problem_links_its_recording_and_says_when_it_passed`.
- The trial's verdict also ended in two periods: a check's sentence that ends with a period ends
  the line now.

**2. Step numbers disagreed.** `hydo_schedule::describe` counted a step window from 1: `@0-1` read
"During step 1", while the engine's line says `before step 0`, the walk's test is `walk step 3`,
and `repro.spec.ts` says `// step 3`. Every user-facing place now names a step by the schedule's
own number, from 0: "during step 0", "during steps 5 to 9" for `@5-10`, "4 ms after step 12
starts". A count stays a count: `C=12` reads "after 12 steps", and `@1` reads "after 1 step" (it
read "after the first step"). `hydo guide inspect` promised steps counted from 1; it says the new
rule now. Only step texts moved in the goldens: one line of each plain-words report golden
(`During steps 24 to 27` became `During steps 23 to 26`), and four answers of the CLI golden
(`after the first step` became `after 1 step`). Test: hydo-schedule's
`a_step_has_the_schedules_number`.

**3. The CI history page contradicted itself.** The headline counted the first line only (the
default branch), so it read `No open problem in redis` above two findings open on `pull/1`, and
the existing test had recorded that wording. The headline now counts the open, not accepted,
findings of every line, a finding open on two lines once, and the lead names the lines: `Open and
not accepted: 2 on pull/1.` `ci-run.json` gains `started` (a results addition, in
`hydo/schema/results-v1.json`): `hydo ci run` writes the UTC time it started, and `hydo ci merge`
takes the earliest shard's. The page's runs table is ordered and labelled by it (`Started`), and a
finding's first sight shows its run's start. A run recorded before has only the time of its
record, and the page says `recorded <time>`. Tests: `the_page_shows_each_finding_across_commits_and_branches`
(changed to the true headline) and `the_runs_show_when_they_started`.

**4. The explorer and the report misstated what happened.**

- `hydo explore` printed `the faults it draws: none of the project's kinds` with `faults:
  [protocol, clock, pause]` and `--protocol-faults`, and then drew `H=` faults. The line now
  lists the kinds that options draw (`--protocol-faults`, `--protocol-cover`, `--grpc-faults`,
  `--storage-faults`, `--cluster-faults`, `--pause-workload`, `--pause-thread`, `--upgrades`), and
  a kind of `faults:` that only an option draws names the option: `it draws no fault. --new-faults
  adds pauses and clock jumps. --protocol-faults adds faults of the outside services.` Test:
  `fault_space_line::the_options_that_draw_their_own_kinds_are_in_the_line`.
- The class `test-failed` read "with no fault that explains it" under a title "while an outside
  service misbehaved". The class means only that no disk fault, damaged file or relaxed setting
  was in the run. Its words now say that the test failed while the schedule's faults ran, or with
  no fault in its schedule, and the advice calls a failure a matter of timing only for a run with
  no fault. Test: `a_test_that_failed_under_faults_says_so`.

**5. A build of `main` could not boot a guest.** `hydo setup --get 0.3.4` said `the release is
damaged or incomplete`, because the tree pins `Image-explore-containers`, which no release has,
and its first line said that it had moved `~/.hydo/bin/hydo`, which it had not.

- A pin that the release does not list, or lists with other bytes, is no longer called damage.
  Setup names the files, says that the release's own files are as published and that this hydo
  needs a newer release's guest files, and names the way out. `hydo setup --check` and `hydo
  doctor` say the same.
- The link note says what happens when the setup succeeds, and a setup that stops prints `...
  still points at hydo <version>`.
- `HYDO_RELEASE_DIR` (a developer variable in `hydo-config`) names a release tree that a hydo
  built in a checkout uses instead of `~/.hydo/versions/<version>`: a tree built from the
  checkout, as `docs/RELEASING.md` section 2 builds one. `CONTRIBUTING.md` documents it, and `hydo
  doctor`'s note for a checkout names it. A released or cargo-installed hydo ignores it.
- `docs/RELEASING.md` section 2 lists every pinned guest kernel, with 0.4.0's new ones:
  `guest/bzImage-kvm-containers`, `guest/bzImage-kvm-smp-containers`, and
  `Image-explore-containers`. They are the only guest files of the trees' pins that 0.3.4 lacks.
- Tests: `a_release_without_a_newer_pin_is_not_called_damaged`,
  `a_checkout_build_takes_the_release_tree_it_is_given`, the changed
  `moving_the_bin_link_to_another_version_is_said_first`, and `docs::`'s
  `the_release_steps_name_every_pinned_guest_kernel`.

**6. The smaller items.**

- `hydo guide values` names the Blnk example's folder, its build steps, and what each of the two
  `arch` options does.
- `hydo fuzz --vm --help` prints the VM's own help. Test:
  `docs::the_vm_fuzz_help_lists_the_options_the_guide_names` reads the options from the guide.
- `hydo ci record` points to `hydo guide ci`, section 12, instead of `docs/design/ci.md`. `hydo
  guide strategies` names no milestone; it says that the numbers come from the project's runs and
  where the examples are. Four other topics lost a milestone number. Test:
  `docs::no_guide_topic_names_a_milestone`.
- An exploration prints a progress line on standard error every 30 s: how long it ran, the
  schedules run and failed, the replays, and the shrink runs, counted as each run is made. Test:
  `walks::the_progress_line_counts_the_runs_by_their_part`.
- `hydo guide web-apps` says that a recording can pass, and that a busy element ends with its
  document.

**The proof on the Mac engine.** A release tree of 0.3.4 with this tree's `hydo` and
`hydo-build` built the web-shop walk image (disk `a3bae636…`), and `hydo explore --seeds 1-8
--protocol-faults` ran it as the trial did. Its first line read `the faults it draws: faults of
the outside services. --new-faults adds pauses and clock jumps.` It printed 21 progress lines in
its 10.5 minutes. Seed 2 passed. Seed 7 failed as in the trial and shrank in 32 runs to the
trial's minimal schedule, with the fingerprint `93b4514a28c3cf83` of the direct run. Its recording
replay ended with the same verdict. `hydo report` reads `During step 3`, as the finding's `walk
step 3` does, and names the recording's folder; the web page links its video, trace and test. The
trial's CI history store gives the headline `2 open problems in redis` and the lead `Open and not
accepted: 2 on pull/1.`, and its two runs, made before `started`, read `recorded 2026-11-17
16:55:53 UTC`. A new `hydo ci run --mode push` of the trial's repository on `main` wrote
`"started": "2026-11-17T18:08:53Z"`, and after `hydo ci record` the page shows that run as
`2026-11-17 18:08:53 UTC` under `Started`. The trial's minimal walk ran once more from the tree's
own `target/release/hydo` with `HYDO_RELEASE_DIR` naming the release tree, with the fingerprint
`fe1bc2e5e2990ead` of the runs above. These fingerprints are of the tree before Milestone 294,
whose RAM hash moves every epoch-4 fingerprint of the Mac engine; the verdicts do not depend on
it. `hydo setup --get 0.3.4` of the tree's hydo, in a scratch install cache with the
0.3.4 archive, names `hv/hvm/explore/out/Image-explore-containers`, calls the release's files as
published, and ends `... still points at hydo 0.3.1`.

**What moved.** The images of `browser:` get new bytes (`hook.cjs` and `check.mjs` are in them),
so the fingerprints in the RESULTS.md pages of web-shop, Memos and Vikunja hold for the images
built before. None of them is in `hydo/onboard/recorded.json`, and nothing recorded moved.

**Checks.** The merge checklist: `cargo fmt --all --check`, the workspace's clippy with `-D

### Milestone 295 (tentative number) - DONE (Meilisearch v1.57.0, one server from its image, onboarded with `hydo onboard` and hunted on the Mac engine against what its task queue promises; three new candidates: an index swap runs twice after a crash between its two commits, a power cut empties the payload of an enqueued document addition, and a succeeded dump is an empty file after a power cut; nothing posted; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**In short.** Meilisearch v1.57.0 (2026-11-16) answers every write with a `taskUid` and
processes its task queue in batches; the queue and each index are LMDB environments.
`hydo/onboard/examples/meilisearch` (RESULTS.md) runs one server from the official image,
imported with `hydo onboard` from a one-service Compose file, with its data folder on a file
system of its own (`storage:`). The test client `mlc` (Go, standard library only) enqueues
additions, partial updates, deletions, settings changes, swaps of two indexes, edits by
function, dumps and snapshots, without waiting for them. Six checks state the documented
promises: every acknowledged task ends succeeded with all its documents and in order per index,
the documents are what the succeeded tasks made of them and the search agrees with them, the
settings are those of the last settings task, the swaps leave the indexes as their count says,
each edit runs once, and every succeeded dump and the snapshot are whole archives. The build
parameter `dumps=no` turns the dumps off, because finding 3 breaks every power cut's run.

**What was found.** Three bugs, new as far as the search found; nothing was posted.

- **An index swap runs twice after a crash.** `process_batch` commits the swapped index
  mapping in its own LMDB transaction (`crates/index-scheduler/src/scheduler/process_batch.rs:434`),
  and `tick` writes the task's `succeeded` status in a second one (`scheduler/mod.rs:279` to
  `:452`). The `processing` status lives only in memory, so after a crash between the commits
  the restart runs the swap again and swaps the indexes back. `disk=none | run
  A=meili.add_acked@20+40:cut` gives 21 succeeded swaps with both indexes at home, and the swap
  task 164 started in the recovery boot (`fp=44a749b10aeef55b`, twice). Kill reactions at 18
  delays never came between the commits. `native/swap-twice.sh` kills the server with
  `pkill -9` inside its Docker container 0 to 45 ms after a swap and 16 additions: a swap ran
  twice in 4 of 48 rounds. The code is the same on `main` (`d15a0866`). Issue #1679 (2021)
  named the case in the design of the task queue.
- **A power cut empties the payload of an enqueued document addition.** The route renames the
  payload file into place with `tempfile`'s `persist` and no `fsync`
  (`crates/file-store/src/lib.rs:147`), then commits the task. After a cut the task succeeds
  with `indexedDocuments` 0, or fails with `No such file or directory (os error 2)` with every
  task of its batch, also a deletion (`disk=cut | run A=meili.add_acked@20+2:cut`,
  `fp=830da5344ced8d40`). Blind in exploration B, seed 26, shrunk to `C=60 A=meili.add_acked:cut`.
- **A succeeded dump is an empty file after a power cut.** `process_dump_creation` writes the
  archive with `File::create` and never syncs it (`process_dump_creation.rs:281-285`). `disk=cut |
  run C=30` leaves all five dumps at 0 bytes (`fp=e4469b79f388a979`); in exploration A 9 of 25
  schedules, and a power loss of the service alone (`L=meilisearch@42+1`).

**What held.** No acknowledged task was lost from the queue, and each index's tasks ran in uid
order. In 75 blind schedules and the directed runs, kills, pauses, and clock steps of 30 s to a
year broke no check; the clock audit found one place, a metric. The settings, the search, and
the edits (but on a lying disk) held. Damage that Meilisearch detects (`MDB_INVALID`, a corrupted
version file) stops it at the start. Every failure with disk I/O errors or a lying disk was the
disk's own loss.

**What hydo lacked** (open item 148; RESULTS.md, section "What hydo lacked"):

- A kill reaction does not come between two commits that a power cut finds; a SIGKILL in Docker
  does.
- One schedule's first violation hides the others: the dumps fail in every run with a power cut,
  and finding 1's verdict line names finding 2.
- Released 0.3.4 (epoch 3) cuts at other moments and misses finding 1 with `+2` and `+40`. The
  moment also moved with the example's own bytes: the build parameter `dumps` moved finding 1
  from `+2` to `+40`.
- The shared Mac VM lock: about 1 hour 40 minutes of waiting.

Retro: Meilisearch v1.57.0, the Mac engine, 2026-11-17
- Time to the first clean run: 46 minutes of wall time, about 28 of them waiting for the Mac VM
  lock.
- Schedules run before the first finding: 5 (4 clean runs and the first directed cut), of which
  1 failed by the rules' mistake (a search for `w3` also found `w30`).
- The findings: 3 new (an index swap that runs twice, an empty payload of an enqueued addition,
  an empty succeeded dump), 0 known, 0 by design or documented.
- What took the most time: waiting for the shared Mac VM lock (about 1.6 hours); the kill scans
  and the native reproduction of finding 1 (about 30 minutes); the write-up and the duplicate
  searches (about 1 hour).
- What hydo lacked: a kill that comes between two commits (open item 148); a way to see every
  broken check of a schedule in its verdict (open item 148); a regression schedule that keeps
  its moment across a change of the client (open item 132 says the same of image bytes); the
  Mac VM lock (open item 148).
- Strategies: reactions at console events found findings 1 and 2 and the payload loss blind;
  power cuts found finding 3; one node's storage faults (`L=`) found finding 3 alone; kills
  missed finding 1 in hydo and found it in Docker; the clock audit and clock steps found
  nothing. `hydo guide strategies` gained Meilisearch's evidence in "Start here", "Power cuts
  of the whole guest", "Kills of the process that holds acknowledged work", "Clock steps and
  the clock audit", "Reactions at console events", "A scan of a reaction's delay", and "A
  forced order in a native script".

**Checks.** Before the commit, on this Mac: `cargo fmt --all --check`, the workspace's clippy
with `-D warnings`, `cargo test -p hydo --test it equivalence::cli_matches_golden`,
`agents_equivalence` and `docs::`, `hydo-agents`'s `public_content::`, `hydo-schedule`'s
`language::`, `hydo-config`, `hydo-explore`'s `it` and `fake_engine`, the control corpus,
`hydo-release`'s `test_tiers`, `sh ci/consolidate-tests.sh --check` and `sh ci/vale.sh`. The
explorer's identity and corpus goldens and the control corpus golden were re-recorded. Besides
the new example's lines, they now also hold the current inputs of four files that changed after
their last recording: the manifests of dragonfly, memos and redpanda (Milestones 283 and 284),
and blnk's `hydo-values.yaml` in the full identity golden. Nothing recorded moved: no engine,
guest program or recorded example changed.

### Milestone 287 (tentative number) - DONE (TiKV v8.5.8 with three PD members and three stores in one hvx guest, against what TiKV promises its clients: snapshot isolation of transactions in real-time order, linearizable raw registers and compare-and-swap, the bank's total and every acknowledged write held under every fault kind, while PD moved, split and merged regions; one new candidate, a clock effect: after a backward step of the wall clock, PD's timestamps keep their physical part, and TiKV judges a lock's time to live by it, so the locks of a client that crashed inside its commit block every writer of their keys for the length of the step; a known PD bug reached blind, tikv/pd#11596: a PD member that restarted shortly before a power cut never starts again; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**In short.** `hydo/onboard/examples/tikv` (RESULTS.md) runs TiKV and PD v8.5.8, the newest
release, from their Docker images on hvx: three PD members and three stores, each store's data
directory on a file system of its own. The stores use API version 2, the one that the
documentation names for RawKV and TxnKV in one cluster. `hydo compose` imported a Compose file
written for the example. A static Go client on client-go v2 (the version of TiDB v8.5.8) records
a list-append history checked for strong snapshot isolation, raw registers with atomic
compare-and-swap checked for linearizability, bank transfers, and acknowledged raw and
transactional writes of new keys. One transaction in three uses async commit and one-phase
commit. Two more commands ask PD's operator API to move, split and merge regions, and play a
client that crashes inside its commit (`anytime_crash`, through client-go's exported test
helpers). Two `eventually` checks say that the keys can be read and written again within 90 s
after the heal.

**What the setup needed.** The first clean run passed 42 minutes after the start, after four
changes:

- `root.share_images: true`. Three unpacked copies of the TiKV image (`tikv-server` is 518 MB
  with debug information, `tikv-ctl` 328 MB) made an 8,836 MiB disk, and an engine maps 4,096 MiB.
- Addresses instead of names between TiKV and PD. By name, TiKV's gRPC calls to PD ended in
  `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` for three minutes, although PD answered HTTP by name.
- Each store listens on its own address. TiKV locks a file named after its listen address in
  `$TMPDIR`, and the stores of the shared tree found one another's file (`0.0.0.0_20160 already in
  use`).
- 7,680 MiB of guest RAM: each store held about 2 GB at its start. At 5,120 MiB the guest's
  out-of-memory killer ended a store.

Later, PD's members got the readiness check `true`. After `K=pds.all` hydo restarted pd1 first
and waited for its readiness, which needs a quorum, so pd1 never became ready (seed 6).

**What was found.**

- **A clock effect, new as far as the search found: after a backward clock step, the locks of a
  crashed transaction block every writer of their keys for the length of the step.** PD's
  `UpdateTimestamp` (`pkg/tso/tso.go`) keeps the physical part of the TSO while the wall clock is
  behind it and only counts the logical part on, as TiDB's TSO page documents. TiKV decides that
  a lock has expired by `lock.ts.physical() + lock.ttl < current_ts.physical()`
  (`src/storage/txn/actions/check_txn_status.rs`, lines 55 and 176). So a lock's 3 s do not pass
  until the wall clock passes the time PD had reached before the step, and a writer that meets
  the lock backs off until its own deadline. Seed 4 of the first exploration reached it blind
  (a step back of 30 days among six faults): bank transfers failed from step 70 on, and the
  final reads of the accounts timed out. Its schedule gave the same error from a fresh boot, and
  passed without the step. With `anytime_crash` in the workload, `disk=none | run T=20:-3600`
  and `T=20:-300` break the `writable` check on every run (`fp=5c55bec66f806d2d` and
  `5e36930d71d80471`, two runs each), a step of 60 s keeps the accounts unwritable for 17 s
  after the heal, and without a step the locks go 2.18 s after the heal. Seed 13 of the second
  exploration reached it blind again. The search covered tikv/tikv, tikv/pd, tikv/client-go and
  pingcap/tidb; RESULTS.md lists the phrases. Nothing was posted.
- **A known bug, tikv/pd#11596: a PD member that restarted shortly before a power cut never
  starts again.** Seed 12 of the second exploration (a kill of PD's leader, a partition of the
  stores, and a whole-guest cut at a flush) ended with a store that could not start. Inside the
  replay, two PD members had stopped in the recovery boot, one with `leveldb: manifest corrupted
  (field 'comparer'): missing`. PD v8.5.8 pins goleveldb from 2019, whose `newManifest` syncs
  `CURRENT` but not the new MANIFEST it names; goleveldb fixed it in 2021. `disk=cut | run
  K=pds.all@40+1 C=46` gives it on every run. The issue was opened on 2026-11-16, and its fix
  (pull request #11598) is on PD's master, not on `release-8.5`.

Not bugs: a flipped bit in a store's RocksDB `OPTIONS` file stops the store at its next start,
and the cluster runs on with two (seed 9). The cluster took clock steps of 30 days either way,
a kill of all three PD members, whole-guest power cuts, and one store's strict power loss without
a broken history.

**The runs.** Every run used hvx on the bare-metal machine, one VM at a time, with this branch's
`hydo`, `hydo-build` and `hydo-hvx` (built at `0038380d`) over the 0.3.4 Linux release, at the
fingerprint epoch 4. A clean run takes 40 to 60 s of the machine and a schedule of the explorer
2 to 3 minutes. One explorer worker of the 7,680 MiB guest used about 19 GB of the host, so the
other workers failed to boot, and `hydo run` beside the explorer ended with `the engine exited`.
Four blind explorations (`--strategy process --new-faults --more-faults --cluster-faults
--storage-faults`) ran 60 schedules on four images. Finding 1 came in seeds 4, 13 and 42, finding
2 in seeds 12 and 83, the readiness mistake in seed 6, and nine stores that did not start after a
damaged file in the others that failed. The fourth exploration left clock steps out, because a
backward step reached finding 1 in most schedules and its shrink took the machine; it ran 44
schedules at 33.7 runs an hour. No swarm exploration ran: the phase reached its limit of 5 hours.
RESULTS.md lists the nine images and their values. The image of the committed
folder gave `OK` for `disk=none | run` twice (`fp=9c236dcfc429f5cf`), and `hydo repro
--regressions` gave `2 of 2 regressions as expected`.

**Tests and checks.** The explorer's `identity-quick.txt` and `corpus-full.txt` and the control
corpus `corpus-quick.txt` were re-recorded with `HYDO_BLESS=1`. The new example's inputs were
added, and the chunks after them in the sorted streams moved. The entries of the Dragonfly, Memos
and Redpanda manifests moved too: Milestones 283 and 284 changed those files without re-recording
the goldens. On this Mac, on `main` at `5c3de108` with this milestone on top, these passed:
workspace clippy with `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, `hydo`'s
`equivalence::cli_matches_golden`, `agents_equivalence` and `docs::`, `hydo-agents`'s
`public_content::`, `hydo-schedule`'s `language::`, `cargo test -p hydo-config`, `hydo-explore`'s
`--test it` and `--test fake_engine`, `hydo-control`'s `corpus::`, `hydo-release`'s
`test_tiers`, `sh ci/consolidate-tests.sh --check` and `sh ci/vale.sh`. Nothing recorded moved:
no engine, guest program or existing example changed.

### Milestone 303 (tentative number) - DONE (Restate v1.8.1-hotfix.2, a durable execution engine, with a deployment of the example's own service on Restate's Rust SDK 0.13.0; one new candidate, not posted: after a backward clock step, a restart of the server holds accepted invocations until the wall clock reaches their creation time, also a plain send without a timer; journaled steps, idempotency keys, one writer per virtual object, awakeables and workflow promises held under kills, pauses, network faults, power cuts at steps, at events and at 49 disk flushes; the explorer reads an image's manifest with its parameter values; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**The example.** `hydo/onboard/examples/restate` (RESULTS.md) runs one Restate server from its
official image `restatedev/restate:1.8.1-hotfix.2` (index `sha256:e3a11e7c…`), imported with
`hydo compose` from a one-service Compose file. Its data directory is a file system of its own
(`storage:`). A second service, `svc`, is the deployment: one static musl program `rsv` on
`restate-sdk` 0.13.0, built for both architectures without a C toolchain (`build.sh`). It serves a
virtual object `Job` (journaled steps, durable sleeps), `Acct` (adds with a sleep inside, one writer
per key), `Wait` (an awakeable) and a workflow `Flow` (a durable promise). Each journaled step
appends a synced line with a nonce to an effects file on the data disk. The same program is the
client: calls and one-way sends with idempotency keys, delayed sends, adds, two resolutions of
each awakeable and promise. A messages check (`no-loss`, `duplicates: forbidden`) and four rules
(`jobs`, `timers`, `objects`, `signals`) judge them. Two clean runs give one fingerprint on the
Mac engine (`5197fd2b05fab330` on the first image) and on hvx (`3be8abae33f86551`).

**Finding 1, new as far as the search found.** Blind at seed 14 of 20 on the Mac engine, shrunk
and confirmed on hvx to `disk=none dseed=d584008bda670834 | run P=svc@28+2 T=30:-300
W=726d723b,p1,q4,r600 L=restate@30+1`: a one-way send acknowledged while the deployment was
paused never starts after the step back and the power loss of the server, for the 250 s that the
checks wait. Without `T=`, or with a step of 30 s, it passes; the same step without a restart
passes. The cause is in VQueues, the scheduler that v1.8.0 turned on for every cluster: an
invocation without a delay gets its record's creation time as `run_at`
(`crates/vqueues/src/lib.rs:295`); a failover moves a running invocation back to the inbox with
that key (`:779`, `:811`); the scheduler takes an inbox head only when `run_at` is not later than
the wall clock (`crates/vqueues/src/scheduler/vqueue_state.rs:357`, `SchedulerClock` in
`scheduler/clock.rs`). So every invocation in flight at a restart after a step back of X waits up
to X. The documentation's note on clocks is about timers. No issue names it (RESULTS.md, "The
duplicate searches"). Native reproduction: none, the cause is plain in the code. The regression is
`hydo/regressions/held-after-a-clock-step-and-a-restart.schedule`.

**Documented.** Durable timers follow the wall clock: after a step back, a timer that the timer
service had armed ends on time by real time, and every later one waits for the wall clock
(`crates/timer/src/service/clock.rs:29`). The rules judge a sleep by either clock, and a job that
waits for a timer due later on the wall clock is listed, not counted as lost.

**What held.** Under kills of the server and the deployment, pauses, network faults between them,
power cuts at steps, power cuts and kills at six events of the client and the service, a stop of
the deployment inside a step past the inactivity timeout, and on hvx 49 power cuts at disk
flushes from `cf=37` to `cf=4000`: no acknowledged invocation lost, no handler completed twice, no
journaled step ran again, one invocation per idempotency key, one add at a time per account and
each add in the state once, and the first resolution of each awakeable and promise kept.
Exploration A (process, seeds 1-20, Mac) had 11 failures: finding 1 (seed 14, and seed 16, which
fails without its `G=` and passes without its `T=`), 5 damaged files that Restate detects at the
start, 1 truncated RocksDB log that loses the writes after the cut (seed 10), a delayed send whose time the ingress computed just
before a step back (seed 13, documented), seed 15 not separated, and a delayed send behind a step
of 30 days (seed 7, documented). Exploration B (swarm, seeds 21-40) had 11 failures, each
with a lying disk, disk I/O errors or a detected damage.

**The explorer's fix.** `hydo explore` read the manifest that an image carries without the image's
parameter values, so `guest.cpu: "{{cpu}}"` (v3 on x86_64, v2 on arm64) stopped it with `got
'{{cpu}}'`, and so did its corpus test, which reads the manifest file. The explorer now applies
the parameters to the `guest:` section only: the image's values from `/etc/hydo/params`
(`Space::from_text_params`, `hydo_manifest::from_embedded_meta_params`), and a manifest file's
defaults (`hydo_manifest::for_explorer`). `hydo run` and the host controller already read the
image's values. The rest of the manifest reads as before, so no other example's fault space
changes; the test is `fault_space_line::a_guest_key_from_a_parameter_is_read_as_built`.

**Tests.** The explorer's identity and corpus goldens and the control corpus-quick golden are
re-recorded for the new example; only its entries moved.

Retro: Restate v1.8.1-hotfix.2, the Mac engine and hvx, 2026-11-17
- Time to the first clean run: 1 hour of wall time (40 minutes of scouting), none of it waiting
  for machines.
- Schedules run before the first finding: 14 blind schedules and about 40 directed runs, of
  which 3 failed by the rules' mistakes (an add in flight at a cut, interleaved console lines,

- The findings: 1 new (a clock effect that breaks a promise), 0 known, 1 documented (wall-clock

### Milestone 302 (tentative number) - DONE (the epoch-4 re-recording before 0.4.0: every value of `hydo/onboard/recorded.json` re-recorded on the three engines at the fingerprint epoch 4, whose `epoch` is now 4; every image has new bytes and every run moved on all three engines; seven verdicts changed, two are accepted and five have new schedules; a tick-jitter schedule that delays no timer at epoch 4 is replaced; the epoch-4 RAM tree hash follows the RAM, shown with whole-RAM dumps; the pinned reproducers keep their values on their images of the epochs 1 to 3; open item 105 is empty; 2026-11-17)

**In short.** Milestones 269, 283, 290 and 294 made the fingerprint epoch 4 and, under the rule
"Re-recording runs in batches" (AGENTS.md), left the recorded values for one pass before 0.4.0.
This is that pass. It ran `hydo-bench rebaseline --write --thorough` on the bare-metal machine
(hvx), on this Mac and on GitHub's runners (KVM). Every image was built twice with the same
bytes, and every run gave the same values twice from fresh boots on all three engines.
`hydo/onboard/recorded.json` now says `epoch` 4. The decisions are in docs/REBASELINE.md
section 26.

| platform | images (bytes moved) | runs (values moved) | verdicts |
|---|---|---|---|
| the Mac (`hvm`) | 21 (21) | 76 (76) | 1 changed, with a new schedule |
| KVM (GitHub's AMD runners) | 6 (6) | 19 (19) | 2 changed: 1 accepted, 1 with a new schedule; 2 schedules replaced |
| hvx (the bare-metal machine) | 43 (43) | 141 (141) | 4 changed: 1 accepted, 3 with new schedules |

**Why the values moved.** An image built at epoch 4 records the epoch in `/etc/hydo/image.json`
and carries no saved regression (M269), so every image has new bytes. Every boot of such an image
mounts cgroup2 before the S0 snapshot (M283), so every boot conversation has one more command,
and every `ctl` value and fingerprint moved on all three engines, hvx included. On the Mac and KVM
the disks' and the RAM's tree hashes (M290, M294) move every fingerprint again. The guest's timing
moved with the mount, and that changed the verdicts below.

**The Mac** (an M2 Pro, this tree's programs over the 0.3.4 Mac release, Go 1.26.5 from go.dev as
`HYDO_GO`). The images were built twice with `--build-only --thorough`, without a VM. Then each
image ran with `--write --thorough --reuse-builds --jobs 1 --only <image>` while the pass held
the Mac's shared VM lock, released after each image, and each image's kept build was deleted once
its values were written. The runs took 1,096 s. Every run moved. One verdict changed:
`hvm/redis-composed-racy` `W=0000002a,p4,q2,r100` passes now, and `W=0000002a,p4,q4,r100`
breaks `total_conserved` with the epoch-3 verdict's words. Of 24 composition seeds with
`p4,q2,r100`, 13 break it. Four verdict lines changed their numbers with the same class, for
example `hvm/ledger` `O=front@0-30:resp:loss,50%` now stores entry 11 twice instead of entry 2.

**KVM.** Neither this Mac nor the bare-metal machine may run KVM, so three one-off workflows ran
on GitHub's runners from temporary branches, deleted afterwards. Each took the published 0.3.4
Linux release (sha256 checked), whose KVM guest kernels with cgroups have their pins, with the
branch's programs, and the Qdrant example's test programs built there with their pins.

- Run 44145027179 (`--write --thorough`, six hosts: AMD EPYC 7763 three times, 9V74 twice, Intel
  Xeon Platinum 8573C): the five AMD hosts wrote the same values. Every `ctl` value was the same
  on all six. Two verdicts changed. The quickstart's KVM section ran there too: a power cut at
  every step from 2 to 19 with `R=everysec`, the exploration, and its repro (13 of 13).
- Run 44149877529 (four hosts: AMD EPYC 7763, Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C, two 6975P-C): the
  Qdrant pause window with `pause-check.sh`, and the tick-jitter question below.
- Run 44155738225 (six hosts: AMD EPYC 9V45, 7763, 9V74, three Intel Xeon 6975P-C): `--write
  --thorough --accept-verdicts` of the final KVM list wrote nothing on the AMD hosts, `--check
  --thorough` of the written list exited 0, and `hv/kvm/kvm-check.sh` passed 15 of 15 on every
  host.

**The tick jitter that delays nothing.** In the first run `disk=none tj=1234 tjpm=300 | run`
gave the fingerprint of `disk=none | run` on every host, AMD and Intel, with another `ctl` value;
at epoch 3 the two differed. That could have meant that M294's tree hash misses RAM that the
guest writes through KVM's mapping. The second run ran both schedules with `HYDO_KVM_DIAG=1` and
the whole 1 GiB of guest RAM dumped at each fingerprint (`HYDO_KVM_DIAG_RAM`), on the epoch-3
image with 0.3.4's hydo and with this tree's hydo, and on the epoch-4 image. At epoch 4 the two
runs' dumps have the same sha256 at the workload's end and at the run's end, with the same
console, vCPU, device and machine hashes and the same exits and guest time. The RESULT line says
`tjn=0`: the seed delays no armed timer of the run's ticks. `tj=99 tjpm=900 tjmax=900` applies 3
delays, and its dumps and fingerprint differ. In all 7 runs per host the RAM hash changed exactly
when the dump's bytes changed. The epoch-3 image gave 0.3.4's fingerprints under this tree's
hydo. So the fingerprint is right, and the denser jitter replaces the old one in the list and in
`hv/kvm/kvm-check.sh`.

**hvx** (the bare-metal machine, this tree's programs over the published 0.3.4 Linux release
unpacked under umask 022, a tree made from an archive of the commit's tracked files, the main
module `91D86B693F4D4035C368F9B`, two VMs at a time): `--write --thorough` took 7,950 s (builds
2,536 s, runs 5,413 s). All 43 images were built twice with the same bytes, and all 141 runs
moved and gave their values twice. Four verdicts changed; the searches for new schedules ran one
VM at a time on the pass's images, and the changed entries were written again with `--write
--thorough --reuse-builds --only`.

- `hvx/stack-errors-fix` `disk=ioerr:5 dseed=1`: the restart that fails after the disk errors is
  now MySQL's, not Redis's. Accepted.
- `hvx/redis-live`: pauses of 20 s at steps 16 and 17 miss the liveness deadline, and the pause
  at step 18 and longer ones there hold. `P=redis@17~0:20000` replaces `@18`.
- `hvx/nats-flaky-buggy`: the default turn sweep (21 runs) found the boundary between `q=19726`

The Linux quickstart's hvx values moved (`2f9186af5e3be2b1`, `d299dc487ceb5e3c`, image
`80643bb1…`, netem `020c9cc8c6182c9f`). Its exploration finds 9 failures with the same classes and

**The quickstarts and the tutorial.** The Mac quickstart's values are the `hvm/release-redis`

**The pinned reproducers** keep their images and values on hvx: the epoch-1 images give

**The full tier.** `cargo test --locked --release --workspace --no-fail-fast` passed on this Mac
with the pass's tree, so no golden of the full tier needed a new recording: the goldens that

### Milestone 304 (tentative number) - DONE (explorations spread over many GitHub runners with KVM: `hydo explore --shard I/N` explores one part of a seed range, and `hydo explore --merge` makes one exploration of the parts without a VM, equal to one exploration of the range on the scripted engine; the results addition `config.shard`, `shards` and `missing_seeds`; the standing workflow `.github/workflows/explore.yml` builds once, explores up to 20 parts and merges them, and `ci/remote-explore.sh` starts it, waits and downloads the result; on GitHub's runners Redis in 8 parts gave one runner's 40 verdicts, signatures and shrinks, Dragonfly in 20 parts found its snapshot finding in 9 of 60 schedules in 31 minutes against 75 on one runner, and Redpanda in 20 parts found findings 1 and 2 at hvx's seeds in 2 h 53 min; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-17)

**What was asked.** Seven agents shared one Mac's VM lock and the bare-metal machine. One
onboarding waited 1 h 40 min of its 3 h 20 min for the lock. GitHub's `ubuntu-24.04` runners have
KVM and cost nothing for this public repository. Every engine run repeats exactly, so the parts
of a seed range can run on separate machines and merge without loss. The task was a standing
workflow that the team and hydo's agents start without pushing a branch, the merge in hydo, a
script that starts the workflow and waits, and the docs.

**The parts: `hydo explore --shard I/N`.** The option takes the I-th of N contiguous parts of
`--seeds`, the first parts one seed longer when the range does not divide evenly. It is the split
of `hydo ci run --shard`: `parse_shard` and `shard_of` moved from hydo-cli to
`hydo_manifest::ci`, and both commands use them. A part's `exploration.json` records it as
`config.shard` (`index`, `count`, `range`), and `config.seeds` is the part. The option is refused
with `--sweep`, `--schedule`, `--steer`, `--steer-match` and `--search state`.

**The merge: `hydo explore --merge DIR... --out DIR`.** The module `merge` of hydo-explore reads
each part's `exploration.json` and `events.jsonl`, sorts the parts by their first seed, and
decides again what one exploration decides over all of its runs:

- The first runs, the re-runs and the failures, in seed order.
- Which failures are shrunk. One exploration shrinks the first failure of each class and
  signature, and with `--shrink-causes N` up to N with other fault kinds, in seed order. Such a
  failure is also the first of its key in its own part, so its part shrank it. The merge keeps
  that shrink and renames its runs to the number one exploration gives the chain (`shrink3-1-0`,
  `min3-a`), in the stream, in `shrinks` and in the console files. A part's shrink of a key that
  an earlier part also found is dropped.
- The error kinds: the counts add up, each kind keeps its first part's details and its first 12
  seeds. The new kinds to shrink are chosen from the merged kinds as one exploration chooses them
  (`errlog::to_shrink`, `--errors-shrink`), and each one's shrink is taken from the part of its
  first new run.
- The property table and the liveness summary, from the parts' tables. Counts add up, a property
  keeps its place of first appearance, and the verdicts are judged again from the counts
  (`results::property_verdict`). The slowest run and the first miss follow the console-name order
  of one exploration's summary.
- The summary's counts. The wall times are the longest part's, because the parts ran side by
  side, and `mean_run_s` is recomputed from the first runs.

The parts must be one exploration: the same hydo, fingerprint epoch, image sha256, engine and
guest, and the same options apart from `--seeds`, `--shard`, `--out` and `--workers`. Their seeds
must not overlap. The merge refuses a sweep, a steered search and a state search. The merged
folder has `exploration.json`, `events.jsonl`, `report.md`, the consoles of every run it keeps, each
part's replays of `hydo explore`'s diagnosis, and each part's own documents and worker logs under
`parts/<n>/`. The results addition `shards` lists each part with its seeds, its counts, its host
CPU, its workers and its wall times, and `missing_seeds` names the seeds of a part that did not
finish. report.md gains the section "Parts (hydo explore --merge)". `hydo explore --merge` in a
terminal ends with the problems in words, as `hydo explore` does.

**No fingerprint across parts.** GitHub assigns each runner an AMD EPYC or an Intel Xeon, and KVM
fingerprints differ between the two vendors (AGENTS.md, "The KVM engine"). Each part re-runs and
shrinks its own failures on its own runner, so `reproduced` and `identical` compare runs of one
machine. The merge compares verdicts and signatures only. When the parts' host CPUs differ, the
merged `engine.host_cpu` is left out, and the merge says that the vendors differ.

**The proof on the scripted engine.** `fake_engine`'s scenario `merge_equals_one_exploration`
explores 60 seeds with `--timing --new-faults --concurrency --more-faults --buggify
--shrink-causes 2 --errors-shrink 3 --known-errors`, once whole and in 7 parts. The merge of the
parts, given in reverse order, equals the whole exploration's `exploration.json`, `events.jsonl` and
`report.md` after the scenario normalisation of the wall times and the workers, and without the
merge's own `shards` and its report section. A merge without the last part names `53-60` in
`missing_seeds`, and parts with another strategy are refused. By hand the merge also equalled one
exploration for six more option sets: `--shrink-causes 3` in 7 parts, the redis-errors manifest
with `--errors-shrink 2` in 3 parts, `--strategy swarm-pos --preempt --durable-only --timing` in 5
parts, the composed Redis plan in 4 parts, the shop's protocol faults in 6 parts, and every stream
in 8 parts.

**The workflow `.github/workflows/explore.yml`.** It starts by `workflow_dispatch` and by
`workflow_call`. Its inputs are `example`, `manifest`, `set`, `seeds`, `shards` (1 to 20),
`explore`, `ref`, `vcpus`, `prepare` and `id`. Every input reaches the shell through the
environment and is checked first: numbers, `lo-hi`, paths inside the repository, and options
without shell characters. The jobs:

1. `build` checks out `ref`, builds `hydo`, `hydo-kvm` and `hydo-build`, and unpacks the newest
   Linux release of `hydo/dist/releases.txt` (0.3.4, its sha256 checked), runs the release's
   own `hydo setup`, and then copies those programs into it. It checks that the release's KVM guest kernels are the ones the commit pins. It
   runs `prepare` in a copy of the example and `hydo build`. An example whose manifest names
   `~/hydo/build/` files builds from the release's copy (the Redis example). It uploads the
   programs and the image as `explore-<id>-build`.
2. `shard`, a matrix of N runners. Each makes `/dev/kvm` usable, records its CPU in `host.txt`,
   and runs `hydo explore --backend kvm --shard I/N`, with `--time-limit 15000` unless the
   options name one. It uploads its folder as `explore-<id>-part-<i>`.
3. `merge` runs when the build passed, also after failed parts. It runs `hydo explore --merge`,
   `hydo report` and `hydo report --html`, writes the problems into the job summary, and uploads
   `explore-<id>-merged`.

`ci/remote-explore.sh` starts the workflow with `gh workflow run`, finds the run by the `id` at
the end of its name, waits at most `--wait` minutes, and downloads the merged artifact into
`hydo-out/remote-<id>`. It prints the inputs and `hydo report`'s problems.

**The proof on GitHub's runners.** `explore.yml` must be on the default branch before
`workflow_dispatch` can start it. So the one-off workflow `tmp-explore-test.yml`, on the branch
`tmp-explore-test` only, called it through `workflow_call`. The runs found four mistakes of the
workflow, one of the merge, and one of the proof's own options:

- Run 44163758070: the release's `hydo setup` refuses a `bin/` that already holds other
  programs. The setup now runs before the commit's programs are copied in.
- Run 44165114222: `hydo build --out` also leaves the build's root trees, whose unreadable files
  stopped the upload. The build job now uploads only the image and the files beside it. The
  merge job did not create `/mnt/w`.
- Run 44168649611: one shard's artifact unpacks into the download path itself, not into a
  folder of its own, so the merge of one shard found no part. The merged time limit listed each
  part's seeds instead of joining them. Both are fixed; the first fix ran only on this Mac's copy
  of the artifacts, because run 44173340814 had 20 shards.
- Run 44168649611 also gave Redpanda's shards `--more-faults`, whose `cf=` cuts only hvx runs.
  The explorer refused it in every shard.

The runs below are run 44168649611 (Redis and Dragonfly, at `0574b90f`) and run 44173340814
(Redpanda, at `0ed3d5ef`). Every runner had 4 CPUs and 15 GB. GitHub gave them AMD EPYC 7763, 9V45
and 9V74 hosts and Intel Xeon 6975P-C, Platinum 8370C, and Platinum 8573C hosts.

| exploration | runners | wall time from the build's start to the merge's end | the exploration's own time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redis, seeds 1-40, the default options | 1 (a Xeon 6975P-C) | 9 min | 12 s |
| Redis, seeds 1-40 | 8 (2 AMD, 6 Intel) | 9.4 min | 2 to 7 s a part |
| Dragonfly, seeds 1-60, `--strategy process --new-faults --cluster-faults` | 1 (a Xeon 6975P-C) | 75 min | 3,996 s |
| Dragonfly, seeds 1-60, the same options | 20 (8 AMD, 12 Intel) | 31 min | 63 to 1,281 s a part |
| Redpanda, seeds 1-40, `--strategy process --new-faults --storage-faults --cluster-faults --workers 2` | 20 (8 AMD, 12 Intel) | 2 h 53 min | 146 s to 9,469 s a part |

Each runner's pool had one worker for Dragonfly (a 2 GiB guest), two for Redpanda (the option) and three for Redis. The build
job took 6 minutes each time, most of it the compile of hydo without a cache.

- **Redis.** The 8 parts and the one runner gave the same 40 verdicts, the same 8 failures with
  the same 3 signatures (`ERROR redis restart failed` 3 times, `ERROR restart after the faults
  (redis)` once, `VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost` 4 times), and the same 2
  minimal schedules from seeds 20 and 31. The first runs' fingerprints were equal on 30 of 40
  seeds: those of the parts on the one runner's CPU model, and none of the 10 seeds explored on
  AMD. The run before the fixes gave the same counts on 4 AMD and 4 Intel parts.
- **Dragonfly.** The merge found the example's finding 1, Dragonfly loading an older snapshot
  after a backward clock step, in 9 of 60 schedules (seeds 4, 6, 7, 12, 16, 37, 48, 49 and 51).
  All 9 reproduced, and the shrink from seed 4 kept `disk=none dseed=5d40003bdb5e0071 | run
  K=df1@21+1 T=10:-162000 W=ddb740e7,p5,q2,r150` after 81 runs. The one runner gave the same 60
  verdicts, the same 9 failures and the same minimal schedule; its part was merged on this Mac
  with `hydo explore --merge`, because that run's merge job had the one-artifact mistake. The
  fingerprints were equal on the 30 seeds explored on Xeon 6975P-C hosts and on none of the 30
  explored on AMD or on a Xeon Platinum 8573C. On hvx (RESULTS.md, ex1) the same seeds gave 26
  failures with the example's first checks: 18 of finding 1, 6 of power cuts, 2 of a check that
  was too strict.
- **Wall time.** For Dragonfly, 20 runners took 31 minutes against 75 on one runner. The part of
  seeds 43 to 45 took 1,281 s without a failure, and the part of seeds 4 to 6 with its shrink took
  454 s, so the slowest part set the time. The 20 parts used 7,536 s of exploration in all. For
  Redis the build set both times.
- **Redpanda.** 14 of 40 schedules failed, and all 14 reproduced on their own runners. The
  merge found two of the example's known findings in the same seeds as hvx's blind explorations:
  - Finding 1, a damaged snapshot that stops its node at every start. Seed 27 damaged a
    partition's `tx.snapshot` and seed 35 the coordinator's `tx.coordinator.snapshot`. Both
    nodes stopped at the assertion in `persisted_stm.cc` (`ERROR n# restart failed`). On hvx seed
    35 gave the same finding.
  - Finding 2, the hanging transaction. Seed 9 broke `tx.no_hanging`, as on hvx.

  Ten more runs broke `rp.no-loss` and one broke `rp.fan-out`, the claims that finding 3 broke on
  hvx; their causes were not read. The shrink of seed 18 kept no fault at all, only the
  composition of the workload (`W=06dd08ca,p2,q1,r500,n30,x0-59`). Seed 22 ended `ERROR workload: exit budget exhausted`. No run on one
  runner was made: the 20 parts used 58,176 s, 16.2 hours, more than a job's 6-hour limit. On
  hvx one worker gave 4 to 20 Redpanda schedules an hour (RESULTS.md). The shards started up to
  13 minutes late, behind the Dragonfly shards of the other run.
- **What set Redpanda's time.** The shrinks. The part of seeds 27 and 28 took 9,469 s, of which
  146 s were its first runs. It shrank seed 28's failure, whose key an earlier part had found
  first, so the merge dropped that shrink (72 runs). It also shrank four new error kinds, 83 runs

  seeds 3 and 4 had no failure and took 6,689 s, 176 s of first runs and one error kind's shrink.

## Milestone 307 (tentative number): enumerations, trait methods, and values built by a constructor in `hydo fuzz`

Both evaluations of `hydo fuzz` (M280, M288) found that most of a real Rust API could not carry a
contract: enumerations were refused as parameters and not read as results, trait methods were
refused, and types that hold pointers could not be generated. This milestone builds the three
parts, and `sorted(v)`, in the crate `hydo-contracts`. `hydo guide fuzz` is the reference, and
`docs/design/function-fuzzing.md`, section "Enumerations, trait methods and built values", has
the decisions.

**Enumerations.**

- The textual reading finds each `enum` of the crate with its variants, their fields, and its
  type parameters, and the standard library's `Ordering`. A crate's type alias with type
  parameters, such as httparse's `type Result<T> = result::Result<Status<T>, Error>`, resolves
  too.
- A variant goes over the wire as `V<variant>` and its fields. The generator picks a variant
  whose fields it can generate, and a shrink tries an earlier variant without fields.
- The language has `matches(e, <pattern>)`. A pattern is `_`, a literal, a tuple, or a variant
  with its path and its fields' patterns: `matches(result, Ok(Status::Complete((_, 0))))`. A
  variant's field reads as a field (`ok(result).Complete.0`), and an `input` line names one as
  `op.Clamp.lo`. A misspelt variant refuses the function before the run, with the variants that
  the type has. `==` on a variant is undecided.

**Trait methods.**

- `with Self = <type>` names the type that a trait's method is fuzzed on, once for each such
  line, through `<Type as Trait>::method`. A required method without a body is fuzzed too.
- `with` lines also name the type parameters of a generic `impl` block and of a trait. A comma
  inside a type no longer splits a `with` line (`with T = (usize, u64)`).
- A method of `impl Trait for Type` is called as `<Type as Trait>::method`.
- A `Self` or a parameter that is a reference to a reference (`&mut &[u8]`) is generated as the
  value it refers to. The harness passes a reference to a local slice and reads it after the
  call, so `len(self) == old(len(self)) - n` judges a reader that advances.

**Values built by a constructor.**

- `// hydo: build <Type> from <constructor>(<name>: <type>, ...)` makes hydo generate the
  arguments and pass the value that the constructor returns. `// hydo: read <Type> as <type> by
  <method>()` reads such a value. Both lines hold for the whole crate.
- A clause names the arguments as fields (`self.v`). `requires` reads only them. `ensures` reads
  the value through `read`, at the entry too: the harness answers the read value before the call
  after the values after it.
- The harness builds the values under `catch_unwind`, so a panic of the constructor is the
  call's panic. An argument passed by reference is leaked, so that the built value may borrow
  it.
- A refused parameter's reason names the `build` line to write.

**Sorted inputs.** `sorted(v)` is true when each element is at most the next. In a `requires`
clause the generator puts the list in order, so the fixture's `search` rejected none of 1,000
inputs.

**A whole-system run.** `contracts:` refuses a clause with `matches()` or `sorted()` with its
reason. Nothing of the run's plan changed.

**Proof.** The fixture `hydo/crates/hydo-contracts/tests/fuzz-m307` has a function for each
part, five with a planted bug. With 1,000 inputs and seed 1:

| Function | What it shows | Smallest input |
|---|---|---|
| `chunk_size` | an `Ok(Status::Complete(..))` result and the RFC rule | `buf = b"\r\n"`, result `Ok(Complete((2, 0)))` |
| `apply` | an enumeration parameter with unit, tuple, and named variants | `op = Clamp { lo: 0, hi: -1 }, x = 0` |
| `<i64 as Halve>::halve` | a required trait method, on `u8` (held) and `i64` | `self = -3` |
| `<&[u8] as Take>::take_uint` | a generic default method on `&[u8]` | `self = b"\x00", n = 0` |
| `Blob::truncate` | a type with a `NonNull` field, built and read | `self = Blob::from_vec(b"\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00"), len = 3` |

`compare`, `Blob::split_to`, `search` and `roundtrip` held. `compare_typo`, a trait method
without `with Self`, and a pointer type without a `build` line were refused, each with what to
write.

The re-run of the second evaluation's six crates and byteorder is the section "After Milestone
307" of `docs/design/function-fuzzing-evaluation-2.md`. Fresh copies from the crates.io
archives, unchanged, with seed 1 and 1,000 inputs:

| Crate | Contracts | Refused before | Refused after | Functions fuzzed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| strsim 0.11.1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 2 |
| hex 0.4.3 | 4 | 3 | 0 | 5 |
| httparse 1.10.1 | 7 | 6 | 2 | 5 |
| bytes 1.12.1 | 23 | 20 | 0 | 23 |
| num-traits 0.2.19 | 15 | 15 | 0 | 19 |
| chrono 0.4.45 | 11 | 11 | 0 | 11 |
| byteorder 1.5.0 | 4 | 4 | 0 | 5 |

"Before" is `main` at `d0159ad0` with the same contracts less the lines it lacks. The broken
contracts were earlier findings, now stated on the API itself: httparse's chunk size line
without a digit, num-traits' `Signed::abs` and `abs_sub` on the trait, and byteorder's
`read_uint` with `nbytes` of 0 or 9. Nothing new was found, and nothing was posted.

**Tests.** `cargo test -p hydo-contracts`: the parse of `matches`, patterns, `build`, `read` and
`with` lines with tuples (`lang::`); enumerations through the wire, the shown form, patterns,
generation and the shrink; the harness of an enumeration, a built value and a reference to a
reference; and the fixture end to end (`fuzz::`). The merge checklist of `AGENTS.md` passes.
Nothing recorded moved: no engine, guest program or image changed.

## Milestone 306 (tentative number): which error paths ran under the faults

The question was the one a team asks after an exploration that found nothing: did the faults
reach the error handling at all? hydo now records which error-handling places of a program ran
in each run, in which schedule each first ran, and which ran only in runs with faults. The design
is `docs/design/error-paths.md`, and the how-to is `hydo guide error-paths`.

**What counts as an error path.** `error_paths: true` in a `contracts:` entry of `hydo.yaml` (a
format-1 addition) makes `hydo build` list the program's places in the plan
`<image>.contracts.json` (the module `paths` of `hydo-contracts`). A place is the first
instruction of a piece of error handling:

- Go: the first line of code in the block of an `if` that compares an error with `nil`.
- Rust: `return Err(`, an `Err(...)` given back, a `match` arm on `Err`, the body of `if let
  Err`, the error branch of a `?` (the code of `<Result as FromResidual>::from_residual` that the
  compiler copied into the function), and the calls of `unwrap_failed`, `expect_failed` and the
  panic functions (bounds and overflow checks left out).
- Both: the first instruction of a function whose name has `retry`, `recover` or `rollback`.
- `// hydo: error path` adds the next line of code. `// hydo: no error path` removes the next
  line, the block it opens, or the function it declares. The contracts' scanner reads both as
  comments.

The line table of the debug information gives a line's statement addresses, one per copy of the
code (a function copied into its callers has a copy in each). The sources' files are matched to
the debug information's paths by the folder that most of them share (`github.com/blnkfinance/blnk/`
with Go's `-trimpath`), so that a dependency's `balance.go` is not the project's. The first
version matched by the end of the path, and Blnk's `database/balance.go` took the lines of the
folder's own `balance.go`.

**How the engine watches them without a change of the run.** The Mac engine has 5 breakpoint
registers for contracts and Blnk has 1,334 addresses, so the engine writes the instruction `BRK
#0x4859` over each place's first instruction in guest RAM (`hydo-hvm`'s module `paths`). The
places are in the program's file, which the Mac engine's root keeps in guest RAM, page by page.
The plan lists each 4 KiB page of the file that holds a place by its first nonzero 8 bytes and
its hash. At each run's start the engine reads 8 bytes of every page of guest RAM, hashes the
pages whose bytes match, and checks each place's instruction there. A hit is a debug exception
(the engine traps them while the contracts are armed). The engine puts the place's instruction
back at all of its addresses, records the first hit with the engine's clock and the boot, and
lets the guest run the instruction. It counts no exit. The breakpoints are out of guest memory
whenever the host reads it: when a run call ends (before every fingerprint), and before a
snapshot that the host takes at a stop. A `BRK` with another immediate is delivered to the
guest's kernel as the CPU would have delivered it (`Vmm::inject_sync`). The engine writes one
line per run, `{"paths":...}`, into the run's records.

**The report.** `result.json` gets `paths` (`RunPaths`: the places that ran, with the clock and
the boot), and `exploration.json` gets `paths` (`PathCoverage`: per place the first runs that
reached it, those without a fault, and the first run with its schedule). Both are results
additions. `hydo run` prints `hydo: error paths: 27 of 1326 places ran`. `hydo report --paths
[DIR] [--against DIR]` prints three lists: the places only runs with faults reached, the places
the workload reaches by itself, and the places never reached, by function. `--against` leaves out
of the first list every place that another exploration reached. `hydo report --html` adds the
section "Which error paths ran" to a run's and an exploration's page. `hydo explore --no-faults`
runs each seed's workload, its composition and walk, without a fault: the baseline.

**The proof on Blnk.** The example's new manifest `hydo/hydo-paths.yaml` runs Blnk built from the
example's commit with its debug information (`build.sh`: `bin/blnk-paths-<arch>`). The plan has
1,326 places at 1,334 addresses on 210 pages: 1,311 `if err != nil` bodies and 15 recovery
functions. 40 more places have no code in the program. All runs used the Mac engine, at the
fingerprint epoch 4.

| Schedule | The four runs (two with the plan, two without) | Places that ran |
|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | `a5028e3b9aed3bf3`, OK | 27 |
| `disk=none dseed=c054734a6f769762 \| run K=redis@21+1 N=worker-*@14-20:delay,100ms W=a36fcf62,p5,q1,r800` | `75eddb844b2c11b9`, VIOLATION | 32 |
| `disk=cut dseed=5 \| run C=10` | `06683fc030390c31`, VIOLATION | 37, 10 in the recovery boot |

The two runs with the plan recorded the same places at the same clock. No place was unwatched in
any run. A third run of the first two schedules with the final engine gave the same fingerprints.

Then seeds 1 to 12 were explored three times, on one worker: with faults (`--strategy process
--new-faults`) and the plan, with `--no-faults` and the plan, and with faults without the plan.
The first and the third gave the same 12 fingerprints. `hydo report --paths x-faults --against
x-clean`:

- Without faults 27 places ran: the lookups that find no row, a busy lock, and the rollbacks of
  the atomic bulks that the workload makes fail on purpose.
- With faults 73 ran, the 27 among them. 46 ran only with faults: 17 database errors that only the
  kills of PostgreSQL reached (seeds 4 and 9), 8 places of the recovery of queued transactions
  (power cuts and kills of Redis), 6 errors of the queue, and 15 others.
- 1,253 places in 606 functions never ran, for example the 18 of `metrics.Init` and the API that
  the workload does not use.
- `main.recoverPanic` and `api.logrusRecovery` are named for a recovery and run at every start of
  Blnk, so the runs that restart Blnk reach them without an error.

Seed 4's first run reached `validateTxn`'s branch at the clock 590,557. `hydo run` of its schedule
reached it at 590,557 again, with the fingerprint `061c17092b845ffe`. The example's RESULTS.md has
the table ("Which error paths the faults reached").

**The cost.** The plan is 570 KB. The search of 1,536 MiB of guest RAM took 10 to 11 ms per run
(16 runs). A run stopped 24 to 54 times, once per place that ran. The engine's time stayed within
the spread of the runs: 1.7 and 1.8 s with the plan against 1.7 and 1.6 s without it for `disk=none
| run`, and 12.5 and 10.9 s against 12.0 and 15.8 s for the power cut. The exploration with faults
took 122 s with the plan and 152 s without it.

**Rust.** The compiler's test builds a small Rust program and finds its `?` with a conversion, an
arm on `Err`, an `Err` given back, a retry function, an `unwrap()` and a `panic!`. A `?` whose
error needs no conversion has no instruction of its own in the optimized build and is no place,
and a `return Err` that shares its code with another return counts among the places without
code. No Rust program ran with the plan in a VM.

**Tests.** hydo-contracts `paths::` (the scanners of Go and Rust, the declarations, the hits'
line, and plans of a Go and a Rust program built in the test); hydo-explore `error_paths::` (a
run's hits in its result, the exploration's lists, `--no-faults`); the committed project and
results schemas with the additions (hydo-schema-compat passes). Nothing recorded moved: without
`error_paths: true` a plan has no places, and the engine writes nothing new.

**What is left.** Open item 155.

### Milestone 305 (tentative number) - DONE (a kill at the moment of a console event: the reaction action `kill-now-<svc>` kills a service from a real-time relay in the guest that the event's own write wakes, before any thread of the service runs on; no engine, agent, kernel or image changed; `hydo explore --reactive fault --kill-now` draws it; Meilisearch's index swap runs twice at 13 and 14 ms after its `202` on the Mac engine and at 34 to 40 ms on hvx, where `kill-<svc>` never did; old schedules keep their fingerprints and control transcripts on both engines; nothing recorded moved; 2026-11-18)

**What was asked.** A reaction's kill (`A=<event>+<ms>:kill-<svc>`) goes through the guest
agent. The host sees the event's record at its next stop, sends the agent a signal command, and
the agent sends SIGKILL when the guest's scheduler runs it. Until then the service's threads run
on, so the service finishes what it was doing. In Meilisearch (M295, finding 1) an index swap
commits the swapped mapping and its task's status in two LMDB transactions. A crash between them
runs the swap again after the restart. A plain SIGKILL in Docker did it in 4 of 48 rounds, and
18 kill reactions in hydo never did. The task was a kill that takes effect at the exact moment an
event is printed, deterministic, on every engine where it can be built, without changing any
existing schedule's commands or values.

**The design.** The new reaction action `kill-now-<svc>` is decided in the guest, by a relay
that the event's write wakes:

1. Before the reaction's step, the main sequence spawns the relay through the agent's existing
   `spawn`: `busybox chrt -f 99 busybox sh -c <script>` (`react::RELAY`). It waits for the
   relay's console line `HYDO-KILLNOW a<i> armed`.
2. The relay makes two FIFOs under `/tmp/hydo-killnow/a<i>/` and a device node of the console
   (from `/sys/class/tty/<tty>/dev`). It bind-mounts the input FIFO over `/dev/console` and over
   the agent's console device (`hydo.tty=`, default `ttyS0`). A process that opens the console
   from then on writes into the FIFO.
3. The write wakes the relay in the writer's own system call (`pipe_write`). No worker thread of
   the kernel stands between them, as one does on the path of a byte that the host types
   (`flush_to_ldisc` runs in a kworker). At `SCHED_FIFO` 99 the relay outranks every normal
   process, so with one vCPU no other process runs until it blocks again.
4. For each line the relay tests whether it is the event's record, as `react::record_of` does:
   the id, and `ok:true` of a `sometimes` or `reachable` record, `ok:false` of the others. At
   the first match it sleeps the delay. It then lists `/proc`, takes the agent's children whose
   standard output is the service's log file (`[ /proc/<pid>/fd/1 -ef /proc/self/fd/9 ]`, the
   log opened at arming), adds their descendants, and sends `kill -9` to all of them. Every step
   from the record to the kill is a builtin of busybox's shell, so no process starts and no
   disk is read in between.
5. Only then does it hand the record to a forwarder at normal priority (`chrt -o 0 cat`), which
   writes every line to the console device. It reports `HYDO-KILLNOW a<i> killed <svc> <n>`
   directly, and drops to normal priority.

The host keeps the books. A run with reactions keeps the `HYDO-KILLNOW` lines as facts. The
reaction's thread marks the reaction fired and the service killed, so the service stays down
until the heal's restart pass, as after `kill-<svc>`. A restart policy's supervisor counts the
relay's kills of its service (`react::kills_of`) and leaves such an exit to the schedule. At the
end of the steps the host removes `/tmp/hydo-killnow/a<i>/on` of a relay that saw no event, so it
only forwards from then on. A relay that cannot start ends the run with `HYDO-ORACLE: ERROR
A=...: <why>`.

**Why not the other options.**

- A kill sent by the agent with priority: the agent cannot change, because its bytes are in
  every image (open item 127). Its only real-time mode belongs to the packet trigger and needs
  a netfilter queue, which the Mac's default guest kernel lacks. And a command typed to the
  agent reaches it through the tty layer's kworker, which runs at normal priority.
- A host call that the guest kernel handles: the guest kernels are pinned, and a new one moves
  fingerprints.
- The cgroup freezer, written by the engine: the engine cannot write a guest file. A freeze
  written by a guest process has the same problem of who runs first, and a SIGKILL from a
  process that runs first needs no freeze.
- A pause of the whole VM: nothing in the guest runs while the VM is paused, so the kill still
  has to happen after the target could run.

The relay needs nothing new in the engines. It is the same controller code on hvx, the Mac
engine and KVM, so KVM needs no run of its own for the mechanism.

**What it guarantees.** With one vCPU, no thread of the service runs between the event's record
and the kill. A thread inside a system call finishes it and dies before it returns to user
space, as with a SIGKILL anywhere. With `+<ms>` the kill comes at the first switch of the guest's
scheduler after the relay's sleep, which the guest's timer ends. The limits:

- The event's writer must open the console after the reaction is armed, as the composer's
  commands and a workload's SDK do. A record written through a file descriptor opened before,
  such as a service's SDK opened at boot, reaches the host but not the relay.
- With several vCPUs the service's threads on other CPUs run until the kill's interrupt reaches
  them.
- One `kill-now-` reaction per schedule (hydo-schedule refuses a second), because one relay sits
  over the console.

**The schedule.** `kill-now-<svc>` (`ReactAction::KillNow`). A service name has no `-`, so no
schedule before this one had `kill-now-`, and `kill-nowhere` stays the kill of the service
`nowhere`. `hydo_control::names` checks the service as for `kill-`. The describe text is "kills
`<svc>` at that moment, before it runs on".

**The explorer.** `hydo explore --reactive fault --kill-now` draws `kill-now-<svc>` where the
reactions draw `kill-<svc>`. The delay of such a kill comes from `REACT_NOW_DELAYS` (0, 1, 2, 3,
5, 8, 13, 20, 30 and 50 ms), from one more draw at the end of the reaction stream. So without
the option every draw is the one before (`reactive::the_reactive_stream_is_pinned` passes
unchanged). The shrinker keeps the action, and its candidates drop the reaction, act at once,
halve the delay or arm it from the start. `Ra::svc` reads the service of `kill-now-<svc>`.

**Meilisearch on the Mac engine.** The example's image built with this tree (`--set
arch=arm64`, `dddbbcab…` initramfs), 0.4.0's guest files. One run per delay of
`disk=none | run A=meili.swap_acked@20+<ms>:kill-now-meilisearch`:

| delay (ms) | verdict |
|---|---|
| 0, 6, 7 | `VIOLATION [edits]`: an edit by function ran twice |
| 13, 14 | `VIOLATION [swap]`: the swap ran twice |
| 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50 | `OK` |

At `+14` the relay killed 2 processes (the service's shell and Meilisearch). Task 75, enqueued at
9.768 s of the guest's clock, ran again at 21.239 s after the heal's restart, and the check said
`sa and sb are swapped otherwise than 3 succeeded swaps say`. Three runs of `+14` gave
`fp=49a613db35d5f480`, and two of `+0` gave `fp=ef86ff1e1fbe26f5`. `kill-meilisearch` at 13, 14
and 15 ms gave `OK`. The window of the swap is 2 ms wide on a grid of 1 ms. The edit's window is
the same split of two commits, of `editDocumentsByFunction` in the counter's index; M295 saw an
edit run twice only on a lying disk. `hydo/regressions/swap-runs-twice-after-a-kill.schedule` is
the regression.

**hvx.** On the bare-metal machine, in `~/hydo-killnow` under umask 022 with the main module and
0.4.0's Linux guest files, the image built from the same files, every run through
`~/bin/hvx-run`. This was the example's first run on hvx. The same scan:

| schedule | delays (ms) with a violation | delays (ms) that passed |

| `A=meili.swap_acked@20+<ms>:kill-meilisearch` | 14, 15, 18, 22: `[edits]` | 6, 8, 10 to 13, 23, 24, 26 |
| `A=meili.swap_acked@30+<ms>:kill-now-meilisearch` | 34 to 40: `[swap]`, the swap ran twice | 0 to 32 in steps of 2, 41, 42, 44 |

At `@30+36` task 111, enqueued at 14.837 s, ran again at 21.897 s after the restart. Three runs
of `@30+36` gave `fp=30ab8d845d6f258b`, two of `@30+40` gave `fp=a4673d9b3c2abb21`, and three of

window of 7 ms it never reached.

**Old schedules keep their values.** The same schedules with the tree before the change

**Tests.** hydo-schedule's `language::the_kill_at_the_event` (round trips, the action, the
