## Milestone 325 (tentative number): the busy Keeper threads of the ClickHouse runs

Milestone 319 found that two `KeeperHandler` threads of a Keeper kept hvx's guest busy in the
ClickHouse runs that never ended, while the Keeper's client port held a connection in
`CLOSE_WAIT`. It did not trace their cause (open items 157 and 164). The threads are ClickHouse
Keeper's own loop: a candidate, not reported upstream, and not posted.

**The run.** Seed 20 of exploration E2, `disk=cut dseed=6711e6dcb424bc7a | run
K=keepers.minority.7@36+3 N=keepers.ring@12-21:loss,100% C=40 P=replicas.all@6+3
W=9580664b,p4,q2,r250`, ran with `hydo run` on hvx from a tree of its own on the bare-metal
machine. The image was M319's `img-x1`, built from the committed example with `--set
fsync=insert`, so with `guest.exact_tick`. The run gave M319's `VIOLATION [converge]` with
`fp=2be840e3c29f36dd`, `inh=50392a9848e8a956` and `ctl=897572c6272fa6fd`, in 419 s of host time.

**What `hydo inspect` showed.** The partition began at stop 292118. Sessions at stops 518232 and
438127 found every handler asleep. A session at stop 364112 found the loop on `keeper2`:

- `ch1` and `ch2` had sessions 3 and 4 on `keeper2`'s handler threads 333 and 338. Both servers
  ended them at 00:03:14.02 of the guest's clock, after `Connection loss` answers.
- Threads 333 and 338 were runnable in every sample and ran 9.2 ms and 8.2 ms in 50 ms of guest
  time. All 100 samples of each kernel stack had `exit_to_user_mode_prepare` on top.
- `keeper2`'s port 9181 held both connections in `CLOSE_WAIT`, each with the FIN unread and no
  data. Each Keeper's port also held 218 to 231 connections in `TIME_WAIT` from the servers'
  repeated connects.
- `mntr`, `stat` and `cons` answered `This instance is not currently serving requests`.
- In steps of 5 s, the loop went on at 00:03:40 and was over at 00:03:46, 30 s after the
  `Close`. The threads then had 2.90 s and 2.92 s of CPU, 78 % of it system time.

**The cause.** In `src/Server/KeeperTCPHandler.cpp` of v26.10.6.18 the handler reads the socket
only when `result.has_requests && !close_received` (line 610). After a `Close` request (line 626)
it waits for the `Close`'s response. Its `poll()` still asks for `POLLIN` on the socket (lines 192
to 220; Linux builds take the `poll()` branch, because `POCO_HAVE_FD_EPOLL` is private to Poco's
network library). The client's `ZooKeeper::finalize` sends the `Close` and shuts its socket down
without waiting (`src/Common/ZooKeeper/ZooKeeperImpl.cpp`, lines 1551 and 1583). The unread FIN
makes every `poll()` return at once. A Keeper without a quorum cannot answer the `Close`, so the
loop ends only at the session timeout (line 711). `master` has the same code on 2026-11-19.

**The label.** A ClickHouse candidate. The partition holds only the links between the Keepers,
and the client closes its own socket, so a real network gives the same loop. The guest's clock was
not the cause: with the exact tick the loop ended after 30 s of guest time. Without it, the
loop kept the guest busy past the engine's limit, which M319 described. The cause is plain in the
code, so it was not reproduced outside hydo. A search of ClickHouse's issues and pull requests
with 22 phrases found no report. `gh search issues --include-prs` returned nothing for phrases of
several words on that day, so the search used `gh api search/issues`. The details and the
searches are in the section "The busy Keeper threads" of the example's RESULTS.md.

Nothing recorded moved, and no tracked code changed.

## Milestone 324 (tentative number): three gaps of a user's onboarding with 0.4.0

A user onboarded a project of their own with hydo 0.4.0 and reported three gaps. The project is
private, so each gap was reproduced with public sources, made-up images, and the repository's
examples. Each fix is its own commit. None moves a recorded value, and the fingerprint epoch
stays 5.

**1. Identical images copied once per service.** Four services of one 1.2 GB image got four
roots in the initramfs (`image sha256:418c… -> /oci/scheduler`, `/oci/executor_1`, and so on), a
2.0 GB `cpio.gz`, and roots that did not fit in the Mac's guest RAM. `root.share_images: true`
shares one tree between services of one image since Milestone 287, but `hydo compose` did not
propose it (open item 147).

- `hydo compose`, and `hydo k8s` through it, writes `root.share_images: true` when two or more
  services run one image, commented out. The lead changed it from on to commented out at the
  merge: services of one shared tree once met one lock file in `/tmp` (open item 147), so
  turning it on by itself could break a project of replicas without a message. The comment
  says to turn it on when `hydo build` warns that the roots do not fit. The key is the image's digest for each architecture, because one
  manifest names one config digest, and hydo-build shares a tree by the config digest. An
  image not resolved to a digest is keyed by its file. A comment names the services of each
  image and says why.
- `hydo build` and `hydo build --check` estimate each image's unpacked size from its layers
  without unpacking them (`Image::unpacked_bytes`): a plain layer's size, and a gzip layer's own
  record of its size in its last 4 bytes. They warn, with the estimate in MiB, in two cases. On
  the Mac, when the roots exceed half of `guest.ram_mib`: the initramfs root is a tmpfs, and
  Linux gives a tmpfs half of the RAM. On hvx, when the root partition (1.3 times its content,
  as the build sizes it) and the data disk exceed the 4,096 MiB that the engine takes
  (`HVX_DISK_MAX`, which the ClickHouse onboarding of Milestone 311 met). The warning names
  `root.share_images` when services share an image. On the Mac it also names `guest.ram_mib`,
  or `guest.root: disk` when 8,192 MiB is not enough, and on hvx `data.size_mib`.

The proof on this Mac, with no VM: a `docker save` archive of one image whose gzip layer holds
1,200 MiB of zeros, and a `hydo.yaml` of four services of it with `guest.ram_mib: 4096`.
`hydo build hydo.yaml --check` printed:

```text
hydo-build: warning: the image services' roots need about 4804 MiB unpacked (scheduler,
executor_1, executor_2 and executor_3: 1201 MiB each), and on the Mac engine the root lives in
the guest's RAM, where Linux gives it at most half of guest.ram_mib (2048 of 4096 MiB): the
guest stops at boot with `Initramfs unpacking failed`. To fix it: scheduler, executor_1,
executor_2 and executor_3 run one image: root.share_images: true unpacks it once, 1201 MiB in all
```

The test `hydo-build::root_fit` checks both engines' limits with and without sharing, and that a
48 MiB layer's estimate is its tar's size. The change of `hydo compose`'s output moves no recorded
value: a manifest that `hydo compose` writes is input, and the examples' Compose-made manifests
were not written again. The importer's goldens were re-recorded for the new lines only: 28 cases
of `tests/golden.json` (the unit projects anchors, health, cluster and restart, and Mastodon and
Sentry) and `tests/golden/k8s-cluster.yaml`. Docker's voting app has no shared image and did not
change.

**2. An exploration keeps no run directory for its failures.** `hydo inspect diagnose
hydo-out/explore` said `no-run: ./result.json: No such file`, and the user replayed the minimal
schedule by hand with `hydo run "<schedule>" --out <dir>`.

- `report.md` gives each minimal schedule the line "a run directory for `hydo inspect`": the
  "by hand" command, with `--backend hvx` on hvx, and `--out <exploration>/runs/seed-<n>` by the
  seed the failure came from. The folder comes from the exploration's command line in
  `exploration.json`, so `hydo report --details` prints the same line.
- `hydo report`'s problem text gives each failing problem two lines, `Why it failed: hydo
  inspect diagnose <dir> --problem N` and `A run directory of it: hydo run [--backend kvm|hvx]
  --image <image> "<schedule>" --out <dir>/runs/seed-<n>`. The command names the image and the
  engine, so it runs from any folder; the Mac has one engine and takes no `--backend`.
- `hydo inspect diagnose <explore dir> [--problem N] [--run]` takes problem N as `hydo report`
  numbers it (default 1). It reads, in this order: the run directory that the command made; the
  explorer's replay of a run that stopped with an error (`replays/<tag>/`, Milestone 247); and
  the exploration's own control transcripts of the run (`consoles/<tag>.control.jsonl`, the
  minimal schedule's first confirmation when hydo shrank it). With none of them it names the
  command, and `--run` runs it once into that folder and diagnoses the result. A problem of
  error lines, a number past the last problem, and `--problem` on a run directory are refused
  with the command to use.

The test `hydo::inspect_explore` runs every path on the scripted exploration of
`tests/fixtures/report/scripted-explore`, with the Redis run of `tests/fixtures/report/redis` as
the files a real run leaves, and `--run` through the scripted engine. The explorer's documents
did not change (`exploration.json` and the event stream). Goldens re-recorded for the new lines
only:

- `tests/golden/report/exploration.txt`: 4 lines.
- 4 answers of `tests/golden/cli.jsonl`: `hydo report` of the composed exploration, now longer
  than 4 KiB and so kept as a digest.
- `report.md` of 19 scenarios of `hydo-explore`'s `fake_engine`: one line per minimal schedule.
  `freeze_call` and `protocol_cover` became longer than 4 KiB and are kept as digests.

Before the re-recording, the old goldens matched the code before the change.

**3. The clock audit's noise.** The user's `hydo rules scan --kind clock` ranked a Rust test
function `[high]` (`test_clean_unpartitioned_table` in a `#[cfg(test)]` module). It also ranked
places in a program that no service of the manifest runs, and its schedules kept `<service>`
although `hydo/hydo.yaml` existed.

- Test code inside a source file is left out by each language's conventions:
  - Rust: an item after `#[cfg(test)]` or `#[cfg(all(test, ...))]`, and a function after
    `#[test]` or another crate's test attribute (`#[tokio::test]`, `#[rstest]`).
  - Go: `func TestX(t *testing.T)`, `BenchmarkX` and `FuzzX`.
  - Python and Ruby: `def test_...` and `class Test...`.
  - Java, Kotlin and C#: JUnit's and .NET's test annotations.
  - JavaScript and TypeScript: `describe(`, `it(` and `test(` blocks, and Vitest's
    `if (import.meta.vitest)`.
  - C and C++: googletest's `TEST(`.
  Its lines are neither places nor readings, and the report's head counts what it left out.
- With a manifest, the audit maps the code to the programs that the services and the workload
  run (`hydo-cli/src/clockmap.rs`). A Cargo binary comes with the packages of the tree that it
  depends on, dev-dependencies left out. A Go main package comes with the packages of its module
  that it imports. A service runs a program that a command of its `entrypoint` and `cmd` starts
  (with the image's, from `hydo-compose.lock.json`), or its `setup` or `ready`. Failing those, it
  runs a program named like its image. The places in the mapped code come first. The head says
  how the audit mapped them, each place says who runs it, and `--json` gives `run_by`.
- A schedule names the one service that runs a place's code instead of `<service>` or
  `<leader>`. When several services run it, none does, or the map cannot tell, a line under the
  schedules says why the placeholder stays.

The proof used the tagged sources of Milestone 248's projects and TiKV v8.5.8, downloaded from
GitHub, each with its example's `hydo/hydo.yaml`:

| project | the head of the report | the known place, rank before and after |
|---|---|---|
| Valkey 9.1.3 | C is not mapped: ranked by words alone | `refreshGoodReplicasCount` 2 and 2, `shouldStartChildReplication` 4 and 4 |
| Temporal 1.32.2 | `temporal` runs `server` (the image's name), built from `cmd/server` and 293 Go packages | `reconnect` 1 and 1 |
| River v0.51.2 | the workers run `riverq`, the example's own program, which River's tree does not build | `river_leader.sql` 2 and 2 |
| TiKV v8.5.8 | `tikv1` to `tikv3` run `tikv-server` (the image's entrypoint), built from `cmd/tikv-server` and 60 packages | `test_from_local_time`, a test, ranked 5 before and left out after |

On TiKV the audit left out 223 test functions and 489 test modules, and 3 of its 7 high places
went. Two were in `#[cfg(test)]` modules. The third, `check_damaged_files`, measures `Instant`,
and only a test's assignment had made its field a wall-clock reading. The two functions left are
Azure's credential code, which `tikv-server` links. On Temporal the schedules of the
places that `temporal` runs name it, as in `K=temporal@2+3`, where the audit wrote `<leader>` and
`<service>`. The tests are the unit tests `test_code_inside_a_source_file_is_left_out` and
`clockmap::tests` (a Cargo workspace, a Go module, and a tree without either), and
`hydo::rules::the_clock_audit_ranks_the_code_that_the_services_run_first`.

**What is left.** Open item 166.

## Milestone 323 (tentative number): hvx's guest clock right by default from the fingerprint epoch 5

Milestone 319 found why a busy hvx guest's clock nearly stopped late in a long run, and made the
fix an opt-in key, `guest.exact_tick` (`clocksource=jiffies`). The user approved making a fix the
default at the fingerprint epoch 5 (2026-11-19). This milestone compares four ways for the guest
kernel to keep time, makes the best one the default for an x86_64 image built at epoch 5, and
checks that images of earlier epochs keep their values. The design note is
`docs/design/guest-clock.md`.

**The four ways.** All ran on the bare-metal machine, from a tree of their own, with the engine's
`HVX_EXPLORE_CMDLINE_EXTRA` adding the words to the guest kernel's command line:

- (d) today's default: nothing on the command line;
- (a) `clocksource=jiffies`, M319's key;
- (b) `tsc=reliable`, which turns the clocksource watchdog off and keeps the TSC as the clock;
- (c) `clocksource=tsc tsc=reliable`;
- (e) `tsc=reliable` and a virtual TSC step of 1,600 instead of 65,536 (1 µs instead of 41 µs of
  the 1.6 GHz TSC), through a temporary engine variable for the comparison.

(e) came from (b)'s result. The module moves the virtual TSC by one step at each `RDTSC` it
emulates and by one more at the exit while a timer is armed, so with the old step every clock read
costs the guest 82 µs of its time.

**The probe.** A static C program `clockprobe` in an image without services ran 500 million loop
passes after each minute of idle time, for 10 steps, and printed how far `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`,
`CLOCK_REALTIME` and the TSC moved during the work. Step 0 and the last step also printed
`clock_getres` and what 100,000 calls of `clock_gettime` saw, and the kernel's clocksource lines.
Each way ran twice with `disk=none | run`:

| | (d) default | (a) jiffies | (b) `tsc=reliable` | (c) both words | (e) (b), step 1 µs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The clock after the boot | `refined-jiffies`, from 10.02 s | `jiffies` | `tsc`, from 11.47 s | `tsc`, from 11.46 s | `tsc`, from 2.25 s |
| Monotonic clock against the TSC during the work, step 0 | 0.082 | 0.443 | 1.0001 | 1.0003 | 1.000003 |
| The same, step 9 (10 minutes of uptime) | 0.010 | 0.443 | 1.0001 | 1.0003 | 1.000003 |
| Uptime against the TSC at the end | 0.021 | 0.787 | 0.990 | 0.990 | 0.998 |
| `clock_getres`, and the smallest step seen | 1 ms, 999,848 ns | 1 ms, 1 ms | 1 ns, 81,920 ns | 1 ns, 81,920 ns | 1 ns, 2,000 ns |
| Guest time of 100,000 reads | 6 ms | 6 ms | 18.0 s | 18.0 s | 0.21 s |
| Fingerprint, both runs | `b7be8240a5b19163` | `cd64262ead35819b` | `44c291ef9bbeb2a1` | `50d435480a3ca259` | `af2c947920e24539` |
| Host seconds of the two runs | 28, 27 | 27, 27 | 20, 18 | 19, 20 | 24, 22 |

In (d) the kernel log has `Marking clocksource 'tsc-early' as unstable because the skew is too
large` at 6.25 s and `Switched to clocksource refined-jiffies` at 10.02 s; at the end
`/proc/timer_list` showed `tick_handle_periodic` and 607,453 local timer interrupts in 607 s. In
(a) the TSC is marked unstable the same way, and the kernel keeps `jiffies`. A busy guest's clock
runs at 0.44 of the TSC there, because each tick's next deadline is set 1 ms after the tick's
handling, which waits for the next tick of the branch clock (2 ms of the TSC). In (b), (c) and (e)
no watchdog line appears, and the timers run in high-resolution mode (`hrtimer_interrupt`,
`nohz_mode 2`, 116,870 local timer interrupts in 708 s). (c) behaved as (b): the TSC has the
highest rating of the guest's clocksources. A step of 6,400 (4 µs) also gave one fingerprint in
two runs.

**ClickHouse seed 20.** M319's schedule `disk=cut dseed=6711e6dcb424bc7a | run
K=keepers.minority.7@36+3 N=keepers.ring@12-21:loss,100% C=40 P=replicas.all@6+3
W=9580664b,p4,q2,r250` ran on the onboarding's image `img-i2` (read only) with each way:

| Way | Verdict | Fingerprint | Host seconds | The workload's TSC | The workload's `RDTSC` exits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (d) | `TIMEOUT workload` at a wall limit of 600 s | none | 626 | n/a | n/a |
| (a) | `VIOLATION [converge] the replicas differ in 1 blocks after the heal` | `56cdb36c4bdaf736`, M319's | 560 | 654.7 s | 9,372,812 |
| (b) | `ERROR service start (ch1)`, twice | `3b0869bf667a6985` | 112, 93 | n/a | n/a |
| (e) | `VIOLATION [converge] the replicas differ in 7 blocks after the heal`, twice | `98ad6346319c3f0a` | 457, 408 | 212.2 s | 28,963,047 |

In (b) `ch1`'s readiness check did not pass in 300 s of guest time: ClickHouse's log ran from
00:00:29 to 00:05:08 while it started, because every read of its clocks moved them 82 µs. In (e)
the log's times have microseconds (`00:03:39.887406`); in (a) they end in `000`. Two runs of (e)
gave one fingerprint, input hash and transcript hash. The runs of (a), (b) and (e) overlapped
with other runs of this milestone on the machine, so the host seconds compare only roughly.

**The pinned reproducer's stack.** `disk=none dseed=4d5cb825dfaab05b | run K=redis@11+1 C=24` on
the epoch-4 images in `~/hydo/build/m302` (Kafka on a JVM, MySQL, Redis) gave its two verdicts
with every way: `VIOLATION [stack.exactly_once] order=11` on the old image and `OK` on the fixed
one. The host seconds were 79 and 41 with (d), 90 and 62 with (a), 176 and 152 with (b), and 104
and 60 with (e). With (b) the workload took 45.5 s of guest time and made 722,911 `RDTSC` exits;
with (a) it took 4.3 s.

**The choice: (e).** It is the only way whose clocks follow the TSC exactly at every uptime and
read in steps finer than 1 ms, while a read costs little guest time: 2 µs, near the 2,666 ns of a
read on the Mac engine. (a) keeps the ticks exact but runs a busy guest's clock at 0.44 of the TSC
and gives programs steps of 1 ms. (b) and (c) are exact but make a clock-heavy program's time run
82 µs per read, which broke ClickHouse's start. The fine step is used only with the PMU branch
clock: on the exit-count clock alone the step is all that moves the TSC.

**What was built.**

- `hydo_image::EpochDefaults::exact_tick`: on for an x86_64 image from epoch 5. hydo-build
  writes `/etc/hydo/exact-tick` with `tsc` when `guest.exact_tick` is `true`, or absent and on by
  the default (`hydo_build::x86::guest_clock`). `false` writes nothing.
- `hydo_engine::image::guest_clock` reads the file's word, `jiffies` (M319's images) or `tsc`, and
  passes `--exact-tick <word>` to hvx or the in-process engine's `Start::clock`.
- `hydo_hvx::engine::GuestClock`: `Kernel` (no file), `Jiffies` (`clocksource=jiffies`) and
  `Tsc` (`tsc=reliable` and the TSC step `FINE_TSC_STEP`, 1,600). A VM that falls back to the
  exit-count clock keeps the old step.
- The project schema says `"default": true` for the key, and the validator's message names the
  TSC. MANIFEST.md's section "The guest's timer tick on hvx" describes the new default.

**Images built at epoch 5.** With the change, the release's Redis example and the probe built at
epoch 5 recorded `tsc`, and the probe with `guest.exact_tick: false` recorded nothing. The probe
booted with `tsc=reliable` and gave (e)'s values: 233,302 stops, the clock at 1.000003 of the TSC,
reads in steps of 2,000 ns, `d9b2ce1e7caaca85` in two runs. The probe with `false` booted with the
old command line and gave (d)'s values (0.010 at step 9). The Redis image ran each schedule twice,
with one fingerprint each:

| Schedule | Verdict | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | OK | `cce52f9e8565f6e2` |
| `disk=none dseed=1 \| run K=redis@5+3 P=redis@12+2 T=8:-86400` | OK | `ee3e7b755122e7d3` |
| `disk=none \| run T=8:3600` | OK | `2ba6fb7c1603fd87` |
| `disk=none tj=5 tjpm=100 \| run` | OK (`tjn=2`) | `df98ec8fec90d043` |
| `disk=none xt=1 xtr=4 xtpm=100 \| run` | OK (`xtn=4`) | `7bcd6f5637d071c1` |
| `disk=none pp=65536 \| run` | OK | `3f9f4cad1ea598e0` |
| `disk=none \| run`, `--vcpus 2` | OK | `fc9769c78faf58c6` |
| `disk=cut \| run C=12 R=everysec` | `VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:1 lost` | `8bee301c59ad1b12` |

The PMU branch clock was on in every run.

**Images of earlier epochs keep their values.** With this tree's engine on hvx, and no developer
variable set:

- the pinned reproducers gave `e153f376096a072c` and `6a5c2fe208174af3` on the epoch-4 images in
  `~/hydo/build/m302`, and `a76d7fe857fdb37c` and `efbde7b57264be0f` on the epoch-2 images in
  `~/hydo/build/m204`;
- the release's Redis example of the epoch-4 re-recording (`80643bb1…`) gave `2f9186af5e3be2b1`
  (`disk=none | run`), `d299dc487ceb5e3c` (`C=12 R=everysec`) and `28275db955114140`
  (`disk=cut | run C=12`), its recorded values.

An empty `HVX_EXPLORE_CMDLINE_EXTRA` still adds a space to the command line and so moves a
fingerprint: the comparison's runs of (d) set it empty, and their values are not the recorded ones.

**The Mac and KVM engines.** The same probe, built for arm64 with 0.4.1 and run on the Mac engine,
showed `arch_sys_counter` as the clocksource and the arch timer on the same counter, in
high-resolution mode, with no watchdog line. The fixed work took 5 µs of guest time at every step
from 1 to 10 minutes: the engine's clock counts exits, and the loop makes none. A read cost 2,666 ns
of guest time. So the Mac guest has no gap. The KVM engine's guest kernel reads one exit clock for
its clocksource `hydo` and its one-shot timer, both in nanoseconds
(`hv/kvm/linux/hydo-kvm-guest.patch`), with the TSC hidden in CPUID; no KVM run measured it. Neither
engine changed.

**What moves.** Every hvx image built at epoch 5 gets the TSC clock, so every hvx value of the list
moves at the re-recording pass, and a verdict can move with the guest's timeouts (open item 105).
The KVM images get `/etc/hydo/exact-tick` as new bytes; the Mac images do not change. Nothing
recorded is re-recorded here.

**What is left.** Open item 164.

## Milestone 326 (tentative number): what Milestone 318 left of the third `hydo fuzz` evaluation

Milestone 318 fixed the first six items of the third evaluation's list
(`docs/design/function-fuzzing-evaluation-3.md`). This milestone fixes the rest, in the order
of what costs a Rust developer most. Each fix is its own commit. None touches an engine, an
image, or a recorded value. The tests are `cargo test -p hydo-contracts --test it fuzz_m326::`,
on the new fixture `hydo/crates/hydo-contracts/tests/fuzz-m326`.

**1. A test module that does not build.** The report showed only the compiler's first line, and
`build.log` could hold a later build's output. The test module is one line in hydo's copy, so
its line and column mean nothing to the user. Now the report gives the first error and its
cause in the user's terms:

- a `build`, `read` or `with` line, with its file and line;
- a parameter and how the test module passes it;
- the call, or a generated closure.

It adds the compiler's labels at the test module's own text, its `help:` and `note:` lines, and
the file `<out>/harness/<function>.log` with the whole output. `<function>.rs` beside it holds
the test module's text, and `--show-harness` prints the log. `build.log` keeps every build under
a numbered heading. A `build` line's arguments now have the line's types, so a type that the
constructor does not take is a compile error at the line. Before, it was a value that did not
fit and a false `broken`. Commit `9caaca7a`.

**2. A private field's refusal.** The refusal said to fuzz a constructor instead. It now names
the `build` line with the crate's public constructor of the type and its parameters, and a
`read` line with a public method that reads the value. `new` comes first, then `from_*`,
`with_*`, the others, `From` and `Default`. A crate without such a constructor gets what to add
instead. The test writes the proposed lines into a copy, and the function holds with them.
Commits `a8394bbb` and `db93baee`; the second gives the same advice for a type with a `read`
line and no `build` line, as percent-encoding's `AsciiSet`.

**3. The language.** Each part is its own commit:

- The bit operators `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<` and `>>` bind as in Rust, exactly on 128 bits, with
  `0b` and `0o` literals. In `hydo fuzz`, `!` on an integer is Rust's bitwise `!` of its type.
  A run's contracts read them too. Commit `5b6f1fcb`.
- `requires len(a) == len(b)` makes the generator give `b` the length of `a`, and the shrink
  shortens both together. Commit `0d3397a2`.
- `matches()` takes `Name { .. }` and `Name { field: <pattern>, .. }`, and refuses a field that
  the type does not have. Commit `a1f3d749`.
- `--fn codec::` selects a module's functions or a type's methods. A name that names no
  function but a module, such as `--fn hydo_props`, selects that module, and a line says so.
  Commit `fd7882b6`.
- A `&'static mut` parameter gets a leaked value behind a raw pointer, read after the call. A
  crate that forbids `unsafe_code` gets a refusal with what to write. Commit `5e6205d7`.
- A type's name resolves through glob imports, renamed imports and re-exports, and re-exports
  that a path names. Commit `fa19ca70`.
- An error in a workspace member's own code names the member, the workspace's root, the error's
  place in the user's files, and `cargo test -p <member> --no-run`. Commit `d113c7e1`.

**4. More shapes of closures.** Two integer arguments add (`|x, y| x + y`). A second argument
of the result's type is returned, and two arguments of one type compare (`x < y`, `x == y`). A
sort's comparison is `|a, b| a.cmp(b)` or its reverse, never a constant, because a sort may
panic on an order that is not total. An `Option` result takes `Some(x)` and
`try_from(x).ok()`. Commit `2a144f18`.

**The proof.** The six crates of the evaluation came fresh from crates.io, with the contracts
that Milestone 318's script writes. The runs used seed 1 and 1,000 inputs on the Mac. `main` at
`bfb38e06` and this milestone gave the same verdict for each of the 71 functions, and the same
smallest input for each of the 15 broken ones. All nine known upstream bugs showed: heck 36, 70
and 71; humantime 67, 68, 69, 78 and 82; `rust-url` 1132. half's `convert_from_f32_slice` threw
away 49,596 inputs for 404 calls before, and none for 1,000 calls after. A second set of
contracts used the bit operators on half and a pattern of named fields on humantime, and every
function kept its verdict. The section "After Milestone 326" of the evaluation page has the
details. Nothing new was found, and nothing was posted.

**What is left.** Open item 163.

## Milestone 327 (tentative number): a fourth evaluation of `hydo fuzz` by a new user

A fresh evaluator, a coding agent that played a Rust developer new to hydo, tried `hydo fuzz`
natively after Milestones 318 and 326. The evaluator learned the tool only from `hydo guide fuzz`
and `hydo fuzz --help`. It read the three earlier evaluations (M280, M288, M308) only for their
method and their crates, and did not read hydo's source. The binary came from `main` at
`7b3d309b`. The page is `docs/design/function-fuzzing-evaluation-4.md`. No code of hydo changed.

Each crate came from its latest stable release on crates.io:

- semver 1.0.28, a parser;
- base64 0.23.1, an encoding with a trait for engines;
- smallvec 1.16.5, a generic data structure;
- time 0.3.55, dates and durations;
- textwrap 0.16.4, text;
- ordered-float 5.5.1, a trait-heavy API of floats.

The evaluator contracted
88 library functions and 60 property functions. hydo fuzzed 71 of the library functions:

- 57 held, 2 were `vacuous`, and 9 were `not judged` because hydo did not read a value;
- 3 broke: two known upstream bugs, and smallvec's `into_vec`, a false verdict of hydo's;
- 8 were refused, all of smallvec for a parameter of type `A::Item`;
- 9 harnesses did not build: semver's five parsers, three of ordered-float, and smallvec's
  `retain`.

Every property function ran, and 58 of 60 held. Each crate's first useful run came 6 to 10
minutes after the first look at its source. Four crates needed a helper constructor in the test
module.

hydo reproduced 3 issues that other people had already reported upstream, and found no new
candidate:

- textwrap: `wrap_columns` panics when a line is wider than its column (pull request 647, merged
  after the release of 0.16.4);
- textwrap: a whitespace-only line stops `dedent` (pull request 654, open);
- ordered-float: `OrderedFloat(NaN) == NaN` is `false` (issue 143, open), found on 20,000 calls
  and missed on 1,000.

The worst problems, in order:

1. A false `broken` verdict: `into_vec`'s `result == old(self)` compared elements of type
   `A::Item`, which hydo does not read, as unequal.
2. A type parameter's associated type (`A::Item`) is refused as a parameter, not read as a
   result, and does not build in a closure.
3. A `Result` whose error type has a field of a private module does not build, although no
   clause reads it: semver's `Error` holds an `ErrorKind`.
4. A `build` line without arguments writes `(,)`, a constructor that returns a `Result` cannot be
   named, and the refusals proposed an ambiguous `from`, an `unsafe` function, and a macro's
   `$src` placeholder.
5. An `impl` block's type parameter is not put into a parameter's type (`&OrderedFloat<T>`), and
   `Self::Output` came from another `impl`.

A bug planted in smallvec's `swap_remove` broke its contract on 25 of 1,000 calls and shrank to
six elements and the index 1. The page lists nine fixes. Open items 139 and 163 have what is left.
Nothing recorded moved.

## Milestone 328 (tentative number): small fixes from a user's second onboarding round

A user onboarded a private system of their own with hydo 0.4.1 on the Mac, in two rounds, and
wrote down what hydo did wrong. The first round's items 1 to 10 are Milestones 316, 317, 320
and 324. This milestone fixes the first round's items 11 and 12 and six items of the second
round. The system is private, so each case was made again with public material: the Redis
example of the Mac release, a file of random bytes, and the scripted engines of the tests. Each
fix is its own commit. None moves a recorded value, and the fingerprint epoch stays 5.

**1. `hydo explore` that refuses exits with status 5.** The user's exploration printed `explore:
one guest of 6144 MiB (guest.ram_mib) needs about 6400 MiB of this machine's memory, and it has
5813 MiB available now` and wrote no report. A script could not tell the stop from an
exploration that ran. Every stop before the explorer hands its first schedule to the pool now
exits with status 5 (`hydo_explore::REFUSED`). Such stops are a refusal for memory, a missing
image, options that do not go together, a `--sweep` that the image cannot run, and an engine
that does not start. With `--json`, or when stdout is not a terminal, the stop also prints one JSON line,
`{"refused": "<reason>", "status": 5}`. The status collides with none of the others: 0 is an
exploration that ran, 1 a stop after runs, 2 a bad option, 3 and 4 the "nothing judged" and
"could not check" of `hydo fuzz` and `hydo update`, and 100 a check's violation. Inside `hydo ci
run` every stop keeps that command's status 2. `hydo compare-versions` and the benchmark, which
use the explorer as a library, keep their status. `hydo guide workflow` lists the statuses. The
test `hydo::explore_refusal` runs a missing image and `--search state --sweep freeze` on the
scripted engine (status 5 and the JSON line, no report) and a wrong option (status 2, no JSON
line).

**2. Inspection sessions that hold guest memory.** The user's `hydo inspect list` showed old
sessions, and a script that read the session id from the wrong key left a session open. Each
session holds a whole guest until it ends.

- `hydo inspect stop --all` stops every running session of the user. It asks each over its
  socket. A session that does not answer in 5 s, such as one still replaying its run, gets
  SIGTERM to its process group, which holds its engine. The answer lists the sessions it
  stopped and says how many and how much memory they held.
- A session counts as running only while its process is still `hydo inspect __serve <id>`.
  Before, a session that ended days ago counted as running when the system had given its
  process number to another program, and `stop --all` would have signalled that program.
- The refusals of `hydo run` and `hydo explore` for memory name each running session with its
  memory and its age, and end with the line that stops them all.
- The idle time of a session is 300 s, not 900 s. The calls of one look come seconds apart, and
  a session that ended costs one replay to start again. A forgotten session held its guest for
  15 minutes, and runs and explorations refused for memory meanwhile.
- `hydo inspect start`'s answer has the id also at the top, `.id`, beside `.session.id`. It is
  an addition to the results format, and `hydo-schema-compat` passes against the released
  schema.

The test `hydo::inspect_sessions` stops two stand-in sessions. It leaves alone a third, whose
process number belongs to the test itself. On this Mac, `hydo inspect start` of a Redis run
answered `.id` and `.session.id` both `i-253783c6`, with `idle_timeout_s` 300, and `hydo
inspect stop --all` answered `stopped 1 session, which held 1024 MiB of guest memory`.

**3. A hint after the second one-shot call.** Each `hydo inspect exec <run dir>` replays the
whole run, and on the user's project each took minutes. After the second one-shot call on one
run directory within 10 minutes, hydo prints a hint on stderr, and in the answer's notes, to
start a session with `hydo inspect start`. The state is one small file per run directory in the
sessions' folder, holding the time of the last call, so the run directory stays unwritten. On
this Mac the second `hydo inspect exec <run> -- redis-cli DBSIZE` printed the hint, and the
first did not.

**4. The class of a failure names its fault families.** Every failure of the user's report had
the class `durable-defaults`, also a liveness failure under a pause without a disk fault. The
class meant that the system failed with its safe settings and a working disk. From now on
`durable-defaults` is kept for such a failure in a run with a power cut (`disk=cut`, `C=`,
`cf=`, `L=`, or a reaction's cut), where the system's durability with its defaults is under
test. Any other such failure is named for its fault families, joined by `+` in a fixed order:

- `process`: kills, pauses, freezes, and reactions that kill or stop;
- `network` and `clock`;
- `protocol`: an outside service's faults (`H=`);
- `timing`: the tick and vCPU tokens;
- `buggify`.

A failure without a fault is `no-fault`. A schedule with a kill, a network loss, a pause and a
clock step reads `process+network+clock`, and a minimal schedule that needs only the pause
reads `process`.

The class does not feed a CI finding key, and `hydo/known-findings.yaml` and
`hydo/onboard/recorded.json` hold no class. It does choose which failures an exploration
shrinks: one per class and signature. So the new classes are one group with `durable-defaults`
(`advice::shrink_group`), and an exploration shrinks the same failures as before. The report
page groups failures the same way and shows each group's own class. The benchmark and the
explorer's identity test with explore.py's answers read the group, so their goldens did not
move. A saved regression's file name starts with its class, so a regression saved from now on
can get a new name; the files already saved keep theirs.

**5. `hydo save`'s unconfirmed form.** A composition too long for one schedule line is saved as
`W=@<key>`, and `hydo save` printed `(unconfirmed)` without saying what it means. The note now
says that the explorer reproduced the failure with the composition's seed form and never ran
the saved form, and that `hydo build` and then `hydo repro --regressions` run it. `hydo guide
composer`, section "Regressions", says the same.

**6. A root too big for guest RAM.** On the Mac an image's root is its initramfs, which the
kernel unpacks into guest RAM. The user's 10 image services unpacked to 1,885 MiB in a 4,096 MiB
guest. The kernel printed `Initramfs unpacking failed: write error` and left files out, and the
run ended later as `ERROR service network setup failed`. The controller now ends the boot at
that console line with an ERROR of its own. It names the root's unpacked size (from the gzip
trailer), the compressed copy that the kernel holds beside it while it unpacks, and
`guest.ram_mib`. It says to raise `guest.ram_mib` or to make the roots smaller. Another reason
of the kernel's says that the image's root could not be unpacked. The verdict stays under the
255 bytes that the engines keep of the verdict that ends a run; the first version was longer, and
a Mac run cut it there. On this Mac the Redis example with a 400 MiB
file of random bytes and `guest.ram_mib: 768` ended with 0.4.1 as `HYDO-ORACLE: ERROR service
start (redis)`, the wrong cause, and with this tree as:

```text
RESULT one fp=c8a3a8601f81176c ... stops=33 ... verdict=HYDO-ORACLE: ERROR the root does not
fit in guest RAM (Initramfs unpacking failed: write error): about 423 MiB unpacked beside 409
MiB compressed, and guest.ram_mib is 768. Raise guest.ram_mib or shrink the roots
(root.share_images)
```

**7. A used-up exit budget.** The Mac and KVM engines end a phase of a run after 50,000,000 VM
exits with `ERROR <phase>: exit budget exhausted`. The user's `eventually_` check started one
client per accepted query at every try while queries stayed stuck. The run ended `ERROR check:
exit budget exhausted`, which named neither the check nor the limit. The controller now keeps
what it waits for: each final check, each `eventually_` check's monitor with its failed tries
and its last output, and the workload's steps. When the engine ends the run by itself, the
controller's verdict replaces the engine's in the RESULT line (`Controller::engine_ended`). The
fingerprint and the transcript stay the engine's.

- An `eventually_` check that failed 3 tries or more gives its violation: `VIOLATION [<id>] not
  satisfied <t>s after <anchor>, deadline <d>s: the engine's exit budget for the phase ran out
  after <n> failed tries of the check (last check rc=1: <its last line>)`.
- Otherwise the engine's words stay, and the verdict names what ran (`... exhausted while the
  check <id> ran`).

Neither part needed an engine change. `hydo guide checks` has a section "The exit budget" on how
to keep a check inside it. The test `hydo-control::engine_end` ends the scripted engine's run at
chosen stops of a plan with an `eventually_` check that never holds. On this Mac the Redis
example with an `eventually_` check that runs 100 clients per try and never holds, and
`HVM_RUN_EXITS=3000000`, ended with 0.4.1 as `ERROR check: exit budget exhausted`. With this
tree it ended as `HYDO-ORACLE: VIOLATION [queries.settle] not satisfied 252.41s after heal,
deadline 600s: the engine's exit budget for the phase ran out after 245 failed tries of the
check (last check rc=1: 3 queries still running)`. The two runs had the same fingerprint
`31a06d63e97092d4` and the same control hash `312d9848c1455e1b`.

The Redis example without faults gave its recorded Mac fingerprint `05f433ee427f8e3c` with this
tree.

**Goldens.** Re-recorded for these changes only, each checked line by line:

- 6 answers of `tests/golden/cli.jsonl`: `hydo explore` without an image, with a missing image,
  and with an image that no engine here runs, on Linux and the Mac. Each now exits 5 and prints
  the JSON line. 2 more: `hydo guide composer` on both platforms.
- `hydo/schema/results-v1.json`: the new field `id` of an inspect answer, and the words on
  `sessions`.
- The explorer's fake-engine goldens (`hydo-explore/tests/golden/fake/`, 58 files): the
  classes only. In the verbatim files `durable-defaults` became `protocol`, `no-fault`,
  `process`, and `process+timing`. In the scenario `stack_sweep_frontkill` one row of 20
  failures became rows of 12 and 8, with the same minimal schedule.

The control transcripts did not change: `hydo-control`'s corpus tests passed unchanged, and the
two Redis runs of part 7 had the same control hash.

**What is left.** Open items 112, 150, 162 and 166 say what stays of each part.

## Milestone 329 (tentative number): conditional writes on the s3 emulator, the s3 proxy's lost uploads, and the shell assertion SDK

A user's onboarding with 0.4.1 on the Mac named three gaps. The user's system writes S3 objects
with Rust's `object_store` and its conditional writes, and the user did not know whether the s3
emulator honours them. Through the s3 emulator's proxy, uploads stored
empty objects (open item 162). And `hydo guide sdks` named the shell assertion SDK
`hydo/stack/hydoassert/hydo_assert.sh`, which no release ships. Each fix is its own commit.

**The s3 proxy's lost uploads (open item 162).** The pinned rclone 1.76.0 ran under Docker on this
Mac, with this tree's `hydo-world` as its proxy, and four clients wrote objects through the proxy
and directly. The cause was the proxy's answer, not the request body:

- The proxy dropped the service's `Content-Length` from every answer. An answer to a `HEAD` has no
  body, so it went out with no size at all. rclone 1.76.0 as a client reads the size after each
  upload: it read 0, printed `corrupted on transfer: sizes differ src 6 vs dst 0`, and deleted the
  object it had just written, three times. `object_store` 0.14.2 failed every `head()` with
  `MissingContentLength`.
- An answer body over 2,048 bytes went out chunked without `Content-Length`, as Go's server writes
  a handler's answer of unknown length. `object_store`'s `get()` of such an object failed with
  `MissingContentLength` too.
- The proxy cut every request body to its first 1 MiB, as a fake does. The AWS CLI's `PUT` of
  3,000,000 bytes failed with `IncompleteBody`, and a body cut that way would be a shorter object.

Now the proxy keeps the service's `Content-Length`: in the answer to a `HEAD` it is written as the
service sent it, and an answer with a body of that length goes out with it, not chunked. Go's
server does the same with a `Content-Length` that a handler sets. An `http` proxy forwards the whole
request body, up to 512 MiB, and answers a larger one `413`. A fake still reads the first 1 MiB.
The `aws-chunked` bodies of the AWS SDKs' signed streaming uploads and `Expect: 100-continue` were
forwarded correctly before and after.

**What rclone does with conditional writes.** `object_store` sends `If-None-Match: *` for
`PutMode::Create` and `If-Match: <etag>` for `PutMode::Update`. rclone 1.76.0 answered both as S3
does, directly and through the proxy, with `curl` and with `object_store` 0.14.2:

| Request | rclone 1.76.0 |
|---|---|
| `If-None-Match: *`, a new key | 200 |
| `If-None-Match: *`, an existing key | 412 `PreconditionFailed`; `object_store`: `AlreadyExists` |
| `If-Match` with the object's ETag | 200 |
| `If-Match` with another ETag | 412; `object_store`: `Precondition` |
| `If-Match` on a missing key | 404 |

In 30 rounds of 8 parallel writers of one new key with `If-None-Match: *`, one writer won each
round. In 30 rounds of 8 parallel updates of one key with its ETag, one won each round. The same
held through the proxy. So no newer rclone is needed, and nothing was re-pinned.

**`H=` faults that answer 412.** A system's code for a lost race runs only when another writer
wins. Two format-1 additions let a project make that happen:

- `if_header:` on a route of a fake or an `http` proxy: the route takes only a request with that
  header.
- `errors:` on a route of an `http` proxy, as on a fake's route since Milestone 249.

The s3 emulator's proxy now has the routes `put_if_absent` (a `PUT` with `If-None-Match`) and
`put_if_match` (a `PUT` with `If-Match`) before `put_object`. Each answers an `H=` rule
`status=412` with S3's `PreconditionFailed` XML, as `application/xml`, without reaching rclone:
`H=s3.put_if_absent@3-6:status=412`. `hydo explore --protocol-faults` draws the statuses of an
`http` proxy's `errors:` too, so it draws 412 on these routes. A manifest with an s3 emulator
gets two more `H=` targets, so the explorer draws other schedules for it. No recorded example
has an s3 emulator: the checkout example is not in `hydo/onboard/recorded.json`.

**The shell assertion SDK.** Both release trees ship it as `hydo/sdk/hydo_assert.sh`
(`build-release.sh` of each platform), and every `hydo` prints it with `hydo guide
hydo_assert.sh`, from a link in `hydo-agents`' `embed/`, so a `cargo install` has it too. `hydo
guide sdks` has the recipe: copy it into the project, list it in `root.files`, and source it in
the workload. hydo puts it into no image by itself, so no image's bytes move. The SDK's default
output is now `/dev/console`, which every engine's guest has, instead of `/dev/ttyS0`, which only
the x86_64 guests have. No image carries the SDK, so no recorded value moved.

**Evidence.**

- Native, under Docker with the pinned rclone image (arm64 digest `fbcca19e…`) and this tree's
  `hydo-world` as the proxy on this Mac:
  - before the fix: rclone 1.76.0's `copyto` of a 6-byte file through the proxy failed as above and
    left no object; `object_store`'s `head()` failed; the AWS CLI's 3 MB `PUT` failed with
    `IncompleteBody`.
  - after it: rclone's `copyto` of 6 bytes and of 20,000,000 bytes in 5 MB parts read back equal
    (`rclone cat | cmp`); `object_store` created, updated, read a 3 MB object and a multipart object
    of two 5 MiB parts with the right sizes; the AWS CLI's 3 MB `PUT` stored 3,000,000 bytes.
  - The AWS CLI's multipart upload (its CRT client) failed directly against rclone too, with
    `AWS_ERROR_S3_MISSING_UPLOAD_ID`, so it is no fault of the proxy.
- `hydo-world`'s test `proxy_s3::the_s3_proxy_carries_real_clients_uploads` runs the request
  shapes through the `hydo-world` program in front of a small S3 service in the test: rclone's
  `PUT` and `HEAD`, the AWS SDKs' `aws-chunked` body after `Expect: 100-continue`, a 3 MB body
  with `HEAD` and `GET`, and the conditional routes with an `H=` rule `status=412`. The unit test
  `a_route_with_if_header_fits_only_a_request_with_the_header`, the manifest's
  `the_s3_proxy_has_routes_of_conditional_writes_that_answer_412` and
  `if_header_and_errors_are_for_http_proxy_routes`. `xcheck`'s transcript of the Go version did
  not move.
- The shell SDK: the test `shell_sdk::the_shell_sdk_s_records_and_a_raw_line_reach_the_property_table`
  of `hydo-explore` runs every function of the SDK with the host's tools and reads the records
  into the property table. On the Mac engine, with the released 0.4.1, a workload that sourced
  the SDK from `root.files` and wrote one raw `printf 'HYDO-ASSERT {...}' > /dev/console` line
  gave a `result.json` whose property table listed `shell.step_ran` (`always`), `shell.reached`
  (`reachable`), `shell.tmp_writable` (`eventually`) and `raw.printf` (`sometimes`), each `PASS`.
  The SDK before the change gave the same table there.

**What moved.** No recorded value. The changed `hydo-world` (the proxy's `Content-Length`, whole
bodies, `if_header:`, the proxies' `errors:`) reaches a release at its next re-pin. A proxied
request body over 1 MiB now changes the record's `body=` hash, which no recorded run has. The
explorer's corpus golden (`hydo-explore`'s `corpus-full.txt`) is re-recorded, because the checkout
example's manifest has two more `H=` targets. hydo-build's and hydo-manifest's equivalence
corpora, which already failed (open items 115 and 165), get the new known keys of a route in 12
and more answers; they were not re-recorded.

**What is left.** Open item 116: the proxy's fix and the conditional routes ran through
`hydo-world` natively and in its tests, not in a VM, because a VM run needs the re-pinned
`hydo-world` in the guest.

## Milestone 330 (tentative number): what a user's second onboarding round taught the strategies and the skill

A user onboarded a distributed query engine of their own with hydo 0.4.1 on the Mac engine
(2026-11-20). The system has schedulers, workers, a control plane of three Raft nodes, an object
store, and caches. The project is private, so no tracked file names it, its services, or its
files. This milestone puts what the user's two rounds taught into `hydo guide strategies`, the
onboarding skill, and the playbook. No code changed.

**The evidence.** The first round ran one control-plane node, one scheduler, the caches off, and
a workload that recorded a stuck query and an unreadable result as unknown. It explored 20 seeds
and found no bug. The second round ran production's shape: two schedulers, three control-plane
nodes, and the replication of results and the caches on. It added two `eventually_` checks:
every accepted query reaches a final state, and a completed query's result stays readable after
the heal. It explored 60 seeds with `--strategy process` and found two bugs. Each shrank to a
small schedule and replayed with one fingerprint:

- A pause of one worker for 8 s, past the failure detector's timeout. A scheduler marked the
  worker dead and never cleared the mark, because it keeps the mark by the worker's id, which
  changes only at a restart. Queries stayed running forever. The shrinker reduced a schedule of
  4 faults to the pause alone.
- A kill of the worker that held a completed query's results, after a pause of one scheduler.
  The query stayed completed, and every read of its results failed.

The guide's entry on kills had said that a pause of a service alone found nothing (a 15 s pause
of a Hatchet engine). The first bug is a counter-example: a kill gives the worker a new identity,
which the stale mark does not name, so only a pause shows the mark.

**The guide.** `hydo/guide/strategies.md`:

- A new section "The system's shape" with two entries. "Production's topology": copy the replica
  counts, the cluster sizes, and the enabled features from the deployment manifests, and shrink
  only the memory; `hydo k8s` gives a Deployment one service only. "The features behind a flag":
  a cache that production turns on runs code, here conditional writes of its manifests to the
  object store, that no fault reaches while it is off. hydo's S3 emulator was not checked for
  conditional writes, and the user ran MinIO as a service instead.
- A new check entry, "How each unknown outcome ends": an outcome that the client records as
  unknown is a property that no check judges. For each, an `eventually_` check says how it must
  end, with `within=` above the system's own timeout, and a second check says that a completed
  result stays readable. Its example stops at the first operation that has not ended, because
  the user's first version, which asked about every query on every poll, ended a run as `ERROR
  check: exit budget exhausted`.
- A new fault entry, "Pauses of a service past its failure detector", after the kills. The kills
  entry gains the second bug and the counter-example.
- The table "Start here" gains a row for a distributed query or compute engine. The findings
  for every type of system gain production's shape, the unknown outcomes, and a second round
  after a clean exploration.

`hydo/guide/checks.md`, "What not to check", says that whether an unknown operation ends is a
property, with a pointer to the entry.

**The skill.** `plugin/skills/onboard/`:

- Step 1: when the user is not the system's owner, derive the promises from the deployment
  manifests and the code (timeouts, leases, retries, replication), and mark each "unconfirmed by
  the owner" in the report.
- Step 3.3 and `references/inventory.md`: copy production's shape from the deployment manifests,
  scaled down only in memory, and tell the user each difference.
- Step 3.4 and `references/choosing-checks.md` (items 3 and 7): the unknown-outcome rule and the
  check that a completed result stays readable.
- Step 4: read the RAM and disk warnings of `hydo build --check` (Milestone 324) before the first
  run (round 1's item 11, a root too large for the guest's RAM that the verdict blamed on the
  network). After a first exploration without a finding, run a second round with more seeds, the
  strategies' fault families, the liveness checks, and production's shape before reporting "no
  bugs".
- Step 5: the report names the unconfirmed promises, the differences from production's shape,
  and the explorations of each round.

The skill keeps its version, 2.4.0, in `metadata.version`, `plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`
and the marketplace entry: the user is deciding the skill's version scheme, and the lead sets it
at the merge. `skill_check::` checks that the three agree, not that a content change raises them.

**The playbook.** `docs/ONBOARDING-PLAYBOOK.md`: section 3's table gains the pause of a service
past its failure detector, and its lesson on pauses names the counter-example. Phase 1 derives
unconfirmed promises and reads the deployment manifests for the shape. Phase 2 fixes the build's
RAM warnings before the first run. Phase 3 starts with the checks of the unknown outcomes and
ends with a second round before a report of no bugs.

**Checks.** The CLI golden `cli.jsonl` moved in 8 answers of `hydo skill install`, 4 on each
platform. Only the hashes of the three changed skill files differ: SKILL.md,
`references/choosing-checks.md`, and `references/inventory.md`. The guide's topics have no

`hydo`'s whole test program (`cli_matches_golden`, `agents_equivalence`, and `docs::` among
