ci/consolidate-tests.sh --check`. Nothing recorded moved: no engine, image, guest program, or
example changed.

**What is left.** The user's other items are outside this milestone: among them, the S3
emulator's conditional writes, `hydo explore` exiting 0 when it refuses for memory, and the
inspect sessions that hold guest RAM.

## Milestone 331 (tentative number): each image service's own `/tmp`, and `root.share_images` on again

A user's onboarding with 0.4.1 on the Mac found exploration speed bound by memory. A guest of
5 GB gave the explorer one worker, at about 50 s per schedule. Each service of one image got a
copy of the image's root, and on the Mac the root lives in the guest's RAM.
`root.share_images: true` gives the services of one image one unpacked tree. Since Milestone 324
`hydo compose` writes it commented out, because of open item 147: in the TiKV example
(Milestone 287), with the key on, each store found the other stores' address lock in `/tmp`,
although MANIFEST.md said that each service of a shared tree has its own `/tmp`. This milestone
finds the cause, gives each image service its own `/tmp` from the fingerprint epoch 5, measures
what sharing saves, and has `hydo compose` write the key on again.

**The cause.** The key was not the cause. Every image service's launcher
(`/etc/hydo/oci/<service>/run`) and its `hydo-oci` helper (`exec`) bind the guest's `/proc`,
`/sys`, `/dev`, `/tmp` and `/data` into the service's root (`hydo-build/src/oci.rs`, `BINDS`).
The bind of `/tmp` is the guest's own `/tmp`, so every image service sees one `/tmp`, with
`root.share_images` and without it. MANIFEST.md said so in its section on image services ("`/tmp`
is shared, so `$HYDO_ACKED` etc. are the same files inside"), and its comment of
`root.share_images` said the opposite ("each on its own mount of it with its own /tmp"). It was
a bind of its own, of the same folder. The TiKV example never ran without the key, because three
copies of the image did not fit the engine's disk, so only runs with the key showed the lock.

**The reproduction.** On the Mac engine, with the public image `alpine:3.20` (`docker save
--platform linux/arm64`) and `guest.ram_mib: 2048`. Three services of the image, `s1` to `s3`,
each run the same shell command, as TiKV locks a file named after its listen address. When
`/tmp/addr.lock` exists, the command prints `addr in use by <the name in the file>` and exits 1.
Otherwise it writes its name to `/tmp/addr.lock` and to `/tmp/own.<name>`, and sleeps. A check
lists each service's `/tmp` through `hydo-oci` and fails when a service sees another's
file. `disk=none | run` gave:

| hydo | `root.share_images` | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 0.4.1 (epoch 4) | false | `ERROR service start (s2)`: `addr in use by s1` |
| 0.4.1 (epoch 4) | true | `ERROR service start (s2)`: `addr in use by s1` |
| this tree (epoch 5) before the fix | true | `ERROR service start (s2)`: `addr in use by s1` |
| this tree (epoch 5) with the fix | true | `OK`; each service sees only `addr.lock`, `hydo` and its own file |
| this tree (epoch 5) with the fix | false | `OK`, the same |

With the fix and the key on, `K=s2@1+1` and `disk=cut | run C=1` passed too: a restart and a
recovery boot bind the service's own `/tmp` again.

**The fix.** From the fingerprint epoch 5 (`hydo_image::defaults`, the new `oci_own_tmp`) the
launcher's block of Milestone 317, under the service's lock and once per boot, binds the
service's own `/tmp`:

```sh
for d in proc sys dev; do hmnt $R/$d || $BB mount --bind /$d $R/$d || exit 125; done
hmnt $R/tmp || { $BB mkdir -p /tmp/oci/s2 && $BB chmod 1777 /tmp/oci/s2 && $BB mount --bind /tmp/oci/s2 $R/tmp; } || exit 125
hmnt $R/tmp/hydo || { $BB mkdir -p /tmp/hydo $R/tmp/hydo && $BB mount --bind /tmp/hydo $R/tmp/hydo; } || exit 125
hmnt $R/.hydo/tmp || $BB mount --bind /tmp $R/.hydo/tmp || exit 125
hmnt $R/data || $BB mount --bind /data $R/data || exit 125
```

- The service's `/tmp` is the guest's folder `/tmp/oci/<service>`, mode 1777, so the workload,
  the checks and `logs:` find a file the service writes to its `/tmp/x` at `/tmp/oci/<service>/x`.
  It is in the guest's `/tmp`, so a power cut loses it as before, and a restart keeps it, as
  Docker keeps a container's `/tmp` across a restart.
- The guest's `/tmp/hydo` is bound at the service's `/tmp/hydo`: `$HYDO_ACKED`, `$HYDO_OUTCOMES`,
  `$HYDO_FAILED`, `$HYDO_LOG`, the launcher's lock and done files, and the pages' records of
  `browser:` (`/tmp/hydo/web`) are the same files inside and outside.
- The guest's own `/tmp` is bound at `/.hydo/tmp`, a new folder of the image's tree beside hydo's
  busybox. The SDKs read the BUGGIFY configuration from the guest's `/tmp/hydo-buggify`, which the
  controller writes, so the launcher passes `HYDO_BUGGIFY_FILE=/.hydo/tmp/hydo-buggify` unless
  the service's `env:` sets the variable. A project whose services shared files in `/tmp` can
  use `/.hydo/tmp` too.

An image built before epoch 5 keeps its launcher and binds the guest's `/tmp`. The test
`hydo-build` `oci::tests::each_image_service_has_its_own_tmp_from_epoch_5` runs the launchers of
epochs 4 and 5, with and without a shared tree, with a busybox stand-in that records the mounts.
Milestone 317's test of the shared tmpfs passes with the new block. The example
`compose-voting-browser` (in no recorded list) read the browser's screenshots in the guest's
`/tmp/gui/shots`; its workload now reads them in `/tmp/oci/browser/gui/shots`.

**What sharing saves.** On the Mac engine, with the public image `ghcr.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v2.1.0`
(arm64, 8 layers, 4,084 entries), three services that only sleep, and `guest.ram_mib: 2048`. The
workload printed `/proc/meminfo` after the services started:

| | initramfs | `Shmem` | `MemAvailable` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root.share_images: false` | 146.5 MiB | 362.3 MiB | 1,548.3 MiB |
| `root.share_images: true` | 51.0 MiB | 125.6 MiB | 1,789.5 MiB |

The initramfs root is a tmpfs, so its files count as `Shmem`. Each copy of the image's root took
about 118 MiB of guest RAM, and sharing gave 241 MiB back. The values were the same at epoch 4
(0.4.1) and at epoch 5, within 3 MiB. For the explorer on a Mac, a worker needs about twice
`guest.ram_mib` plus 256 MiB of the host (`hydo_engine::Engine::max_workers`). So each MiB that
sharing takes off the guest saves 2 MiB per worker. Sharing does not make the guest smaller by
itself: the project's `guest.ram_mib` is the user's. For four services of an image of 1,201 MiB
unpacked (Milestone 324's proof), sharing takes 3,603 MiB of roots off the guest. A guest that
held four copies can then be about 3.5 GiB smaller, and a worker about 7 GiB smaller. On the
user's Mac, with 5.8 GB free, a 5 GB guest gave one worker. A 2.5 GB guest would give two.

**`hydo compose`.** It writes `root.share_images: true` again for services of one image, with a
comment that names the services of each image and says what the key does:

```yaml
  # kv_0, kv_1 and kv_2 run one image, registry.example.com/kv/server:2.1.
  # They share one unpacked copy of their image in the root, each service with its own
  # /tmp and mounts. false gives each service a copy of its own, and on the Mac the root
  # lives in the guest's RAM (MANIFEST.md, "root").
  share_images: true
```

The importer's goldens were recorded again for these lines only: the 28 cases of
`hydo-compose/tests/golden.json` that Milestone 324 moved, and `tests/golden/k8s-cluster.yaml`.
hydo-build's `tests/golden/oci/answers.json` was recorded again for the new launchers and the
folder `/.hydo/tmp` only, and the CLI golden for the new text of `hydo guide manifest`. MANIFEST.md (the
`root:` comment, the section on image services, the compose table, `mounts:`), `hydo guide
services`, `hazards` and `error-logs` say what an image service's `/tmp` is now.

**What moves.** Every image built at epoch 5 with an image service has a new launcher, a new
folder `/.hydo/tmp` in its tree, and the variable `HYDO_BUGGIFY_FILE` in its services'
environment. These are the 7 images that Milestone 317 moves already (`hvm/voting`,
`hvm/redis-oci`, `hvx/redis-oci`, `hvx/restate-oci`, `hvx/voting`, `hvx/voting-generated`,
`hvx/voting-loopback`; 21 runs). Their workloads and checks reach the services through `hydo-oci`
and `/tmp/hydo`, so no verdict is expected to move. They wait for the pass before 0.5.0 (open item
105, docs/REBASELINE.md section 29). A manifest that `hydo compose` writes is input, and the
examples' Compose-made manifests were not written again.

**What is left** (open items 147 and 166). The TiKV example did not run again at epoch 5. A
manifest that `hydo compose` wrote from Milestone 324 to this one keeps the line commented out.
A `logs:` or `errors.files` path under an image service's `/tmp` must name `/tmp/oci/<service>/`;
hydo does not map it. A socket that an image service makes in its `/tmp` is not reachable at the
same path from the workload. hvx and KVM did not run the new launcher; it is the same shell on
every engine.

## Milestone 332 (tentative number): the onboarding skill has hydo's version

The user decided on 2026-11-20 that the onboarding skill's version is hydo's version from hydo
0.5.0 on. Until then the skill had a version line of its own, 1.0.0 to 2.4.0, released as GitHub
releases tagged `skill-v<version>` (Milestone 170). There are no outside users, so nothing keeps
the old line beyond the version order below.

Where the version lives. The four version fields equal `hydo/VERSION`, now 0.4.1:
`metadata.version` and `metadata.hydo-min` in `plugin/skills/onboard/SKILL.md`, the `version`
of `plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, and the `version` of the plugin entry in
`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`. `metadata.hydo-min` stays and equals the version. The skill
ships in hydo's release and needs the hydo of its own version, and the skill's step 0 reads
`hydo-min` to tell the user to upgrade an older hydo. Keeping the key changes no text of the
skill's steps. `skill_check::` fails when a field differs from `hydo/VERSION`, so a version bump
changes them together. `hydo/dist/registries.sh versions` checks the four fields too.

How the release carries the skill. Both `build-release.sh` scripts run
`hydo/dist/skill/build-skill-release.sh` into their output folder. It refuses a skill whose
version is not `hydo/VERSION` (or `HYDO_VERSION`), packs `hydo-skill-<version>.tar.gz` twice,
compares the bytes, and prints the archive's line for the release's `SHA256SUMS`. The release
`v<version>` gets the archive as a sixth file, with its line in `SHA256SUMS`
(docs/RELEASING.md, steps 2, 6 and 7). From 0.5.0 on, `registries.sh release`, which the release
workflow's `check` job runs, requires the archive. `hydo skill update` and `hydo update` take the
skill from the newest `v<x>.<y>.<z>` release of the release list that they already read. Each
command still makes one request (Milestone 322). `hydo update` takes the skill of the release it
installs, also with `--version V`. The kept answer `~/.hydo/update-check.json` no longer has a
`skill` key, and a kept `skill` key that an older hydo wrote is not read. A release before 0.5.0
carries no skill, and `hydo skill update` then says so and changes nothing.

How 2.x compares. `hydo_agents::release::skill_lt` orders every version from 1.0.0 to 2.4.0, the
ended line, before every other version. Within one line the numbers decide. `hydo skill update`
and `hydo update` compare installed copies and Claude Code's plugin installs with it, so a copy
of 2.4.0 is behind 0.5.0. The skill's step 0 runs `hydo update --check`, so it gets the same
answer. `hydo doctor` compares only hydo's own version. `skill_check::` refuses a `hydo/VERSION`
from 1.0.0 to 2.4.0, because hydo would then take its own skill for an old one.

Claude Code's plugin update. Claude Code's documentation ("Plugin loading reference", section
"Versions and updates", and "Host and maintain a marketplace", section "Release a new version")
says that Claude Code installs a new copy when the plugin's computed version differs from the
recorded one. It compares the strings, not their order, so 2.4.0 to 0.5.0 is an update. This Mac's
Claude Code setup was not changed to try it. If Claude Code does not offer the update, the user
runs `claude plugin marketplace update hydo` and `claude plugin update hydo@hydo`, and if it still
says that the plugin is current, `claude plugin uninstall hydo@hydo` and `claude plugin install
hydo@hydo`. `hydo guide update` and docs/RELEASING.md say so.

What changed in the documents:

- docs/RELEASING.md: the section "Releasing the onboarding skill (separate from hydo releases)"
  is now "The onboarding skill (ships with each hydo release)". A skill change ships with the
  next hydo release, and a small fix with a patch release. Steps 1, 2, 6 and 7 name the skill's
  archive. The new subsection "Once, after 0.5.0 is published" gives the lead three steps:
  - write a "Before you upgrade" line into 0.5.0's notes, because hydo 0.4.1's `hydo update`
    updates hydo only;
  - delete the releases and tags `skill-v1.0.0` to `skill-v2.4.0`;
  - check the update from a copy of 2.4.0.
- docs/PUBLISHING.md, docs/INSTALL.md, `hydo guide update` and the skill's
  `references/install.md` describe one version. The text of the skill's steps did not change.

The tests: the fake release server of `tests/update.rs` publishes the skill in hydo's release
`v<newest>` beside an old `skill-v2.9.0` tag that nothing may read. Copies of 2.0.0, 2.1.0 and
2.3.3, and a plugin install of 2.0.0, are updated to the release's version. `hydo skill
update`'s unit tests cover a copy of 2.4.0 updated to 0.5.0 and a release before 0.5.0 without a
skill. `skill_check::` has a test of a hydo version bump without the skill's.

What is left: between this commit and 0.5.0, hydo 0.4.1 compares the plugin's 0.4.1 on `main`
with the release `skill-v2.4.0`, so it offers a Claude Code plugin update that changes nothing.
Deleting the `skill-v` releases after 0.5.0 ends it. No real release carries the skill yet, and
`claude plugin update` from 2.4.0 to a lower version ran only as the documentation describes it.
Nothing recorded moved.

## Milestone 333 (tentative number): what the fourth `hydo fuzz` evaluation found, fixed

The fourth evaluation (Milestone 327, `docs/design/function-fuzzing-evaluation-4.md`) listed
nine fixes, worst first. This milestone makes them, each its own commit. None changes an
engine, an image, or a recorded value. The tests are `cargo test -p hydo-contracts --test it
fuzz_m333::`, on the new fixture `hydo/crates/hydo-contracts/tests/fuzz-m333`.

**0. Line tables.** A `debug = false` for the dev profile in the user's cargo configuration
left a panic inside the standard library at the library's line, because the backtrace that
places it at the crate's frame needs the line tables. The harness's builds now set
`CARGO_PROFILE_<P>_DEBUG=1` unless the environment sets it. Commit `5fad3587`.

**1. No false `broken`.** A comparison of a list, an option, a tuple, or a structure that holds
a value that hydo does not read is undecided, and the reason names the type. smallvec's
`into_vec` had broken with `result = [<not read>]`. Commit `e3e01775`.

**2. Associated types of a type parameter.** `A::Item` and `<A as Array>::Item` resolve through
the `with` line's type and the crate's `impl` of the trait for it, matched by the block's type
parameters: `impl<T, const N: usize> Array for [T; N] { type Item = T; }` makes `A::Item` a
`u8` for `with A = [u8; 4]`. It works in parameters, results and closures' arguments. An
associated type of an `impl` block (`type Item = T::Item;`) no longer counts as a type alias of
the crate, and `Self::<name>` now binds the block's type parameters
(`impl<T> Add<T> for NotNan<T>` for `NotNan<f64>`). smallvec's 18 contracts all ran and held.
Commit `9ec807ce`.

**3. An error with a field of a private module.** The test module writes a type of the crate
that the function's module does not import by its path from the crate's root
(`crate::error::ErrorKind`). semver's five parsers built and ran. The `use` lines are also kept
by the inline module they stand in. Commit `59745d86`.

**4. Constructors.** A `build` line without arguments builds (`VersionReq::default()`). A
constructor that returns a `Result` or an `Option` is found in the crate's sources, or marked
with `)?`. The harness passes its `Ok` or `Some` value and answers `Z` for `Err` or `None`, and
the report counts such inputs apart from `requires`. The refusals leave out `unsafe` functions
and macro metavariables. They name the trait of an ambiguous `from` and rank `Default` last.
For a type with a `build` line already, they name a line for the argument's type. Commit `fa8aaba4`.

**5. The `with` lines' types in parameters' types, and more values read.** A generic structure
whose fields are all `pub` is generated field by field (`OrderedFloat::<f64>`), a built type's
text takes the `with` types, and `with T = &[u8]` passes a slice. From the evaluation's sixth
friction:

- a structure with a lifetime parameter or a reference field is read field by field;
- `Cow<str>` and `Cow<[T]>` read as the value they hold;
- a built type's public fields read without a `read` line;
- a variant behind `#[cfg(...)]` is never generated.

Commit `22659074`.

**6. The smaller items.**

- A `with` line of no type parameter is refused.
- A nested `input` path names the constructor's arguments.
- `--fn <Trait>::` selects a trait's methods, and `--features F` passes features.
- Reports name the crate's library name (`ordered_float::`), while the seed keeps the package's
  name.
- The copy allows dead code.
- Two floats are both NaN, or equal, in about one input in six of a function with two of them.
- An index that `requires index < len(v)` names is generated inside the list.
- A clause reads a string's byte by index, and two values of one enumeration compare with `==`.

Commit `30da22c8`.

**7. `build` lines across modules and of generic `impl` blocks.** Following the refusals
without a helper showed two more gaps. A `build` line's type and constructor are written by
their path from the crate's root when the function's module does not import them (base64's
`Alphabet` in `engine`). A constructor's `impl` block's type parameters bind to the type's
arguments, so `NotNan::new(val: T)` takes an `f64` in `impl NotNan<f64>`. Commit `e6d6c8e0`.

**The proof.** The six crates came fresh from cargo's registry folder with the evaluator's first
contracts, which have no helper, using seed 1 and 1,000 inputs on the Mac. `main` at `99aba8ed`
fuzzed 51 of the 88 library contracts, and this milestone 76. The other 12 have no `build` line
in those contracts, and each refusal names a line that builds. With those lines all 88 build
without a helper. No verdict after is hydo's own error. The 56 property functions kept their
verdicts. All three known upstream issues showed again: textwrap's pull requests 647 and 654,
and ordered-float's issue 143, now on 1,000 calls instead of 20,000. The third evaluation's
either, with 14 contracts written again from its page, went from 13 held and 1 `not judged` to
14 held. The section "After Milestone 333" of the evaluation page has the tables. Nothing new was
found, and nothing was posted.

The checks used a target folder outside the checkout, because other sessions shared the
checkout's. Two tests of `cargo test -p hydo --test it` failed with it from the first check on:
`onboard::the_fetch_step_names_the_release_fetcher_when_it_is_not_on_path` and
`update::a_checkout_build_is_left_alone_with_the_commands`. Both read where `hydo` was built,
which this milestone does not change.

**What is left.** Open item 163. Nothing recorded moved.

## Milestone 334 (tentative number): the failing run's own frames, and the pages read back

Two gaps of the walks through a web app's pages (Milestones 258 to 273) are closed, each in its
own commit.

The first gap was the evidence of a failure. Only one step was recorded, the step that a finding
names, because a run copied at most 1 MiB of files out of the guest (Milestone 264). The
recording was a second run with `,rec` and timing of its own, so a failure that depends on the
timing could pass in it, and then no video showed the failure (open item 151). A walk that a
power cut ended left nothing at all, because its files stayed in the first boot's `/tmp` (open
items 124 and 137).

The second gap was what a user sees. The page checks judged what a page did, and a project's own
rule judged the database. No check said whether the pages still showed what the server had said
it saved.

### Part 1: every run keeps its own frames

What the walker does now, in images built from this commit on:

- After the page opens and after every action, it takes a JPEG of the viewport at three eighths
  of its size (480 by 270 pixels, quality 50). It uses the page's DevTools session
  (`Page.captureScreenshot` with a scaled clip), not `page.screenshot`, which a trace records as
  an action. It writes one line to `shots/film.jsonl`: the step, the action's number, the file
  and its size, the action's sentence, the page's path, the guest's time, and `notes`. The notes
  are the uncaught errors, the failed requests and the error elements that the watcher recorded
  since the frame before.
- Every step records a Playwright trace (DOM snapshots, no screenshots). Its index line says
  `only: failed`. With `,rec` the recorded step's video and trace are copied as before.
- The expansion of `browser.explore` writes `/etc/hydo/walk-film`. `agent::plan_of_image` reads
  it and sets `Plan::film`. An image built before, of any fingerprint epoch, sends the commands
  that it sent before. The epoch could not decide this, because an image built at epoch 5 before
  this commit has the older walker.

What the controller does for an image with the mark (`schedule/screens.rs`):

- After the verdict it copies the index's files, then `film.jsonl` and every frame that it
  names, then, when the verdict is not OK, the traces. The step that the verdict names ("walk
  step 3") comes first, then the latest steps.
- A boot copies at most 5 MiB (`BOOT_BYTES`), each file up to 3 MiB (`FILE_MAX`). An image
  without the mark keeps Milestone 264's copy, at most 1 MiB per run.
- The reads go 16 at a time (`text::WINDOW`) before the controller waits for their replies. A
  frame's size is in its line, so every chunk of a group of frames is sent at once. A read that
  waits alone costs about a tenth of a second on hvx (Milestone 264).
- At a host power cut (`C=`, a reaction's `:cut`, and the flush of `cf=`), with every service
  frozen and after the ids are read, it copies the filmstrip and the trace of the last step before
  the engine cuts the power. `/tmp` is a tmpfs, so the reads touch no disk. The recovery boot
  copies its own files after its verdict. `agent::take_screens` now also takes the recovery
  transcript's files, adds the index lines that are new, and appends a second `film.jsonl` to
  the first.

The engines' channels: 5 MiB as hex with its notes is about 10.5 MiB of agent lines. The hvx
engine keeps 16 MiB per boot (Milestone 264). The Mac and KVM engines read the agent's lines from
the console, which kept 4 MiB per boot; `CONSOLE_MAX` is 32 MiB now. A fingerprint hashes the
console up to its length, and a boot that wrote more than 4 MiB lost the agent's later lines and
never reached its verdict. So no recorded run has a different console, and no recorded value
moves.

`hydo report --html` of a run has a section "The walk, action by action" with one row of frames
per step: each frame with its action, its path and its notes. The step that a failing check
names, and every frame with notes, are marked. The read-back check's frames come last. The page
of an exploration shows each failure's filmstrip from `consoles/<tag>.screens/` in the
failure's details, under its timeline.

### Part 2: the pages read back

`browser.read_back` (a format-1 addition, with `explore` only) adds the invariant
`<browser>.acked_shown` after the other page checks. Its entries name the acknowledged writes
that make an object (`writes`, a regular expression over `<METHOD> <path>` of the
`<METHOD>:<path>=<id>` words of `$HYDO_ACKED`, Milestone 273). They also give the page that lists
such an object (`page`), the Playwright selector by which it shows (`shows`), and the later
writes that remove it on purpose (`unless`). `{id}` and the named groups of `writes` fill them.
`read_back: true` takes one entry of defaults: every object that a POST or a PUT returned an id
of, on the start page, as a link whose path ends with `/<kind>/<id>`.

The check is `node walk.mjs --read-back "$HYDO_ACKED"` in the browser's service:

- It runs at the end of the run and in the recovery boot after a power cut, whose `$HYDO_ACKED`
  starts with the first boot's words.
- It starts a fresh browser with the walk's saved session. A recovery boot has none, so it then
  runs `read_back.setup`, or the walk's own setup.
- It opens each page once and waits up to `wait_ms` (10 s) until every object of that page
  shows.
- A page that lacks an object gets a screenshot, `read-back-<n>.png`, which the finding names,
  and a frame in the filmstrip. Exit 0: every object shows, or no write named one; 1: one does
  not, or the pages could not be opened.
- It runs after the other page checks, because in a recovery boot it makes the record folder
  that they read as "no page ran in this boot".
- The explorer blanks generated ids in its signatures (`report::page_violation`), so a loss of
  two tasks and of three tasks is one signature.

The check is not on by default. The default entry guesses where an object shows, and a guess that
does not fit an app is a false finding. It judges an object's presence, not its content, and it
cannot see an object that the app shows only on a page that it does not open, or hides on
purpose.

## Milestone 335 (tentative number): copy-on-write guest RAM on the Mac engine

The user decided on 2026-11-20 to build copy-on-write VMs on the Mac engine (open item 36). An
explorer worker on the Mac was a whole VM. It held its guest RAM, locked with `mlock`, and S0 and
S1 in files of their own. The explorer counted twice the guest RAM and 256 MiB per worker. A user
with a 5 GB guest on a 32 GB Mac got one worker, and 60 seeds took about an hour. The design is
`docs/design/mac-cow.md`.

What changed in the engine (`hydo/crates/hydo-hvm`):

- A snapshot is a RAM base (`mem::Base`): a file in `HVM_SNAP_DIR` named
  `ram-v1-<length>-<tree hash>`, which holds the RAM's pages that are not zero and nothing writes
  after it is made. Another engine whose snapshot has the same bytes finds the file by its name.
  It uses the file only when each of its extents equals its RAM and its RAM is zero between them.
  A base is written to a temporary file and linked to its name, so a named file is complete. Each
  process holds a shared `flock` on its bases, and a base that nobody holds is removed when it is
  dropped and when an engine starts.
- Guest RAM is mapped from a base with `mmap(MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_FIXED)`, so the kernel copies a
  page at its first write. A restore destroys the VM, maps the base again and makes the VM
  (`Vmm::fresh_vm_from`). Right after a snapshot, guest RAM is mapped from the new base in the same
  VM and vCPU (`Vmm::rebase`, with `hv_vm_unmap` and `hv_vm_map`), except in the rewind mode. The
  instruction cache is made coherent over the base's extents.
- Guest RAM is not locked with RAM bases. A probe locked a private mapping of a 256 MiB file, and
  its footprint grew by 256 MiB, so `mlock` would copy every page.
- The RAM's part of a fingerprint still reads every page. The engine does not use
  `mach_vm_page_range_query` to skip pages, because its answer for a private page that macOS
  compressed was not shown.
- `HVM_RAM_SHARE=0` (`hydo-config`, INVENTORY.md) gives the engine of before.

What changed in the explorer: `hydo_engine::WorkerMemory` says what a pool needs, once for all
workers and per worker, and `Engine::worker_memory` gives it. For the Mac engine with RAM bases
(`hydo_engine::hvm::worker_memory`) it is half of the guest RAM once and half of the guest RAM and
256 MiB per worker. A worker still writes all of its guest's RAM before S0, so the pool's new boot
gate (`pool::BootGate`) lets only as many workers boot at once as fit. The pool line then says
`, 1 booting at once`. The memory warning names the shared part and the part per worker.

The images of the proofs. The release 0.4.1 built `release/examples/redis` (`31e90668…`) and
`release/examples/ledger-spin` (`0214abba…`) at the fingerprint epoch 4, the bytes of the list's
`hvm/release-redis` and `hvm/release-ledger-spin`. The Redis example was also built with
`guest.ram_mib` 2048 and 4096. Meilisearch's image of Milestone 295's example (2,048 MiB, an image
service, `network: bridge`) came from a platform run. "Before" is the engine of `main` at
`14e94083`.

Exactness. Every run below gave the same fingerprints, verdicts and control transcripts:

- The 7 recorded runs of `hvm/release-redis` and the 2 of `hvm/release-ledger-spin` gave their
  recorded `fp` and `ctl` with RAM bases and with `HVM_RAM_SHARE=0`. The quickstart's two are
  `05f433ee427f8e3c` (`ctl` `f8953914130df454`) and `2174995ebfb4d2d6` (`20a90cbaf59735ae`).
  ledger-spin's runs go through the rewind mode.
- `hydo explore` of Redis seeds 1-40 with its shrinks: before on 4 workers, and after on 4 and on
  1 worker and with `HVM_RAM_SHARE=0`. The `exploration.json` files are equal but for `--out`,
  and so are the 64 events of `events.jsonl` (every run's `fp`, `wfp` and `ctl`, the 8 failures,
  2 shrinks and the replays).
- Without shrinks: Meilisearch seeds 1-12 (18 events) and 1-60 (84 events), Redis 2,048 MiB seeds
  1-20 (23 events), Redis 4,096 MiB seeds 1-20 (23) and 1-60 (72). Before ran on 1 or 2 workers,
  after on 3 to 6.
- `hydo explore --search state`, Redis seeds 1-30, one worker: the 42 events and the 31 records of
  `state-search.jsonl` (15 snapshots, 10 branches) are equal but for the jobs' wall times.
- An `hydo inspect` session at the end of the power-cut run: six looks, each a restore of the
  stop's snapshot, printed the same 60 lines but for one `wall_ms`.

`hydo-bench rebaseline --check` did not run. Its images are built from this tree at the
fingerprint epoch 5, whose Mac values wait for the pass (open item 105), and its prefix takes the
tree's shared `target/release`. The recorded runs above are the list's epoch-4 values.

Memory. `footprint <pid>` was sampled every 3 s for every engine of each exploration, and the
bases' allocated size came from `du -k`. A worker after its boot:

| Example | Guest RAM | Before | After, median and largest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redis | 1,024 MiB | 1,133 MB, and 1.1 to 2.0 GB of snapshot files | 36 to 113 MB, 137 MB |
| Redis | 2,048 MiB | 2,119 MB | 119 MB, 129 MB |
| Redis | 4,096 MiB | 4,118 MB | 68 MB, 87 MB |
| Meilisearch | 2,048 MiB | 2,155 MB, and 2,220 MB of snapshot files | 171 MB, 1,153 MB |

In an exploration of 16 Meilisearch seeds with its shrinks a worker held 1,058 MB in the median
and 1,172 MB at most. The cause was not traced. A worker held all of its guest's RAM while it
booted: 1,252 MB for 1,024 MiB about 1 s after its start, and 102 MB after S0. Each base holds 60
MB of data for Redis and 535 MB for Meilisearch. The fingerprint reads every page, so a base's
holes become clean pages of zeros in the page cache, once for all workers: 4,096 of 4,096 MiB for
a base of the 4,096 MiB guest. A version that mapped only the extents and left the holes anonymous
was measured and dropped: macOS gives a process its own page for an anonymous page that is read,
and a 4,096 MiB worker held 3,957 MB in the median.

With 9.4 GB available, the explorer's count gives 4, 2 and 1 workers for 1,024, 2,048 and 4,096
MiB before, and 11, 6 and 3 after. The schedules per hour with those workers, without shrinks:

| Example, seeds 1-60 | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Redis, 4,096 MiB | 1 worker, 297 s, 742 schedules an hour | 3 workers, 54 s, 4,143 schedules an hour |
| Meilisearch, 2,048 MiB | 2 workers, 308 s, 1,285 schedules an hour | 6 workers, 320 s, 1,241 schedules an hour |

Two Meilisearch runs took 115 s and 130 s (`ERROR check: exit budget exhausted`), and they set
how long the exploration ran on any number of workers. The 6 workers used one core together most of that
time. A restore no longer compares every page of the RAM and the snapshot. Redis seeds 1-40 with
shrinks took 65 s before on 4 workers. After, they took 14 to 41 s on 4 workers and 18 to 19 s on
1 worker. The state search's jobs
took 42.1 s before and 27.0 s after. Other sessions shared the Mac, with load averages from 4 to
93, so the times are not exact.

What is left is in open item 36 and in `docs/design/mac-cow.md`, "What is left". hvx and KVM
workers share nothing between them. A worker still boots on its own. The estimate per worker
comes from two examples. Nothing recorded moved.

## Milestone 336 (tentative number): statistics of an exploration

The user asked for the statistics of an exploration. A person, and later a program that reads
hydo's files, needs to see how much was explored and decide how much more to run, with how many
workers or shards. Before, `exploration.json` counted the schedules, the failures and the wall
time, and nothing said whether more seeds would show anything new.

What was built. `hydo explore` writes `stats.json` beside `exploration.json`. It is a new
document of the results format (`StatsDoc`, type `stats`, an addition). Every number in it is the
host's record of the runs, so no run, fingerprint or verdict moved. It has four parts:

- The curve of new behaviour (`StatsCurve`). After each first run in seed order, it counts what
  the runs showed so far:
  - the distinct run fingerprints;
  - the distinct verdicts, by kind and signature;
  - the distinct property outcomes (`<id>: held`, `<id>: failed`, `<id>: reached`);
  - the distinct error kinds, for an image built with `errors:`;
  - the distinct error paths, when the engine watched them.

  It keeps the counts after 1, 2, 4, 8, ... runs, after every `total/64`-th run, and after the
  last. It also keeps the run numbers at which each judged measure grew. The judgement looks at
  the last quarter of the runs, at least 10, and gives `growing`, `flat` or `too-few` with one
  sentence. The fingerprints are counted but not judged, because two schedules almost always give
  two runs.
- The cost (`StatsCost`). It has the runs and the engine's seconds by role: first runs, re-runs,
  shrink runs, shrink runs of error kinds, and others. It has the spread of a first run's seconds
  and the engine's clock over the first runs, read from their control transcripts (VM exits on
  the Mac and KVM engines). The host CPU seconds and the largest resident memory of the explorer
  and of one engine process come from `getrusage`. Each worker's time busy, starting its engine,
  waiting for a quiet window, and idle comes from the pool's new ledger (`pool::Ledger`), with the
  share of the busy time that re-runs and shrinks took.
- The faults drawn (`StatsCoverage`). Each fault kind of the first runs' schedules has its runs,
  its targets, and its workload steps. The kinds that the manifest's `faults:` allows and no
  schedule drew are listed with the option that draws them, and so are the services that no fault
  named.
- The estimate (`StatsEstimate`). It says how many first runs fit in a budget:
  `shards × ⌊(budget − start) × workers ÷ job × (1 − share)⌋`. It works out an hour and
  eight hours on the exploration's workers, an hour on the workers this machine fits, and an hour
  on 4 and 20 shards. `hydo ci run`'s `seeds_from: history` now counts with the same function
  (`hydo_explore::stats::fit_count`).

`stats.json` also lists each first run with its seconds, its clock, and what it showed first
(`StatsRun`). `hydo explore --merge` reads the parts' files and makes the statistics of the whole
range. It puts the runs in seed order and keeps each key at its first run, so the curve is the one
that an exploration of the whole range gives. The costs and the coverage add up, and each part's
workers keep their part number. A part's own `stats.json` goes to `parts/<n>/`.

Where it shows. `hydo stats [DIR] [--json] [--budget TIME] [--workers N] [--shards N]` is a
command of its own, because it answers another question than `hydo report`. The report says what
broke, and the statistics say whether to run more, and on what. `hydo report <explore dir>`
prints a short section "How much was explored" and names `hydo stats`. The section has the cost,
the judgement, the kinds never drawn and an hour's estimate. `hydo report --html` has the same
section with one small chart per judged measure. The charts are inline SVG: a step line with a
dot at each run that grew, and the judgement's window shaded. The numbers and the faults drawn
are two folded tables. The page still loads nothing and runs no new script. `hydo guide workflow`
has the section "How much was explored, and whether to run more", which says how to read the
curve.

What a flat curve means, in the guide's words: more seeds of the same strategy and options mostly
repeat what these runs showed. It does not say that the system has no more bugs. Other fault
kinds, other strategies, a longer workload, or other checks can still find more.

The proof on the scripted engine. The scenario `merge_equals_one_exploration` now also checks
the statistics. The exploration of seeds 1-60 has 60 runs, four measures, shrink runs, three
workers, and fault kinds with targets and steps. The merge of its seven parts has the same curve,
the same runs with the same new keys, and the same coverage, with 21 workers in 7 parts. Unit
tests cover the curve and its judgement, the merge's renewal of keys, the reading of fault
tokens, the budget rule, and the property outcomes.

The proof on the Mac engine. The Redis quickstart (`~/.hydo/examples/redis`, built by the
released 0.4.1, epoch 4, 1,024 MiB of guest RAM) was explored with `hydo explore --seeds 1-60
--strategy swarm --workers 4`. Its `stats.json` is the example
`hydo/schema/examples/results/v1/mac-redis-stats/`:

- The curve was flat over the last 15 runs: 4 distinct verdicts, which grew at runs 1, 2, 12 and
  13, and 2 property outcomes, at runs 1 and 2. All 60 runs had their own fingerprint.
- The cost: 60 first runs took 66.7 s of the engine, 24 re-runs 27.1 s, and 9 shrink runs 14.9 s.
  Re-runs and shrinks took 39 % of the workers' busy time. A first run took 1.11 s of the engine
  on average (median 1.4 s, the longest 3.1 s) and 23,184 VM exits. The host CPU was 152 s for 62
  s of wall time. The largest engine process had 3,109 MiB resident and the explorer 742 MiB.
  The workers were busy 89 % of their time, starting their engines 7 %, and idle 4 %.
- The faults drawn: disk faults in 48 runs, network faults in 35 (at 15 of the 20 workload
  steps), power cuts in 34 (17 steps), crashes in 29 (11 steps), and the setting `R=` in 26. The
  manifest allows pauses, one-way network faults and clock jumps, and no schedule drew them: the
  swarm strategy draws them only with `--new-faults`.
- The estimate: a first run took 2.21 s on one worker and a worker 4.3 s to start, so an hour on
  4 workers fits about 3,945 first runs. The exploration measured 3,658 first runs an hour while
  its first runs ran.
- The same seeds in 2 parts (`--shard 1/2` and `2/2`) and `hydo explore --merge` gave the same
  curve, the same runs with the same new keys, and the same faults drawn. The merge has 18 shrink
  runs, because each part shrank its own failures (open item 153).
- An earlier exploration of the same seeds, on a busier machine, took 108.7 s instead of 62 s and
  gave the same 24 failures and the same curve.
- `hydo run` gave the quickstart's fingerprints `05f433ee427f8e3c` (`disk=none | run`) and
  `2174995ebfb4d2d6` (`disk=cut | run C=12 R=everysec`).

The explorer's goldens did not move, because `stats.json` is a file of its own, outside
`exploration.json` and `events.jsonl`. The main help of `hydo` gained the lines of `hydo stats`:
11 answers of `cli_matches_golden`, the main help on both platforms. `results-v1.json` gained the
new types, and `hydo-schema-compat` passes. The page's test reads the example: two charts, the
plain words, nothing loaded, and `hydo stats`'s lines within 80 columns.

What is left (open item 169):

- Guest time is not in the cost. The explorer has no guest clock for a run on every engine; the
  engine's clock is VM exits on the Mac and KVM and hvx's own units on hvx.
- The host CPU and the memory are the whole explorer's and its engine processes', not one run's.
  An engine in the explorer's process, as hvx's, counts with the explorer.
- The estimate assumes that each shard runs on a machine like this one, and that shrinking takes
  the same share of a longer exploration. It does not count the build and the download of a
  shard on a runner.
- Only the Mac engine ran it. hvx and KVM, an image with `errors:`, and an image whose error paths
  the engine watched did not run with it on a VM; the scripted engine covers the error kinds.
- An exploration made before this milestone has no `stats.json`, and `hydo stats` says so instead
  of reading `events.jsonl`.
- The waits for the Mac's shared VM lock are outside hydo, so the workers' time does not show
  them; the engine's own waits are inside its start.

## Milestone 337 (tentative number): shared beginnings of an exploration's runs, research

The question was whether the explorer can run a beginning that many schedules share once, take
a snapshot where they part, and continue each schedule from it, with every run exact. The
research note is `hydo/explore/RESEARCH-shared-prefix.md`, and its scripts are in
`hydo/explore/shared-prefix/`. Nothing of the product changed.

How it was measured. A run's inputs to the guest are its host part and the host controller's
sends, each at a guest clock value, and the control transcript records every send. Two runs with
the same host part are the same up to their first differing send. `prefix.py` builds a tree of an
exploration's runs from their transcripts and measures the clock that an earlier run already ran.
The data were 15 hvx explorations of nine examples (ClickHouse, Dragonfly, Iggy, Redpanda,
SurrealDB, TiKV, VictoriaMetrics, seven PostgreSQL image services, and web-shop's walk), read on
the bare-metal machine without a VM. The planned Mac explorations of the Redis quickstart, the
composed Redis example, and a state search did not run. The shared Mac VM lock stayed with another
session for more than 40 minutes, and this Mac's free disk fell to 12 GB with 17.7 GB of swap.

What is shared today. With the explorer's draws, the first runs of 13 explorations of databases
and queues shared 0.07 % of 12,590 s, even with `dseed=` left out and `disk=cut` counted as
`disk=none`. By the whole host part they shared nothing, because each seed draws its own `dseed=`.
The 184 runs of `disk=none | run` of the PostgreSQL exploration had one transcript and 184
fingerprints: on hvx `fnv_snapshot` hashes the disk's fault seed, classes, and probability, and
the Mac engine hashes the device's struct with its seed.

What keeps runs apart. The first range of the workload ends at the first fault's step, and its
program gets `HYDO_TO` of that step. A composed workload draws its own `W=` and a walk its own `I=`
per schedule, and both differ at the first workload command (0.1 % of a run on Iggy). A setting
token with a value other than the default and a strict power loss act before step 0. The timing tokens and the disk's policy act from the
workload's first instruction.

Other draws. Drawing the composition, the walk, and the setting tokens once per exploration would
save 3.3 % of the first runs' time (an estimated 415 s). Also starting the workload program once
per step, which needs a new fingerprint epoch, would save 10.9 % (1,366 s). Both lose search, and
drawing the first fault later loses more: 73 of the 106 failing first runs (69 %) had their first
fault in the first quarter of the steps.

Shrinks. A shrink's candidates share a beginning with earlier candidates: 43 % of the clock on
Dragonfly, 28 % on TiKV, and 10 % on web-shop. Only 5 % to 12 % of it is shared with the failing
run or the last failing candidate. Exact repeats of an earlier schedule took 88 s of Dragonfly's
418 s of shrinks, 238 s of TiKV's 1,124 s, and 300 s of web-shop's 2,988 s. The PostgreSQL
exploration drew 13 distinct schedules for 300 seeds, and its repeats took 800 s of 848 s.

The engines. `SNAP`, `RESUME`, and `agent::check_branch` exist since Milestone 212. A snapshot
keeps the run's disk policy and seed, and no command changes them at a stop. hvx holds 8
snapshots of every non-zero page and refuses them for `cf=` and timing schedules. The Mac engine
and KVM hold 64 snapshots of the pages written since S1. Continued runs gave their fingerprints
again on hvx (6 of 6) and on the Mac (9 of 9 fault and 9 of 9 timing branches) in Milestone 212,
and KVM has no such proof on a real host.

The recommendation. A tree of snapshots over the first runs is a no-go. The first version to
build is a change of the explorer only: a repeated schedule takes the earlier result without a
VM, and the reruns and confirmations keep their VMs. A repeat must not claim the earlier
fingerprint for its own text, or the explorer stops drawing a `dseed=` that decides nothing. The
second version continues shrink candidates from their own snapshots on the Mac engine and KVM.
Open item 167 has what is left. Nothing recorded moved.

## Milestone 338 (tentative number): hard links in the root, the root's estimate, `/sys` of an image service, and the pause of threads

Four fixes that give images built at the fingerprint epoch 5 new bytes or new commands, so they
come before 0.5.0 (user, 2026-11-20). Each fix is its own commit, and each is keyed on the image's
epoch in `hydo_image::defaults`, so an image built before keeps its bytes and its transcripts.
The measurements used the Mac engine with this tree's `hydo` and the installed 0.4.1 release's
engine and guest files. "Before" is the release 0.4.1 (epoch 4), whose builder writes the same
roots as this tree's before the fixes.

**1. Hard links stay links (open item 162; `cpio_hard_links`).** An arm64 root is a newc cpio
archive: the initramfs, or the archive that the helper VM unpacks into the root of `guest.root:
disk`. The builder wrote each path of a file as a whole copy with its own inode, so the busybox
image's 405 paths of one program became 405 copies of it in the guest's RAM. From epoch 5 the
paths of one file get one inode number and their count of links, and the first path in sorted
order carries the bytes. The kernel's unpacker (`init/initramfs.c`, `maybe_link`) links the later
paths to the first, and so does busybox's `cpio -i`, which unpacks the disk root. A link to a
file outside the tree counts only the tree's paths. An x86_64 root is made by `mke2fs -d`,
which keeps hard links already. The measurements, with `network: bridge`:

| image (arm64, one service) | initramfs before | after | `Shmem` before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `busybox:1.36.1` | 259.2 MB | 6.4 MB | 445.9 MiB (2,048 MiB guest) | 13.5 MiB (1,024 MiB guest) |
| `postgres:16.4` | 149.9 MB | 148.6 MB | 470.9 MiB | 467.3 MiB |

The busybox image's root did not boot in a 1,024 MiB guest before (`Initramfs unpacking failed:
write error`), and it boots with 0.9 GiB free now. Inside the service, `ls -li` shows
`/bin/busybox`, `/bin/ls` and `/bin/sh` as one inode with 405 links; PostgreSQL's
`/usr/bin/perl` and `/usr/bin/perl5.36.0` are one inode with 2. The test `hydo-build`
`cpio::tests::hard_links_stay_links` checks the headers of both forms.

**2. The root's estimate counts the whole root (open items 162 and 166).** PostgreSQL 16.4 still
does not fit in 1,024 MiB with its links: its root of 467 MiB is less than half of the RAM, and
the guest stops with `Initramfs unpacking failed`. The kernel holds the compressed archive in
RAM while it unpacks it into a tmpfs, which Linux sizes at half of the RAM it has then
(`totalram_pages() / 2`). `MemTotal` was 935 MiB of 1,024 and 1,942 MiB of 2,048, so PostgreSQL's
root had room for about 396 MiB. The estimate of Milestone 324 compared the layers with half of
`guest.ram_mib` and gave no warning. Now:

- `hydo_build::oci::initramfs_room` is half of the RAM less what the kernel keeps (80 MiB and
  1/56 of the RAM) and less the archive. The test `root_fit::the_room_of_an_initramfs_root` checks
  it against the four measured cases above: both roots fail in 1,024 MiB and fit in 2,048.
- The estimate before the build, also with `--check`, counts the layers 8 % higher for their files'
  whole pages, and adds hydo's own files, 12 MiB unpacked and 5 MiB compressed. The archive is the
  layers as stored.
- The build measures the staged root too: each file once, in pages of 4 KiB
  (`oci::tmpfs_mib`), beside the written `cpio.gz`. It warns when the estimate did not, for
  example for a large `root.files` tree.

`hydo build --check` of the imported PostgreSQL project with `guest.ram_mib: 1024` now prints:

```text
hydo-build: warning: the image services' roots need about 440 MiB unpacked (db: 440 MiB), and the
whole root about 488 MiB of the guest's RAM with hydo's own files. On the Mac engine the root
lives there: the kernel holds the compressed root, about 150 MiB, while it unpacks it into a
file system that Linux gives half of the RAM it has then, about 388 MiB of guest.ram_mib: 1024.
The guest stops at boot with `Initramfs unpacking failed`. To fix it: guest.ram_mib: 1280 or
more gives the roots the room (now 1024)
```

With 2,048 MiB, and for the busybox image with 1,024 MiB, it prints no warning. The hvx check of
the root partition and the data disk is unchanged.

**3. An image service sees cgroup2's files (open item 144; `oci_sys_rbind`).** The launcher's
block of Milestones 317 and 331, which runs once per boot under the service's lock, binds `/sys`
with `mount --rbind` from epoch 5. `/proc` and `/dev` stay plain binds. In the busybox and
PostgreSQL services, `ls /sys/fs/cgroup` listed `cgroup.controllers`, `cgroup.procs`,
`cpu.stat` and the other files, beside the `0::/` line of `/proc/self/cgroup`. With 0.4.1 the
folder was empty. The test `oci::tests::sys_is_bound_recursively_from_epoch_5` and the launcher
goldens check the block; an image built before keeps the plain bind.

**4. The timed pause of threads (open item 80; `pause_largest_session`).** On an image built at
epoch 5, the timer of `P=workload/<thread>@...` uses the freeze script of a reaction (Milestone
296). It takes the session with the most processes among the leaders with `HYDO_FROM`, not the
first in `/proc` order, which can be a watcher of busybox's `timeout`. A thread that ended before
its move into the cgroup is left out. `agent::plan_of_image` reads the image's epoch into the
plan (`Plan::pause_largest_session`); a plan read from a manifest keeps the old script, so the
controller's corpora did not move. A probe ran `timeout 60 sh -c '...'` with 8 sleeps of 3 ms at a
time, under `P=workload/sh@0~<off>:20`, on the Mac:

| image | `off` 100, 300, 500 |
|---|---|
| built by 0.4.1 (epoch 4) | `ERROR P=workload/sh: unexpected output "sh: write error: No such process"` each time |
| built by this tree (epoch 5) | `OK`, `PAUSED workload/sh (timer, threads 33 sh)` each time |

The probe did not show the watcher's session: both scripts found the workload's session there.

**The pinned reproducers.** On the bare-metal machine, this tree's `hydo` and `hydo-hvx` in
`~/hydo-m338`, every VM through `~/bin/hvx-run` under umask 022, `disk=none dseed=4d5cb825dfaab05b | run K=redis@11+1 C=24` on the epoch-4
images in `~/hydo/build/m302` gave `e153f376096a072c` (VIOLATION, order 11) and `6a5c2fe208174af3`
(OK), their recorded values. The four fixes do not touch an epoch-4 image.

**What moves.** Every image built at epoch 5 has new bytes already. These fixes add, at the
re-recording pass (open item 105): the Mac images whose roots have hard links, the 7 images with
image services (their launchers), and the three KVM runs of the Qdrant example's thread pause.

The four commits are `df4692ad` (hard links), `79f6c26a` (the estimate), `352d430f` (`/sys`) and

## Milestone 339 (tentative number): repeated schedules, error shrinks, and `hydo run`'s refusal

The user chose three changes of the explorer and the command line for hydo 0.5.0 on 2026-11-20.
Each part is its own commit. No engine, image, or recorded value changed.

**1. A repeated schedule takes the earlier result** (commit `80da883e`). Milestone 337 measured
that exact repeats of an earlier shrink candidate took 10 % to 21 % of the shrinks' seconds, and
that an exploration of a small fault space repeated 94 % of its first runs
(`hydo/explore/RESEARCH-shared-prefix.md`, recommendation 1).

- The new module `hydo_explore::repeats` answers a first run (tag `seed-`) or a shrink
  candidate (`shrink…`, `errshrink-…`) whose schedule the exploration already ran. It takes the
  earlier run's result and copies its consoles to its own tag, without a VM. A schedule whose
  run is still in flight is not started twice: the second run waits for the first one's result.
  A cancelled candidate that another run waits for still runs.
- The re-runs that check that a failure repeats (`repro-`) and the two confirmations of each
  minimal schedule (`min-`, `errmin-`) keep their VMs. So does every other run, and a run that
  lost its engine is no result to repeat.
- The pool keeps the answers off unless the explorer turns them on, so hydo-bench's pools, the
  rebaseline among them, run every schedule as before. `hydo explore --rerun-repeats` turns them
  off.
- `exploration.json`'s summary counts the runs answered so (`repeats`) and the seconds of their
  earlier runs (`repeats_saved_s`), a results addition. `report.md` shows both, and `hydo
  explore --merge` adds up the parts' counts. The counts depend on which runs were in flight
  together, as the wall times do.

The disk's seed. The engines' fingerprints cover `dseed=` even where it decides nothing, so two
first runs of `disk=none` with two seeds were one run of the guest with two fingerprints. Two
ways were open. The first keys the answers on the text without such a seed and reports the
earlier run's text and fingerprint. Then a first run would name another seed's schedule, and
the shards of `hydo explore --shard` could not merge into one exploration: a shard without the
earlier seed runs its own text. The second way, taken here, stops writing a seed that decides
nothing. The explorer's `sched::dseed_shown` writes `dseed=0` for `disk=none`, and for
`disk=cut` without a block fault (`torn=`, `mis=`, `lse=`, `hang=`). `disk=ioerr` and
`disk=lying` keep their seed. The seed is still drawn, so every later draw of a generator is
unchanged. No recorded value moves: `hydo/onboard/recorded.json` and the saved regressions are
fixed texts, and `hydo run` keeps a written schedule's `dseed=`. Drawn schedules have new texts
and so new fingerprints, with the same guest runs.

The proofs:

- The scripted engine. A script ran every scenario of the fake engine with the binary before
  and after the change. Every run record (tag, role, verdict, class, schedule), every failure
  with its re-runs, and every shrink and minimal schedule were the same up to the `dseed=`
  values. 10 % to 30 % of the runs were answered, for example 109 of 382 runs of
  `stack_swarm_errors_fail` and 44 of 323 of `stack_random_all_streams`.
- The goldens. The explorer's fake-engine goldens, `identity-*.txt`, `corpus-*.txt`,
  `reactive.txt`, and hydo-bench's `schedules.golden` were recorded again. After the `dseed=`
  values and the stream hashes are blanked, each moved line equals the line before (all 72 lines
  of hydo-bench's file). The fake-engine goldens leave the two counts out. hydo-bench's test now
  records its file again with `HYDO_BLESS=1`.
- The new scenario `repeats_take_the_earlier_result` explores the stack (shrinks of several
  signatures, causes and error kinds) and the AVX2 example's manifest of clock steps only, each
  with and without `--rerun-repeats`. `exploration.json`, `events.jsonl` and `report.md` are the
  same file for file. On the AVX2 manifest the random strategy draws `disk=none dseed=0 | run` for
  all 40 seeds, and one VM runs it: 39 runs are answered. `merge_equals_one_exploration` holds.
- The Mac engine, on the Redis quickstart (`~/.hydo/examples/redis`, an image built by 0.4.1 at
  the fingerprint epoch 4, 2 workers, the tree's `hydo` and `hydo-hvm`):

| exploration of seeds 1-40 | runs | answered | their seconds | wall s, answered / in VMs | failures | minimal schedules |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--strategy swarm` (the quickstart's) | 65 | 1 shrink candidate | 0.1 | 20.4 / 21.4 | 16 | 2 |
| `--strategy random --shrink-causes 3` | 67 | 4 first runs and 6 shrink candidates | 1.3 | 17.2 / 20.9 | 8 | 3 |
| `--strategy process --new-faults` | 40 | none | 0 | 33.0 / 14.9 | 0 | 0 |

With and without `--rerun-repeats`, every run record, its fingerprint, every failure, and every
minimal schedule was the same. The 4 answered first runs were `disk=none dseed=0 | run`, which
four seeds drew. The Redis runs take 0.1 s to 0.3 s each on this Mac, so the seconds saved are
small. The measured shares on hvx are in the research note. The process exploration's wall
times differ because the Mac was busy with tests during the first one.

**2. The explorer shrinks the system's errors** (commit `a9baeacb`). Until now it shrank
violations only. A service that never starts again after a crash kept its first schedule, and
the Redpanda and Temporal onboardings shrank such errors by hand (open items 112 and 142).

- `report::shrinks` decides which first failures are shrunk: a violation, and these errors of
  the system, by their signature (the verdict with every number left out):
  - a service that does not start again: `ERROR <svc> restart failed`, also with a reason in
    parentheses, and `ERROR restart after the faults`;
  - a workload or a check that does not end: `TIMEOUT workload`, `TIMEOUT check`, `TIMEOUT
    recovery`, and the Mac engine's `ERROR workload: exit budget exhausted` and `ERROR check:
    exit budget exhausted`.
- A candidate keeps an error when it ends with an error of the same signature
  (`report::same_outcome`), within the shrink's budget of 40 runs. Every other error is
  hydo's or its engine's, such as a lost worker, a refused schedule, or a setup that failed, and
  is not shrunk.
- The system's documented detection of damage is left out by default (`report::detected_damage`).
  This is a service that does not start again in a run of the class `corrupted-files` (`G=`) or
  `damaged-disk` (the block faults and `G=...:bad|rot`), or whose restart's reason is `its
  files were corrupted`. An error kind of the error logs that was first new in such a run is
  left out too: open items 140 and 158 had explorations whose shrink of detected corruption ran
  for 25 minutes or more. `hydo explore --shrink-detected-damage` shrinks both.
- `hydo explore --merge` chooses with the same functions. An `eventually_` check that failed 3
  tries or more is still a violation (Milestone 328).

The proofs:

- The scripted engine's new scenario `restart_errors_are_shrunk` uses the RAUC example's
  manifest with `--storage-faults` and the error logs. There a service killed for 3 steps or more
  does not start again, and a `G=` gives `ERROR device restart failed (its files were
  corrupted)` with a log line about a checksum. The first error was shrunk to its kill alone,
  `disk=none dseed=0 | run K=device@4+3` from seed 25 in 12 runs. The detected damage (22 runs)
  and the checksum's error kind were not shrunk. With `--shrink-detected-damage` both were
  shrunk to their `G=` alone. Four shards merged gave the same shrinks and error shrinks. Every
  other scenario kept its golden.
- The Mac engine, the Redis quickstart's `--strategy swarm` seeds 1-40: `ERROR redis restart
  failed` (class `io-errors`) shrank from seed 12's `disk=ioerr:3 dseed=fd403ef8d08fa636 | run
  K=redis@16+1 N=redis@0-8:loss,7%` in 9 runs to `disk=ioerr:3 dseed=fd403ef8d08fa636 | run
  K=redis@16+1`. `ERROR restart after the faults (redis)` shrank from seed 13 in 11 runs to
  `disk=ioerr:3 dseed=281cc34161f446f4 | run K=redis@1+1`. Both confirmations of each gave one
  fingerprint (`4c0e5bbda39117c7`, `f35cff425a07c7c2`). With `--rerun-repeats` the same 79 runs
  gave the same records.

**3. `hydo run`'s memory refusal exits 5** (commit `ff7b422f`). `hydo explore` exits with status 5
when it refuses before any schedule (Milestone 328). `hydo run` stopped for a guest that does not
fit into the machine's memory with status 1. Now `runs::memory_refusal` gives the reason with
the running `hydo inspect` sessions. `hydo run` checks it before any VM and exits with status 5.
With the new option `--json` it also prints the explorer's line, `{"refused": "<reason>",
"status": 5}`. Inside `hydo ci run` the status stays that command's. The proof was on this Mac
with the Redis quickstart built with `guest.ram_mib: 8192`, while about 5 GiB were available:
`hydo run --json "disk=none | run"` exited 5 with the JSON line, and without `--json` it exited
5 with the reason on stderr only. No test forces the refusal, because the reader of an image
refuses `guest.ram_mib` above 8192 and a test machine's free memory varies.

**Checks.** `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`,
the tests of hydo-explore, hydo-results, hydo-schema-compat, hydo-bench, `public_content::`,
`sh ci/vale.sh` and `ci/consolidate-tests.sh --check` passed. `cargo test -p hydo --test it`
passed but for `onboard::the_fetch_step_names_the_release_fetcher_when_it_is_not_on_path` and
`update::a_checkout_build_is_left_alone_with_the_commands`, which fail in a target folder
outside the checkout.

**What is left.** Open items 142 and 167. Nothing recorded moved.
