## Milestone 363 (tentative number): a test of the guide's topics, and the trial's smaller frictions

Status: done on 2026-11-26, in the tests on this Mac; no VM ran. Each fix below is its own
commit. Nothing recorded moved: every change is in the host's import, scans, reports and
commands, in the public Go module, and in a test. The fingerprint epoch stays 6.

**1. A test that every guide topic prints text.** On 2026-11-25 a scripted merge emptied
`hydo/guide/strategies.md`. `hydo guide strategies` printed nothing on `main`, and every check
passed, because the CLI's golden answers were recorded again with the empty topic. The new test
`hydo-agents::guide_topics` runs `hydo guide <topic>` for each of the 29 topics of `hydo guide
--list`. A topic fails when it prints nothing, or less than three quarters of its size in
`hydo/crates/hydo-agents/tests/guide-sizes.txt`. A topic without a recorded size fails too.
`HYDO_BLESS=1 cargo test -p hydo-agents --test it guide_topics::` records the sizes again. The
test is in the fast tier. With `strategies.md` emptied in the checkout, it failed with
`` `hydo guide strategies` prints nothing ``, and it passed with the file restored.

**2. The trial's smaller frictions** (open item 183, the trial's section "The frictions, ranked",
item 9):

- The import's unused `data.dirs` folder. NSQ's import wrote `data: dirs: [vol/nsqd-data]` for
  a volume on `/data` whose mount its own warning left out. A volume, an image's `VOLUME` and a
  missing bind source now get their folder only when the mount was added.
- The workload placeholder against the wrong service. The placeholder named the first service
  with a port, NSQ's `nsqlookupd`, which only tells the clients where `nsqd` is. It now starts
  from that service. When other services with a port depend on it, it names the first of them
  that keeps data (a named or anonymous volume, or an image's `VOLUME`), else the first of them.
  So NSQ's import names `nsqd` (port 4150), and an application listed after its database is
  named instead of the database. The test `hydo-compose::placeholder` imports the trial's
  Compose file.
- The clock scan's `<database>` for a known service. A place of `nsqlookupd` whose words name a
  connection got `K=<database>@2+3` under `Run by nsqlookupd`, because hydo.yaml has no database.
  Such a place now names the one service that runs it, with that service's words. With a
  database in hydo.yaml the schedules name it as before. The test
  `rules::the_clock_audit_names_the_service_when_there_is_no_database` failed before the change.
- The Go SDK's call for `drained`. `(*History).Drained(proc, channel, group)` writes `ok
  drained <channel> <group>` with the Rust SDK's item encoding. Its test runs the test program
  again with `HYDO_HIST_OUT` set and compares the line with the shared case
  `sdk/cases/history/messages`. The call and its test are files of the public module only
  (`hydohist/messages.go`, `hydohist/messages_test.go`). A new file in the frozen copy in
  `hydo/stack` would change the order service's bytes inside recorded images, so hydo-release's
  `sdks::` lists the two files as public-only, and `sdk/README.md` says why. The shared case's
  description names both checks. The Go page and `hydo guide messages` show the call.
- `hydo inspect diagnose --text` printed JSON. The view now prints lines: the run, the verdict,
  why it failed, what failed and where, how the process ended with its output, the readiness
  check, the other processes, the likely causes, the kernel's lines, the evidence, and the next
  commands. The plain report's line names it: `Why it failed: hydo inspect diagnose <dir>
  --problem N --text`.
- `(no error code)` for a lost message. Without an error code in the read-back, `acked-outcome`
  now says `m0 was acknowledged and has no final state: the read-back found it still pending or
  not at all`. With an error code the words keep it, as before.
- The title `Nsq` for NSQ. The report reads the project's README, in the folder above `hydo-out`
  or above the project's `hydo/` folder. It takes the most frequent spelling of the manifest's
  name as a whole word there, when that spelling has a capital letter. A word inside a path, an
  address or a file name does not count. A README in the form of NSQ's gives `NSQ failed your
  check`. Without a README, or with a lower-case spelling only (`etcd`), the name is capitalised
  as before.

**3. A long `W=` word hides the faults after it.** When a command's schedule has a `W=` word
longer than 40 characters and a fault after it, the problem now says under the command: `After
its long composition word W=, the command has the fault L=nsqd@6+2.` The command stays exact.
The terminal's report of an exploration and of a run and the web page's problem cards show the
sentence. A fault before the word stays in sight and is not named again: the recorded
exploration of redis-composed has such faults, and its report gained no sentence.

**4. A regression found on the default build names its parameters.** When the exploration
image's manifest has `params:`, `hydo save` now writes `# params:` with every value the image was
built with, the defaults too: `# params: memq=0` for the trial's default build. `hydo repro
--regressions` on the `--set memq=10000` build then prints `SKIP` with the build command, as for
any `# params:` line (Milestone 355). A manifest without `params:` gives no line, so the
examples' regressions keep their form. A value with white space cannot be a word of the line and
is left out. The unit test `save_keeps_every_finding_and_names_the_build_parameters` checks the
line of a default build and that the build check holds such a regression back on the other
build.

**The recorded answers that changed**, each recorded again with `HYDO_BLESS=1` for the reason
named:

- `hydo-compose/tests/golden.json`: 46 of 185 cases, the placeholder's service in 35 and the
  `data.dirs` line in 14. The new targets are applications and proxies instead of their
  databases: Mastodon's `web`, n8n's `n8n`, Temporal's `temporal`, Sentry's `web`.
- `hydo-compose/tests/golden/k8s-cluster.yaml`: the placeholder names `api`, which depends on
  `kv-0`.
- `hydo-cli/tests/golden/report/exploration.txt`: two "Why it failed" lines with `--text`.
- `hydo-cli/tests/golden/cli.jsonl`: `hydo report` of the recorded exploration (5,213 to 5,241
  bytes) and `hydo guide manifest` (258,397 to 258,449 bytes), on Linux and on the Mac.
- `sdk/cases/history/messages.json`: its `about` text only.

## Milestone 364 (tentative number): SeaweedFS, three masters, three volume servers and a filer

The onboarding of SeaweedFS 4.55 (2026-11-23, the newest release) on hvx, 2026-11-26, by
`docs/ONBOARDING-PLAYBOOK.md`, with the released hydo 0.6.0 installed into a prefix of its own on
the bare-metal machine. The example is `hydo/onboard/examples/seaweedfs`; its RESULTS.md has the
evidence. No new bug of SeaweedFS: every failure was a server that refused its own damaged files,
on purpose or within a documented limit. Nothing was posted. Nothing recorded moved.

**The example.** `hydo/onboard/examples/seaweedfs` (RESULTS.md) runs the shape of the wiki pages
"Failover Master Server" and "Replication" on one host, imported with `hydo compose`: three
masters with Raft, three volume servers with the replication `001` (two copies of every volume),
one filer on its default store, leveldb2, and the S3 gateway, in one hvx guest of 2,048 MiB. Each
server's `/data` is a file system of its own. The first command writes the filer's path rule
`fsync` for `/buckets/` (the build parameter `fsync`, `true` by default) and makes the bucket. The
client `swc` (`client/main.go`, the AWS SDK for Go v2 and Go's standard library) writes every key
through S3 (PutObject, overwrite, DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, multipart uploads of 5 MiB parts
and their aborts, CopyObject) or through the filer's HTTP API (PUT, overwrite, DELETE), reads
each acknowledged write back through the other API, and orders compactions of the volumes during
the workload (`anytime_vacuum`). A `type: messages` check with the claim `acked_outcome` and
`effect: recorded` judges every write after a compaction of every volume; final checks compare
the listing with the keys, the multipart uploads with the aborts, and both copies of every chunk,
read from each volume server directly. Two clean runs on the final image (`f6e18b43…`) give one
fingerprint, `353f5b2b1913660a`.

**By design and the environment.** A volume server stops at every start when a volume's
superblock names an unknown version, here after hydo zeroed bytes of its file (pull request
#8047 made it stop on purpose). A master stops at every start after hydo damaged its Raft state,
with a message about `/data` being writable. The rule over both copies of each chunk found a copy
that answers 404 after hydo damaged a volume server's files; SeaweedFS documents that it repairs
no copy by itself, and every read took the other copy. Without the fsync rule, SeaweedFS's
default, 5 of 20 power cuts lost acknowledged writes, and `hydo explore --configs` labeled it the
documented trade-off; with the rule none of 20 did. The saved regression
`acknowledged-write-lost-at-a-power-cut-without-fsync.schedule` carries `# params: fsync=false`,
and `hydo repro --regressions` reproduced it on that build.

**What held.** With the fsync rule no acknowledged write was lost or read wrong, no deleted key
came back, and every listing and upload list agreed with the keys. That held through kills,
pauses past the masters' election timeout and the volume servers' heartbeats, partitions and
one-way loss, clock steps both ways, one server's power loss, power cuts of the guest at steps
and at disk flushes, and compactions concurrent with all of them. It also held through 60
reactions 0 to 40 ms after acknowledgements and compactions (power cuts and power losses of the
filer and of a volume server), 65 kills of each master, a volume server and the filer 0 to 3 s
into writes of 4 MiB or more, and volumes of 8 MB that filled during the runs. SeaweedFS issue
#4557, a write left empty by a failover of the master leader, did not reproduce.

**Explorations.** 342 schedules in eight explorations on two workers or one: e1 and e2
(process strategy with cluster, storage and more faults, seeds 1-37), e3 (seeds 101-160 with
fault reactions at the acknowledgements and the compactions), e4 (the aimed grid of power cuts
and power losses), e5 (`--configs` over `fsync`), e6 (the kills inside large writes), e7 (volumes
of 8 MB, seeds 201-240) and e8 (swarm with new faults, seeds 301-340). Eleven directed runs
checked the clean run, pauses of the Raft leader and of volume servers, the filer's power loss,
power cuts inside the workload, clock steps, and an isolated master.

**hydo.** No code of hydo changed. The guide's strategies have the SeaweedFS evidence in two
entries. The new example enters the explorer's and the controller's corpora: their goldens are
re-recorded with `HYDO_BLESS=1` in a copy of the tree without git on the bare-metal machine, in
the default modes and with `HYDO_CORPUS_QUICK=1` and `HYDO_IDENT_FULL=1`, and checked there. In
that copy `identity::local_outputs_are_no_inputs` fails, because it needs git's list of ignored
files. It passed, and so did `public_content::` over 3,921 files, after the copy was made a git
repository of its own (`git init`, `git add -A`).

Retro: SeaweedFS 4.55, hvx, 2026-11-26
- Time to the first clean run: 1 hour 5 minutes of wall time (scouting 30 minutes, the import,
  the client and two blockers 35 minutes).
- Schedules run before the first finding: no finding of SeaweedFS in 342 schedules and 11
  directed runs. The first failure, at e1's seed 3, was a damaged file; no failure was a mistake
  of the rules after the multipart parts were made 5 MiB.
- The findings: none new, none known; by design or documented: the fail-fast on a damaged
  superblock, the copies that nothing repairs, and the default without fsync; the environment:
  a master's damaged Raft state.
- What took the most time: the shrinks of power-cut losses in the configurations exploration
  (40 minutes on one worker); the FIPS entropy panic of every server (20 minutes); a shrink of a
  violation with damaged files that had to be stopped (10 minutes).
- What hydo lacked: a Go program in FIPS mode cannot start in the guest, whose clock has no
  jitter; `--check` does not count the services' own file systems against hvx's 4,096 MiB; the
  import takes the image's first `EXPOSE`; a stopped exploration leaves its engine under sudo;
  a violation with damaged files is shrunk; the write-route scan sees no gorilla/mux route with
  a variable path; the verdict line names a claim that judged nothing. Open item 186.
- Strategies: "Settings that trade durability" (the fsync rule, labeled by design) and "A scan
  of a reaction's delay" (the grid after acknowledgements and compactions found nothing) are
  updated.

**What is left.** Open item 186.

## Milestone 365 (tentative number): one findings store for every run

The user's idea (2026-11-26): the findings of hydo's runs should be kept in one light store that
any tool can read, not only by CI. Before this milestone only `hydo ci record` wrote the history
store, and only from the `ci-run.json` of a `hydo ci run`. A finding is one failure of a check,
named by its key `f1:<kind>:<10 hex>` (docs/design/ci.md section 4.2).

**The design.** The store keeps the format of the CI history store, with additions only:
`v1/<project>/runs/<id>.json` (one `ci-run` document per recorded run), `findings.jsonl` (one
`finding-event` per change of state) and `state.json` (the `ci-ledger`, their fold). A store
written before reads as before.

- `hydo findings record [RUN_DIR | EXPLORE_DIR]` makes a `ci-run` document from a plain `hydo
  run` or `hydo explore` folder and records it with the fold of `hydo ci record`. The document
  has `ci.name` `local`, `trigger` `manual`, no base, and the new field `recorded_from` (`hydo
  run` or `hydo explore`). An exploration's findings come from the function that `hydo ci run`
  uses (`ci::run::findings_of`), and a run's from its verdict and its new error kinds.
- A finding seen failing is `new` on its branch the first time, `present` while it is open, and
  `reappeared` after a fix. A finding of the branch adds a sighting, never a second entry.
- A `hydo run` whose schedule is one of an open finding's recorded schedules is a replay. When
  its verdict is `OK`, the finding is `fixed` (proof `head-replay-ok`). When it fails with
  another key, the finding is `changed` and keeps its state. A run of any other schedule, and an
  exploration that does not find a finding, change nothing: absence proves nothing.
- A record's id is `local:<first 16 hex of the sha256 of result.json or exploration.json>`.
  Recording one folder twice says `already in` and changes nothing.
- The store is `--store DIR`, else `HYDO_FINDINGS_STORE` (new in `hydo-config`), else
  `~/.hydo/findings`, the folder `findings` of `HYDO_HOME`. A per-user folder works without a
  setting, and one variable points every run of the machine at a team's checkout.
- The project is `--project`, else the `name` of the manifest in the image's build record, else
  the `name` in `./hydo/hydo.yaml` or `./hydo.yaml`, else the image's file name. The commit and
  the branch are the folder's git `HEAD` and branch, else the branch `local`.
- `hydo findings list|show|history` fold the recorded runs of each branch again, as `hydo ci
  page` does, and give each finding its line: `new`, `failing`, `not-found` (still open),
  `fixed`, `back`. `--json` prints the new results document `findings` (`FindingsDoc`, with
  `StoredFinding`, `FindingSighting`, `FindingPoint` and `FindingsFilter`), an addition to
  `hydo/schema/results-v1.json` that `hydo-schema-compat` checks against the released schema.
- `hydo run --record-findings` and `hydo explore --record-findings` record at the end. They are
  off by default. With `--json`, or when stdout is no terminal, `hydo explore` prints the
  record's line on stderr, so the summary stays on stdout.
- `hydo ci page` reads the same runs, so it shows these records. Its column `Trigger` names the
  command of a record that has `recorded_from`.

Other additions: `CiFinding.verdict` (the whole verdict line), and `image_sha256`, `epoch`, `fp`
and `time` on each `finding-event`, which `hydo ci record` now writes too.

**What a record holds.** A record keeps small values only. It holds no path of this machine:

- the image and the exploration's folder by their file names;
- no engine arguments (they name the guest kernel's path), and the guest kernel by its file name;
- no command line of the explorer;
- a replay line `hydo run <image file name> '<schedule>'`, made by hydo, instead of the explorer's
  `repro_command`, which names the image's full path.

It holds the host's CPU model (`Apple M2 Pro`), as `ci-run.json` does. The verdict line is the
guest's own text, so a check that prints a secret puts it there. The scripted test checks every
file of the store, but the page, for the test folder's path and for the engine's arguments. The
store of the Mac proof below has no `/Users` and no `/private` outside its `index.html`, which
names the store as `--store` gave it.

**The proof on the scripted engine.** `hydo/crates/hydo-cli/tests/findings.rs` runs the scripted
engine (`HYDO_SCRIPTED_ENGINE`), which fails a power cut with `MODE=lazy`. In one test:

- `hydo explore --record-findings` records `new VIOLATION [db.acked_writes_survive]`, and a second
  record of the folder changes nothing;
- a second exploration of the lazy image adds a sighting, and one of a changed image finds
  nothing and keeps the finding open;
- a `result.json` of the minimal schedule that passes proves it fixed, and a passing run of
  another schedule does not;
- a failing run brings it back. `hydo findings history <part of the key> --json` gives the line
  `new, failing, not-found, fixed, back` and 3 sightings;
- `--since`, `--class` and `--state` filter, `hydo ci page` shows the records, and the store
  holds no path of the test folder.

A second test reads an empty store and refuses a folder that does not exist.

**The proof on the Mac engine.** The Redis quickstart example of the 0.6.0 release ran with this
tree's `hydo` (`HYDO_RELEASE_DIR` named the unpacked release) under the shared Mac VM lock. Its
manifest kept `faults: [kill, pause, cut, clock]`, so that the lying disk did not hide the
replay. Image A is the example, and image B the same example whose setting `R` always sets
`appendfsync always` (the fix):

```text
$ hydo run --image hydo-out/explore-ob-redis-arm64.cpio.gz "disk=cut | run C=12 R=everysec" --out runs/a1 --record-findings
hydo findings: recorded local:c4bc61380bd51f0f of redis on local into .../store: new VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost
$ hydo findings record runs/a1
hydo findings: local:c4bc61380bd51f0f of redis is already in .../store; nothing changed
$ hydo explore --image <A> --seeds 1-20 --out ex1 --no-diagnose --record-findings
hydo findings: recorded local:367c8544757dedf1 of redis on local into .../store: seen again VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost
$ hydo explore --image <B> --seeds 1-20 --out ex2 --no-diagnose --record-findings
hydo findings: recorded local:5c7f55e9891d36c6 of redis on local into .../store: no finding
$ hydo run --image <B> "disk=cut | run C=12 R=everysec" --out runs/b1 --record-findings
hydo findings: recorded local:9eeb7cdf4f472c85 of redis on local into .../store: fixed by replay VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost
$ hydo run --image <A> "disk=cut | run C=12 R=everysec" --out runs/a2 --record-findings
hydo findings: recorded local:4665667d9d6b098a of redis on local into .../store: back again VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost
$ hydo findings history 5ef675c8c9
  f1:invariant:5ef675c8c9  VIOLATION [redis.acked_writes_survive] key k:# lost
    back again; first seen 2026-11-26 07:48:35 UTC, last seen 2026-11-26 07:49:01 UTC; 3 sightings
    class unsafe-knob
    minimal schedule: disk=cut | run C=12 R=everysec
    2026-11-26 07:48:35 UTC  hydo run      first seen  fp=275a3d143726e6ad  image df2bb1f559b4
    2026-11-26 07:48:47 UTC  hydo explore  seen failing again  fp=18b18bd983b8a4a0  image df2bb1f559b4
    2026-11-26 07:48:53 UTC  hydo explore  not found (still open)  image 12360f0ff79e
    2026-11-26 07:48:57 UTC  hydo run      fixed: its schedule passed  fp=eb1d238c59246a8f  image 12360f0ff79e
    2026-11-26 07:49:01 UTC  hydo run      back again after a fix  fp=275a3d143726e6ad  image df2bb1f559b4
```

The two runs of the schedule on image A gave one fingerprint, `275a3d143726e6ad`, and image B
passed it (`acked=12 all present`). `hydo findings show` named
the second schedule the exploration recorded (`disk=cut dseed=0 | run C=10 R=no`), the replay
line, and the last sighting's hydo 0.6.0, epoch 6, engine `hvm/Apple`, image and fingerprint.
`hydo ci page --store` wrote a page of 12 KiB with the five records. The whole proof took about
40 s. `hydo/schema/examples/results/v1/mac-redis-findings/` keeps the store's ledger, two of its
`ci-run` records, and the `list` and `history` documents.

**Nothing recorded moved.** No engine, agent, image or fingerprint changed. The CLI goldens
changed in the 11 answers of the main help, which names `hydo findings`.

**What is left** (open item 187):

- A key names the check, not the cause. A passing replay of one schedule proves the key fixed
  while another schedule may still fail it; the next sighting marks it `back again`.
- `hydo findings record` replays nothing itself. A finding found by an exploration is proven fixed
  only by a `hydo run` of one of its schedules; a command that replays every open finding of a
  store on an image is not built.
- A record of a laptop goes to the branch that git names, also `main`, which `hydo ci run
  --history` reads. `--branch` keeps it apart; nothing refuses it.
- `hydo ci run --history` did not read a store with such records, and the page read only the
  scripted test's store and the Mac proof's store, not a history branch on GitHub (open item 67).
- A store has no lock. Two records into one store at once can lose one ledger update.

## Milestone 366 (tentative number): Typesense, a replay that applies a delete by a filter out of order

Typesense 30.2 became the example `hydo/onboard/examples/typesense` (RESULTS.md), by
`docs/ONBOARDING-PLAYBOOK.md`, with hydo of `main` at `8a60fcb2` on hvx on the bare-metal
machine. Three new candidates; nothing was posted, and nothing recorded moved.

**The example.** Three Raft nodes of Typesense 30.2 from the official image, as a cluster at
fixed addresses with a nodes file, imported with `hydo compose`. Each node's data is on a file
system of its own; the snapshot interval is the build parameter `snap` (30 s), and the batch size
of the client's deletes by a filter is the build parameter `batch` (2). The Go client `tsc` sends
each write once, through a node that the seed picks, so most writes take the forwarding path to
the leader. It writes creates, upserts, partial updates, deletes, deletes and updates by a
filter, deletes by a filter in batches, imports of 2 to 100 documents and of 240 KB bodies, and
schema changes. A messages check with `acked_outcome` and `effect: recorded` reads every document
back from the leader after a barrier write. Seven checks judge the rest: every follower holds the
leader's documents, a write through each node is readable everywhere within 15 s, an export
with the default batch size ends, a delete by a filter ends whole or not at all, a search finds
each stored version, each acknowledged schema change is everywhere, and the cluster has a leader
while two nodes answer. The last one reads a probe of every node's `/debug` once a second.

**Finding 1, new.** A node that replays its Raft log applies a delete by a filter in several
batches out of order with the writes after it, and then lacks acknowledged documents for good.
`del_remove_documents` deletes one batch (`src/core_api.cpp` line 2166) and posts the rest with
`defer_processing(req, res, 0)` (line 2196): a timer of the HTTP event loop, whose callback runs
the next batch on a thread pool (`src/http_server.cpp` lines 867 and 892). The batched indexer
called the handler once (`src/batched_indexer.cpp` line 299) and goes on to the next write
(lines 338 to 343). A replay applies the next writes at once, so an upsert that creates a deleted
document again updates the old one in place, and a later batch deletes it. Typesense deletes at
most 1,000 documents a batch (`src/core_api_utils.cpp` line 6), so a delete of more than 1,000
matches runs in batches with the default `batch_size` too. `K=ts3@40+20 W=5479b87f,p6,q1,r500`
left `ts3` without three documents, with `eventually_converge` failing for 120 s. The kill alone
was enough, and so was `K=ts3@50+3`; the composition without a fault passed. Four failing
schedules, the kill above, `K=ts3@50+3`, and the blind seeds 49 and 53, passed on an image built
with `--set batch=1000000000`. In seed 53 a node's search index named an older version of a
document than its store. Typesense's #3181 reports `num_documents` that differs between nodes
under deletes by a filter and restarts, with `async_reference` fields, and names no cause.

**Finding 2, new, a clock effect.** After a backward step of the wall clock, every answer that
Typesense makes in several parts stops after its first part, for the step's length. h2o's event
loop reads `gettimeofday` (`lib/common/socket/evloop.c.h` line 792) and its timer wheel returns
no timer while the time is before its last run (`lib/common/timerwheel.c` lines 304 to 308,
`detected rewind`). Typesense makes each later batch of an export from a 1 ms timer
(`response_proceed`, `src/http_server.cpp` line 945) and each later batch of a delete by a filter
from a 0 ms timer. So after `T=20:-3600` an export with its default batch of 100 ends after the
first batch, and each delete by a filter of the run deleted 2 documents and answered nothing.
h2o/h2o#2321 (open since 2020) and the open pull requests #2339 and #2822 propose a monotonic
clock for h2o.

**Finding 3, new, a clock effect.** After a backward step, a failure of the leader is followed
by no election for the step's length. braft's `RepeatedTimerTask` schedules the next run of the
election timer at `butil::milliseconds_from_now` (`src/braft/repeated_timer_task.cpp` lines 128
to 130), and brpc's timer thread compares with `gettimeofday_us` (`src/bthread/timer_thread.cpp`
lines 372 and 427). `T=20:-120 P=nodes.primary@30+25` left the two other nodes followers without
a leader for 116 s, until the late timer fired 120 s plus one election timeout after the step
(the check's probes saw 68 s of it); the same pause without `T=` got a new leader in 11.8 s. The
released hydo 0.6.0 from a fresh clone at `e2058be0` gave both clock findings again on hvx, each with
one fingerprint over two runs (finding 2 `7d80c69637796b19`, finding 3 `ec4fae531d94d397`).

**The runs.** The final image `explore-ob-typesense-disk.img` (`02024a5f…`) gives
`097b8fcffac8545b` on two clean runs. Each regression gave one fingerprint over two fresh runs:
finding 1 `2d653b8a28652520`, finding 2 `c3653bc7d18e8f42`, finding 3 `8675611411642625`. `hydo repro --regressions` gave 3 of 3 as expected with the same values. RESULTS.md has the runs that separate the causes, with their fingerprints.

**Finding 1 with the released hydo 0.6.0.** From a fresh clone at `0fe1e269`, the published 0.6.0
Linux release built the image `de22e524…` on hvx with the example's steps. The regression gave
`converge` with `ts3` lacking the same two documents, `881d375553ca3742` on two runs; the client
built from the committed sources differs from the onboarding's in its line numbers. In that
schedule `ts3` is the leader when it is killed. A kill of the follower `ts1` or `ts2` with the
same composition gives the same violation (`f7e81ca6d9185872` twice), and passes on the image
whose deletes run in one batch. The table is in RESULTS.md.

**The explorations.** e1, `--seeds 1-30 --strategy process --new-faults --cluster-faults
--storage-faults` on 3 workers of an earlier image, failed 10 of 30: finding 2's export in 5,
each shrunk to one step back, detected damage in 4, and the group's primary during an election
in 1. e2, seeds 31 to 90 of the final checks, failed 22 of 60: finding 1 in 3 without a step
back (seeds 43, 53 and 61), finding 2 with the nodes it leaves apart in 8, detected damage in 10,
and one not judged. e2 was stopped during its shrinks; the directed runs separated its failures.

**Tests.** The new example enters the explorer's and the controller's corpora. Re-recorded with
`HYDO_BLESS=1`: the explorer's corpus goldens (full and quick), its identity goldens (quick and
full), and the controller's quick corpus golden, which adds the example's entries only. With a
target folder of this task's own on the bare-metal machine, in a copy of the worktree with an
index of its tracked files: `cargo test -p hydo-explore --test it` (61 passed), the controller's
corpus tests, `-p hydo --test it -- equivalence:: agents_equivalence::` (9 passed) and `-p
hydo-agents --test it` (16 passed). The copy has no `AGENTS.local.md`, so `public_content::`
checked the generic patterns, and a `grep` of the listed values found none in the new text. `sh
ci/vale.sh` finds nothing. No Rust code changed.

Retro: Typesense 30.2, hvx, 2026-11-26
- Time to the first clean run: 1 hour 10 minutes of wall time, about 20 minutes of it waiting for
  builds and runs.
- Schedules run before the first finding: 3 (e1's seed 3, finding 2); finding 1 at e2's seed 43,
  the 43rd blind schedule. No failure was a mistake of the rules, but the first client's history
  records overflowed hvx's console (64 KiB) and made the messages check undecided.
- The findings: 3 new (the replay out of order, the parts of an answer after a step back, no
  election after a step back), 14 schedules of detected damage, none known or documented.
- What took the most time: separating finding 1 from the clock effects (about 1 hour: the
  probes, the A/B image, and the faults one by one); the console's limit and the history's one
  operation per process (about 40 minutes); the leader probe dense enough to see an election
  (about 30 minutes).
- What hydo lacked: no warning when hvx's console is full; one record per process for a batch;
  `primary:` tried 10 times a second apart; a shrink that kept an unneeded `G=`; no write routes
  of a C++ route table; two images of one manifest in one folder (open item 188).
- Strategies: a new entry "Every replica compared with the leader after a restart", and the
  Typesense evidence in "Clock steps and the clock audit" of `hydo guide strategies`; the first
  table names Typesense.

**What is left.** Open item 188.

## Milestone 367 (tentative number): the gaps of the NSQ and SeaweedFS onboardings

Status: done on 2026-11-26, on the bare-metal machine (hvx and the tests) from this Mac. Each fix
below is its own commit. Nothing recorded moved: every change is in the host's build check,
explorer, commands, scans and reports, and in the guide. No engine's guest behaviour, agent,
image or fingerprint changed, and the fingerprint epoch stays 6. The gaps are the "What hydo
lacked" sections of the NSQ and SeaweedFS examples' RESULTS.md (open items 184 and 186).

**1. `--check` counts the services' own file systems.** The SeaweedFS onboarding gave the data
disk 1,792 MiB beside eight file systems of `storage.size_mib`. `hydo build --check` printed `OK`,
and the build stopped only after it had unpacked the images: `the disk with the services' own
file systems is 4488 MiB, more than the 4096 MiB an engine maps`. The disk holds the root
partition, the data partition of `data.size_mib`, and each own file system with 1 MiB before it.
Two changes:

- The known parts of the disk are 1 MiB, a root of at least 1 MiB, `data.size_mib`, and the
  file systems. When they already pass the 4,096 MiB, `--check` and the build stop before
  anything is unpacked, with the words of the disk's assembly
  (`hydo_build::image::disk_refusal`). The
  message adds that the file systems come on top of `data.size_mib`, which needs only the run's
  own files.
- The estimate of the image services' roots (Milestone 324) adds the file systems on top of the
  data disk, and its advice names smaller `storage.size_mib` values.

The test `root_fit::the_services_own_file_systems_count_against_the_disk` checks three cases.
Data of 2,048 MiB beside three file systems of 512 fits (3,779 MiB). Data of 2,400 passes only
with the roots' estimate (4,131 MiB: a warning). Data of 1,792 beside three of 768 passes with
the known parts alone (4,101 MiB: the refusal).

**2. A stop of `hydo explore` stops its engines.** The SeaweedFS onboarding stopped an
exploration by its process group, and its engine `hydo-hvx`, which runs under `sudo`, kept 14
GB of the host; nothing named its pid. The chain of an hvx worker is `flock` (the module lock),
`sudo`, and `hydo-hvx` as root. This user cannot signal the root engine. It can signal its
`sudo`, whose real user is this one, and `sudo` passes SIGTERM on to its command (tried on the
bare-metal machine with `sudo sleep`). On the bare-metal machine, SIGTERM and SIGINT to the
process group ended a healthy engine with 0.6.0 too. `sudo` passed the signal on, and an engine
also ends when its input closes. What stays is an engine that neither the signal nor its input
reaches, such as one in a long call. A stand-in engine that ignores SIGTERM, SIGINT, and the
end of its input showed it: with 0.6.0, SIGTERM to the exploration's process group left both
stand-in engines and their `sudo` processes as root.

The new module `hydo_engine::children` keeps every engine program this process starts:

- `hydo explore` (and `hydo explore --configs`) installs handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM. A
  signal that the process inherited as ignored stays ignored. On the signal, hydo sends SIGTERM
  to each engine child and every process under it that this user may signal, and waits up to
  10 s. Then it sends SIGKILL to what is left, and a root engine that its `sudo` did not end
  gets `sudo -n kill -KILL`. It says on stderr how many engines it stops and names any that
  stayed. Then it ends by the same signal (status 143 for SIGTERM).
- The processes under each engine child are remembered every 2 s. So the stop also reaches an
  engine whose `flock` the process group's own signal ended first.
- While the stop runs, no engine starts, and a worker that sees its engine end waits for the end
  of the process. Before that wait, an exploration stopped in its workers' boot wrote 40
  failures of 40 seeds.
- While engines run, the exploration's folder has `engines.txt`. It is rewritten when an engine
  starts, becomes ready, or ends, and every 2 s. Each line names the engine program's pid, the
  processes it runs under, and the command that stops it. The first engine's start prints the
  file's path. `hydo guide workflow` has the section "Stop an exploration and its engines."

```text
hydo-hvx 367456 (under sudo 367454, flock 367451; stop it with: sudo kill 367456)
```

The proof ran in this tree on hvx, with the pinned stack image of epoch 6
(`explore-ob-stack-fix-disk.img` of `~/hydo/build/rel060`, read only) and two workers:

| run | stopped by | left after 30 s |
|---|---|---|
| 0.6.0, stand-in engine | SIGTERM to the process group | both `hydo-hvx` and both `sudo`, as root |
| this tree, stand-in engine | SIGTERM to the process group | none; the explorer ended with status 143 |
| this tree, `hydo-hvx` | SIGTERM to the process group | none |
| this tree, `hydo-hvx` | SIGINT to the process group | none |
| this tree, `hydo-hvx` | SIGTERM to `hydo explore` alone | none |

Each run matched the processes by the pids that `pstree` showed under the explorer before the
signal, and `engines.txt` named the same pids. The stand-in engine was a shell loop that ignores
the signals, given to the explorer by `HYDO_HVX_EXPLORE`.

**3. `hydo save` keeps one regression per class and finding.** The SeaweedFS configurations
exploration shrank five power cuts of one class, whose verdicts named other objects of one
check. `hydo save` wrote five files, named after each verdict's first words, while the
configurations table showed one finding. A save now takes the shrinks of one class, one finding
key (the check, as `hydo ci` names it) and one cause (`--shrink-causes`) as one regression. It
writes the first, and names each other one as `the shrink of seed N is another failure of the
finding of seed M ... left out`; the summary line counts them. The unit test
`save_takes_one_shrink_per_class_and_finding` checks that another check, class, or cause stays
apart.

**4. The write scan reads gorilla/mux chains and a switch on the method.** `hydo rules scan
--kind writes` found no S3 route and no filer write of SeaweedFS. Three shapes are read now:

- A route whose matchers come before its handler, as a chain of calls:
  `bucket.Methods(http.MethodPut).Path(objectPath).HandlerFunc(...)`, also over line ends. The
  path comes from `Path` or `PathPrefix`, a constant or a variable (`{name}`). The keys of
  `Queries` follow after `?` and the header of `Headers` or `HeadersRegexp` in brackets, so the
  routes of one path stay apart (`PUT /{object:(?s).+}?partNumber&uploadId` and
  `PUT /{object:(?s).+}[X-Amz-Copy-Source]`). Of a wrapped handler
  (`track(s3a.iam.Auth(s3a.cb.Limit(s3a.PutObjectHandler, ACTION_WRITE)), "PUT")`) the name that
  ends with `Handler` is taken.
- A registration without a method (`mux.HandleFunc("/", fs.filerHandler)` of net/http, or a
  gorilla/mux route without `Methods`). Its handler's body decides: each write method of a
  `case` of `switch r.Method` is a route, with the `...Handler` call that the case makes most,
  the last of a tie. SeaweedFS's filer gives `POST /` and `PUT /` to `PostHandler` and `DELETE
  /` to `DeleteHandler`. A handler without such a switch, and a case of reads, give no write.
- A route of the older form with a variable or a concatenated path
  (`r.HandleFunc(prefix+"/items", h).Methods("POST")`) was read before; the test checks it too.

Three more pieces make the real case right:

- A loop over a list of groups gives its variable the group's prefix. SeaweedFS writes
  `routers = append(routers, apiRouter.PathPrefix("/{bucket}").Subrouter())` and then `for _,
  bucket := range routers {`, so its S3 routes read `/{bucket}/{object:(?s).+}`.
- A path that starts with a variable (`{handlePath}`) keeps the variable's name in the key that
  joins the routes of one path. Before, two such paths were one route with a parameter.
- Of handlers of one name, the one of the switching function's receiver type is taken. Both
  SeaweedFS's filer and its volume server have a `PostHandler`.

On SeaweedFS 4.55's sources 0.6.0 listed 231 write routes, none of `s3api_server.go` and none of
the HTTP servers of `weed/server`. This tree lists 290, 40 of them in `s3api_server.go`.
The filer's `PUT /` and `DELETE /` go to `PostHandler` and `DeleteHandler` of
`filer_server_handlers_write.go`, and its upload protocol's `PATCH` and `DELETE` to
`tusHandler`. Routes of one method and path in several servers stay one route, with the others
under `elsewhere`. So the filer's `POST /` is listed under the IAM API's `POST /`, and the
volume server's writes on `/` under the filer's.

The test `gorilla_chains_variable_paths_and_handlers_that_switch_on_the_method` holds the shapes
of SeaweedFS's `s3api_server.go`, `filer_server.go` and the filer's and volume server's handler
files. The earlier projects' scans keep their tests.

**5. The verdict names a check that judged.** Every passing SeaweedFS run ended `checks=2 held
(objects.no-phantom: ... (0 judged, 0 undecided))`, while `objects.acked-outcome` judged 81 to
95 writes. The verdict now names the first check whose summary does not say `(0 judged`. It
names the first check only when every check judged nothing. No recorded verdict has such a
summary.

**6. `hydo stats` counts `disk=cut` with the cut.** Every power cut needs `disk=cut`, and the
statistics counted it as a disk fault that `faults:` did not list. With `cut` in `faults:`, the
`disk=cut` of a schedule is now no fault of its own; `disk=ioerr` and the others count as
before.

**7. A failed check keeps the services' logs.** A run whose check failed while every service ran
had no `logs/` folder. The NSQ onboarding needed a `hydo inspect` session for `nsqd`'s log and
its log before the restart (`/tmp/hydo/nsqd.log.old`). The diagnosis replay of `hydo run` and of
the explorer's problem replays now runs for every violation. Before, it ran only for an error, a
recovery boot without agent lines, and a violation that names a service. It also reads each
service's log before its last restart, kept as `logs/<service>.before-restart.log`. The cost is
one more replay of a failed run; `hydo run --no-diagnose` leaves it out.

**8. `hydo inspect exec --service` enters an image service's root.** It ran in the service's
network namespace only, where NSQ's data path was the empty mount point. For a service from a
Docker/OCI image it now runs the program through `hydo-oci <service>`, and a `--sh` line through
the image's `/bin/sh -c`. `--guest-root` keeps the guest's root and its tools. The help, `hydo
guide inspect`, and a unit test say so.

**9. Words.** `hydo guide hazards` names the limit of a Go program with `GODEBUG=fips140=on`. The
FIPS entropy source keeps the low byte of timed memory accesses, and hvx's clock moves by the
same 2 µs at every read, so the repetition test fails at start. `hydo guide messages` says that a
`sub ... from=start` record from a `first_` command has no effect, because the command runs in
provisioning, and that the workload, a driver, or the drain writes it. `hydo compose` warns when
services of one image without `ports:` that run other commands get the image's first `EXPOSE`
as their port and readiness check. It comments each such service (as open item 121), and it
still writes the port. Services that run one command of the image, as a Redis cluster's nodes
do, listen where the image says, and get no warning.

**The recorded answers that changed**, each recorded again with `HYDO_BLESS=1`:

- `hydo-compose/tests/golden.json`: 6 of 185 cases, Sentry's self-hosted import in its six
  variants. Its services of the `sentry` and `snuba` images run other commands with the image's
  `EXPOSE` port, and the import now warns and comments them.
- `hydo-agents/tests/guide-sizes.txt`: the topics `hazards`, `inspect`, `messages` and
  `workflow` grew.

The command's golden answers (`equivalence::`, `agents_equivalence::`) and every other test of the changed
crates passed unchanged on the bare-metal machine, with `cargo clippy --workspace
--all-targets` clean.

**10. Not built: a guard for a shrunk reaction delay.** A shrink moves a reaction's delay towards
`+0`, and the NSQ trial's in-flight losses shrank into the window of finding 1. A guard would
keep a smaller delay only when its run gives the same finding key and the same first lines of
the failing check's output (`HYDO-CHECK-OUT`), and else keep the original delay. The shrink
compares verdicts by their signature. The check's output is in the controller's records, not in
the results the shrinker reads, so the guard needs that output carried into each candidate's
result. That was more than this round's time (open item 184).

## Milestone 368 (tentative number): the gaps of the Typesense and Pulsar onboardings

Status: done on 2026-11-26, on the bare-metal machine (hvx and the tests) from this Mac. Each fix
below is its own commit. Nothing recorded moved: every change is in the host's side of the hvx
engine, the controller, the explorer, the checkers, the scans, the commands and the words. No
engine's guest behaviour, agent, image or fingerprint changed, and the fingerprint epoch stays
6. The gaps are the "What hydo lacked" sections of the Typesense and Pulsar examples' RESULTS.md
and the guard that Milestone 367 left (open items 181, 184 and 188).

**1. A cut console says so.** hvx keeps the first 64 KiB of a VM's console
(`HVX_CONSOLE_SZ`). The Typesense and Pulsar onboardings wrote more, and no run warned, although
`hydo guide hazards` said that `hydo run` warns. The cause: the hvx engine wrote its note `hvx:
console full` only when the module's count passed the buffer's size, and `hvx.c` stops counting
at the size. So the note never came. Now:

- The engine notes a buffer that is full (`hydo_hvx::engine`, `console_full_note`). It leaves
  `<tag><suffix>.console-cut` beside the console it saves, a host file that no hash covers. The
  module and the console's bytes are unchanged, so no fingerprint moves.
- The controller takes that file when it writes the run's console and ends the console with a
  `HYDO-CONSOLE-CUT <words>` line (`hydo_control::agent::console_cut_note`).
- A run with the line gets a warning first (`hydo_explore::results::console_cut_warnings`).
  `hydo run` prints it, `result.json` keeps it, `hydo report <run dir>` shows it, and an
  exploration counts such first runs apart from its passes that checked nothing.
- A `type: messages` claim that is violated or undecided in a run with the line is an ERROR whose
  words start with `the console <name> was cut at 64 KiB ...`, with the claim's own words after
  them (`hydo_history::console_cut`). A claim that held stays held.

The limit stays: it is the kernel module's, and the module does not change.

The proof ran on hvx in this tree, with the 0.6.0 release's guest files, on a copy of the
Typesense example in a folder of its own. The copy adds a command `eventually_noise` that prints
700 lines of 100 bytes to the console. The other session's tree was only read.

| run | programs | console | warning | fp | ctl |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | 0.6.0 | 314 of the 700 lines kept | none | `00bfacca721662f2` | `228425142b44cf81` |
| `disk=none \| run` | this tree's `hydo` with 0.6.0's `hydo-hvx` | the same | none | the same | the same |
| `disk=none \| run` | this tree's `hydo` and `hydo-hvx` | the same, then the `HYDO-CONSOLE-CUT` line | `hydo run`, `result.json`, `hydo report`, and `hvx: console full` in engine.log | the same | the same |

The fingerprints and control transcripts of the three runs are equal, so the change moved
nothing that a run hashes. The second row also showed that a `hydo` copied out of its checkout
starts the release's `hydo-hvx`, as open item 182 says; `HYDO_HVX_EXPLORE` named this tree's.
In this copy the check's read-back ran before the noise, so its records were whole and the check
held; a claim that the cut breaks is shown by the tests `messages::a_cut_console_makes_a_loss_an_error`
(hydo-history) and `messages_results::a_cut_console_is_a_warning_and_no_loss` (hydo-explore).

**2. Several operations of one process in flight.** The Typesense client's import recorded one
`send` per document from one process, and the checker counted 337 of 352 sends as unknown: a
process has one operation in flight, so each invocation closed the one before. A process token
`<process>#<op>` now names one operation of the process. The messages checker pairs a completion
with the open invocation of its whole token, and the claims that compare processes (`members`
and the members' leases) take the part before the first `#`. A token without `#` reads as
before. No recorded history has a `#` in a process token. For list-append and register checks
each token is a process of its own, as it was. The Rust SDK's `history::messages::op_proc(3,
"d17")` writes `3#d17`; it is at the end of the module behind the feature `messages`, so the
programs built without the feature keep their bytes. The other SDKs keep their frozen scope; a
client of theirs writes the token as its process. `hydo guide messages` and HISTORIES.md say so,
and that a batch of one request is one `send` with several items.

**3. A group's primary during an election.** hydo asked a group's `primary:` command 10 times a
second apart, and Typesense's Raft election after a kill of its leader took longer. It asks 30
times now. Only a run whose probe named no member within 10 tries runs otherwise, and such a run
ended in an ERROR. The ERROR names the likely cause: a first line that is no member's name (a
node id or an address) or no primary for 29 s of guest time, with what to do.

The proof ran on hvx on a copy of the Typesense example whose `primary:` command asks once
(`timeout 2 /bin/tsc primary`), without the 15 s that the example's command waits itself:

| schedule | 0.6.0 | this tree |
|---|---|---|
| `K=nodes.primary@10+20 P=nodes.primary@11+2` | the primary after 4 tries | the same, with one fingerprint |
| `K=nodes.all@10+1 P=nodes.primary@11+2` | after 4 tries | the same, with one fingerprint |
| `K=nodes.all@10+30 P=nodes.primary@11+2`, no member up | `ERROR ... named no member in 10 tries (exit status 143, first line "")` | `ERROR ... in 30 tries, a second of guest time apart (exit status 143, first line ""); the group had no primary for 29 s of guest time, or the command failed. ...` |

Typesense's elections after these kills ended within 4 tries, so no run here reached the case of
the onboarding, an election that outlasted 10 tries; the third row shows the longer wait and the
words. The passing runs gave 0.6.0's fingerprints and control transcripts.

**4. The shrinker leaves out a storage fault that the failure does not need.** Seed 3 of the
Typesense exploration shrank to `T=35:-21600 W=... G=ts3@8+3:zero,...` with the class
`corrupted-files`, although the step alone fails. Its events show why: every round kept the
candidate that halved the clock step, which comes before the one without `G=`, and the budget
of 40 runs ended the rounds first. After its rounds the shrinker now tries, one at a time, the
schedule without each storage fault that is left (`G=`, `L=`, each block fault;
`Ex::storage_removals`), whatever the budget, and skips one it already decided. The minimal
schedule's class (`min_class`) is named by the faults it keeps, as before.

**5. The write scan reads C and C++ registrations.** `hydo rules scan --kind writes` found none
of Typesense's routes. It now reads `<server>->post("<path>", <handler>, ...)` and its kin
`put`, `patch`, `del` and `delete` (also with `.`) in C and C++ files, with the handler's
definition in any C or C++ file. A path is a literal that starts with `/`, an HTTP client's call
is no route, and a handler named for its method (`post_multi_search`) is judged by the words
after the method. On Typesense 30.2's sources it lists 54 routes that write and leaves out 3
`POST` routes whose names say that they read; the file has 57 such registrations. The earlier
projects' reports keep their bytes: their tests passed unchanged.

**6. Two images in one folder.** A build of a copy of `hydo.yaml` with `--set` wrote a second
image beside the first, and `hydo run`, `hydo repro` and the other commands that find the image
stopped. Of several images they now take the one whose build record (`<image>.json`) names a
manifest called `hydo.yaml`, when exactly one does, else the newest, and print a note that names
it, the reason, and the others with `--image`.

**7. A kept address says nothing.** `hydo compose` warned `ipv4_address 10.89.0.11 ignored; the
service is at 10.89.0.11`. An `ipv4_address` that hydo's own order gives the service too gives no
warning now; another address is still named. No recorded import had an equal pair.

**8. The guard of a shrunk reaction delay.** Milestone 367 left it (open item 184): a shrink moved
the NSQ trial's in-flight loss to `+0`, into finding 1's window, and the report named the wrong
cause. A candidate whose only change is a shorter delay of a reaction is kept now only when it
fails with the same key and the same first violation text as the schedule kept so far. The text
is the first line of the violated check's `HYDO-CHECK-OUT` note, else of a host check's
explanation, else the verdict, with every number left out (`report::first_violation_text`).
Otherwise the earlier delay stays.

The scripted engine's new scenario `guard_shrinks_keep_the_cause` shows both shrink rules. A kill
of redis 30 ms after an event loses the message in flight, and earlier than 20 ms it fails the
same check with another cause; its shrink keeps `+30`. A kill of mysql fails alike at every delay
and shrinks to `+0`. On the RAUC manifest with storage faults, where only a step back of the
clock fails, no shrink keeps a `G=`. With the guard turned off the first part fails, and with the
storage pass turned off the second (`T=10:-168 G=device@3+3:zero,...` kept its `G=`).

**The recorded answers that changed**, recorded again with `HYDO_BLESS=1`:

- `hydo-control/tests/golden/groups.txt`: the transcript of `K=deaf.primary@3+1`, a probe that
  never names a member, now 30 tries and the new words.

- `hydo-cli/tests/golden/cli.jsonl`: the answers of `hydo guide manifest` (linux c007 and mac
  c033), which prints MANIFEST.md.

On the bare-metal machine `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` was clean, and these passed:
the tests of hydo-history, hydo-hvx, hydo-control, hydo-explore (with the 32 scenarios of the
scripted engine), hydo-compose, hydo-agents, the Rust SDK with the feature `messages`, and
`cargo test -p hydo --test it` with `equivalence::` and `agents_equivalence::`. Three tests
failed there for reasons outside this milestone:

- `skillupdate::tests::each_agent_gets_its_folder` (hydo's unit tests) and
  `identity::local_outputs_are_no_inputs` (hydo-explore) need a git checkout; the copy on the
  bare-metal machine is an rsync of the tracked files, without `.git`.
- `value_properties::a_broken_value_property_is_a_violation_with_one_signature` failed once under
  a load of 19 and passed alone.

## Milestone 369 (tentative number): rqlite, queued writes answered and then lost, and a removed node that never joins again

rqlite 10.8.0 became the example `hydo/onboard/examples/rqlite` (RESULTS.md), by
`docs/ONBOARDING-PLAYBOOK.md`, with hydo of `main` at `e2058be0` on hvx on the bare-metal
machine. One known bug was reached and two new candidates were found; nothing was posted, and
nothing recorded moved.

**The example.** Three Raft nodes of rqlite 10.8.0 from the official image, at fixed addresses,
each with `-bootstrap-expect 3` and the three Raft addresses, imported with `hydo compose`. Each
node's data is on a file system of its own, which `setup:` gives to the image's user; the
snapshot threshold is the build parameter `snap` (64 log entries). The Go client `rqc` sends each
request once, through a node that the seed picks. It writes inserts, upserts, updates, deletes,
transactions of 2 or 3 writes, and queued writes with `wait`, all recorded in a messages check
with `acked_outcome` and `effect: recorded`. Transactions of list appends and of reads at level
`linearizable` or `strong` go into a list-append history checked at strict serializability.
Other checks judge every node's lists against the leader's (at level `none`, during the run), a
backup in SQL against the acknowledged appends, a removal of a follower and its join after a
restart, every node against the leader after the heal, the writes through each node, and the
leader itself. A serial driver behind the build parameter `qstop` sends queued writes without
`wait` and stops that node with SIGTERM.

**Finding 1, known (pull request rqlite#3027, open).** A queued write with `wait` is answered 200
although it was never committed. `runQueue` (`http/service.go` lines 1949 to 2019) retries a
batch once after a second and then runs its success path, whose `req.Close()` releases every
waiting caller. `K=nodes.primary@35+3` kills the leader at the step of a queued write through a
follower: the follower logs `execute queue write retry limit (1) limit reached`, and the client
got 200 after 1.05 s. Blind at seed 28 of e1, and in seeds 46, 62 and 77 of e2b. Seed 46 shrank to
a 500 ms delay of the leader's links without a kill
(`N=nodes.primary@17-20:delay,500ms W=2da25f11,p3,q1,r2000,oanytime_backup`).

**Finding 2, new.** A graceful stop of a node loses the queued writes that it has acknowledged.
At SIGTERM `rqlited` closes its HTTP service first (`cmd/rqlited/main.go` line 284).
`Service.Close` closes the queue, whose goroutine returns at `case <-q.done` (`queue/queue.go`
line 236) without writing the batch it holds, and then stops `runQueue`. With `--set
qstop=yes`, 3 queued writes and SIGTERM to that node lost all three in a run without any fault.
The node's log shows a clean stop with a snapshot on close. rqlite's page "Queued Writes" names
only a crash as the risk.

**Finding 3, new.** A node removed while it was down never joins again after its restart. The
aimed grid e3 (`--reactive-at rq.write_acked@20 --react-delays 0..40/10 --react-actions
cut,powerloss,kill-now`) failed at one cell of 35, `A=rq.write_acked@20+10:powerloss-rq2`. The
node `rq2`, the leader then, lost its power and stayed down, and the removal driver removed it (200). At the
heal `rq2` started with `-bootstrap-expect 3` and `-join`. hashicorp/raft's leader makes
one last best-effort replication to a removed server and heartbeats it until then, so `rq2` heard the
leader at once. The bootstrapper's done check is a known leader (`cmd/rqlited/main.go` lines 643
to 646), checked before every join (`cluster/bootstrap.go` lines 151 to 156): `boot operation
marked done`, no join, then `not part of stable configuration, aborting election`, and a failed
snapshot every few seconds to the end. rqlite#1290 (fixed in 7.20.1) was a removed node that did
not join for another reason.

**The runs.** The final image `explore-ob-rqlite-disk.img` (`c4d29886…`) gives
`943d6c299867d55d` on two clean runs. Each regression gave one fingerprint over two fresh runs:
finding 1 by a kill `b99061a1e2c70785`, finding 1 by a delay `11279983f35ccb8b`, finding 2 on the
image built with `--set qstop=yes` (`a3078a27…`) `7d26ebb2631121b3`, finding 3
`c6b10c11a878e130`. `hydo repro --regressions` gave 3 of 3 as expected on the default image, with finding 2's
regression left out for its `# params: qstop=yes`, and 3 of 3 on the `qstop` image before finding
3's file existed.

**The explorations.** e1, `--seeds 1-40 --strategy process --new-faults --cluster-faults
--storage-faults` on an image whose list-append check hydo had dropped, failed 3 of 40: finding 1
and detected damage (2). e2 on an image with a removal driver that waited was stopped after 19
runs; its one failure was that driver. e2b, `--seeds 41-100 --strategy process --more-faults
--cluster-faults --storage-faults`, failed 9 of 60: finding 1 (3), detected damage (3), an
undetected damage of one node's Raft log (seed 51), and a removal of unknown outcome that the
driver did not follow with a restart (2, a mistake of the rules, fixed). e3, the aimed grid of 35
cells, failed once, with finding 3. The list-append check held in all 95 schedules of e2b and
e3.

**Tests.** The new example enters the explorer's and the controller's corpora. Re-recorded with
`HYDO_BLESS=1`, in a copy of the worktree with an index of its tracked files and a target folder
of its own on the bare-metal machine: the explorer's corpus goldens (full and quick), its
identity goldens (quick and full), and the controller's quick corpus golden, which adds the
example's entries only. Then `cargo test -p hydo-explore --test it` (61 passed), the controller's corpus
tests, `-p hydo --test it -- equivalence:: agents_equivalence::` (9 passed) and `-p hydo-agents
--test it` (16 passed). The copy has no `AGENTS.local.md`, so `public_content::`
checked the generic patterns, and a `grep` of the listed values found none in the new text. `sh
ci/vale.sh` finds nothing. No Rust code changed.

Retro: rqlite 10.8.0, hvx, 2026-11-26
- Time to the first clean run: 30 minutes of wall time, with the client written while the first
  builds ran beside two other onboardings.
- Schedules run before the first finding: 28 (e1's seed 28, finding 1); finding 2 at the first
  run of its driver; finding 3 at cell 10 of the aimed grid. Three failures were mistakes of the
  rules: the client's transactions sent a `DELETE` for every write, the removal driver waited 90
  s inside a serial driver, which stretched a pause of one step to 90 s, and it did not restart a
  node after a removal of unknown outcome.
- The findings: 1 known (pull request #3027), 2 new (the queued writes at a graceful stop, and
  a node removed while it was down that never joins again), and one undetected damage of a Raft
  log by hydo's `G=`, the environment.
- What took the most time: the slow builds, runs and tests on the shared machine (about 2
  hours of the 5); the client and its checks (about 1 hour); the list-append check that hydo
  dropped and the three mistakes of the rules (about 1 hour, with two rebuilt images).
- What hydo lacked: a `checks/list_append_*` file dropped without a word when hydo.yaml has a
  `checks:` section; no write routes of a `switch` on the path; no clock place found; a pause by
  steps stretched by a serial driver; two images in one folder; no fault that stops a service
  gracefully; no fault that changes a cluster's members (open item 189).
- Strategies: a new entry "A graceful stop after answers that are not durable yet", and the
  rqlite evidence in "Kills of the process that holds acknowledged work", "Reactions at console
  events" and "History checks"; the first table names rqlite.

**What is left.** Open item 189.

## Milestone 370 (tentative number): RabbitMQ, a stream that loses a confirmed message after a power loss of one node while a second node is away

RabbitMQ 4.4.1 became the example `hydo/onboard/examples/rabbitmq` (RESULTS.md), by
`docs/ONBOARDING-PLAYBOOK.md`, with hydo of `main` at `e2058be0` and the guest files of the
published 0.6.0 Linux release, on hvx on the bare-metal machine. Two new candidates and one
documented loss, all of the stream; nothing was posted, and nothing recorded moved.

**The example.** Three nodes of the official image `rabbitmq:4.4.1`, which find each other from
fixed names with classic peer discovery, imported with `hydo compose`. Each node's data is on a
file system of its own, and the stream plugin is on. A node is ready when its Erlang distribution
port answers, the nodes start together, `net_ticktime` is 15 s (the build parameter `ticktime`),
and `consumer_timeout` is 30 s. The Go client `rmqc` (amqp091-go v1.17.0,
rabbitmq-stream-go-client v1.10.0, `hydohist` of the Go SDK v0.6.0) declares a quorum queue `j`
with a delivery limit of 2 that dead-letters at least once into `jd`, a quorum queue `k` with a
single active consumer, and a stream `s` of three replicas. It publishes with publisher confirms,
consumes with acknowledgements that a passive declare on the channel confirms, crashes on poison
messages, deduplicates stream publishes by producer name, and reads the stream as a consumer
whose offset the server keeps. Three messages checks judge `j` (`lease`, `dead_letter`,
`acked_outcome`), `k` (`order: fifo` per key) and `s` (`duplicates`, `order: log`, `after_ack`,
`fan_out` over the reader and a group that reads from the first offset). One drain takes all five
groups in parallel and starts with one recorded publish to `j` and to `s`. The build parameter
`replicas` (3 or 1) is the example's `configs:` entry. RabbitMQ 4.3 removed the partition
handling strategies with Mnesia, so the example has no such setting.

**Finding 1, new.** A power loss of one node while a second node is away loses a confirmed
message of the stream for good. A stream's writer confirms a chunk once a majority of the members
wrote it (`agreed_commit/1`, `osiris_writer.erl` line 653), and osiris 1.14.1 never syncs, as the
documentation says. Blind at seed 2 of e2: `K=rabbit2@1+3 N=nodes.bridge.6@21-23:loss,100%
P=rabbit1@16+11 W=5764a73c,p3,q2,r1000 G=rabbit3@20:flip,n=4,seed=4979bdc4 L=rabbit3@21+3`. The
pause of `rabbit1` is 11 workload steps, about 100 s, past the net tick time of 15 s. Epoch 2
began with `rabbit3` as the writer and `rabbit2` as its replica, and they confirmed `s29`. Then
`rabbit3` lost its power and its unsynced chunks of epoch 2, while `rabbit1` was still down. When
all three ran again, the coordinator elected `rabbit1` from the quorum of stopped members
`rabbit1` and `rabbit3`. `rabbit2`, which held `s29`, waited on a retry timer after
`writer_unavailable`. When it joined epoch 3, it deleted its whole log, `s29` with it, and copied
the log again from `rabbit1`. On e2's image it needed the kill, the pause and the power loss; on
the final image each run without one of the five faults passes, a narrow window. The
documentation says that a single node's loss "would typically just be re-replicated from the
other nodes". No issue or discussion names it. The paragraph "Finding 1 checked again with hydo
0.7.0" below has the trace.

**Finding 2, documented.** A power cut of the whole guest loses confirmed messages of the stream,
and a new message can take a lost one's offset (`C=12`: "share offset 0"); a reader's stored
offset can go back too. The documentation's "Data Safety when using Streams" says that streams do
not flush their data. The quorum queues lost nothing at any cut.

**Finding 3, new, a clock effect.** After a backward step of the wall clock by a day, a kill of the
stream's writer leaves the stream without a writer for the size of the step: every publish answers
`Leader not Ready yet` for the rest of the run, while every node runs. The coordinator logs `failed
to stop member ... nodedown` and nothing more. Seed 10 of e3 (`K=nodes.primary@12+2 ...
T=7:-86400 ... G=rabbit3@7+2:trunc`) needed the step, the kill and the restart that `G=` makes;
seed 4 of e4 failed the same probe after `K=rabbit1@21+9 P=rabbit1@8+1 T=10:-2592000`, not
separated. The paragraph "Finding 3 checked again with hydo 0.7.0" below has the trace: the
coordinator's leader parks failed restarts with a retry time from a system time that is still a
day ahead, because every node runs with `multi_time_warp`.

**What held.** The quorum queues kept every confirmed message under kills, pauses past the net
tick time, partitions, one-way loss, one node's power loss, damaged files, power cuts and clock
steps. A consumer's crash gave its message back, poison messages were dead-lettered at least once,
the single active consumer kept each key's order, and the stream stored no message twice.

**The runs.** The final image `explore-ob-rabbitmq-disk.img` (`0f93b104…`) gives `08ff275ad7f8aac4`
on two clean runs. Each regression gave one fingerprint over two fresh runs: finding 1
`46d06ab61b82f53e`, finding 2 `2d220bcd3276c1b7`, finding 3 `efcd83d18848454a`. Finding 1 on e2's
image gave `83cc413c2d60d1ae` twice, and finding 3 on e3's image `33f9b1d69512cda5` twice. Both
windows move with the image's bytes: finding 3's saved schedule kills the leader a step later than
e3's seed did. `hydo repro --regressions` gave 3 of 3 as expected with the same values.

**The explorations.** All with one worker and `--no-shrink`, because the stream's documented loss at
a cut would have taken every shrink; directed runs judged each failure. e2, 20 schedules without
power cuts (`explore-nocut.yaml`) and `--cluster-faults --storage-faults`: finding 1 (seed 2),
hydo's restart of a killed group one node at a time (3), detected damage of the metadata store
(3). e3, 15 schedules of the final client with `--new-faults`: finding 3 (seed 10) and a drain
that did not end (seed 4). e4, 12 schedules with power cuts and a stream check without
`delivery` (`explore-cutqq.yaml`): probably finding 3 without a damaged file (seed 4) and finding
2 at 3 of 5 cuts. e5, the grid `--reactive-at rmq.pub_confirmed@10,rmq.stream_confirmed@10
--react-actions kill-now,powerloss`: 24 schedules, no failure. The configs exploration of `replicas` (3 and 1, seeds 1 to 6, `--storage-faults`)
found finding 1 again blind in its default combination (seed 2, without `N=`). With one replica,
seed 1 lost a confirmed stream message at the power loss of that replica's node, the setting's
documented trade-off; with three it passed. With one replica 3 of 5 seeds failed, with three 2 of
6. The exploration was stopped during its shrinks, so `configs.json` has no table.

**Tests.** The new example enters the explorer's and the controller's corpora. Re-recorded with
`HYDO_BLESS=1` on the bare-metal machine, in a copy of the worktree with an index of its files and
a target folder of this task's own: the explorer's corpus goldens (full and quick), its identity
goldens (quick and full), and the controller's quick corpus golden, which only adds the example's
entries. `cargo test -p hydo-explore --test it` (61 passed), the controller's corpus tests (2
passed while recording), `-p hydo --test it -- equivalence:: agents_equivalence::` (9 passed)
and `-p hydo-agents --test it` (16 passed). The copy has no `AGENTS.local.md`, so
`public_content::` checked the generic patterns; a `grep` of the listed values found only the
repository's own GitHub path in the client's module paths, as in the other Go clients. `sh
ci/vale.sh` finds nothing. No Rust code changed.

Retro: RabbitMQ 4.4.1, hvx, 2026-11-26
- Time to the first clean run: 40 minutes of wall time, about 20 of them waiting for the build
  of this tree's programs and the image.
- Schedules run before the first finding: 2 (e2's seed 2, finding 1). None of the failures was a
  mistake of the rules, but four changes of the client were: the poison crash needed a recorded
  give-back, the consumers' give-up a requeue, the probe had to move into the drain, and the
  declaration had to wait for every node to join.
- The findings: 2 new (the stream's loss after a power loss of one node while a second node is
  away, the stream without a leader after a clock step), 1 documented (the stream's loss at a
  power cut), 3 schedules of detected damage and 3 of hydo's restart of a group one node at a
  time.
- What took the most time: images that the client's changes made over again, about 2 hours with
  the clean runs; timing-sensitive candidates that passed on the next image, about 1 hour; the
  restart of a killed group, which needed the readiness on the distribution port.
- What hydo lacked: a group restarted one node at a time; a messages check's `final:` before the
  `eventually_` commands; one drain for several histories; no `Drained` in the tagged Go SDK; no
  way to leave one fault kind out; two images in one folder; no Erlang in the clock audit; a
  forward step written with `+` (open item 191).
- Strategies: the RabbitMQ evidence in "Power cuts of the whole guest", "One node's storage
  faults" and "Clock steps and the clock audit" of `hydo guide strategies`; the first table names
  RabbitMQ.

**Finding 1 checked again with hydo 0.7.0.** A check of the record with the released hydo 0.7.0,
from a fresh clone at `1c318f23`, on hvx, found that the first version of this section and of
RESULTS.md described finding 1's trigger wrongly. That version said three things:

- that the pause of `rabbit1` was shorter than the net tick time;
- that one node's power loss alone was enough;
- that the quorum of the election was not traced, and that `rabbit2` followed the new writer.

The image built again had the sha256 of RESULTS.md (`0f93b104…`). The schedule gave `VIOLATION
[stream.no-loss] s29 was acknowledged to process 29 at 84.029 s and never delivered ...` with
`46d06ab61b82f53e` twice. Without `L=rabbit3@21+3` it passed with `30301878046ba223`, and without
`P=rabbit1@16+11` it passed with `5f708bb378946198`. The nodes' logs and the code of RabbitMQ
4.4.1 and osiris v1.14.1, the same on `main`, give this order:

- The pause is 11 workload steps, about 100 s of guest time. `rabbit2` logged `node
  rabbit@rabbit1 down: net_tick_timeout` at 00:01:06.4, and `rabbit1` came back at 00:02:33.66.
- Epoch 2 began with `rabbit3` as the writer at 00:01:05.88 and `rabbit2` as its replica.
  `rabbit1` got the role `{replica,2}` without a member that ran in it
  (`rabbit_stream_coordinator.erl` line 2098).
- `rabbit3` and `rabbit2` confirmed `s29` (`osiris_writer.erl` lines 321 and 653, the middle
  tail). Nothing syncs a segment file: osiris has no `file:sync` call in `src/`, and osiris pull
  request 87 left fsync "to be implemented separately".
- `rabbit3` lost its power at about 00:01:21, while `rabbit1` was down too, and only `rabbit2`
  ran. `rabbit3` lost its two chunks of epoch 2, and its tail on disk was `{1,4}`.
- All three nodes ran again before the election. The replica on `rabbit2` failed to start with
  `writer_unavailable`, and the coordinator parked that action for about 6 s (lines 2392 to
  2398), so `rabbit2` was no candidate.
- The old writer of epoch 1 on `rabbit1` wrote a tracking chunk at offset 5 in epoch 1 and
  stopped with the tail `{1,5}`. The coordinator elects as soon as a quorum has stopped (lines
  1414, 1744 to 1747 and 2056) and takes the newest tail (`select_leader/2`, lines 2534 to 2548).
  `rabbit1` and `rabbit3` were that quorum, and `rabbit1` became the writer of epoch 3 at
  00:02:33.706.
- At 00:02:39 `rabbit2` started as a replica. The writer named offset 5 as epoch 1, and
  `rabbit2` held offset 5 in epoch 2. So `truncate_to` (`osiris_log.erl` lines 948 to 1022)
  deleted every segment of `rabbit2`, and `rabbit2` copied the log again from offset 0. After it
  all three nodes report `{{0,7},[{1,5},{3,7}]}`, and none holds `s29`.

So the loss needs the documented absence of a sync ("they do not explicitly flush (fsync) the
data", the streams page, "Data Safety") and a second node away during the power loss. The
candidate is the part that no page documents. The coordinator elects from a quorum that leaves
out the member with the confirmed chunk, because that member waits on a retry timer. Then that
member deletes its copy. The documentation says that a lost copy on one node "would typically
just be re-replicated from the other nodes". No duplicate names this loss. The closest are
rabbitmq-server issue 9457, osiris issue 145, osiris pull request 87 and issue 79, discussion
18370 with osiris pull request 246, and rabbitmq-server issues 16822 and 9275. RESULTS.md, finding
1, has the corrected text. The regression file's comment and the explorer's four corpus goldens,
which hold that file's sha256, changed with it.

**Finding 3 checked again with hydo 0.7.0.** The released hydo 0.7.0, from a fresh clone at
`4eb78297`, on hvx, traced finding 3. The first version of this section and of RESULTS.md said two
false things: that Erlang starts without a time warp, so that a node that starts after a step back
keeps a system time a day behind, and that the wait needs the coordinator's leader to move between
such nodes. It also named pull request 17450, which has no part in it.

The saved regression gave `VIOLATION [eventually_probe] ... no publish was confirmed within 60 s
after the faults` with `efcd83d18848454a` twice, on the final image (`0f93b104…`). Without
`T=7:-86400` it passed with `5c593130087afccd`, without `K=nodes.primary@13+2` with
`056c67d4bc69ded8`, and without `G=` (so without the restart of `rabbit3`) with
`af49e5ec61e49f53`. Held runs read each node's clocks and the coordinator's state at four points.
With the code of RabbitMQ 4.4.1 (`rabbit_stream_coordinator.erl`, the same on `main`) and Ra 3.2.0
they give this order:

- Every node runs with `multi_time_warp`. The runtime moves its time offset only at its next check
  of the OS clock, every 15 s and later every 60 s (`erl_time_sup.c` lines 316 to 318 and 497 to
  505). 19 s after the step, `rabbit1` and `rabbit2` had an `erlang:system_time` 86,400,543 ms
  ahead of `os:system_time`; `rabbit3`, restarted after the step, matched. 23 s after the step
  `rabbit2` matched too.
- The kill came between those points. `rabbit2` led the coordinator in term 2. `rabbit1`'s member
  was `{down,1}` and `{sleeping,nodeup}`. `rabbit2`'s replica was `{sleeping,1795651263161}`
  with the target `stopped` (`writer_unavailable`), and `rabbit3`'s `{sleeping,1795651264168}`
  (`noproc`).
- Each retry time is the command's system time plus 5,000 ms and a jitter (`park_action/8`, lines
  2392 to 2399; the `.hrl` lines 12 and 17). The system time is the Ra leader's
  `erlang:system_time(millisecond)` at the command (`ra_server_proc.erl` lines 2524 to 2529,
  `ra_server.erl` lines 3443 to 3447). `rabbit2` stamped it before its check, so after the check
  each retry was a day away.
- The relative timer of 5 to 10 s fired (`ra_server_proc.erl` lines 1812 to 1813 and 628 to 629).
  Its `{timeout, retry_reconcile}` carried the corrected time, `expire_parked/4` found nothing due
  (lines 2440 to 2442), and the timer was armed again for about 86,400 s (lines 2403 to 2430).
- `rabbit1`'s `nodeup` woke its member (`{stopped,1,{1,1}}`), but one stopped member of three is no
  quorum (lines 1412 to 1415 and 1744 to 1747). `wake_timed_sleep` (lines 2605 to 2615) wakes a
  member parked on a time only when a writer goes down or fails to start, which cannot happen
  without a writer.
- The commit index stayed at 27 for the rest of the held run, about 7 minutes, and at its end
  `rabbit2`'s retry was still 85,994,948 ms away. The wait would be about 86,406.6 s.

Without the restart `rabbit3` led the coordinator, `rabbit2`'s replica stopped cleanly, and only
`rabbit3`'s replica was parked. With `rabbit1` back two members were stopped, a quorum, and the run
ends in epoch 2 with every member running. So the restart changes which node leads and how many
replicas are parked, not the clock's part. The parked retries came with pull request 16515
("Stream coordinator: v8 optimisations and bug fixes", merged on 2026-08-19, commits
`c5a668ef1f`, `f712c3d228` and `fd80774359`) in 4.4.0 (2026-10-19): "Failed operations are now
retried after a short randomised delay". No duplicate names it. The closest are issue 18475 (a
