## Milestone 371 (tentative number): Garnet, a slot without an owner after a failover that follows a migration

Microsoft Garnet 2.2.14 became the example `hydo/onboard/examples/garnet` (RESULTS.md), by
`docs/ONBOARDING-PLAYBOOK.md`. The image and the directed runs used the published 0.6.0 Linux
release on hvx on the bare-metal machine, and the explorations ran on GitHub's KVM runners with
`explore.yml`. One new candidate, one finding that needs Garnet's default of a setting, one known
bug, and three candidates whose cause was not traced; nothing was posted, and nothing recorded
moved.

**Finding 2, new.** A default `CLUSTER FAILOVER` right after a `MIGRATE ... SLOTS` into the same
shard leaves the migrated slot without an owner on every node, for good. The client waited until
the source and the target named the target as the owner, and then failed the target's shard
over at once. The replica takes over the slots that its own copy of the configuration gives its
primary (`ClusterConfig.TakeOverFromPrimary`, `libs/cluster/Server/ClusterConfig.cs` line 1393),
and gossip had not brought it the migration yet. The old primary becomes a replica and serves
no slot. So the slot's keys, which the new primary replicated, are served by no node:
`CLUSTERDOWN Hash slot not served` through the new primary, and `MOVED` to the old primary through
the source. The exploration e2 failed seeds 96, 99 and 120 so; the first two showed it in the recovery boot
after a power cut.
On hvx seed 96 failed with its faults, without its power cut, and without its clock step. Its
composition alone passed on the final image, where the gossip came before the failover, so the
race depends on that moment. `native/slot-lost-after-failover.sh` reproduces it with Docker, also across a restart of
every node, and passes with a wait of 6 s between the two steps. No issue names it. The paragraph
"Findings 1 and 2 checked again with hydo 0.7.0" below has why gossip never repairs it.

**The example.** Six nodes of Garnet 2.2.14 from the official image, in cluster mode as three
primaries with one replica each, at fixed addresses, imported with `hydo compose`. Each node's
AOF, checkpoints and cluster configuration are on a file system of its own. The build parameters
are `--aof-commit-wait` (`wait`, `yes`), `--aof-commit-freq` (`freq`), `--checkpoint-freq`
(`ckpt`), `--device-type` (`device`), and `--cluster-replication-reestablishment-timeout`
(`reest`, `5` in the example, `0` in Garnet), each a `configs:` entry. The Go client `gnc` forms
the cluster with `CLUSTER MEET`, `ADDSLOTSRANGE` and `REPLICATE`. It sends each write once to the
owner of its slot and follows `MOVED` and `ASK` itself. The writes are strings, expiring keys,
hashes, counters, lists, sets, sorted sets, `MULTI`/`EXEC` and Lua scripts over 16 hash tags. As
a control plane does, it fails a shard over with `CLUSTER FAILOVER` and a late write to the old
primary, moves slots with `MIGRATE ... SLOTS`, and takes checkpoints with `BGSAVE`. A messages
check with `acked_outcome` reads every write back from the owner of its slot. Four checks judge
the rest: each replica holds its primary's keys and none of a slot that left its shard, every
node names one owner per slot, transactions and scripts apply whole, and counters stay within
their `INCR`s. Garnet has no `WAIT`, so replication is asynchronous and the client never forces
a failover.

**Finding 1, a deployment setting with a status that hides it.** With Garnet's default
`--cluster-replication-reestablishment-timeout 0`, a kill of a primary and its start with
`--recover` leave its replica without replication for good. The primary drives the AOF stream
only to a replica that attached, and a replica attaches again by itself only in
`ReplicationManager.EnsureReplication`, which returns at once when the option is 0
(`libs/cluster/Server/Replication/ReplicationManager.cs` line 189). The replica's
`master_link_status` is its gossip connection (`Gossip.GetPrimaryLinkStatus`), so it says `up`.
`disk=none | run K=g1@15+3` left `g4` at offset 1,668 while `g1` was at 5,984, without 18 keys
that `g1` acknowledged after its restart, and with 5 keys of two slots that moved away after it.
With `reest=5` the same schedule passes. A kill of the replica passes with either value.
`native/replica-after-primary-restart.sh` reproduces it with Docker: 0 of 10 keys on the replica
60 s after the restart, `connected_slaves:0` on the primary, and 10 of 10 with `REEST=5`. A
default `CLUSTER FAILOVER` in that state aborts (`native/failover-after-primary-restart.sh`); a
forced one would promote the stale replica. microsoft/garnet#2087 reported the same
`master_link_status:up` for a write through `READWRITE`, and was closed with a fix of that
trigger only.

**Known: microsoft/garnet#2281.** With the default device, a power cut of the guest loses writes
that Garnet acknowledged with `--aof-commit-wait`: `disk=cut | run C=10` lost 5 of 20. With
`--device-type FileStream`, the issue's workaround, the same cut and `C=30` lost none.

**Three candidates whose cause was not traced**, each with a regression on the `fs` image and two
equal fingerprints on KVM: a kill of a primary 10 ms after a `BGSAVE` leaves its replica
answering nothing after the heal; a pause of a migration's target and failovers of both shards
after the migration lose two acknowledged writes; and after a kill of a new primary and a power
cut, its replica holds other data at the same replication offset.

**The runs.** The final images were built with the client `f3951b59…`: the default image
`explore-ob-garnet-disk.img` (`f9d61a2f…`) gives `96eee05052238c8b` on two clean runs. Each
regression gave one fingerprint over two runs on hvx: finding 1 on the `reest=0` image
(`c5bc4e25…`) `982a16effdb11bfa`, finding 2 on the `device=FileStream` image (`57aaef25…`)
`5a4771d51585eeff`, and #2281 on the default image `bb4299751e2f04c0`. `hydo repro --regressions`
on each image replayed the regression of its build parameters as expected and left the others
out. Kills of a migration's source and target at the migration's events, of a newly promoted
primary, power cuts at the client's events and at the 300th and 600th flush (`cf=`, with
`device=FileStream`), and steps of the clock by an hour each way passed.

**The explorations** ran on GitHub's KVM runners with `explore.yml`, 20 parts each, from the
branch's first version of the example. A first run took 200 to 350 s there, four times hvx's.
e1, the default image with `--strategy process --new-faults --cluster-faults --storage-faults`
over seeds 1-60, was cancelled after 9 first runs: its one failure was #2281, and its shrink took
81 runs. e2, the same options on the `device=FileStream` image over seeds 61-120, read 51 first
runs from 17 parts. It found finding 2 in seeds 96, 99 and 120, the candidates B (seed 89) and C
(seed 115), damaged files in 8 seeds, one run whose group `primary:` named no member, and one
`SPIN` of KVM in a recovery boot. e3, `--strategy swarm --new-faults
--cluster-faults --reactive fault` at the client's five events with `--kill-now`, over seeds
121-160, read 32 first runs from 16 parts and found candidate A (seed 144). The last 3 parts of
e2 and 4 of e3 were still shrinking when the round ended and were cancelled, so no merged report was
made; the parts' reports were read one by one.

**Tests.** The new example enters the explorer's and the controller's corpora. Re-recorded with
`HYDO_BLESS=1`: the explorer's corpus goldens (full and quick), its identity goldens (quick and
full), and the controller's quick corpus golden. With a target folder of this task's own on the
bare-metal machine, in a copy of the worktree with an index of its tracked files: `cargo test -p
hydo-explore --test it` (61 passed), the controller's corpus tests, `-p hydo --test it --
equivalence:: agents_equivalence::` (9 passed) and `-p hydo-agents --test it` (16 passed). The
copy has no `AGENTS.local.md`, so `public_content::` checked the generic patterns, and a `grep` of
the listed values found none in the new text. `sh ci/vale.sh` finds nothing in the changed
documents. No Rust code changed.

Retro: Garnet 2.2.14, hvx and KVM, 2026-11-26 and 27
- Time to the first clean run: 1 hour of wall time, about 25 minutes of it waiting for builds.
  The first run stopped at `--logdir` without a storage tier.
- Schedules run before the first finding: 3 directed runs (finding 1 at the first kill of a

- The findings: 1 new (a slot without an owner after a failover that follows a migration), 1

- What took the most time: the KVM runs at four times hvx's run time and the shrinks of finding

  (about 1.5 hours).
- What hydo lacked: no `depends_on` links between a Compose cluster's nodes, so no network
  faults until they were named by hand; no way to leave one fault kind out; the class
  `durable-defaults` for a failure on the durable device; the diagnosis that named a
  `kill-now-` reaction's SIGKILL the kernel's out-of-memory killer; the console of 64 KiB (open
  item 192).
- Strategies: "Failovers by the client, with a late write" gained finding 2 (two control-plane
  steps next to each other), and "Every replica compared with the leader after a restart" gained
  finding 1; the first table names Garnet.

**Findings 1 and 2 checked again with hydo 0.7.0.** The released hydo 0.7.0, from a fresh clone
at `67ccb6ee`, built the three images again on hvx with the sha256 values of the paragraph on the runs. Each schedule
gave its recorded value twice:

- finding 2's seed 96 on the `fs` image `5a4771d51585eeff`. A held run asked every node: only

- finding 1's `K=g1@15+3` on the `r0` image `982a16effdb11bfa`. `INFO replication` gave `g1`
  `connected_slaves:0` at offset 5,984, and `g4` offset 1,668 with `master_link_status:up`.
- the same schedule on the default image (`reest=5`) OK, `179ac0194c742e8d`. This value is new;
  the record had only `8ccf4e5c0b279c83` of an older client.

The Docker script of finding 2 gave two end states in three runs on this Mac, both with the slot
unserved for good. In two, the nodes named owners as in hydo's run. In one, `a`, `b` and `c`
named the new primary `ra`, and `ra` named none: `ra` had set the slot `OFFLINE` right after the
migration (`MergeSlotMap`, `ClusterConfig.cs` line 1248). With `MIGSLEEP=6` every node named
`ra`. The code shows why gossip never repairs it. `MergeSlotMap` (line 1217) sets a slot
`OFFLINE` when its believed primary's message does not claim it (lines 1239 to 1258). A
replica's message never gives such a slot an owner (line 1277, from pull request #2089). No
primary claims it: `TakeOverFromPrimary` (line 1393) claimed only the slots of the new primary's
own slot map (`GetLocalPrimarySlots`, line 334). For finding 1 the record now names three
lines. `defaults.conf` line 598 sets the option to 0, its declaration in `Options.cs` (line 777)
has no help text, and `EnsureReplication` returns at once for 0 (`ReplicationManager.cs` lines
183 to 190). `master_link_status` is the cluster connection's state (`Gossip.cs` line 232), not
the AOF stream's. RESULTS.md, the AGENTS.md paragraph and open item 192, and the use-cases rows
say this now. No regression file changed.

## Milestone 372 (tentative number): one service's own wall clock

Status: a prototype, done on 2026-11-26 on the bare-metal machine (hvx and the tests) from this
Mac. Every service of a guest reads one wall clock, so `T=` moved every service's clock at once.
The idea "Clocks per service" of `docs/USE-CASES.md` asked for one node's clock ahead of or
behind the others, the cause of lease and timestamp bugs that the TiKV, Prometheus and Typesense
onboardings could not test (open items 117, 147 and 170). The design and the options are
`docs/design/service-clocks.md`. Nothing recorded moved, and the fingerprint epoch stays 6.

**The options, checked.** The hvx guest kernel's configuration, extracted from `guest/bzImage`
(`0a9ede35…`) with the kernel's own `scripts/extract-ikconfig`, has `CONFIG_TIME_NS=y`,
`CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER=y` and `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH=y`. Linux 6.6's time namespaces do not
help: `struct timens_offsets` has only `monotonic` and `boottime`, `proc_timens_set_offset`
refuses every other clock with `EINVAL`, and the offsets are frozen once a process entered the
namespace. A preloaded library reaches only programs that read the clock through a shared libc,
not static Go, Rust or C programs. A realtime offset per time namespace in the guest kernels
covers every program without a tracer, but it touches the timekeeping core of four kernels. The
prototype takes the fourth option of the design page: seccomp and ptrace, with the vDSO hidden.

**What was built.** Five parts, none of which changes the agent, a guest kernel, or an image
without the new key:

- `hydo/crates/hydo-clock`, a static x86_64 program with its own lock file (std and libc), built
  by its `build.sh` with hydo-agent's recipe (414,624 bytes, `de24fd93…`). `hydo-clock <offset
  file> <program>` installs a seccomp filter that sends the reads of the wall clock and the
  waits until a wall-clock time to it, traces the program's whole tree, and hides the vDSO at
  every `execve` (`AT_SYSINFO_EHDR` becomes `AT_IGNORE`). At a read it writes the guest's time
  plus the offset and skips the call; at a wait it gives the kernel the deadline minus the
  offset. Its unit tests check the filter's jumps, the time conversion, and the offset file.
- `services[].clock: own` (a format-1 addition, x86_64 only): `hydo build` stages
  `/bin/hydo-clock` from `HYDO_CLOCKBIN` (default `<build dir>/hydo-clock`), and the controller
  starts the service as `hydo-clock /tmp/hydo/clock.<svc> <its command>`.
- The token `T=<svc>@<at>:<change>` in `hydo-schedule` (`ServiceClockChange`): `<n>` seconds,
  `<n>ms`, or a drift `<n>ppm`, each with one spelling (test `service_clocks`). Every such token
  applies; the guest's own `T=` still replaces an earlier one.
- The controller (`features/clock.rs`, `service_clock`) writes `<offset ns> <drift ppm>` into
  the service's file before the step, logs `CLOCK of n2 5 before step 3 (offset 0 ms -> 5000 ms,
  drift 0 ppm -> 0 ppm)`, and gives a step the records of a guest clock step. `hydo_control::names`
  refuses the token for a service without `clock: own`, before any VM.
- The example `hydo/onboard/examples/service-clocks`: two nodes that hold a lease by their own
  wall clocks, read with a static Go program.

**Outside a VM first.** On the bare-metal machine, hydo-clock with an offset of +5 s made the
static Go program read 5.24 s ahead (the 0.24 s are the time between the two calls). An offset of
-1 h moved glibc's `date` and Python's `time.time()` back by an hour. `clock_nanosleep` with
`TIMER_ABSTIME` and `pthread_cond_timedwait` on a deadline of the program's clock plus 1 s each
took 1.000 s with offsets of +1 h and -1 h, with a dynamic and a static glibc. Exit statuses
passed through (7, and 143 after a SIGTERM).

**The hvx runs.** This tree's `hydo` and `hydo-hvx` over the 0.6.0 Linux release's guest files,
every VM through `~/bin/hvx-run` under umask 022. Every schedule ran twice with one fingerprint;
the table is the example's RESULTS.md:

| Schedule | Verdict | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | OK, the lead changed 0 times | `57d19bbc77f8360b` |
| `disk=none \| run T=3:5` | OK | `1ff65322865695d5` |
| `disk=none \| run T=n2@3:5` | VIOLATION `[lease.one_leader]`, two leaders at once | `9feba06d7a2b47c3` |
| `disk=none \| run T=n2@3:-5` | OK | `fad0820e66206c18` |
| `disk=none \| run T=n2@0:500000ppm` | VIOLATION `[lease.one_leader]` | `bd68cd0ff4c2b957` |
| `disk=none \| run T=n1@3:1500ms T=n2@3:-1500ms` | OK | `1df85a95a9dee374` |
| `disk=none \| run T=n1@0:4 T=n2@0:4` | OK | `beeb8a7a0e432b60` |
| `disk=none \| run P=n1@2+3` | OK, the pause of a traced service | `61ccc82fa554b277` |
| `disk=none \| run K=n1@2+2 T=n1@1:2` | OK, the offset kept across a restart | `07c13db36f21324b` |

The same lease passes a step of the guest's clock (`T=3:5`) and fails a step of one node's clock
(`T=n2@3:5`), the case that `T=` could not make. At the end the nodes read 5,006 ms apart after
`T=n2@3:5` and 4,411 ms apart after 8.8 s at 500,000 ppm.

**The cost.** 20,000 reads of the wall clock by the static Go program took 4.4 µs of guest time
each as the guest's own program and 40.5 µs each under hydo-clock. On the bare-metal machine
outside a VM they took 0.12 µs and 21.9 µs.

**Nothing recorded moved.** The pinned reproducers' epoch-6 images in `~/hydo/build/rel060` gave
`db33d71069816103` (VIOLATION, order 11) and `c421af1ccb714225` (OK) with this tree, their
recorded values. The release's Redis example built by the 0.6.0 release and by this tree gave one
image, `8fae6946…`.

**The tests.** On the bare-metal machine: the tests of hydo-schedule, hydo-manifest, hydo-config,
hydo-build, hydo-control and hydo-explore, `cargo test -p hydo --test it -- equivalence::
agents_equivalence::`, `cargo test -p hydo-agents --test it`, clippy with `-D warnings`, and
`cargo fmt --check` passed. Re-recorded with `HYDO_BLESS=1`:

- the project schema, with the key `clock`;
- the answers of the hydo-build and hydo-manifest equivalence corpora, whose messages list the
  known service keys;
- the corpus and identity goldens of the explorer and the controller's corpus golden, with the
  new example;
- the CLI golden (the length of `hydo guide manifest`), the agents recording's hash of the skill
  folder, and the inventory of environment variables (`HYDO_CLOCKBIN`).

**What is left** (open item 190): the explorer does not draw the token, and the clock audit does
not propose it. The KVM and Mac engines did not run it: their guest kernels have seccomp only in
the `containers` variants, and the Mac needs an arm64 build of hydo-clock. The design page names
the programs and the timers it does not cover.

## Milestone 373 (tentative number): the NSQ, SeaweedFS and Typesense examples on KVM

The examples of Milestones 362, 364 and 366 ran on the KVM engine for the first time, on GitHub's
runners. NSQ and SeaweedFS gave the verdicts of the Mac engine and of hvx. Typesense does not
start on KVM, because the KVM guest kernels have no `/proc/<pid>/io`. Nothing recorded moved.

**How it ran.** A one-off workflow on the branch `tmp-m373-kvm` (deleted after the runs), made
from `e2058be0`, built this tree's `hydo` and `hydo-fetch-image`. It took the 0.6.0 release's
guest files (`hydo-linux-0.6.0.tar.gz` `12fe3299…`) through `hydo setup`. Each job ran the
example's `build.sh` (Go 1.27.3), its fetch script for x86_64, and `hydo build`: NSQ with `--set
arch=amd64`, and SeaweedFS also a second image with `--set fsync=false`. Each schedule ran twice
from fresh boots with `--backend kvm`, and `hydo repro --regressions` ran once per image. The
main run is 45890568477 (9 jobs). Run 45894112875 added three NSQ jobs and three SeaweedFS jobs,
and two jobs of the Typesense diagnosis. Runs 45891967817 and 45893037519 were the diagnosis.

**NSQ, the first time on x86_64.** The image is `d6f8de9a…` at the fingerprint epoch 6, and the
client `nsqc-amd64` is `25adf549…`. Every schedule gave one fingerprint over its two runs on every
host, and the same fingerprint on every host of one vendor. `hydo repro --regressions` gave 5 of
5 as expected on each host. Every verdict is the Mac engine's:

| schedule | verdict | AMD EPYC 9V45, 9V74, and two 7763 | two Xeon 6975P-C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | OK, `no-phantom` judged 24 deliveries | `ac7ebf20a1d9588e` | `488679fb6b91528e` |
| `topic-queue-restarts-empty-after-kill` | `VIOLATION [jobs.no-loss]` | `4afbbef778eed026` | `3e2e59c7802f597c` |
| `channel-queue-restarts-empty-after-kill` | `VIOLATION [jobs.no-loss]` | `70ba4f0f0e2960ad` | `2acf18f6433087b3` |
| `in-flight-message-lost-at-kill` | `VIOLATION [jobs.acked-outcome]`, 1 of 4 | `2a0834d1bbed8d50` | `7e4814758448a48f` |
| `publish-waits-after-backward-clock-step` | `VIOLATION [eventually_publish]` | `42d2ad65fc452352` | `3fd1a6f3d2c3fcfe` |
| `topic-queue-restarts-empty-after-power-cut` | `VIOLATION [jobs.no-loss]` | `4f0cf10a9072cd5c` | `292a26f1d32d656f` |

The regression `topic-queue-restarts-empty-after-kill` says that six acknowledged messages are
lost, and RESULTS.md finding 1 gives `6 of 7 judged operations` on the Mac engine. On KVM, on
both vendors, its `acked-outcome` reads `5 of 6`: `m0` to `m4` were answered `OK` and are lost.
The sixth publish, `m5`, overlapped the kill, so `nsqd` did not answer it, and the client recorded
it as failed. The publish after the restart (`m9`) reached a consumer. The comment's six lost
messages are the Mac engine's run.

**SeaweedFS.** The default image is `f6e18b43…`, hvx's bytes, and the image with `--set
fsync=false` is `c56d8263…`. The client is `37dcd648…`. Each schedule gave one fingerprint over
its two runs, and both verdicts are hvx's. `hydo repro --regressions` left the regression out on
the default image by its `# params:` line (`0 of 0 regressions as expected, 1 left out`), and
passed it on the `fsync=false` image:

| schedule | image | verdict | AMD EPYC 9V74 and three 7763 | two Xeon 6975P-C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `disk=none \| run` | default | OK, 92 acknowledged writes judged | `bbf6243b4dc5d2b1` | `611bba1f54237e68` |
| `acknowledged-write-lost-at-a-power-cut-without-fsync` | `fsync=false` | `VIOLATION [objects.acked-outcome]` for `fover.k0.0.v0x0` | `909e6e48aa11058c` | `08fdc426d9c908e2` |

**Typesense does not start.** The image `de22e524…` (the client `tsc-amd64` `5109fe4d…`) is the
one that the fresh clone built on hvx in Milestone 366. On KVM every run ends `ERROR service
start (ts1)`: `ts1` exits with SIGSEGV (status 139) before its readiness check passes. The clean
run and the three regressions gave `d7f5d6359ab95efb` on three Xeon 6975P-C hosts, twice each.
The clean run gave `ce4ff2694a847f79` on an EPYC 7763 and on two EPYC 9V74. An image with `guest.cpu:
v3` (`93dc08be…`) gave the same ERROR, `aeb47edf1016f135` on a Xeon 6975P-C and
`15302d9d3b1eb9b9` on an EPYC 7763.

**The cause.** The diagnosis runs found it in three steps:

1. In the guest, at the stop after the failed start, `ls /proc/self/` lists no `io`, and `cat
   /proc/self/io` answers `No such file or directory`. The KVM guest kernels are allnoconfig with
   the fragments of `hv/kvm/linux/`, and no fragment sets `CONFIG_TASKSTATS`, `CONFIG_TASK_XACCT`
   or `CONFIG_TASK_IO_ACCOUNTING`.
2. On a runner, `typesense-server` from the image's root prints its usage and exits 1. With a
   preloaded library that makes every open of `/proc/<pid>/io` fail with ENOENT, it exits 139.
3. The backtrace of that run under gdb is `bvar::read_proc_io` in a static initializer of brpc,
   then `google::ErrnoLogMessage`, then `google::LogMessage::Init`, which calls
   `std::string::empty()` on a null pointer (`0x5e30064` in the program). brpc logs the failed
   read with glog's `PLOG_ONCE` before Typesense has set glog up.

Typesense's commit `b708744220` (#3093, 2026-10-28, after v30.2) replaces that log line with
`fprintf`; no Typesense release has it yet. apache/brpc's own `default_variables.cpp` has the
`fprintf` too. The Mac engine's kernels are built the same way (`hv/hvm/linux/hvm.config` on
allnoconfig) without the options; the Mac engine did not run the example. hvx's kernel is nixpkgs's `linux_6_6`, which has the file. The section "No
`/proc/<pid>/io` in the guest" of `docs/design/kvm-engine.md` names the other programs that read
the file and proposes new kernel builds at a new fingerprint epoch. No kernel was built.

**Records.** An engines note in each example's RESULTS.md, and open items 184, 186, and 188.
`hydo guide hazards` names the missing file. `HYDO_BLESS=1` re-recorded

## Milestone 374 (tentative number): the gaps of the rqlite, RabbitMQ and Garnet onboardings

Status: done on 2026-11-27, on the bare-metal machine (hvx and the tests) from this Mac. Each fix
below is its own commit with its tests. The gaps are the "What hydo lacked" sections of the
rqlite, RabbitMQ and Garnet examples' RESULTS.md (open items 189, 191 and 192). Nothing recorded
moved: the two keys of `groups:` are opt-in and change nothing without them, and the other fixes
are in the controller's reading of an image, the explorer, the importer, the diagnosis, the
parser, the build's warnings, the input key and the words. No engine's guest behaviour, agent,
image or fingerprint changed, and the fingerprint epoch stays 6.

**How the proofs ran.** On the bare-metal machine in this round's own tree, with the 0.6.0 Linux
release's guest files and this tree's `hydo`, `hydo-build`, `hydo-fetch-image` and `hydo-hvx`.
The examples were copied, inputs only, from the trees of the rqlite, RabbitMQ and Garnet sessions,
which were only read. "Before" is the programs of the rqlite or RabbitMQ session (built from
`main` before this round) on the same image.

**1. A history check file beside a `checks:` section.** The host controller took the history
checks from the embedded `hydo.yaml`, and read the image's `manifest.sh` only when that list was
empty, or to replace a messages check's declaration with the built one. So a
`checks/list_append_*` or `linearizable_*` file was dropped without a word when `hydo.yaml` had a
`checks:` section, although `hydo build` compiled it and said `+ 2 history checks`. Now
`hydo_control::agent::merge_history` keeps the declared checks, takes a messages check's built
declaration as before, and adds every built check that `hydo.yaml` does not name. An image
without such a pair gets the list it got before; no example has one, so no recorded run moves.
The other way, refusing at `hydo build`, was not needed: both kinds run together.

The proof is a copy of the rqlite example whose list-append check `la` is the file
`checks/list_append_la` (`# hydo: history=la consistency=strict-serializable`, `exec /bin/rqc
lafinal`) beside the messages check `writes` of `hydo.yaml`, as its first images had it. The
image `cc9693a0…` has both checks in its `manifest.sh` (`HYDO_CHECK_c0_id='writes'`,
`HYDO_CHECK_c1_id='la'`). One clean run each:

| programs | `HYDO-CHECK` lines | final read-backs | checks | fp | wfp |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 1 (`writes`) | `writes` | `checks=2 held` (`writes.no-phantom`, `writes.acked-outcome`) | `422b6fc2dfc83cc0` | `0c59c193e97c8665` |
| this tree | 2 (`writes`, `la`) | `writes`, `la` | `checks=3 held`, `la` PASS | `1dfdc81cd750869a` | `0c59c193e97c8665` |

The workload's fingerprint is the same; the run's fingerprint differs by the declaration line of
`la` and its read-back, which the run did not have before. The test
`a_checks_file_beside_a_checks_section_is_kept` (hydo-control) covers the merge.

**2. A group's killed members restart together (`restart: together`).** After a `K=` that killed
several services, the controller started each one and waited for its readiness check before it
started the next (`start_svc`), and the heal's restart pass did the same. A member whose
readiness needs a quorum then never gets ready: a RabbitMQ node that restarts with data opens
AMQP only after its peers answer, and 3 of the onboarding's 20 schedules ended `ERROR rabbit1
restart failed` (open items 147 and 157 have the same for TiKV's PD and ClickHouse's Keepers).

`groups[].restart` (a format-1 addition, `one-by-one` by default, or `together`) says how a
group's members come back. With `together`, the controller starts the setup and the process of
every killed member first (`launch_tracked`, as `start_after: started` does at the first start),
and then runs each one's readiness check in the order of `services:` (`start_together` in
`hydo-control/src/schedule.rs`). It does so at the end of a `K=` whose services are all members of
the group, and in the heal's restart pass for the members that are down then, so also after `X=`
and the reactions' kills. A check that fails ends the run with `ERROR <service> restart failed`,
as before. The restarts of `G=` and `L=` stay one by one. Without the key the code takes the
paths it took before, command for command. MANIFEST.md ("Groups of services and partitions" and
"Starting services together") says so.

The proof is two copies of the RabbitMQ example whose readiness is AMQP (`ready: "tcp:5672"`), as
its first images had it: `rabbitmq-amqp` (image `3828aa4a…`) without the key, and
`rabbitmq-together` (`ebe80987…`) with `restart: together` on the group `nodes`. The schedule
`disk=none | run K=nodes.all@10+2` kills the three nodes before step 10 and starts them again
before step 12:

| image | programs | what the controller did | verdict | fp | ctl |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rabbitmq-amqp` | before | `restarting rabbit1 before step 12` | `ERROR rabbit1 restart failed` | `0f45ddf6d366629f` | `5dc13f225e88e839` |
| `rabbitmq-amqp` | this tree | the same | the same | `0f45ddf6d366629f` | `5dc13f225e88e839` |
| `rabbitmq-together` | this tree, twice | `restarting rabbit1 rabbit2 rabbit3 together before step 12` | `OK`, `checks=14 held` | `08574ee52da3936d` both | `4e7942b717d3f76f` both |

The run without the key gave the old programs' fingerprint and control transcript, so the
change is inert there. With the key the three nodes came back, the drain and the checks ran, and
two fresh boots gave one fingerprint. A clean run of the `together` image gave `OK` (`checks=14
held`, `4cd28b60387e8707`). The example itself keeps its readiness on the Erlang distribution
port and has no key, so its recorded runs are unchanged.

**3. The links between a cluster's nodes (`links: all`).** With `network: bridge` the explorer
draws a link fault only between two services where one names the other in `depends_on`. When no
service names any, it draws every pair (`hydo_explore::space`, `bridge_links`). The probe below
shows that this was the case of Garnet's import: its six nodes name no `depends_on`, and the
explorer had all 15 links of them. The Garnet onboarding's "What hydo lacked" item 4 read the rule
as "no links", which holds only once any service names a dependency. A usual Compose file names
some: a replica on its primary, an application on its database, a job's dependents. Then the
nodes that do not name each other get no link fault, as in open items 97 and 111.

`groups[].links` (a format-1 addition, `depends_on` by default, or `all`) makes every two members
of the group linked for the explorer. `hydo compose` writes a group with `links: all` for the
services of one image that run one command and are no one-shot job: the nodes of one cluster.
It names the group after the image (`garnet`, `rabbitmq`), prints a line that names its
services, and adds the key to a converted Kubernetes StatefulSet's group too. A manifest
without the key gets the links it got before. On one loopback network every two services with
`addr:` are linked anyway.

The probe asks the explorer's fault space (`Space::links`) of five manifests:

| manifest | `depends_on` | group | links of the nodes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Garnet's import with this tree, the group taken out | none | none | all 15 pairs and each node against the rest |
| Garnet's import with this tree | none | `garnet`, `links: all` | the same |
| `garnet-deps`: the example with each replica on its primary | `g4` on `g1`, `g5` on `g2`, `g6` on `g3` | the shards' groups | `g1-g4`, `g2-g5`, `g3-g6` only |
| `garnet-links`: the same with a group `cluster` of the six | the same | `cluster`, `links: all` | all 15 pairs and each node against the rest |
| the RabbitMQ example | none | `nodes` | all 3 pairs and each node against the rest |

The import of Garnet's Compose file with this tree's `hydo compose` printed `g1, g2, g3, g4, g5 and
g6 run one image with one command: the group garnet (groups:) with links: all, ...` and wrote
the group with a comment.

On hvx `hydo explore --seeds 1-6 --workers 1 --no-shrink` of `garnet-links` (image
`fae5f7db…`) wrote those links into its `fault-space.json`. Two of its six schedules cut a node
from all its peers, `N=g6-*@23-29:duplicate,36%,loss,57%` (seed 2, after `K=g1@13+2`) and
`N=g2-*@20-27:duplicate,27%` (seed 3), links that `garnet-deps` does not have. All six passed:
the faults ran, and Garnet's checks held.

The goldens of the importer moved with the new group, and were recorded again with `HYDO_BLESS=1`:
`hydo-compose`'s `tests/golden.json` (the hashes and answers of the imports whose
services share an image and a command) and `tests/golden/k8s-cluster.yaml` (`links: all` on the
StatefulSet's group).

**4. A kill that hydo sent from the guest is hydo's.** The diagnosis called a SIGKILL the kernel's
out-of-memory killer when the host had sent no `signal` command to the process. A
`kill-now-<svc>` reaction kills from a relay in the guest, and a kill of threads from a script
there, so in the Garnet onboarding `hydo inspect diagnose --evidence` blamed the memory for
`A=garnet.bgsave+10:kill-now-g1`. Every kill of hydo leaves the controller's note `KILLED <svc>
...` in the control transcript: `K=`, `X=`, `G=`, and the reactions. The diagnosis now counts a
SIGKILL of a process whose conversation has such a note for its handle as sent by hydo
(`hydo_cli::inspect::diagnose`, `killed_by_hydo`), and says nothing of memory then. The test
`a_sigkill_of_a_reaction_relay_is_hydos` adds the relay's note to the recorded out-of-memory
run of the fixtures; `a_sigkill_nobody_sent_in_provisioning` keeps its words. The note names the
service, not the moment, so a second SIGKILL of the same service by the kernel later in the same
conversation would be counted as hydo's too.

**5. Which Go SDK has `Drained`.** The module's tag `sdk/go/v0.7.0`, published with 0.7.0, has
`History.Drained`; `sdk/go/v0.6.0` lacks it, as the RabbitMQ onboarding found (`git grep` of both
tags). `hydo guide messages` and the Go SDK's README now name v0.7.0, and the guide gives the
generic record for an older module: `q.Record(9, "ok", "drained", hydohist.Enc("jobs"),
hydohist.Enc("-"))`. No SDK code changed, and the frozen copy in `hydo/stack` stays.

**6. The end of a run, and one drain for several histories.** After the heal hydo runs every
check's `final:` in the order of `checks:`, then the `eventually` checks and the composer's
`eventually_` commands, then the `final` checks and `finally_` commands (`finish` in
`hydo-control`). No guide said so, and the RabbitMQ onboarding's probe after the faults was an
`eventually_` command whose messages the drain had not waited for. `hydo guide messages` ("Write
the drain") and MANIFEST.md now give the order. A messages check without `final:` is no longer
refused for a claim that reads the end of its history when another messages check of the
manifest has a `final:`: that drain writes its `drained` records too (`hydo_manifest::messages`,
`validate`'s `shared_drain`). A claim the drain leaves undecided stays an ERROR that names it, so
nothing passes unjudged. A list-append check's `final:` is a read-back, not a drain, and does not
count. The test `a_check_without_final_shares_another_checks_drain` (hydo-manifest).

**7. `T=<step>:+<secs>`.** The parser takes a forward clock step with its sign: `T=10:+120` is
`T=10:120`, and it prints so (`hydo_schedule`, the `T=` arm; `++`, `+-` and `+0` are refused). The
guest sees the printed text, so a schedule with the sign is the run of the one without it.
`hydo run` and `hydo explore --schedule` take the canonical text (`Schedule::canonical`), and
`hydo run` prints it when it differs. The service clock's `T=<svc>@` form is not touched. The
test `a_forward_clock_step_takes_its_plus_sign` (hydo-schedule).

**8. A file system of `storage:` that the image's user cannot write.** An image service that
runs as another user than root and has `storage:` with `size_mib:` gets a warning at `hydo build
--check` and at `hydo build`. hydo makes that file system empty and owned by root, so the rqlite
nodes (uid 1000) stopped with `permission denied`. The warning names the user, the folder and
where the service sees it, and the fix: `setup: chown <uid>:<gid> /data/<dir>`, with the user's
numbers when the image names the user by name, because `setup:` runs in the guest
(`hydo_build::oci::storage_owner_warnings`). A `setup:` with `chown`, root, or a storage folder
without a file system of its own gives none. `hydo build --check` of a copy of the rqlite
example without its three `chown` lines gave one warning per node, for example `rq1: the image
runs as the user rqlite. Its storage /data/vol/rq1 (the service's /rqlite/file) is a file system
of its own, which starts empty and owned by root, so the service cannot write to it. ...`; the
example as it is gave none. The test `a_storage_file_system_its_user_cannot_write_is_named`
(hydo-build). `hydo compose` writes no `storage:`, so its import is unchanged.

**9. The input key reads no output of hydo.** `hydo explore --configs` builds its images through
the image cache of `hydo versions`, keyed by the image's input key
(`hydo_cli::ci::inputkey`). The key hashed every file of the `hydo/` folder. The RabbitMQ
example's folder held, beside its 173 input files (0.13 GiB), the build folder `.hydo` with the
copies' unpacked roots and disk images, the runs and the explorations: 46,359 files and 37 GiB
as the key's walk counts them, following links. Hashing the 173 files took 2.5 s on the
bare-metal machine; at that rate the 37 GiB take about 12 minutes for each key, and `--configs`
makes one key per combination, which matches the 23 minutes. The key now leaves out `.hydo`,
`hydo-out`, and every folder with a `result.json` or an `exploration.json` (`is_output_dir`). A
folder without such outputs keeps its key; one with them gets a new key once, so an image cache
builds that image again, with the same bytes. The test `the_key_leaves_out_hydos_outputs`.

**Tests.** On the bare-metal machine: `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D
warnings`, and the tests of hydo-schedule, hydo-manifest, hydo-control, hydo-compose, hydo-build,
hydo-explore, hydo-config, `hydo --bins`, `hydo --test it` and `hydo-agents --test it` passed. Two
goldens moved on purpose and were recorded again with `HYDO_BLESS=1`: the importer's (fix 3) and
the `hydo guide manifest` answers of `hydo`'s `tests/golden/cli.jsonl`, which hash MANIFEST.md.
The schema `hydo/schema/project-v1.json` (regenerated with `HYDO_BLESS=1 cargo test -p
hydo-manifest --test it format::`) gained the two keys of `groups:`, an addition to the released
schema. In two runs of `hydo --test it` four and six of the `update::` tests failed at the spawn of a fake program (`update.rs` line
388); they pass alone and with `--test-threads=1`, and this round changed nothing they run.

**What is left.**

- `restart: together` acts at the end of a `K=` and in the heal. The restarts of `G=`, `L=` and a
  recovery boot's start stay as they were; a recovery boot starts its services as the first boot
  does, where `start_after: started` already starts a cluster together. The TiKV and ClickHouse
  examples did not run with the key.
- `hydo compose` groups the services of one image by their entrypoint and command. Nodes of one
  cluster whose commands differ, such as a primary and its replicas started with other flags, get
  no group; nodes built from several images neither.
- The diagnosis counts a SIGKILL as hydo's when the conversation has a `KILLED <svc>` note for
  the service, wherever it is. A later kill of the same service by the kernel in the same
  conversation would count as hydo's too.
- No example sets a messages check without `final:` yet; the RabbitMQ example keeps its
  placeholders.
- The warning for a `storage:` file system names the user as the image gives it; a name needs its
  number from the image's `/etc/passwd`, which hydo does not read for it.

## Milestone 375 (tentative number): one service's own clock in the explorer and on real systems

Status: done on 2026-11-27 on the bare-metal machine (hvx and the tests) from this Mac. Milestone
372 built `clock: own` and `T=<svc>@<at>:<change>` as a prototype that the explorer did not draw
and that no real project ran (open item 190). This milestone makes the explorer draw it, lets the
clock audit propose it, and runs it on TiKV, Typesense and Prometheus. One node's clock ahead of
or behind the others is a classic cause of bugs there. Nothing recorded moved, `clock: own`
stays opt-in, and the fingerprint epoch stays 6.

**The explorer draws it.** `hydo explore --service-clocks` (an option, not a default) draws one
service's own clock for a manifest with services of `clock: own` and `clock` in `faults:`, from
the stream `SERVICE_CLOCK_SALT` of `hydo-explore`'s `gen.rs`. Every other field of a seed's
schedule stays as it was. Most drawn schedules get one service's change:

- a schedule with a step of the guest's clock gives it up in half of the schedules, for one
  service's change before the same step;
- a schedule without one gets a service's change in 60 % of the schedules;
- the change is a step of `±250ms`, `±1500ms`, `±5`, `±30` or `±300`, or a drift of `±200ppm`
  or `±50000ppm`, of one service of `clock: own` at random;
- with two or more such services a quarter of the changes put two of them apart: a second
  service gets the opposite change before the same step.

The shrinker removes each token, and halves a step longer than 250 ms and a drift larger than
200 ppm, towards 0. The explorer's schedule struct keeps the tokens (`S::ts`), and its parser reads
`T=<svc>@<at>:<change>`, which it refused before, so `hydo explore --schedule` takes such a
schedule. A schedule with a service's clock is in the class of the clock faults. `stats.json`
counts the token as a clock fault of its service. The fault-space line names the draws, and
says `--service-clocks adds steps and drifts of one service's own clock` without the option.
The explorer refuses the option before any run without a service of `clock: own` (exit status
5, with the other option refusals of `run.rs`), and when it draws nothing because `faults:` has
no `clock` (`refuse::nothing_drawn`).

The option is opt-in, not the design page's default for manifests with `clock: own`: a default
would change the draws of the manifests that have the key already, the `service-clocks` example
among them. The explorer's corpus and identity goldens did not change. The new example manifests
are in folders of their own (`<example>/skew/hydo.yaml`), which the goldens do not read, so not
even their pinned inputs moved.

**The clock audit proposes it.** For a place whose code a service of `clock: own` runs (the map
of Milestone 324), `hydo rules scan --kind clock` adds two schedules: `own-ahead`, that service's
clock alone forward by more than the place's limit, and `own-behind`, back by as much. A project
without `clock: own` gets the report of before (the test
`the_clock_audit_steps_the_own_clock_of_the_service_that_runs_a_place`).

**How the real systems ran.** Each example got a folder `skew/` beside its `hydo/`:
`skew/hydo.yaml` is `hydo/hydo.yaml` with `clock: own` on the nodes, another name, and the image
files of `../hydo/images`. `skew/workload` and `skew/checks` are links to `hydo/`'s, and
`skew/regressions/` holds the new regressions, so the recorded images and their regressions stay
as they were. Every VM ran through `~/bin/hvx-run` under umask 022, with this tree's `hydo`,
`hydo-hvx` and `hydo-build` over the 0.6.0 Linux release's guest files, hydo-clock `de24fd93…`
(Milestone 372's bytes), and each onboarding's client and images. No other VM of this
milestone ran beside TiKV's, and each waited for 20 GB of free memory. Directed
schedules came first: one node ahead or behind by seconds and minutes, two nodes apart, and
drifts. The final images were built from `skew/hydo.yaml`. Building them again with the
regressions beside them gave the same sha256, and `hydo repro --regressions` replayed each.

**TiKV (image `21ef8adf…`).** PD's leader was `pd3`. `T=pd3@10:300 K=pds.primary@30+4`, the
leader 5 minutes ahead and then killed, failed `eventually_writable` twice with one fingerprint
(`f04bf542d4fd5a11`). The new leader `pd1` logged `system time may be incorrect` with the saved
window `last=00:05:39.728` against its clock's `00:00:47.006`, went on from the window, and kept
the timestamps' physical part for 5 minutes. TiKV judges a lock's time to live by that part, so
the locks of a client that crashed inside its commit blocked every writer. That is finding 1 of
the example, known as pingcap/tidb#44822, through a failover instead of a step of every clock.
These passed: the same step of a follower with the same kill, the leader's step without the
kill, the leader 30 s ahead with the kill, a PD follower 5 minutes ahead (also killed), a
follower's clock 5 % fast, and one store 5 minutes behind or ahead (tikv/tikv#17995's setting).
The exploration `--seeds 1-8 --strategy process --new-faults --service-clocks --no-shrink` ran
alone (133 s a run). Three schedules drew a node's own clock, one of them the leader 5 minutes
ahead without a kill, and passed. Its two failures were finding 1 under steps of the guest's
clock back by 30 days.

**Typesense (image `84f22e51…`).** The leader was `ts1`. One new candidate, a clock effect:

- `T=ts3@20:-60`, one follower's clock back by 60 s, failed `eventually_converge` twice with
  `b1761b4adaaa1c6c`: `ts3 lacks i29x4, which the leader ts1 holds as w122`. Each node applies a
  delete by a filter from its Raft log and runs the later batches from a timer of its own h2o
  event loop. That loop fires nothing while the node's clock is behind its last run (finding 2).
  The follower applies the writes after the delete first, and its late batch deletes their new
  versions (finding 1's order, without a restart). `T=ts3@20:-30` lost another document
  (`2e6ed47ae01bae13`), and `T=ts3@20:-5` passed (`67e4f101dedb6526`). `T=ts3@20:-3600` left
  `ts3` with 64 documents that the delete removed on the other nodes (`e4c433aa042301fd`, two
  runs).
- Finding 3 needs the followers' own clocks. With both followers 120 s behind, a pause of the
  leader left no leader for 69 s (`4d3093d8b68377e2`, two runs). With one follower behind, the
  other took over (`4b63eff2c4e21276`).
- Forward steps of 30 s and 5 minutes and drifts of 50,000 ppm either way held.
- typesense/typesense#2626 (open) reports nodes that answer one search with different counts;
  its cause is not known.

The exploration `--seeds 1-20 --strategy process --new-faults --service-clocks` drew a node's
own clock in 8 of 20 schedules (11 changes: steps of 1.5 s either way and 5 minutes forward, and
drifts). None of them failed. Its 5 failures were finding 2 under steps of the guest's clock,
shrunk to `T=28:-324000` and `K=ts3@0+13 T=18:-300`. No drawn step put one node 30 s or more
behind, so finding 4 came from the directed schedules only.

**Prometheus (image `bbb797c9…`, built with `ooo_snapshots=skip` and `scrape_times=skip`).** Two
clock effects, both by design:

- The agent 11 or 15 minutes ahead of the server failed `eventually_scrape` (`53ae7f9900601e58`,
  three runs, one of them by `hydo repro --regressions`). The remote-write receiver refuses a
  sample more than 10 minutes ahead of its clock (`maxAheadTime`, `out of bounds: timestamp is
  too far in the future`), and the agent drops the refused batch as non-recoverable. Five minutes
  ahead passed (`ec36af3d9534d723`).
- The server 11 or 15 minutes ahead of its senders refused their samples as `Out of order sample
  from remote write`. The example's check calls that by design (`not judged`,
  `436888e860eea95a`). Five minutes passed.

The exploration `--seeds 1-20 --strategy process --new-faults --service-clocks` drew a service's
clock in 8 of 20 schedules and found no failure. Its three new error kinds came from steps of the
guest's clock of 30 days back. The drawn steps stay below the two 10-minute limits.

**Upstream.** Nothing was posted. The TiKV effect is pingcap/tidb#44822, accepted upstream. The
Typesense candidate has no issue; the user's typesense/typesense#3203 is finding 3. Prometheus's
limits are in its code (`maxAheadTime`, added after prometheus#13573) and in the field reports
#10169 and #8243.

**The KVM and Mac engines.** Read, not built (the section "The KVM and Mac engines" of
`docs/design/service-clocks.md`). Only the `containers` kernel lists have
`CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER`, and no list has `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, which hydo-clock's
`process_vm_readv` and `process_vm_writev` need. So even the `containers` kernels would answer
`ENOSYS`. A fallback to `PTRACE_PEEKDATA` and `PTRACE_POKEDATA` in hydo-clock needs no kernel
change. The Mac needs an arm64 hydo-clock.

**Nothing recorded moved.** No image of `hydo/onboard/recorded.json` has `clock: own`, and a
schedule without the new form gives the controller's commands of before. The explorer's corpus
and identity goldens passed unchanged.

**The tests.** On the bare-metal machine: `cargo fmt --check`, clippy with `-D warnings`, the
tests of hydo-explore (with the new `service_clocks::`), `cargo test -p hydo --test it` and the
CLI's unit tests, `-p hydo-agents --test it`, `-p hydo-control --test it`, `-p hydo-config`,
`-p hydo-schedule` and `-p hydo-manifest`. Re-recorded: the CLI golden's length of `hydo guide
manifest`. Two tests read the tree through its version-control index
(`identity::local_outputs_are_no_inputs`, `equivalence::same_as_hydo_build`); they passed once
the synced tree had an index. The `update::` tests failed once with `Text file busy` beside other
tests and passed when they ran alone.

**What is left** (open item 190): the KVM and Mac engines, the cost of a read (40.5 µs of guest
time), the programs and timers that hydo-clock does not cover, and the explorer's steps of at
most 5 minutes, below limits such as Prometheus's 10 minutes.

## Milestone 376 (tentative number): the guest kernels with `/proc/<pid>/io`, the fingerprint epoch 7

Status: done on 2026-11-27 for the KVM engine; the Mac kernels are built and pinned, and the Mac
engine did not run them. The fingerprint epoch is 7. No value of an older epoch moved, and the
epoch-7 values wait for the 0.8.0 pass.

The Mac and KVM guest kernels are allnoconfig with hydo's fragments, and no fragment set
`CONFIG_TASKSTATS`, `CONFIG_TASK_XACCT` or `CONFIG_TASK_IO_ACCOUNTING`. So the guest had no
`/proc/<pid>/io`, and Typesense 30.2 stopped with SIGSEGV at every start on KVM: its bundled brpc
reads `/proc/self/io` in a static initializer and logs the failure before glog is set up
(Milestone 373, open item 188). VictoriaMetrics' `metrics` package, psutil's `io_counters()`, and
the process statistics of Apache Doris, Apache Impala, Dovecot and cyrus-imapd read the file too.
The user agreed to the proposal of Milestone 373, which this milestone builds.

**The kernels.** docs/BUILD-PINS.md "The guest kernels with /proc/<pid>/io" has the pins.

- `hv/kvm/linux/hydo-kvm-procio.config` and `hv/hvm/explore/hvm-procio.config` set the three
  options and keep `CONFIG_TASK_DELAY_ACCT` and `CONFIG_BSD_PROCESS_ACCT` off: delay accounting
  reads the clock at every wait, and process accounting writes a file. `CONFIG_TASKSTATS` needs
  `CONFIG_NET` and `CONFIG_MULTIUSER`, which every list has.
- The KVM kernels: `hv/kvm/linux/kernel-procio.nix` (`PROCIO=1 [CONTAINERS=1] [SMP=1] sh
  hv/kvm/linux/build-kernel.sh`) makes the list of `kernel-cg.nix` or `kernel-containers.nix`
  and appends the lines. No other recipe changed, so every older pin stays.
- The Mac kernels: `build-guest-cg.sh` and `build-guest-containers.sh` take `PROCIO=1`, which
  appends `hvm-procio.config` and checks each of its lines in the `.config`. Without it they
  build what they built before.
- Each new `.config` differs from its predecessor's in four lines: the three options and `#
  CONFIG_TASK_DELAY_ACCT is not set`, which Kconfig writes once `CONFIG_TASKSTATS` is on.

**How they were built.** On the bare-metal machine, in a directory of this milestone's own:

- The Mac kernels twice each, in two directories, with the same bytes: `Image-explore-io`
  `21928f71…` (6,866,952 bytes), `Image-explore-netns-io` `40b1a3e2…` (7,411,720 bytes) and
  `Image-explore-containers-io` `81fb1b5c…` (9,105,416 bytes).
- The KVM kernels with the single-user Nix, outside a sandbox: `bzImage-kvm-io` `4aef551c…`
  (store path `7yxpz7r4…`), `bzImage-kvm-smp-io` `e5b9cf4a…` (`q8bcs2hi…`),
  `bzImage-kvm-containers-io` `e61bdc8e…` (`dqb2cha3…`) and `bzImage-kvm-smp-containers-io`
  `51ea6c6e…` (`vvyap1zp…`). A `nix-build --check` of `bzImage-kvm-io` there gave another
  output, as Milestones 159, 234 and 256 saw outside the sandbox. So the pins are the sandboxed
  builds of GitHub's runners below, which gave these bytes.
- The RDTSC audit (`hv/kvm/linux/audit-rdtsc.sh`) of each new `vmlinux` lists the same 10 sites
  as before.

**Which kernels need the options.** An image built at epoch 7 boots one of the kernels with cgroups
or one of the variant `containers`. So each of those has a build with the file: four on KVM
(`bzImage-kvm-io`, `bzImage-kvm-smp-io`, `bzImage-kvm-containers-io`,
`bzImage-kvm-smp-containers-io`) and three on the Mac (`Image-explore-io`,
`Image-explore-netns-io`, `Image-explore-containers-io`). `bzImage-kvm`, `bzImage-kvm-smp`,
`Image-explore` and `Image-explore-netns` boot only images built at epoch 2 or before, which keep
their kernels, so they have no new build.

**hvx.** hvx's kernel did not change. `extract-ikconfig` of `bzImage` (`0a9ede35…`) on the
bare-metal machine shows `CONFIG_TASKSTATS=y`, `CONFIG_TASK_DELAY_ACCT=y`, `CONFIG_TASK_XACCT=y`
and `CONFIG_TASK_IO_ACCOUNTING=y`, as nixpkgs's `linux_6_6` sets them. No hvx default changed.

**The code.**

- `hydo-image`: `EPOCH` 7; `EpochDefaults::proc_io` (from epoch 7); `ImageRecord::proc_io`, an
  optional field that only `guest.proc_io: false` writes, and `ImageRecord::proc_io()`, which says
  whether the engines boot a kernel with the file; `kernels::ARM64_KERNEL_IO`,
  `ARM64_NETNS_KERNEL_IO` and `ARM64_KERNEL_CONTAINERS_IO`, `arm64_kernel_of(netns, proc_io)` and
  `record_opts(arch, netns, variant, proc_io)`. `record_for` and `record_with` give the kernels
  with the file. `KNOWN` has 10 files. The image schema gains the field (`HYDO_BLESS=1`).
- `hydo-kvm`: each `Twin` says whether it has the file (`proc_io`); `KERNEL_IO`, `KERNEL_SMP_IO`,
  `KERNEL_CONTAINERS_IO`, `KERNEL_SMP_CONTAINERS_IO`, and `CURRENT` and `CURRENT_SMP` for the
  default of this epoch; `twin_for` takes the record's `proc_io()`. `Twin::build_vars` names the
  variables of `build-kernel.sh` that build it, for the refusal and for `hydo doctor`.
- `hydo-engine`: the KVM boot files take the record's `proc_io()`.
- `hydo-manifest`: `guest.proc_io` (a format-1 addition, `true` by default), its validation and
  its schema text; `Guest::proc_io`.
- `hydo-build`: `record::record_of` makes the record from the manifest, and the x86_64 and arm64
  builds write it inside and beside the image. An arm64 image that needs another kernel than the
  default names it in `/etc/hydo/kernel` from the record. `guest.proc_io: false` prints a line.
- `hydo` (`doctor`, `setup`) and `hydo-release`: the new kernels are release assets, and `hydo
  doctor` checks the kernels of this epoch. Both releases' `build-release.sh`, `assets.sha256` and
  `third-party.json` ship them; the Mac's script takes `HYDO_KERNEL_IO`, `HYDO_KERNEL_NETNS_IO`
  and `HYDO_KERNEL_CONTAINERS_IO`. docs/RELEASING.md names them, and the release lines of
  `hydo/dist/releases.txt` come with the first release that ships them.

**The proof on KVM.** Neither this Mac nor the bare-metal machine may run KVM, so a one-off
workflow on the branch `tmp-m376-kvm` ran on GitHub's runners; the branch is deleted. Each check
printed a `PASS` or `FAIL` line, and each step counted its `PASS` lines against the number it
expected, so a step that checked nothing failed (Milestone 373's lesson).

- **The kernels, in a sandbox** (run 46004050833). Four runners (two Xeon 6975P-C, two AMD EPYC
  7763) with a multi-user Nix 2.18.9 (`sandbox = true`) built one kernel each with `nix-build` and
  then `nix-build --check`: the same bytes twice, the store paths of the bare-metal machine, and
  the pins. Run 46006123647 built all four again with the same result.
- **The checks** (run 46006123647, six runners: four Xeon 6975P-C, an AMD EPYC 7763 and an
  EPYC 9V45). The runner took the published 0.7.0 Linux release, `hydo setup`, and the four new
  kernels in its `guest/`. This tree's `hydo` ran beside the release's.
- **`/proc/self/io` in the guest, 9 of 9 checks on every host.** The release's Redis example got a
  first invariant that reads `/proc/self/io` and the `/proc/<pid>/io` of `redis-server`, and
  prints the latter. Built by this hydo (epoch 7), it ended `OK` with 1 and with 2 vCPUs, twice
  each with one fingerprint, and printed `rchar: 4285 wchar: 2173 syscr: 58 syscw: 54
  read_bytes: 3239936 write_bytes: 90112 cancelled_write_bytes: 0` (one vCPU, AMD). With
  `guest.kernel: containers` it ended `OK` with both kernels for containers. With `guest.proc_io:
  false`, whose record says `"proc_io": false`, it ended `VIOLATION [procio.readable] no
  /proc/self/io` with 1 and 2 vCPUs. Built by hydo 0.7.0 (epoch 6), it ended the same `VIOLATION`
  under this hydo. Every schedule gave one fingerprint per CPU vendor: the AMD EPYC 7763 and 9V45
  agree, and the four Xeon hosts agree.
- **An epoch-6 image keeps its values, 13 of 13 checks on every host.** hydo 0.7.0 built the
  release's Redis example with the recorded bytes (`8fae6946…`, epoch 6). This tree's hydo ran
  the 12 schedules of `kvm/release-redis` of `hydo/onboard/recorded.json`. On both AMD hosts every
  run gave the recorded `fp` and `ctl`, from `b222402de473ea1b` (`disk=none | run`) to
  `d73115b82e1e7897` (`disk=cut dseed=1f16055b6d41c6d9 | run C=9 R=no`). On the four Intel hosts
  every run gave hydo 0.7.0's own values on the same host, with the recorded verdicts.
- **Epoch 7 gives one fingerprint per schedule, 8 of 8 checks on every host.** This hydo built the
  Redis example at epoch 7 (`24592035…`). Seven schedules ran twice each with one fingerprint, and
  `disk=none | run` with 2 vCPUs too. On AMD: `disk=none | run` `abe369f236f79c57` (OK, `ctl`
